items.content:
Pakistan will continue to push for maintaining close relations with the United States irrespective of which party holds power in Washington, as the Democrats swept the US midterm elections, dealing a major political setback to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.
The Foreign Office on Friday said Pakistan viewed the United States as an important partner and would continue to engage with both sides of the political divide, signalling that Islamabad's approach to Washington would remain guided by long-term strategic and economic interests rather than political changes in the US administration.
"We have maintained excellent relations with all governments, irrespective of who is in power, and this will continue," Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said during his weekly briefing.
He identified trade, investment, security, counterterrorism and investment in minerals as key areas of cooperation between the two countries.
The briefing also focused on Pakistan's continuing diplomatic efforts to prevent a renewed escalation of the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran, amid concerns over possible fresh military action against Tehran.
Responding to questions about the prospects for renewed US-Iran negotiations, the spokesperson said Pakistan had extended all possible facilitation in its capacity as an honest mediator.
He described the signing of the Islamabad MoU as a significant achievement, saying Pakistan had brought two countries to the negotiating table after decades without direct engagement.
"The fact that we were able to bring the two countries, which had not even been talking to each other for the past 47 years, to the same table for discussions, culminating in the successful signing of the Islamabad MoU, is a testament to Pakistan's commitment to building peace and promoting peace and stability in our region," he said.
Haider said Pakistan would continue facilitating diplomatic engagement, adding that peace could only be achieved through political dialogue rather than military confrontation.
Asked whether there was a specific opportunity to secure a permanent end to the conflict, he said mediation remained an ongoing process, with Pakistan, Qatar and other regional countries playing active roles.
He also identified Israel as one of the actors undermining regional peace when asked about potential spoilers in the diplomatic process.
"Well, you have mentioned one name yourself. There could be others, but I am sure that peace in the region is certainly not in Israel's interest," he said.
The spokesperson also confirmed that a Pakistani-linked liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier had been struck by projectiles while transiting the Persian Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz, but said no crew members were injured.
He identified the vessel as Al Maida, registered in the Marshall Islands, operated by QatarEnergy and carrying LNG destined for Karachi.
According to the Foreign Office, the vessel was hit last Friday night while travelling eastbound through the Persian Gulf in international waters. It was carrying 25 crew members from different countries, including Pakistanis.
The incident caused a small fire onboard, but all crew members remained unharmed. The vessel subsequently returned safely to Qatar.
"The concerned Pakistani authorities are coordinating with the relevant parties to establish further details of the incident," Haider said.
However, the spokesperson was less forthcoming on the continuing disruption of cross-border trade between Pakistan and Iran, with traders and transporters facing difficulties following the closure of border crossings.
Despite repeated questions about the status of the crossings and the reasons for the disruption, he declined to provide a specific explanation.
Initially, he said the Foreign Office would check the situation with the Ministry of Commerce. When pressed again after the ministry referred journalists back to the Foreign Office, Haider said: "My comment is that I have nothing further to add on this matter."
He did clarify that there was no general ban on Pakistani pilgrims travelling to Iran by land, although recent security concerns and clashes along the border had disrupted their movement.
The spokesperson said Pakistan was also examining a reported US plan to deport Afghan nationals through Pakistan, but stopped short of confirming any arrivals or a final arrangement.
"The matter is currently under consideration, and all relevant aspects are being carefully examined in consultation with the concerned stakeholders. We are hopeful that a mutually agreeable way forward will be reached," he said.
Clarifying reports that Afghan refugees were expected to arrive in Pakistan by air, he said he had not confirmed that the individuals were arriving or had already arrived.
Meanwhile, the Foreign Office reiterated Pakistan's willingness to facilitate Indian religious pilgrims despite the strained relations between the two neighbouring countries.
Haider said Pakistan had issued 9,318 visas to Indian religious pilgrims in 2025, including 9,070 Sikh pilgrims and 248 Hindu pilgrims. A further 4,002 visas had been issued to Sikh pilgrims during the first half of 2026.
"Pakistan welcomes pilgrims of all faiths and recognizes the deep spiritual significance that visits to religious sites hold for devotees and their families," he said.
Preparations were underway to receive Sikh pilgrims for the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji at Nankana Sahib later this month.
The spokesperson said the Kartarpur Corridor remained open from Pakistan's side, despite India suspending pilgrim movement through the crossing since May 2025.
He said Pakistan remained ready to facilitate visa-free visits by up to 5,000 pilgrims daily under the 2019 agreement, but the resumption of movement depended on India's decision.
"It is now for India to decide whether it allows Indian Sikhs to undertake this religious pilgrimage to Kartarpur Sahib," he said.
Haider added that Pakistan had not imposed a visa ban on Indian nationals and would continue facilitating visits to religious sites under the existing arrangements.

Iran has submitted a nuclear proposal to the United States through Qatar but insists that Washington meet seven demands before negotiations can begin, as fresh attacks on shipping, missile interceptions and a crackdown on clerics in Bahrain underscored mounting tensions across the Gulf.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday that Washington was reviewing the proposal, which would only be discussed after the United States addressed Tehran's conditions. Iran's demands include lifting US sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian assets and paying war reparations.
Iran's deputy security chief Ali Bagheri Kani said that Tehran was not satisfied with "paper commitments" and wanted practical American steps before any new diplomatic engagement. Senior security official Mohsen Rezaei had also warned that Iran would neither reopen the Strait of Hormuz nor negotiate without its seven conditions.
Meanwhile, a seafarer was killed in an explosion believed to have resulted from a missile attack on an oil products tanker in the Gulf on Thursday. The Marshall Islands-flagged MT Velos Sapphire was sailing towards Bahrain when it was struck. Its remaining crew extinguished a fire, while the vessel was taken to Bahrain's Khalifa Bin Salman Port for investigation.
Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said a tanker reported an explosion near its port-side waterline while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, 16 nautical miles east of Oman's Khasab. The vessel remained operational and all crew members were safe.
In Bahrain, authorities have intensified a crackdown on clerics accused of promoting allegiance to Iran. More than 50 clerics and religious figures were arrested between May and June over alleged efforts to incite rebellion and overthrow the government with Iranian backing.
Bahrain's security chief Tariq Al Hassan said the authorities were confronting an ideology that placed obedience to Iran's leadership above national sovereignty. However, lawyers and relatives of the detained clerics denied the allegations.
Elsewhere, Saudi-led coalition air defences intercepted two ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Houthi group towards Najran on Friday. Meanwhile, the Houthis said 30 people were killed and eight injured in a separate strike on a market in Yemen's Taiz province, blaming Saudi aircraft for the attack.

items.content:
A widening wave of hoax bomb threats targeting passenger flights and news organisations disrupted air travel across Europe for a third consecutive day on Friday, prompting evacuations, flight diversions and military escorts, although no explosives were found.
Broadcasters in Ireland and Bulgaria received emailed threats from a purported sender named Mikhail Andropov, warning of further attacks on transport across Europe. Ireland's public broadcaster RTE evacuated its offices and suspended programming, while Bulgaria's Nova TV also received a threat.
Britain's Sky broadcaster reported a security threat. Reuters could not establish the sender's identity or determine whether the emails originated from the same source as threats affecting dozens of flights since Tuesday. All aircraft landed safely, and no explosive devices were discovered.
Disruptions were considerably fewer on Friday than Thursday, when more than two dozen flights were affected. An Italian airport authority source said a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome was diverted to Venice.
Hungarian fighter jets escorted airliners travelling from Brussels to Sofia and from Prague to Bucharest and Cyprus through Hungarian airspace. Hungary's defence minister said NATO had ordered air patrols in the region, marking the first reported involvement of the military alliance.
Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares described the developments as apparent "hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare". European officials have increasingly blamed Russia for such operations, although Moscow has denied involvement.
EU technology commissioner Henna Virkkunen said Europe had faced sabotage, drone incursions, cyber breaches and election interference since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. "The reason behind these operations is to destabilise our societies and create mistrust among our citizens," she told Reuters.
Meanwhile, Vladislav Pozdniakov, founder of Russia's banned far-right misogynist movement Male State, denied involvement in the threats. Emails sent to Rome and Sofia airports had reportedly been signed by the movement's supporters.
Pozdniakov said the group had ceased to exist in 2021, when Russian authorities banned it for extremism, accusing unidentified individuals of exploiting its name for their own purposes.

items.author: Business Desk
items.content:
The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) has proposed a new licensing system for Internet of Things (IoT) services in Pakistan, setting an initial licence fee of Rs. 100,000 for companies seeking to operate Low Power Wide Area Networks (LPWAN).
The proposed Internet of Things and Low Power Wide Area Networks (IoT-LPWAN) Licensing Regulations 2026 introduce separate licensing and registration requirements for businesses providing IoT connectivity, private networks and related digital services.
Under the draft framework, IoT services will be divided into three categories: licence-exempt operations, registration and licensing.
Companies planning to provide LPWAN connectivity and related services to third parties, including consumers, will need to obtain a PTA licence. The licence will remain valid for five years, with applications submitted through the regulator’s online system.
PTA has proposed a non-refundable application processing fee of Rs. 5,000 in addition to the initial Rs. 100,000 licence fee.
The proposed registration charges are lower for other categories. Companies operating private IoT networks and providers of IoT platforms or applications will each pay an initial registration fee of Rs. 10,000, along with a Rs. 5,000 processing fee. These registrations will remain valid for five years.
The draft also introduces a separate regulatory sandbox registration for research, development, testing and trials. It will cost Rs. 2,000, with an additional Rs. 1,000 processing fee, and remain valid for one year.
The proposed rules also require licensed operators to begin providing services within one year of the regulations taking effect. They must obtain a commencement certificate from PTA, or their licences could be cancelled. The regulator may allow an extension of up to six months.
In addition, licensed operators will have to register their gateways and submit quarterly reports detailing their active IoT connections and gateways. They must also comply with applicable spectrum regulations.
Existing LPWAN licensees will be required to register their gateways within 90 days after the new regulations come into force.
The post PTA Sets Rs. 1 Lac Internet Company Fee appeared first on ProPakistani.

items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
The National Cyber Emergency Response Team (NCERT) has warned of a growing use of artificial intelligence (AI), automated bots, botnets and agentic tools in coordinated cyberattacks, saying banks and critical infrastructure face heightened risks.
"These capabilities may help threat actors and sophisticated cyber criminal groups to broaden the scale, speed and sophistication of their operations," NCERT said in an advisory dated Nov 5.
It warned that banks could face attacks targeting core banking systems, digital banking platforms, payment systems and customer-facing applications. Potential threats include disruption of online services, automated credential attacks and manipulation of displayed account balances.
Critical infrastructure could also be exposed through vulnerabilities in third-party service providers, connected internet of things (IoT) devices, industrial control systems and insecure remote access, the advisory said.
Such weaknesses could expose oil and gas facilities, water utilities, power generation and distribution networks, manufacturing plants and transport systems to cyberattacks. "A compromise could disrupt physical processes and critical services," NCERT warned.
The team cited recent cyberattacks in Europe targeting supermarket refrigerators and freezers as examples of the physical and commercial consequences of attacks on connected operational systems. However, it said the involvement of AI in those incidents had not been confirmed.
The advisory listed several indicators of potential attacks on financial institutions, including frequent automated login attempts, repeated authentication failures and unusual application programming interface (API) requests.
Other warning signs include abnormal transaction patterns, discrepancies between core banking records and displayed account balances, and unauthorised access to payment systems.
For critical infrastructure, changes to refinery, pipeline, electricity grid, power generation or distribution parameters could signal an attack. Unexpected alterations to pressure, temperature, cooling or heating controls, as well as unusual remote access sessions and unauthorised changes to IoT and operational technology (OT) configurations, were also identified as potential indicators.
NCERT urged financial institutions to review the security of core banking systems, APIs, third-party integrations, payment gateways and digital banking applications. It recommended multi-factor authentication, safeguards against automated login attempts and integrity checks to ensure that customer-facing applications accurately reflect core banking records.
Financial institutions were also advised to monitor bot-driven login attempts, potential service disruptions and abnormal API activity.
For utility providers, NCERT recommended restricting direct internet exposure and remote access, while reviewing the security of IoT devices and industrial control systems.
It also called for stronger separation of operational technology and IT networks, continuous monitoring of access to operational systems, regular security updates and backup procedures for essential operations.
The advisory urged all organisations to assess their preparedness for AI-driven, bot-based cyberattacks, maintain incident logs and strengthen incident response, business continuity and security monitoring arrangements.

items.title: Pakistan, UK to strengthen anti-drug cooperation
items.summary:

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said that 330 cases involving attempts to smuggle drugs into the United Kingdom had been foiled over the past few years.
The two sides also agreed to convene a meeting of the working group established between the interior ministries of Pakistan and the United Kingdom soon.

items.content:
A senior official of the National Database Registration Authority (NADRA) was gunned down outside his office in Peshawar on Friday morning in an apparent case of targeted killing.
The incident took place in front of the NADRA Region Office in the upscale Hayatabad neighbourhood.
Eyewitnesses said NADRA deputy assistant director Fahad was walking toward his office building after parking his car in a lot across the street when unknown assailants on a motorcycle opened fire on him.
According to police, the NADRA official died on the spot as the attackers fled the scene unchallenged. The gruesome incident was also captured on a CCTV footage widely circulated on social media.
Soon after the incident, police and security forces reached the site and cordoned it off to collect evidence. The police also established pickets across the city and launched a search operation.
Sources said investigators were collecting CCTV footage from neighbouring buildings. They said police were also looking into the CCTV recordings at the Peshawar Safe City project to identify the killers. They were also investigating the possibility of some personal enmity.
According to some officials, the police had found images of the assailants and had also shared them with NADRA for identification.
Officials said the assistant director, who was a nephew of MNA Noor Alam Khan, usually arrived at the office with guards in a bullet-proof car, but on Friday he arrived alone, driving his vehicle.
NADRA was established during Musharraf era in a bid to create a comprehensive database of Pakistan's citizens.
The institution in the past couple of years has cancelled thousands of Computerised National Identity Cards (CNICs) issued to foreign nationals particularly Afghan refugees as part of a government campaign which also includes repatriation of Afghans who have been living in Pakistan for decades.

items.summary:
Xiaomi has launched the Mijia Smart Waist Massager 2 in China, featuring four massage heads, dual-sided heating, smartphone controls, and a larger battery.
The device is available through Xiaomi’s Youpin crowdfunding platform for approximately $56, while its recommended retail price is around $74.
The new model improves on its predecessor with a larger massage area, additional massage functions, and longer battery life.
Design and Massage Features
The Mijia Smart Waist Massager 2 features four massage heads, compared with two on the previous model, allowing it to massage the lower back and upper hips simultaneously.
The massage heads cover an area of 46,500 mm² and support two techniques: kneading and acupressure.
One pair of heads performs broader kneading movements, while the other applies more focused pressure. The acupressure heads extend 8mm outward to reach deeper muscle areas.
The device also includes a dual-sided heating system with three adjustable temperature settings.
items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Xiaomi has launched the Mijia Smart Waist Massager 2 in China, featuring four massage heads, dual-sided heating, smartphone controls, and a larger battery.
The device is available through Xiaomi’s Youpin crowdfunding platform for approximately $56, while its recommended retail price is around $74.
The new model improves on its predecessor with a larger massage area, additional massage functions, and longer battery life.
Design and Massage Features
The Mijia Smart Waist Massager 2 features four massage heads, compared with two on the previous model, allowing it to massage the lower back and upper hips simultaneously.
The massage heads cover an area of 46,500 mm² and support two techniques: kneading and acupressure.
One pair of heads performs broader kneading movements, while the other applies more focused pressure. The acupressure heads extend 8mm outward to reach deeper muscle areas.
The device also includes a dual-sided heating system with three adjustable temperature settings. The device operates at a noise level of 50dB(A) or lower and comes in Light Sand and Dark Gray color options.
The front side warms the lower back across a 15,000 mm² heating area, while the reverse side can be used to warm the abdomen.
Xiaomi has used slow-rebound memory foam and skin-friendly fabric for the cushion, which also functions as a regular lumbar support when the massage system is switched off.
Smart Features and Battery
The massager connects to the Mi Home app, allowing users to select seven preset massage modes and create three additional custom modes.
Users can also adjust the heating temperature and set massage sessions lasting between 2 and 30 minutes.
For those who prefer not to use a smartphone, Xiaomi has included large physical buttons on the side of the device.
The Mijia Smart Waist Massager 2 packs a 3,150mAh battery, an upgrade from the 2,400mAh battery in the original model.
It delivers up to 110 minutes of operation per charge, compared with 90 minutes on its predecessor, and supports USB-C charging.
Price and Availability
The Xiaomi Mijia Smart Waist Massager 2 is currently available for crowdfunding in China at approximately $56.
Its regular suggested retail price is around $74.
The crowdfunding campaign began on November 4, 2026.
Xiaomi has not announced international availability or pricing for other markets, including Pakistan.

items.author: Peter Moses
items.content:
The Alaafin of Oyo, Oba Abimbola Akeem Owoade I, says he remains the number one traditional ruler in Yorubaland, citing the historical significance and contributions of the old Oyo Empire to Yoruba civilisation.
He said this during an interview with a broadcaster, Edmund Obilo.
Responding to questions on whether the Alaafin was the supreme king in Yorubaland, Oba Owoade said: “Historically, yes. If you want to go by history and the contribution of Oyo to Yoruba civilisation, then I would say that the Alaafin is number one.”
He dismissed suggestions that he was in competition with other prominent Yoruba monarchs, particularly the Ooni of Ife, Oba Enitan Ogunwusi, over traditional supremacy.
ADC PCC: We&#8217;ve appealed judgement against Mark, Atiku and notified INEC
INEC: Why we&#8217;re yet to act on judgement nullifying Atiku&#8217;s candidacy
“I don’t fight for supremacy or whatever with anybody,” Oba Owoade.
On his commitment to the Yoruba race, the monarch said he regularly prayed for the progress of the people, stressing that the success of Oyo would bring honour to the entire Yoruba race.
“I believe that when Oyo succeeds, the Yoruba in their entirety get honoured. That’s my belief,” he said.
Daily Trust reports that in August last year, the age-long supremacy battle between the two major traditional stools in Yorubaland reared its ugly head again.
Oba Owoade had given a 48-hour ultimatum to the Ooni of Ife to revoke the Okanlomo of Yorubaland chieftaincy title he conferred on Ibadan business tycoon Dotun Sanusi, had reopened debate and bitter rivalry between the highly revered monarchs.
Owoade argued that the Ooni’s instrument of office restricts his authority to three council areas in Osun State and that he has acted “unlawfully, derogatorily, and in contempt of the apex court.”
He warned that unless the title was revoked within 48 hours, the Ooni should be prepared to face unspecified “consequences.”
But the spokesperson for Ooni of Ife, Moses Olafare, said the Ooni would not react to the 48-hour threat by the Alaafin of Oyo.
Olafare, in a Facebook post, said the Ooni will not dignify what he described as “undignifiable” with an official response.
He said, “My principal has directed me against issuing a press release on the empty threat. I beg to disappoint you, gentlemen of the press.
“We cannot dignify the undignifiable with an official response. We leave the matter to be handled in the public court of opinion, as it is already being treated.
“Let’s rather focus on narratives that unite us rather than the ones capable of dividing us. No press release, please. 48 hours my foot!”
Speaking further during the interview, Oba Owoade expressed optimism about ongoing infrastructure projects in Oyo, particularly the proposed circular road and its planned dualisation.
He said the project, which would connect areas including Infinity and Sabo, would improve the city’s appearance and contribute to its development.
The Alaafin also discussed the forthcoming Oyo Empire Day, describing it as a three-day celebration expected to attract about 40,000 people.
He explained that the event was designed to bring together communities and people historically connected to the old Oyo Empire, irrespective of their present locations.
According to him, the celebration would provide an opportunity to reconnect with their roots, preserve Yoruba culture and deliberate on the future of coming generations.
Explaining why the event was named Oyo Empire Day rather than Oyo Day, the monarch said the empire had a wider historical reach beyond the present-day Oyo community.
“The Oyo Empire comprises a number of people and cities, not just one. That’s why we are trying to make sure that we come together, reconnect to our roots, preserve our culture, deliberate on how to move forward and make a better future for our children together,” he said.
Oba Owoade further disclosed that a Hall of Fame would be established as part of the celebration to recognise individuals and communities that had made significant contributions to Yoruba civilisation, Oyo Empire history, culture and heritage.
He added that attendance would not be restricted to people with ancestral links to Oyo, noting that anyone interested in Yoruba culture was welcome.
“Everybody is invited. If you are a lover of culture, you love the way Oyo is doing its things, you are part of it. We are not excluding them,” he said.
On expectations surrounding his reign, the Alaafin urged the people to remain optimistic, describing himself as a resilient person determined to make a positive impact.
“I am a go-getter and very resilient. I don’t give up easily. I try as much as possible to make a positive impact wherever I belong to,” he said.

items.author: Rilwan Muhammad
items.content:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) says it is yet to receive the Certified True Copy (CTC) of the Federal High Court judgement which sacked the David Mark leadership of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and nullified the nomination of candidates produced via its primaries.
Following the judgement, reports started circulating on social media that INEC had removed the name of former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, ADC Presidential Candidate, and his running mate, Rotimi Amaechi, from its portal.
But Malam Mohammed Kudu Haruna, INEC National Commissioner and Chairman of the Information and Voter Education Committee (IVEC), said the commission had yet to receive a copy of the judgment and had not discussed the matter.
A check on the commission’s portal by our reporter on Friday, however, showed that the names were still listed, contrary to the claims circulating online.
Judgment against ADC leaders poses Threat To 2027 Elections &#8211; Coalition
Judgment against ADC leaders poses Threat To 2027 Elections &#8211; Coalition
Haruna questioned the source of the information, insisting that the commission had not received the court judgment.
“I don’t know where that statement came from. Somebody just forwarded it to me. We haven’t received the judgment yet,” he told Daily Trust.
He explained that obtaining CTC of a court judgment takes time, adding that the commission could not be expected to act on a judgment it had not officially received.
“Usually, it takes about a week for you to get a CTC of the tribunal,” Haruna said.
He further indicated that the commission had not met to deliberate on the judgment, stressing that its position remained guided by the existing judicial process.
The clarification comes a day after Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court in Abuja nullified the leadership of the ADC led by former Senate President David Mark and invalidated the party’s actions, including the process that produced Atiku as its presidential candidate for the 2027 general elections.
The judgment followed a suit instituted by a former ADC Deputy National Chairman, North-East, Nafiu Bala Gombe, who challenged the emergence of the Mark-led leadership.
The court held that the process through which the leadership emerged did not satisfy the requirements for democratic elections under the relevant provisions of the Electoral Act.
It consequently nullified the actions taken by the disputed leadership, including the nomination of candidates presented by the party to INEC for the 2027 elections.
The ruling has generated political reactions, with the ADC rejecting the judgment and describing it as legally indefensible.
The party has also indicated its intention to challenge the decision in court.
Atiku has equally rejected the ruling, vowing to appeal and insisting that his presidential campaign would continue.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Luxury smartphone customization company Caviar has introduced a new Zodiac collection for Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo, allowing buyers to personalize their phones with precious metals, gemstones, exotic leather, and even meteorite fragments.
The collection features 12 zodiac-inspired designs, with prices starting at approximately $14,800. Customers can choose their preferred materials and finishes through an online configurator rather than purchasing a fixed design.
Caviar says the collection offers more than one million possible combinations for each zodiac sign, giving buyers extensive control over the appearance of their devices.
Design and Customization
The Zodiac collection features designs inspired by all 12 astrological signs, with a decorative zodiac wheel and constellation elements on the back.
Customers begin by selecting their zodiac sign, which loads a default design. They can then customize the phone’s frame, back panel, zodiac circle, and central medallion.
Available frame materials include silver, gold plating, natural titanium, and titanium with a black PVD coating.
For the rear panel, buyers can choose forged carbon or different types of leather, including calfskin, python, and crocodile leather.
Decorative options include Swarovski crystals, gemstones, jewelry enamel, and meteorite inlays. Caviar also offers textured metal finishes, including clous de Paris and chevron patterns.
The company says these options allow customers to create approximately 15 million design combinations across the collection.
Price and Availability
The default Capricorn model, featuring a black titanium frame and forged carbon back panel, starts at an estimated $14,800.
Meanwhile, the Aquarius configuration, which uses silver and navy crocodile leather, costs approximately $18,615.
Both models are based on the 256GB iPhone Duo, which has a standard starting price of $1,999.
The final price depends on the materials and finishes selected by the buyer.
Unlike conventional online shopping, customers cannot complete their purchase directly through the configurator.
After finalizing a design, the website generates a unique code that must be shared with a Caviar sales manager. The manager then confirms the final price and processes the custom order.
Caviar says each customized iPhone Duo undergoes additional hinge and display testing before delivery and comes with a 12-month warranty.
Caviar’s Other Luxury iPhones
The Zodiac collection follows several other expensive iPhone modifications introduced by Caviar.
In October, the company launched its World Treasures collection, featuring customized iPhone Duo models costing up to $90,000 and incorporating materials such as 18K gold, platinum, and diamonds.
Caviar also previously introduced Black Edition versions of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, featuring redesigned bodies without functioning cameras.
The new Zodiac collection takes a different approach by allowing customers to choose their own combinations of materials instead of purchasing a predetermined luxury design.

Oppo’s upcoming Find X10 Ultra flagship smartphone may have been cancelled or put on hold, according to a new leak suggesting that development of a high-end smartphone has been suspended.
The Find X10 Ultra was previously expected to launch in the first half of 2027 with a powerful camera system, a flagship processor, and a large battery.
However, tipster Digital Chat Station has now suggested that another manufacturer’s top-end flagship project has undergone major changes.
Oppo Find X10 Ultra Project Reportedly Suspended
In a recent Weibo post, Digital Chat Station claimed that another ultra-premium smartphone project had changed direction.
The tipster did not identify the manufacturer or device. However, the post has raised speculation that Oppo’s Find X10 Ultra could be affected.
When a user suggested that the next-generation model had been discontinued, Digital Chat Station replied that the change involved the current generation.
The exchange has fueled reports that Oppo may have suspended or cancelled the Find X10 Ultra.
However, Oppo has not officially confirmed the development, and it remains unclear whether the project has been permanently cancelled, temporarily paused, or simply changed direction.
If the reports prove accurate, the existing Find X10 Pro Max could remain Oppo’s highest-end flagship for this generation.
Oppo Find X10 Ultra’s Expected Specifications
Previous leaks suggested that the Find X10 Ultra would feature a major camera upgrade over the Find X10 Pro Max.
The rumored camera system included a 200MP primary camera with a large 1/1.12-inch sensor and LOFIC technology, a 200MP periscope telephoto camera, and a 50MP periscope lens offering 10x optical zoom.
Reports also suggested that Oppo was considering a 200MP Samsung HP5 ultrawide camera and a 100MP square selfie camera.
The phone was also tipped to feature a 6.89-inch display with 2K resolution and a 144Hz refresh rate, alongside an approximately 8,000mAh battery.
Earlier reports indicated that the device could use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor.
However, more recent leaks suggested that Oppo was also testing MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro with specialized image-processing algorithms.
None of these specifications has been officially confirmed for the Find X10 Ultra.
Xiaomi and Vivo Ultra Flagships Also Face Uncertainty
Oppo is not the only Chinese smartphone manufacturer reportedly reconsidering its upcoming Ultra flagship.
Recent leaks have suggested that Xiaomi may have cancelled the Xiaomi 18 Ultra to focus on its Pro Max model instead.
Meanwhile, Vivo’s X500 Ultra has also faced reports of changes to its global launch plans, although the device was still reportedly in development for a 2027 release.
For now, Oppo continues to offer the Find X10 and Find X10 Pro Max, which have already launched in multiple markets.
The company has not announced whether the Find X10 Ultra will proceed, be delayed, or be cancelled entirely.

items.author: Shahbaz Rana
items.content:
Pakistan's trade deficit increased 16% to nearly $15 billion during the first four months of this fiscal year after imports hit $26 billion amid continued sluggish export growth, a gap that may keep Islamabad dependent on foreign creditors longer than planned.
The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) reported on Friday that the gap between imports and exports widened to $14.6 billion during July to October, $2 billion or 16% more than the same period last year.
The factors behind the peak deficit remained unchanged: a surge in imports averaging $6.5 billion a month and sluggish exports averaging $2.8 billion a month.
The figures were released two days after Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb disclosed that Pakistan had secured yet another rollover of $3 billion in debt from Saudi Arabia last month.
Finance Secretary Imdadullah Bosal told a parliamentary committee that external debt repayments were estimated at $21.5 billion, of which the government would seek $10.5 billion in rollovers of bilateral and commercial debt.
Beyond these rollovers, the government remains in constant search of new foreign loans to build reserves, which are already the product of foreign borrowing and the central bank's domestic purchases of foreign currency.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has promised that the 25th International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme, ending next September, would be the last in the nation's history, a vow that will face its real test before the next general elections.
Official data showed imports jumped to $26 billion in the first four months, higher by $2.9 billion or 12.5%. For the current fiscal year, the central bank has projected imports rising to $71 billion on the back of higher energy import bills.
The PBS said cumulative exports during July to October increased to $11.4 billion, a rise of just $890 million or 8.5% over the same period last year. The government has tried everything in its toolkit to lift exports to a level that reduces dependence on foreign creditors.
For this fiscal year it has retained Rs88 billion in subsidies in the budget to provide cheaper loans, mostly to large exporters. Exports have traditionally remained in the vicinity of $2.5 billion to $3 billion a month, and even a devaluation of Rs100 against the dollar could not give them a major boost.
The rupee appreciated by one paisa to Rs276.66 to the dollar on Friday, according to the central bank.
The government has now projected goods exports of $34 billion this fiscal year, against $30.8 billion last year. At this pace, it would miss its 2029 target of $60 billion.
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal had said earlier that taking exports to $60 billion was a prerequisite to avoiding any future IMF programme.
So far, the government's trade liberalisation policy has not helped exports, contrary to projections by the Ministry of Commerce, the World Bank and the IMF. Under the policy, the ministry and the World Bank had predicted a 14% increase in exports and only a 7% rise in imports.
In the last fiscal year, exports fell 6% to less than $31 billion.
The PBS data showed exports flat at $2.9 billion month-on-month in October over September, while imports rose 5.7% to over $6.8 billion. The monthly trade deficit was up 10.3%, or $364 million.
On an annual basis, imports increased 11.8%, or $719 million, while exports rose 2.8%, or just $81 million. The trade deficit widened 19.7% to $3.9 billion, $638 million more than the previous year.
One reason for the absence of an export surplus is the government's preference for large industries, unlike much of the world where small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) play a major part in expanding exports.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has lately begun focusing on SME financing initiatives, but these meetings have not yet translated into meaningful benefits, whether cheaper financing or other advantages available to large traditional players.
This week the National Assembly Standing Committee on Finance expressed concern over the impact of closing three international borders for security reasons on exports.
Minister of State for Finance Bilal Kayani agreed there would be an impact but said the government had to shut the border with Afghanistan on security grounds.
The only open land route is through China, MNA Mirza Ikhtiar Baig said during a session arranged by the Sustainable Policy Development Institute on Wednesday.

items.content:
A Turkish seismic vessel will arrive in Karachi between November 17 and 20, 2026, reviving Pakistan's offshore exploration efforts after nearly two decades, Federal Minister for Petroleum Ali Pervaiz Malik said while chairing a meeting to review preparations for its arrival.
He described the occasion as a special milestone in Pakistan-Türkiye relations, particularly following the signing of the Mecca Agreement, and said the arrival represented a new chapter in the longstanding friendship and cooperation between the two countries.
"This is a special moment for Pakistan-Türkiye friendship. I will try to personally receive the vessel upon its arrival in Karachi," he said.
The minister said the government was fully committed to facilitating the offshore exploration initiative and ensuring all necessary arrangements for the successful commencement of operations.
He assured the Turkish delegation of Pakistan's full support and said both countries would work together to achieve a landmark success that would be remembered for generations to come.
The secretary petroleum also expressed enthusiasm over the upcoming arrival, saying the Petroleum Division was looking forward to welcoming the vessel.
He underscored the importance of coordination among all relevant departments and stakeholders to ensure smooth arrangements. The project manager expressed confidence in the project and appreciated the support extended by Pakistan. He said the team had received encouraging support from Pakistani authorities and hoped for a successful outcome from the offshore exploration effort.
The meeting reviewed operational, logistical, maritime, security and interdepartmental arrangements for the vessel's arrival and the commencement of the offshore exploration campaign to build Pakistan's energy security.
Relevant departments were directed to maintain close coordination to ensure timely facilitation of the vessel's arrival and the start of operations.
The meeting was attended by the project manager, the secretary petroleum, the additional secretary petroleum, the director general petroleum concessions, the managing directors of the Oil and Gas Development Company, Pakistan Petroleum Limited and Government Holdings, and representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the National Hydrographic Office Pakistan, the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Interior, the Board of Investment and the Directorate General of Ports and Shipping, Karachi. Pakistan's offshore exploration has been largely dormant for nearly two decades, and officials said the arrival would also strengthen bilateral energy cooperation between the two countries.

items.author: ZAFAR BHUTTA
items.content:
Pakistan's economic managers have expressed the desire to end the federal government's role in fixing tobacco prices and have directed the Ministry of Food Security to come up with a deregulation mechanism within three months.
The Economic Coordination Committee (ECC), in a recent meeting, agreed with the price fixing proposal approved by the Pakistan Tobacco Board (PTB), stressing that it was the need of the hour to chalk out an exit strategy for the federal government from price fixation.
During discussions, the Ministry of National Food Security and Research informed the ECC that the subject had been deferred previously to fulfill the missing prerequisites. It was highlighted that Section 8 of the Pakistan Tobacco Board Ordinance, 1968 required the fixation of the maximum price. The ECC deliberated at length the mechanism for determining the minimum indicative prices (MIPs) for tobacco, keeping in view the formula approved by the PTB.
Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) chairman drew the attention of the forum that, given the high production of tobacco and low local consumption, the aspect of exportable surplus should also be discussed so that farmers could avoid losses.
The food security ministry pointed out that a summary on the minimum indicative price of tobacco crop (2026) and the revision in tobacco cess rates for financial year 2026-27 had been presented to the ECC in its meeting held on September 7, 2026. The committee deferred the decision and directed the ministry that a case be submitted with justifiable analysis, along with a workable strategy for deregulation of the PTB in line with the vision of the federal government.
PTB is mainly mandated to promote the cultivation, manufacturing and export of tobacco and tobacco products. MIPs for different grades of tobacco are notified by the federal government under Section 8(1) of the PTB Ordinance, 1968.
The ministry apprised the ECC about the key questions raised. These included why did the proposed MIP for 2026 show a decrease as compared to 2025? Why did White Patta/Rustica appear to cost more while all other types declined? And why did different types of tobacco show different MIP trends from year to year?
The ECC was told that the maximum price was calculated on the basis of the cost of production plus average inflation spanning eight cropping months (January to August) of the previous year and a fixed 5% profit margin. Since the Price & Grade Revision Committee generally meets in November or December for the forthcoming crop, the average inflation of the previous crop year is used.
For 2026, the cost of production for Flue-Cured Virginia (plain) tobacco was calculated at Rs473.61 per kg. With addition of the previous year inflation rate of 5.43% (January to August 2025), the MIP came in at Rs523/kg. While forwarding a draft summary to the food security ministry, the PTB, in its letter dated May 5, 2026, reported the prevailing inflation trends and the hardships of growers while considering the revised MIP. PTB stated that the average inflation for August 2026 was 9.26%, compared with 5.43% for the corresponding period of 2025. If the 2026 inflation rate of 9.26% was applied, it indicated an MIP of Rs541.14/kg.
It was pointed out that Punjab and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa had separate cost of production committees comprising growers, tobacco companies and provincial agriculture departments. Each committee assesses the prevailing local production costs and gives its recommendations.
Keeping in view the prevailing economic conditions and in the best interest of tobacco growers, the Ministry of Food Security proposed that MIPs and cess rates notified for the previous year (2025) may be maintained for the 2026 crop. The ministry also submitted a proposal to find a workable solution for the deregulation of PTB. The ECC considered a summary titled "Minimum Indicative Prices of Tobacco Crop (2026) and Revision of Cess Rates on Tobacco for the year 2026-27" and approved the proposal with the directive that the food ministry should come up with a proposal for deregulation of the price mechanism within three months.

items.author: editorial
items.content:
Pakistan's initiative to institutionalise dialogue as a mechanism for peace has received an endorsement from the UN Security Council. A presidential statement from Islamabad - which called on member states to "continue diplomatic engagement even after the outbreak of armed conflicts" - was recognised as the way forward. It is, indeed, a great contribution to international efforts aimed at resolving conflicts peacefully. This squarely means shunning wars and discouraging rival states from going over the brink, even in times of extreme adversity and the breakdown of communication.
This achievement is a de jure recognition of Pakistan's earlier submission to the world body, which called for affirming the importance of peaceful settlements in international disputes. UNSC Resolution 2788, tabled by Pakistan last year, was a breakthrough of sorts; it gathered unanimous support from all major powers and was seen as a South-South stride toward realising the objectives of the UN. The core message is that diplomacy "must not end even if hostilities break out". Moreover, the prospects of dialogue remain "indispensable" at any stage of inter-state relations. The statement, titled "The Role of Diplomacy during Active Hostilities", could not have come at a more opportune moment, as the world sits on tenterhooks amid quasi-peace and uncertainty.
The UN and other regional bodies have long relied on institutional statecraft to manage and resolve conflicts. Thus, this statement is an extension of that spirit, calling for the protection of civilians, the containment of violence, the prevention of conflict spillover and the facilitation of humanitarian assistance. These outcomes can only be ensured through an unrelenting belief in the dialogue process, rather than through coercion and aggression.
This UNSC resolution necessitates deep reflection and extraordinary efforts to see the light of day. It is a pity that the US spent over $8 trillion on wars and conflicts in the post-9/11 era. The reality is that more than 3.7 billion people live in destitution on an income of less than $8 a day, even as global military expenditures exceed $2.7 trillion annually.

items.author: Farrukh Khan Pitafi
items.content:
Drubbing, shellacking, bloodbath, extinction-level event and blue tsunami: pundits and politicians have used every description for the US midterms. When Texas, which Democrats have tried unsuccessfully to flip for decades, elects a Democrat to every statewide office on the ballot, you understand the quantum of change. While dozens of House races remain uncalled, Democrats picked up seven Republican Senate seats, bringing their tally to 54 in a chamber of 100, flipped more than 40 districts to bring their projected House total to 257, broke the Republican one-party lock on Georgia, Iowa and Texas, and gained five governorships (Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Iowa and Nevada), losing none. In Kansas, they won a Senate seat for the first time since 1932. They took Lindsey Graham's seat in South Carolina and Susan Collins' in Maine.
Dr Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim US senator. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, whom I pushed unceasingly as Biden's running mate in this space before he chose Harris, became Georgia's first black female governor. A sitting Pope submitted a mail-in ballot in a historic first. Countless other firsts.
So what just happened? Was it a repudiation of all things Trump or something more? It is hard to detach Trump from this result: many poor-performing candidates were his handpicked choices. But when did his own numbers seriously start tanking? By the end of 2025, his approval and disapproval numbers were relatively stable. That suggests many controversial policies, such as ICE raids, had not materially shifted them. Then the Iran war began and all hell broke loose. Add the intensifying AI debate, exemplified by Pope Leo XIV's encyclical, Bernie Sanders and AOC's advocacy, and growing public opposition to data centres, and a pattern emerges. Politicians can offset long-term anxieties with short-term financial relief and benefits. The Iran war's cost-of-living crisis, compounded by DOGE-driven cuts and massive tech layoffs, robbed incumbents of that luxury.
Notice, too, the money pouring in from two major interests: AIPAC and tech billionaires led by Elon Musk. Their supported candidates got thrashed. DOGE co-founder Vivek Ramaswamy, for instance, was defeated in Ohio's gubernatorial race. One has to conclude that Israel's role in the Iran war and tech-related anxieties played a huge part. This second factor is especially important because it is symptomatic of an existential dread about the future.
Across the country, this dread translated directly into votes against tech infrastructure and AI itself. Voters backed bans, moratoria or power limits on data centres in 45 of 47 local ballot measures, according to Ballotpedia. Goldman Sachs estimates that states likely to tighten data-centre rules hold 45 per cent of planned US capacity. The software side drove equal panic. National polling shows overwhelming majorities fear AI will eliminate jobs and fundamentally disrupt communities. The public has stopped believing in a frictionless technological utopia and is voting to protect its own survival.
I wrote the following on 4 April in "AI filter and reset":
"The soft reset could materialise as a leftist tsunami across the world. The political right has never been more powerful. But as its rise marked the death of political centrism, its antithesis also emerged in Bernie Sanders' democratic socialism. In political groups like the Democrats, the general impulse is to elect another centrist, but on the left wing of the party, the growing resentment at having allegedly been cheated out of victory three times is reaching a fever pitch.
Zohran Mamdani's rise, the weakening of far-right momentum in Europe and the failure of right-wing governments to restrain billionaire ambitions, leading to existential dread, indicate an impending shift. Add to this the consequences of the ongoing Iran war, its economic impact and the fragmentation of the far-right ecosystem."
This on 25 April in "Capital, code, counterstrike":
"The second accelerant is sheer political dread. Billionaires are watching shifting global political winds. Recognising right-wing electoral losses in places like Hungary, they anticipate a severe left-leaning, pro-labour correction in upcoming elections. A newly empowered political centre-left would demand wealth taxes, algorithmic audits and mandated human oversight in automated systems. Knowing this regulatory window is closing fast, capital is pre-emptively gutting its human dependencies. They intend to force future regulators to negotiate with an AI-driven economy that already exists, rather than one still in the planning stages."
And this on 30 May in "Human premium, or not":
"Politicians like Bernie Sanders and AOC are on to something when they focus on the hardware requirements of the tech growth model. And other fallouts of hyperscale data centres are just being discovered today. I think in its dying hour democracy has one last pushback to offer before it flatlines. The rulers of the new tech architects of dominance are seriously worried about the upcoming US midterms. The far right wave that swept the world and created born-again libertarians among tech billionaires is ebbing away. In this situation a leftward correction can bring back all the regulatory frameworks that they so painstakingly took apart brick by brick in the name of tech competition and cold war. Given this challenge I see... panic reactions. A surge in crypto assets to keep their wealth portable. Peter Thiel has already temporarily relocated to Argentina, remember?"
And this on 8 November 2025, in "This moment, Zohran!":
"So what is the antidote? Three things. Honesty. Flexibility. And... community. Honesty to level with his constituents and manage expectations. Flexibility to negotiate with Albany, Washington, DC, and the billionaires he intends to tax. And community because he has effectively mobilised the New York community through a common dream."
Over the past year, Mamdani has demonstrated exactly that. He has kept his platform but understood that winning office is only the beginning. Delivery requires negotiation with Albany, Washington, DC, and powerful economic interests. His model is neither capitulation to the establishment nor permanent confrontation with it. It means making politics deliver tangible improvements, giving communities a say in decisions affecting their future, and ensuring technological progress serves people rather than simply extracting value from them. If Democrats follow that example, they could establish a global precedent for how human dignity survives the technological upheaval ahead. The message is hiding in plain sight.

items.author: Imtiaz Gul
items.content:
The costs of the unjust Iran war has piled misery on Republicans not many had anticipated. Iranians refused to give in to the unwarranted blackmail by the Trump administration and the younger Americans, too, delivered their stinging rebuke of this policy.
Initial data suggests that Gen Z (voters aged 18–29) emerged as consequential bloc – with a sharp leftward swing – to punish Donlad Trump's strident foreign policy ventures.
The Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) at Tufts University describes this as one of the highest youth preferences for Democrats recorded in a national election. Up to 60 per cent Millennials too favoured Democratic candidates.
CIRCLE data says about 250 millennial candidates ran in the general election (alongside 22 Gen Z candidates). Roughly 38% of these younger candidates won. At least 95 Millennials were elected (or re-elected) to Congress, according to Future Caucus data (as of early November 5–6, 2026 reporting) i.e. 90 in the House of Representatives, 5 in the Senate. Jon Ossoff was reelected while James Talarico (Texas), Abdul El-Sayed (Michigan), Annie Andrews, and Julia Letlow won seats.
As many as 66% of youth supported Democratic US House candidates while 31% backed Republicans, producing a 35-point Democratic margin, CIRCLE and Future Caucus said.
The Iran war and its direct consequences (high energy price and rise in inflation) clearly shifted the voter sentiment.
Abdul El-Sayed epitomises this massive shift in sentiment. Ridiculed and jeered by both President Trump and Vice President JD Vance, the Egyptian-born senator-elect rallied on equal rights and democratic ideals for everyone. And it resonated with the Gen Z and Millennials, who are not ready to stomach unqualified support for Israel, Egypt or any other country that the DC Administration or the US security establishment chooses.
El-Sayed argues that Egypt operates as a military dictatorship propped up in part by US taxpayer-funded military aid. In multiple interviews, he described Egyptians as living under a military dictatorship funded by "our tax dollars". Foreign military aid puts a "chokehold" or "strangling grip" on the Egyptian people. El-Sayed groups Egypt with other recipients of US military aid (Israel, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, etc), arguing the money should prioritise domestic needs like schools and healthcare in Michigan instead.
Egypt receives roughly $1.3 billion annually in US Foreign Military Financing (with some portions subject to human-rights conditions that have been waived). This aid dates largely to the Camp David Accords era and is justified by successive US administrations on grounds of regional stability, the Egypt-Israel peace treaty, counterterrorism cooperation, and other strategic interests.
This aid package also ignores human rights organisations and opposition groups which call the post-2013 Sisi government (which came to power via military coup against the elected President Mohamed Morsi) as highly repressive, with extensive military economic and political dominance, limits on dissent, and restrictions on civil liberties.
In a post-victory CNN interview, El-Sayed called both Trump and Vance as "odious… they've taken us down the path", when calling them out for the consequences of the Iran war.
As a whole, El-Sayed comes across an outspoken critic of US military aid for authoritarian regimes, such as that of Sissi, and wants redirecting of "our tax dollars" domestically. He used his personal heritage and a consistent stance against foreign military aid to underline the widely documented authoritarian realities of the present Egypt. But that passion for equal human rights is not restricted to Egypt only; he made an explicit reference to Pakistan's democratic crisis during his 2026 Michigan Senate election campaign too. Addressing a Pakistan Independence Day gathering in Detroit on August 23, 2026, El-Sayed did not merely speak about democracy in general but referred directly to Pakistan's former prime minister Imran Khan and the treatment of political opponents.
According to a report published by ThePrint on August 24, 2026, El-Sayed said: "Democracy requires that all people get to run for public office rather than be subject to jailing and intimidation simply because they would have a voice in our public office… Whatever one feels about the former prime minister of Pakistan, democracy only works when we have the freedom of our speech and our own freedom to be able to articulate and run for public office."
The 2026 US midterm elections have brought about a significant generational shift to Congress. Though the core of big US geopolitical ventures (such as China or Iran policies) may not change and strategic interests and security partnerships will most probably continue to influence Washington's approach. Yet the entry of Millennial and Gen Z representatives could inject fresh perspectives into American politics, particularly on democratic accountability, civil liberties, political participation and human rights. Younger American lawmakers could possibly push for more consistent congressional attention to democracy, human rights and civilian constitutional governance. But whether this translates into stronger advocacy for democracy, both at home and abroad, will depend on their political priorities and willingness to challenge established power structures and their reliance on "strategic nodes". The Democratic majority in the Congress amounts to literal termination of the carte blanch that Trump held thus far. That should ring alarm for all those who had latched on to the president as their lease of life.

items.author: Shazia Malik
items.content:
Americans did it again, and showed that no amount of hate has any place in the American politics. On Tuesday night, they gave their verdict against the Trump administration's divisive policies, its unnecessary war against Iran, high gas prices and a tariff war with the world, especially Canada. In fact, the vote was not so much for the Democrats but against Trump and his billionaire friends, who according to them, did not care for "small people" of America.
Early results show Democrats sweep both the House of Representatives and the Senate. Among those elected is Abdul El Sayed – the first Muslim Senator in US history, who was sadly mocked by being labelled 'jihadist' and 'extremist'. After winning the primary in August, where the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent over $30 million against him, El Sayed has been constantly speaking against Israel and its genocidal policies in Palestine. He also called for investing the money being spent on foreign wars to fix issues at home.
So Trump's next two years will look very, very different. The implications would extend well beyond Washington, and affect not only its foreign policies but relationship with allies, discredited by Trump. This would also mean that now Democrats would influence legislative talks, federal appointments and confirmation of judges and senior government officials. But removing the President would require a two-thirds majority in the Senate, which is impossible to gain. Impeachment question might return to the political debate, as would the financial assistance to Israel and Ukraine.
The key question here is, would Trump's policies be reversed now that Democrats control both the houses? No, because the President retains executive powers. Democrats' victory would only ensure balance of power in the world's biggest democracy. It will put a check on the unbridled power of the Trump administrations and the President's billionaire friends. The midterms also revealed a pushback from Americans against political polarisation, confrontational leadership, high inflation, the rising cost of living, controversial decisions, and dissatisfaction with Trump's leadership.
A strong turnout among young people, women and suburban voters facing economic difficulties paved the way for a sweeping Democratic victory. Democrats also made gains among Hispanic voters and independents, including in traditionally Republican states. The Muslim population, angered by the administration's pro-Israel policies at the utter disadvantage of the Palestinians, also dented the Republican campaign. So, what's the key takeaway or vital political message here? It is that criticising Israel, supporting Palestine and opposing anti-Semitism are not mutually exclusive issues, and conflating them can alienate voters.
Allies are also happy as they will now have greater leverage in trade talks. At a broader scale and at the level of the EU, those governments will now find more support in the US on Nato commitments, climate policies, etc. And although the US foreign policy has not fundamentally changed, a greater Congressional scrutiny on Israel, accountability over Gaza and settlement policies will be brought to the fore.
The most expensive midterm election in the history of the country saw total campaign spending by the candidates, political parties and the outside organisations exceeding $11.9 billion. Although the final nationwide voter turnout has not yet been officially established, early estimates show approximately 53.14 million Americans voted this time around, compared to approximately 46 million in early voting in 2022. Also, over 58 million early ballots came in. In comparison the turnout among the eligible voters was 46.6% in 2022 midterms, and 50% in 2018.
In the wake of this verdict, the central question remains: will Mr Trump heed the American public's message and reconsider the divisive policies that eroded democratic institutions, fractured international alliances, and prioritised the interests of his inner circle over the country?

items.title: Lemon Water and the Detox Myth
items.summary:

items.content:
Every morning, in kitchens from Lagos to London to New York, someone squeezes half a lemon into a glass of warm water. They drink it with a small sense of virtue. Social media has told them it flushes toxins, resets the liver and melts away last night’s indulgence. It is a pleasant ritual. The only problem is that basic physiology does not support that promise.
Start with the word detox. In medicine, it describes treating poisoning or dependence. A hospital managing alcohol withdrawal is doing detox. So is a clinic treating someone who has swallowed a dangerous substance. The wellness industry borrowed the word and stretched it into something vague and marketable. Ask a promoter which toxins their product removes, and you will rarely get a name, a quantity or a study. That silence tells you most of what you need to know.
Now, your body has been running its own detoxification service since before you were born. The liver converts harmful compounds into forms that can be expelled. The kidneys filter your blood around the clock. The gut, lungs, and skin all contribute to this process. No lemon is required for any of this to work. Lemon water does not speed up the process, and no trial has shown it does. In 2009, a group of British scientists examined claims made for commercial detox products and found no credible evidence behind them. That conclusion has aged well.
What lemon water offers is modest. A lemon contains vitamin C; however, a squeezed half gives you only a small amount. It also adds flavour to plain water. This helps people who find water boring to drink more of it. Citrate in lemon juice may help reduce the risk of some kidney stones, and doctors sometimes suggest it to people who form them. These are real benefits. They are not the same as cleansing your organs.
Troops Arrest Suspected Terrorist in Kaduna, Raid Hideouts in Zamfara
HURIWA Asks DSS To Probe Possible Political Motive Behind Southern Kaduna Attacks
There are small downsides too. Lemon juice is acidic, and sipping it all day can wear away tooth enamel over time. If you drink it daily, use a straw and rinse your mouth with plain water afterwards. Wait a while before brushing. People with reflux may find that lemon worsens their heartburn. None of this is dramatic, but it shows that even harmless-looking habits deserve a little thought.
Globally, the picture is one of enormous enthusiasm and thin evidence. The wellness industry is worth trillions of dollars worldwide, and detox is one of its most persistent selling points. Teas, juice cleanses, foot pads and colon treatments all sell on the same idea. Modern life fills you with poison, they say, and only their product can help. Regulators in Europe and North America have challenged these claims and have taken action against some companies. Yet the message keeps circulating, because it flatters us. It suggests that one cheap habit can undo a week of poor choices.
Nigeria has its own version of this story, and it is a lively one. Walk through any market, and you will find bundles of herbs, bottled concoctions and powders. They promise to clean the blood, wash the kidneys or purge the system. Some of these traditions carry genuine knowledge. Many others are sold without testing, dosage and accountability. NAFDAC has repeatedly warned the public about unregistered products, and for a good reason. Some herbal mixtures have been linked to liver and kidney injury. That is a bitter irony for people who were trying to protect those very organs.
The truth is that lemon water is at the gentle end of this spectrum. It costs little, is easy to find and will not hurt most people. My concern is not the lemon. It is what the lemon can distract us from. Someone who starts the day with lemon water and believes the work is done may feel excused from the harder tasks. They may drink heavily at weekends or ignore the blood pressure reading they meant to check.
Now, consider the health problems Nigerians face at scale. Hypertension is widespread and often undiagnosed. Diabetes is climbing, especially in cities. Hepatitis B remains a serious burden. Studies put its prevalence at nearly one in ten Nigerians, and most people who carry the virus do not know it. Alcohol, sugary drinks and highly processed snacks have become ordinary parts of urban life. No morning tonic offsets these. A glass of lemon water will not lower your blood sugar. It will not repair a liver that has been steadily overworked.
So what supports the organs that really do the cleansing? Drink enough water throughout the day, and let thirst and your urine’s colour guide you. Eat vegetables, beans, fruit and whole grains. Go easy on fried food and sweet drinks. Move your body for at least 30 minutes most days, even if that means walking briskly around your estate. Limit alcohol. Sleep properly. Get vaccinated against hepatitis B if you have not been. Know your numbers, meaning your blood pressure, blood sugar and weight. These habits do more for your liver and kidneys than any potion, and they cost less than most detox teas.
Personal responsibility is at the heart of this. Nobody can hand you health in a bottle. Before buying any product that promises to cleanse you, ask three plain questions. Is it registered with NAFDAC? Can the seller name the toxin it removes? Would a doctor or pharmacist you trust recommend it? If the answers are no, no and no, keep your money.
It also helps to be kind to yourself. Many people reach for detox because they feel guilty after a heavy festive season or a stretch of poor eating. You do not need to punish your body or purify it. You need to return to sensible routines, and you can begin today.
If you enjoy lemon water, continue doing so. It is pleasant, it may help you drink more fluid, and it does no harm to most people. Just be honest about what it is. It is flavoured water, not medicine. Your liver and kidneys are already on the job, and they ask only that you treat them decently. That means nourishing food, regular movement, moderate drinking and proper checkups.
Ojenagbon, a health communication expert and certified management trainer, lives in Lagos.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir and Sudanese Interior Minister Lieutenant General (Police) Babiker Samra Mustafa Ali on Friday reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations, particularly in security and counterterrorism, the military's media wing said.
According to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the Sudanese minister called on Field Marshal Munir at the General Headquarters (GHQ) in Rawalpindi.
During the meeting, the two sides discussed matters of mutual interest, evolving regional and global security dynamics, and avenues for enhancing bilateral cooperation.
“Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening relations between the two countries, particularly in the fields of security, counterterrorism and institutional cooperation,” the ISPR said.
The visiting dignitary appreciated Pakistan's role in promoting regional peace and stability and acknowledged the longstanding fraternal ties between Pakistan and Sudan.
CDF Munir "reaffirmed Pakistan's desire to further deepen bilateral engagement with Sudan" and underscored the importance of close cooperation in addressing shared security challenges, the statement added.
Earlier in the day, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Senator Mohammad Ishaq Dar also met Sudan's interior minister, the Foreign Office said in a statement.
"Pakistan remains steadfast in its support for Sudan's sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity," Dar said, according to the statement.
Deputy Prime Minister/Foreign Minister Senator Mohammad Ishaq Dar @MIshaqDar50 held a meeting with the Federal Minister of Interior of the Republic of Sudan, H.E. Mr. Babeker Samra Mustafa Ali, at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs today.
The DPM/FM reaffirmed Pakistan’s steadfast… pic.twitter.com/ISk977BpKc
— Ministry of Foreign Affairs - Pakistan (@ForeignOfficePk) November 6, 2026
He underscored the importance Pakistan attached to its relations with Sudan and its commitment to further strengthening the brotherly ties between the two countries.
The Sudanese minister expressed appreciation for Pakistan's support and continued solidarity with his country. He highlighted the strength of relations between the two nations and underscored Sudan's desire to further deepen cooperation in areas of mutual interest.
Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry also attended the meeting.
Meeting with PM Shehbaz
A day earlier, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had met the Sudanese interior minister, according to a statement issued by the Prime Minister's Office.
The prime minister warmly welcomed the visiting dignitary and said Pakistan attached great importance to its longstanding and fraternal relations with Sudan.
"We want Sudan to emerge from its current crisis as a peaceful, stable and prosperous country," he said.
Interior Minister of Sudan H.E. Lt. General Babiker Samra Mustafa Ali called on Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif in Islamabad, today. pic.twitter.com/Y0TxouGKoP
— Prime Minister's Office (@PakPMO) November 5, 2026
PM Shehbaz said Pakistan was keen to further strengthen bilateral relations, particularly in trade and investment, adding that there were vast opportunities for cooperation in agriculture, defence, education and other sectors.
"Pakistan values Sudan's cooperation at the United Nations, the OIC, the G-77 and other multilateral forums," he said.
The Sudanese minister thanked the prime minister and the Pakistani government for the warm reception and hospitality extended to him. He also expressed gratitude for the humanitarian and medical assistance provided by the Pakistani government and people during difficult times.
The visiting minister appreciated Pakistan's support at international forums for efforts to restore peace and security in Sudan and praised its role in promoting regional peace and mediation, the statement said.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
The federal government on Friday slashed the price of petrol by Rs6.59 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs4.25 per litre for the next four days.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs346 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs378 per litre from November 7 to November 10.
The latest reduction brings petrol prices below Rs350 per litre for the first time since September 7, exactly two months after the government raised the rate by Rs12.90 to Rs358.77 from Rs345.87.
The revision also comes a day after the government slashed the price of petrol by Rs9.41 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs5.56 per litre for November 6.
Read: Govt slashes petrol by Rs9.41, diesel by Rs5.56 for Nov 6
On November 2, the government announced that oil refineries would bear a burden of Rs15 billion per month, which would allow petrol to be sold Rs15 cheaper than it was in the global market amid the US-Israeli war on Iran.
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.

The handset was earlier spotted on the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) database with the same model number, hinting at an imminent launch in the country. The Geekbench listing suggests that the Indian version of the Vivo V80 FE will be powered by the MediaTek MT6878 chipset, which is the octa-core MediaTek Dimensity 7400-Turbo SoC. It appears to have four efficiency cores clocked at 2.0GHz and four performance cores, delivering a peak clock speed of up to 2.6GHz. The Vivo V80 FE has been spotted with 7.31GB of RAM, which could be marketed as 8GB of RAM. Further, the handset is listed with Android 17. It managed to score 911 points on Geekbench’s single-core performance test and 3,041 points on the multi-core performance test.
