items.author: Anne Florentyna
items.content:
Ecommerce enablement platform Shiprocket turned profitable in the September quarter, reporting a consolidated net profit of ₹0.6 Cr against a net loss of ₹20.3 Cr in Q2 FY26.
Operating revenue rose 34.7% to ₹673.6 Cr during the quarter under review from ₹500.2 Cr a year ago.
Shiprocket, which listed on the NSE and BSE in August, had posted a net loss of ₹13.7 Cr in Q1 FY27. Sequentially, operating revenue increased 13.8% from ₹592.1 Cr.
Revenue grew faster than expenditure during the quarter, with total expenses increasing 29.6% to ₹692.9 Cr from ₹534.8 Cr.
Other income increased to ₹19.9 Cr from ₹14.3 Cr, taking total income to ₹693.5 Cr, marginally above total expenses. The company reported no tax expense for the quarter.
Shiprocket’s adjusted EBITDA rose to ₹14.2 Cr from ₹4.3 Cr a year ago, while its adjusted EBITDA margin expanded to 2.1% from 0.9%.
Emerging Business Drives Growth
Shiprocket reports its operations under two segments: core business and emerging business. The latter includes marketing technology, checkout, cross-border, and omnichannel solutions.
Core business revenue grew 25.3% to ₹461.5 Cr from ₹368.3 Cr a year ago, while adjusted EBITDA increased 28.9% to ₹59.1 Cr. The segment’s adjusted EBITDA margin improved to 12.8% from 12.4%, with transactions growing 31% during the quarter.
Emerging business revenue rose 60.9% to ₹212.2 Cr from ₹131.9 Cr, increasing its share of overall revenue to 31% from 26%.
However, the segment’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹44.9 Cr from ₹41.6 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA loss margin narrowed to 21.2% from 31.5%, reflecting faster revenue growth.
Within emerging businesses, martech revenue jumped 102%, while omnichannel revenue rose 79%.
Shiprocket attributed omnichannel growth to brands using its services to replenish quick commerce dark stores, including appointment-based deliveries with visibility into purchase orders from platforms such as Blinkit and Zepto.
Its martech offerings, grouped under Fastrr, span advertising, checkout, and customer engagement tools.
Transactions And Merchants Grow
Shiprocket processed 233 Mn unique transactions involving goods worth ₹37,398.7 Cr in gross merchandise value (GMV) during the trailing 12 months ended September 30. It served 2.36 Lakh active merchants over the same period.
For Q2 FY27, the company reported 33% growth in GMV, 34% growth in transactions, an 8% increase in merchants, and a 25% rise in average revenue per user.
The number of merchants using its emerging business offerings increased 75% to 62,025 on a trailing 12-month basis. Meanwhile, 9.3% of core business merchants used an emerging product, up from 7.9% a year ago.
Around 17,300 new merchants joined Shiprocket through its emerging products during the quarter, compared with about 5,400 a year earlier.
Borrowing Repayment Supports Profit
CFO Tanmay Kumar attributed the turnaround to growth in core business transactions, improving contribution from emerging businesses, and the repayment of borrowings using IPO proceeds.
“… IPO proceeds retired all our borrowings, which cut finance costs, and the surplus now earns interest income,” Kumar said.
Finance costs declined to ₹4.9 Cr from ₹6.7 Cr a year ago. The company had no outstanding borrowings at September-end as against ₹242 Cr at March 31, although lease liabilities remained on its books.
Net cash generated from operating activities stood at ₹55.1 Cr in H1 FY27 compared with ₹23.8 Cr a year ago.
Founded in 2017 by Saahil Goel, Gautam Kapoor, Vishesh Khurana, and Akshay Ghulati, Shiprocket started as a logistics aggregator for online sellers, partnering with third-party delivery providers. It has since expanded into a broader ecommerce enablement platform.
Shares of Shiprocket ended today’s trading session 0.80% lower at ₹130.80 on the BSE.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Nigerian startup Mytherapist is helping people find qualified therapists, book appointments and attend sessions via video, audio or chat, while also offering tools to support their wellbeing between sessions.
Founded in 2021 by Oluwaseun Raphael Afolayan and Dedoyin Ajayi, Mytherapist launched a pilot in October 2022 before going public and beginning paid therapy bookings in January 2023.
“The idea came from the difficulty of finding reliable, affordable support during the pandemic and the aftermath of the EndSARS protests. That experience affected me and people around me,” Afolayan told Disrupt Africa.
Mytherapist is built around what Afolayan describes as the practical questions people face when looking for help. “Who should I speak to? What will it cost? When are they available? How do I fit a session into my day?” he said.
“We saw a gap between deciding you need support and actually receiving it. Someone may be willing to try therapy but still struggle to identify a suitable professional, understand the price or arrange an appointment.”
Alongside therapy sessions, the platform offers mood tracking, journaling, meditation and breathing exercises. “These give users ways to reflect and support their everyday wellbeing alongside professional care,” said Afolayan.
The startup serves individuals and couples, and also offers access pathways through employers and health maintenance organisations (HMOs).
“Our approach combines therapist discovery, booking and remote sessions with tools people can use between appointments. We also now offer routes through employers and HMOs, so access does not depend entirely on someone paying out of pocket,” he said.
Mytherapist makes money by taking a commission on therapy sessions booked through the platform. It also offers paid corporate wellbeing services and Prime, an optional membership, which provides additional features and benefits.
Traction has been solid. The startup has more than 25,000 users and over 4,000 completed paid bookings, and has onboarded more than 120 therapists, with over 90 active. Afolayan, however, was careful to put those figures in context.
“Those measures represent different things. Users are not the same as paying clients, and bookings are not the same as completed sessions,” he said. “The next stage is improving how reliably people move from signing up to receiving care and returning when they need further support.”
The startup was initially bootstrapped, and in 2024 received a US$5,000 grant from 54Collective, as well as around US$7,500 in combined grants from Wema Bank Nigeria, ABC Health and FATE Foundation. Afolayan cited the launch of paid bookings, the introduction of couples sessions and corporate wellness services, and the addition of Prime as key milestones.
Nigeria remains Mytherapist.ng’s core market, though it has seen users access the platform from abroad.
“We distinguish that cross-border usage from establishing a local operation in another country,” said Afolayan.
“Our priority is to strengthen the care experience and distribution in Nigeria. Any expansion needs suitable professionals, workable payments and dependable delivery, and we’re currently working on expanding properly, while still maintaining low operational costs, with the help of Paystack and the Startbutton Africa team.”

Motorola has expanded its G-series smartphone lineup with the launch of the Moto G47 Power 5G in Europe and the UK. The handset focuses on battery endurance, offering a 7,000mAh battery, a 108MP main camera and 5G connectivity.
The Moto G47 Power was introduced on October 27, 2026, as a battery-focused alternative to the standard Moto G47. While the smartphone is available in selected international markets, Motorola has not confirmed its launch plans for Pakistan.
The biggest highlight is its 7,000mAh battery, compared with the 5,200mAh battery in the regular Moto G47. Motorola claims up to 78 hours of battery life under its testing conditions.
The handset supports 30W TurboPower charging and 6W reverse wired charging for compatible accessories.
The Moto G47 Power features a 6.67-inch IPS LCD screen with a 120Hz refresh rate, 720 × 1604-pixel resolution, claimed peak brightness of up to 1,050 nits, and Gorilla Glass 7i protection.
It is powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 6300 processor, paired with 4GB RAM and 128GB internal storage, with microSD expansion support of up to 1TB.
For photography, Motorola has equipped the phone with a 108MP primary camera, which the company says supports 3x lossless zoom, alongside a 2MP macro camera. An 8MP front camera handles selfies and video calls.
The handset runs Android 16 with Motorola’s Hello UI. Other features include stereo speakers, a side-mounted fingerprint scanner, a 3.5mm headphone jack and an IP64 rating for dust and splash resistance.
Despite its large battery and high-resolution main camera, the 4GB RAM and HD+ display could limit its appeal against competing mid-range handsets offering more memory and sharper screens.
Moto G47 Power 5G Expected Price and Release Timeline in Pakistan
Motorola launched the Moto G47 Power in the UK at £299.99, with a reported European price of approximately €339 for the 4GB RAM and 128GB storage version. These figures are for international markets and should not be treated as official Pakistani retail prices.
According to unofficial Pakistani smartphone price listings, the Moto G47 Power is expected to cost approximately Rs. 83,999 in Pakistan. The final price, if the device launches locally, could differ based on memory configurations, taxes, duties and distribution arrangements.
Regional certification reports have raised the possibility of wider international availability, but such listings do not guarantee an official launch in Pakistan.
Some local listings indicate a possible December 2026 release. However, Motorola has not confirmed a Pakistan launch date or availability timeline, so this should be treated only as an unofficial expectation.
If introduced locally, the Moto G47 Power could appeal to customers looking for extended battery life, 5G connectivity and everyday reliability. Pricing will be crucial in a competitive Pakistani mid-range market where rivals offer AMOLED displays, faster charging and more RAM.
For now, the phone’s official price and release date in Pakistan remain unannounced.

Other Brands Are Also Exploring Wide-Screen Phones
Xiaomi is not the only manufacturer reportedly interested in this category. Oppo is also developing a wide-screen smartphone under its Reno series.
According to earlier leaks, Oppo’s upcoming device could feature a 6.35-inch display, an 8,000mAh battery, dual 200MP rear cameras, and MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600M chipset.
Other manufacturers, including Doogee and Coolpad, have also introduced or previewed wide-screen smartphone designs. Meanwhile, Huawei is reportedly preparing a more affordable model under its new Osta sub-brand.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
WhatsApp is rolling out a new AI photo expansion feature for Android users. The tool allows users to adjust their photos to a vertical 9:16 format without manually cropping or stretching the original image. The new feature is part of WhatsApp’s drawing editor and uses Meta AI to generate additional content around the edges of an existing photo. It can be particularly useful for users who want to share pictures as full-screen WhatsApp Status updates.
WhatsApp Rolls Out AI Photo Expansion Feature on Android
The feature has been spotted in WhatsApp beta for Android version 2.26.44.8 by WABetaInfo, available through the Google Play Store. It is currently rolling out to some beta testers, with wider availability expected over the coming weeks.
How WhatsApp’s AI Photo Expansion Works
Users can access the new option by opening a photo in WhatsApp’s drawing editor. After opening the editing interface, they need to swipe up to find the photo expansion option in the Edit section.
Once selected, Meta AI processes the original image and generates a taller version in the 9:16 aspect ratio. Users can then review the result, confirm it, or generate another version if they are not satisfied with the outcome.
Unlike traditional image resizing, the feature does not simply stretch the original picture. Instead, Meta AI analyzes the image and creates additional details around its edges to fill the empty space. This helps maintain a natural appearance while adapting the picture to a vertical format.
However, the final result may depend on the amount of visual information available around the edges of the original photo.
Works with Chats and Status Updates
Since the feature is integrated into WhatsApp’s drawing editor, users can access it when preparing photos for both chats and Status updates.
It will be particularly helpful when sharing square or landscape images as vertical Status updates. Instead of cropping important parts of a picture, users can expand it to fill the screen.
WhatsApp may also show the feature differently depending on the user’s account. Some beta testers may find it available when sharing photos in chats, while others may see it only when creating a new Status update.
The expansion option may not appear for images that already use the supported 9:16 format because they do not need additional space. Users can try it with a square 1:1 image to check whether the option is available.
See Also: WhatsApp Introduces Separate Meta AI Chats on Android
Availability on Android
WhatsApp is gradually rolling out AI photo expansion to beta testers using Android version 2.26.44.8. Installing the latest update does not guarantee immediate access, as the company is enabling the feature for selected accounts in stages.
More beta testers are expected to receive it over the coming weeks. WhatsApp has not yet shared a timeline for its wider public release or confirmed when it will reach all Android users.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
HugoHub, a Singapore-based financial infrastructure company, has gone live in Pakistan. HugoBank has opened its first pilot customer account on the platform, which makes this HugoHub’s first deployment for a regulated bank.
The account sits inside a controlled pilot. HugoBank runs it under a restricted licence from the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) that permits limited-scope operations as a digital retail bank. It was one of five applicants selected for the country’s first digital-bank cohort.
This is a test phase, not a commercial launch. HugoBank plans to hand the results to the SBP and then ask for approval to operate more widely.
What is HugoHub?
HugoHub sells the software a bank needs to run. Its pitch is one connected platform in place of separate systems bought from different vendors and joined together afterwards.
The company grew out of Hugosave, a consumer financial app in Singapore. HugoHub says that experience of running regulated services and moving live systems shapes how it works with clients. Its holding company, Atlas Consolidated, has raised more than USD 40 million from venture capital and strategic investors. HugoHub reports clients in Singapore, Pakistan, the UK and the US.
New banks are not the only target. The company is also talking to mid-tier banks, insurance brokers, multifinance companies and fintech groups. Some of those talks involve large system changes; others are smaller upgrades.
How the platform works
The HugoBank builds links three layers: the back end that holds the money, the app customers use, and the tools staff use to run the bank.
Layer
What it covers
Core banking
Ledgers (the record of every balance and transaction), account servicing, payments, card management, savings tools
Customer app
The mobile experience for opening and using an account
Operating portal
Administration, customer service, risk monitoring
HugoHub calls the design modular. In plain terms, a bank can replace or upgrade one part without rebuilding the rest. The company says this suits existing institutions that want to modernise gradually as much as it suits a new bank starting from nothing.
David Fergusson, HugoHub’s Chief Executive Officer, said a bank’s technology choices shape what it costs to serve customers and how easily products can improve. Braham Djidjelli, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer, said the single platform lowers the cost of serving each customer. Neither company has published figures to test that claim.
Fitted to Pakistan’s payment and identity systems
A foreign platform only works here if it plugs into local infrastructure. HugoHub says the deployment connects to the following:
NADRA, the national identity authority, for biometric verification of customers.
1LINK, the interbank payment network, and Raast, the SBP’s instant payment system.
Local tax and religious rules, including withholding tax and Zakat deductions, and the annual levy applied to eligible savings balances.
Local reporting formats for regulators, plus support for multiple languages.
Asim Hasan, Chief Executive Officer of HugoBank, said the HugoHub team worked with his staff to adapt the platform to Pakistan’s identity, payment and regulatory requirements. The pilot, he said, lets the bank watch real account-opening journeys and see how products and operating processes fit together.
Why the market matters
Pakistan has a population of nearly 260 million. World Bank data cited by the companies puts account ownership, at a bank or on a mobile-money service, at only slightly more than a quarter of adults in 2024.
The SBP introduced its digital-bank framework in 2022 to reach people that conventional banks serve poorly or not at all. HugoBank is building on identity and payment systems that already exist, which is the argument Djidjelli made when he said new banks can leapfrog legacy infrastructure.
What the pilot will test
The pilot is expected to cover current and savings accounts, money pots and debit cards. Retail lending and small-business products are meant to follow later.
The real test is the joins between systems. A digital bank here depends on identity checks through NADRA and money movement over Raast and 1LINK working smoothly for ordinary customers. HugoBank chose one platform to cut the handoffs between vendors, and the pilot will show whether that choice holds up.
A single supplier also means concentrated dependency. If the ledger, app and risk tools all come from one company, replacing any of them later means negotiating with that same company. HugoHub’s modular design is meant to ease this, but the announcement does not say how.
It also leaves out several basics: pilot customer numbers, fees, interest rates and a date for commercial launch. The SBP has not commented in the material released.
What to watch next
The pilot results go to the SBP, and the regulator’s decision will matter more than any vendor claim. For a market where roughly three in four adults lack an account, the measure is simple: whether the next account opened belongs to someone the existing banks never reached. A pilot confined to a handful of accounts cannot answer that. HugoBank’s first retail lending and small-business products, whenever they arrive, will say more about whether the model works.

items.author: Team Inc42
items.content:
PhysicsWallah Back Among Profits
PhysicsWallah had a blockbuster Q2 FY27. The quarter saw the edtech giant swing back to profitability. With South India emerging as its next growth frontier and a NEET slowdown still lingering, can PW build on its Q2 momentum?
Here’s a quick glance at the edtech firm’s Q2 FY27 performance:
Net profit more than doubled YoY to ₹143.6 Cr
Operating revenue jumped 18.2% YoY to ₹1,242.3 Cr
Total expenses also rose nearly 11% YoY ₹1,105.4 Cr
EBITDA improved 52.6% YoY to ₹348 Cr
PW’s Growth Engines: The edtech major’s Q2 show was driven by healthy revenue growth, tighter cost control and improving operating leverage. Online business remained PW’s primary growth engine, while the offline network continued to add centres and enrolments. The company also benefited from a shift away from direct lending, reducing balance sheet risk.
The startup’s next priority is its AI tutor (currently in pilot), which could reduce the cost of personalised learning and extend its reach beyond physical classrooms.
NEET Slowdown: The quarter was not without challenges. A delayed NEET exam cycle slowed enrolments and collections, impacting both online and offline verticals. To offset the gap, PW is launching full-length crash courses and increasing non-NEET enrolments. As a result, the management expects some collections to spill into the next quarter, while anticipating stronger recovery in the next academic session.
The Next Frontier: PW has now identified South India as its next major growth opportunity, which is home to a large student base. PW is pursuing the region through an online-first playbook rather than relying primarily on new physical centres. It also plans to tap into AI-led live translation to reach students across multiple Indic languages without adding significant academic cost.
With profitability improving and AI becoming central to its strategy, here’s how PhysicsWallah fared on the financial front in Q2…
From The Editor’s Desk
Elo Elo Group Bags $80 Mn
Microdrama platform Story TV’s parent has raised nearly ₹756 Cr in its Series C round led by NBCUniversal and Hornbill Capital to invest in premium original content across Indian languages, expand globally and strengthen its AI capabilities.
Founded in 2020, EloElo Group’s portfolio spans four products. Story TV offers microdramas, while Master is a microlearning platform. It also sells AI-powered tools for creators and an AI companion agent called Voxy. It has raised $130 Mn to date.
Microdramas are gaining global popularity as they are specifically built for mobile-first users and rely heavily on high-octane storytelling. The global microdrama industry is projected to generate $14 Bn in revenue by 2026-end.
Razorpay All Set For IPO
The fintech major has received SEBI’s approval for its proposed IPO. The startup is now eyeing a listing between January and March 2027. This comes five months after Razorpay filed its IPO papers via the confidential route in June.
The ₹5,000 Cr to ₹6,000 Cr public issue is expected to value the company at around ₹47,300 Cr. The IPO will likely comprise both a fresh issue and an offer-for-sale component.
Founded in 2014, Razorpay offers payment processing, business banking, payroll, and lending solutions. It has raised more than $800 Mn in funding to date from the likes of Y Combinator, Tiger Global Management, Ribbit Capital and Lightspeed.
NPCI Goes Beyond Payments
Moving beyond its mainstay, the National Payments Corporation of India has set up a new subsidiary, called NPCI Tech Solutions Ltd, to build capabilities in AI, blockchain, and digital financial infrastructure.
The payments body has appointed Vishal Kanvaty as the subsidiary’s MD and CEO. The new vertical will oversee GCC services, the Unified Ticketing Platform and other digital public infrastructure programmes.
The NTSL formation comes as advances in AI and other emerging technologies open up new opportunities across digital infrastructure and financial services. The subsidiary will pursue these opportunities and strengthen NPCI’s technology capabilities.
Nykaa’s Profitable Q2 Show
The beauty and fashion ecommerce major reported a 206.8% YoY jump in its net profit to ₹101.2 Cr in Q2 FY27. This came on the back of a stronger show by the beauty vertical and narrowing fashion losses.
Meanwhile, operating revenue also rose 28.1% YoY to ₹3,006 Cr in the quarter under review. EBITDA surged 65% YoY to ₹263 Cr. However, expenses also continued to bite and rose 24.8% YoY to ₹2,867.1 Cr in Q2 FY27.
On the operational front, Nykaa’s GMV grew 30% YoY to ₹6,151 Cr during the quarter. Meanwhile, its quick commerce offering, Nykaa Now, expanded to 15 cities in Q2 FY27. The company is targeting more than 25 cities by the end of FY27.
Mapping Agentic AI Liabilities
The Data Security Council of India has proposed a new framework to determine liability when AI agents cause harm. It has recommended that the responsibility of harm should be assigned based on each participant’s decisions and degree of control.
DSCI identifies 12 categories of potential harm, including privacy breaches, security threats, discrimination, safety risks, inaccurate outputs, IP violations, deepfakes, loss of control and AI-enabled cybercrime.
DSCI argues that accountability should be traced via decisions such as model selection, system configuration and human oversight. It also pitches six safeguards, including monitoring model behaviour, restricting permissions and deploying scoped kill switches.
Inc42 Markets
Inc42 Startup Spotlight
How Karta Is Automating Customer Service For Banks
Most voice bots can answer questions. But banking calls often require action, be it checking loan status, retrieving documents or updating records. Karta AI is building voice agents that can resolve these complex financial calls end to end, thereby reducing queues and support costs.
Built For Banks: Founded in 2024, Karta operates an omnichannel customer communication platform spanning voice AI, chat, email and WhatsApp. Its AI agents use a predictive context engine that draws on knowledge bases, past interactions and live data to execute workflows across enterprise systems.
This allows the startup to handle multiple customer intents in a single conversation rather than routing callers through multiple agents.
Healthy Early Traction: The startup claims to handle around 20 Lakh user conversations every month across 25+ languages. Karta claims that its inbound servicing agent resolves about 70% of borrower queries and cuts cost per query by nearly 50%. The Bengaluru-based startup also claims to have 10-12 paying customers, including the likes of PhonePe, Pine Labs, Bajaj and Aavas.
Eye On The Prize: Going forward, Karta plans to strengthen its end-to-end automation and multilingual capabilities, expand BFSI deployments, and grow its engineering and GTM teams. The startup’s challenge will be maintaining accuracy, security and compliance as it handles increasingly sensitive financial workflows.
With India’s conversational AI market projected to become a $3.7 Bn opportunity by 2033, can Karta make voice agents the default layer for BFSI customer service?

items.title: Fintech firms lose $420bn as investor confidence weakens

items.content:
… Partners PAU on research, fact-checking, ethical journalism
By Sola Ogundipe
The International Organisation for Migration (IOM) and Pan-Atlantic University (PAU) have entered into a partnership to tackle misinformation, negative narratives and irresponsible media reporting on migration in Nigeria through research, journalism training and improved media education.
The partnership, formalised through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed by IOM and the university’s School of Media and Communication, seeks to strengthen public understanding of migration and equip journalists, students and communication professionals with the skills to report migration issues accurately, ethically and responsibly.
The initiative comes amid growing concerns over how migration is portrayed in public discourse, particularly the tendency to frame it largely around crises, irregular movement and negative experiences, often overlooking its human, economic and social dimensions.
Under the agreement, both institutions will develop academic content, organise training programmes for journalists and communication professionals, conduct joint research and create practical learning opportunities for students.
The collaboration will also explore digital storytelling, fact-checking, multimedia journalism and public awareness campaigns to counter misinformation and promote more balanced discussions on migration.
Speaking at the signing ceremony, IOM Nigeria Chief of Mission, Sharon Dimanche, said the partnership represented an investment in the people responsible for shaping public understanding of migration.
She observed that migration was frequently reduced to statistics, crises and negative headlines, with the human experiences behind it receiving inadequate attention.
“Migration is often reduced to numbers, crises or negative headlines. But behind every movement is a person, a family and a story. If we want people to understand migration better, we must invest in those who shape the conversation, particularly journalists, students, researchers and communicators. This partnership will help bring evidence, practical experience and human stories into classrooms, newsrooms and public discussions,” Dimanche said.
She stressed that improving public understanding required deliberate investment in journalists, students, researchers and other communicators who influence how migration is discussed.
According to her, the partnership would bring evidence, practical experience and human stories into classrooms, newsrooms and public conversations.
The Vice-Chancellor of Pan-Atlantic University, Professor Enase Okonedo, FCA, welcomed the agreement, describing the collaboration as an opportunity to connect academic research and teaching with the realities of migration in communities.
Okonedo said the partnership would give students, faculty members and media professionals opportunities to engage directly with migration experts while strengthening their knowledge and professional competencies.
“Migration affects economies, communities and individual lives in many different ways. Universities have an important role in helping society understand these issues through research, education and informed debate. Our partnership with IOM will create opportunities for students, faculty and media professionals to engage directly with migration experts and strengthen their knowledge and professional skills,” she said.
Also speaking, Dean of the School of Media and Communication, Dr Ikechukwu Obiaya, said the collaboration would promote public awareness, strengthen ethical journalism and equip media professionals and students to address migration-related issues more effectively.
He said that students would benefit from practical learning opportunities, while joint research initiatives would generate evidence-based findings to inform public discourse and migration policies.
“Migration affects economies, communities and individual lives in many different ways. Universities have an important role in helping society understand these issues through research, education and informed debate. Our partnership with IOM will create opportunities for students, faculty and media professionals to engage directly with migration experts and strengthen their knowledge and professional skills,” he noted.
The agreement builds on previous cooperation between IOM and the School of Media and Communication on migration communication and journalist capacity development, including initiatives associated with the Global Migration Media Academy, which promotes ethical and responsible reporting on migration.
Both institutions are also expected to explore joint lectures, research projects, mentorship programmes, workshops and public dialogues involving journalists, government agencies, civil society organisations, academics and migration practitioners.
The partnership comes as IOM marks 25 years of operations in Nigeria, while Pan-Atlantic University’s School of Media and Communication celebrates its 20th anniversary. Although the MoU does not involve financial commitments, specific activities will be implemented through jointly agreed work plans.
The collaboration is expected to strengthen the capacity of a new generation of journalists and communication professionals to interrogate migration issues beyond sensational headlines and contribute to more accurate, evidence-based public conversations.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Cleantech startup altM has raised $10.3 Mn (₹97.5 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by new investors Rainmatter and Mela Ventures. Existing investors Omnivore, Theia Ventures, Aureolis Ventures and Spectrum Impact also participated.
The Bengaluru-based startup plans to use the fresh capital to expand manufacturing, build its sales pipeline and continue investing in research and development (R&D). A large chunk of the funds will go towards setting up a 1,000-tonne-per-year commercial manufacturing facility by 2028.
“We have three large focus areas for the company today. In the short term, we want to start converting revenues and building our sales pipeline from the pilot plant. From a manufacturing perspective, a large chunk of our investment will go into building the next 1,000-tonne-per-year commercial plant,” cofounder and CEO Apoorv Garg told Inc42.
The startup will also continue developing alternative materials and biochemicals. It plans to expand its sales team following the funding round. “The major influx will be on sales,” Garg added.
Founded in 2022 by former Tesla executives Garg and Yugal Raj Jain, altM develops specialty chemicals and biomaterials from agricultural residue for industrial applications.
Its platform converts lignocellulosic biomass, including sugarcane bagasse, rice straw and other agricultural residues, into materials for use in beauty and personal care, textiles, industrial chemicals, construction, packaging and consumer goods.
The platform uses the major fractions of biomass, including cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin, to produce multiple products from a single feedstock, offering an alternative to fossil-derived raw materials.
The latest round comes nearly three years after altM raised $3.5 Mn in a seed round in 2023. Since then, the startup has built an integrated R&D and pilot manufacturing facility in Bengaluru, bringing laboratory research, demonstration manufacturing and pilot production under one roof.
It has expanded its laboratory footprint nearly 5X, commissioned a demonstration manufacturing facility and advanced six molecules to the demonstration stage, with three selected for pilot production.
The first products advancing towards commercialisation include a lignin-derived SPF booster for suncare, a cellulose-based rheology modifier and bio-derived ferulic acid for cosmetics and personal care formulations.
The startup is currently focused on the BPC segment, while its R&D pipeline spans construction, electronics, automotive, polymers and battery materials.
Garg said altM has completed the installation of its 70-tonne-per-year pilot plant in Bengaluru’s Electronic City and is preparing to begin commercial production.
“We have been installing it since late 2025 and finally finished the installation in 2026. It’s still in pre-production, and we’re getting the right certifications and validations to take it to production this month,” Garg said.
The startup expects to begin fulfilling purchase orders in the current quarter, with its first product launches planned for the following quarter. It currently works with nearly 30 BPC customers at different stages of product development, testing and commercialisation. Around 16-18 of them are in testing and active validation, Garg said.
altM’s process involves breaking down plant matter into core polymers and upgrading these fractions into chemicals. Garg said the startup has filed six patents in India covering its deconstruction technology and processes for upgrading individual molecules. It is working on a seventh patent and plans to file patents in international markets as well.
The startup has carried out more than 15,000 reactions at the laboratory stage and translated over 500 reactions to the demonstration stage. It has also reduced the time taken to develop new molecules from 12-15 months to under six months, Garg said.
Looking ahead, altM aims to sell out the capacity of its existing pilot plant by the first quarter of FY28. Over the next five years, it plans to expand its manufacturing capacity to 10,000 tonnes per year, with the potential to generate 100-200 Mn in annual revenue, depending on the molecules produced.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
… Women record twice men’s prevalence as state targets wider coverage
By Chioma Obinna
Lagos State has recorded significant progress in HIV treatment, with 93.4 per cent of people living with the virus who know their status receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), a new survey has revealed.
However, only 58.3 per cent of people living with HIV know their status, highlighting a major testing gap that could undermine efforts to control the epidemic.
The 2025–2026 Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) Impact Survey also found that HIV prevalence among adults aged 15 to 64 was twice as high among women as men, at 1.6 per cent and 0.8 per cent, respectively.
The findings were presented at the dissemination of the Lagos State Summary Sheet of the survey at the Sheraton Hotel, Ikeja, on Wednesday.
The survey has prompted renewed calls for intensified HIV testing, improved access to treatment and sustainable funding to close existing gaps in the state’s response.
Speaking at the event, the Permanent Secretary, Lagos State Ministry of Health, Dr Dayo Lajide, described the survey as an important milestone in strengthening the state’s HIV response through credible evidence and informed decision-making.
She said the findings would help assess progress since the 2018 Nigeria HIV/AIDS Indicator and Impact Survey and support efforts towards achieving the UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets.
Lajide disclosed that “the 2025 HIV Health Sector Report estimated that 192,911 people were living with HIV in Lagos, while 129,977 were receiving antiretroviral therapy, representing 65.7 per cent treatment coverage and leaving more than 60,000 people outside treatment.”
She also highlighted gaps in services for mothers and children, noting that although prevention of mother-to-child transmission coverage increased from 45 per cent in 2018 to 57.6 per cent in 2025, early infant diagnosis and paediatric treatment remained areas of concern.
The Permanent Secretary called for targeted interventions to improve case identification, treatment linkage, retention in care and services for children exposed to HIV.
She reaffirmed the state government’s commitment to sustaining services through the procurement of rapid diagnostic kits and antiretroviral medicines, strengthening health systems and integrating HIV services into routine healthcare.
Lajide also stressed the need for domestic resource mobilisation and sustainable financing amid changes in the global healthcare funding landscape.
Presenting the survey findings, APIN/PHIS3 Survey Lead, Dr Ubong Okon, said the assessment examined HIV prevalence, testing, treatment access and viral load suppression.
Conducted between November 2025 and February 2026, the survey covered 205 enumeration areas and 6,450 households. Okon disclosed that 93.5 per cent of the 6,748 eligible households completed household interviews.
The findings showed that while 93.4 per cent of people living with HIV who knew their status were receiving treatment, 88.9 per cent of those on treatment had achieved viral load suppression.
Health Assistant Coordinator in the Office of the US Embassy’s Department of State, Abuja, Omoshalewa Oyelaran, identified awareness of HIV status as a major priority, stressing that people who do not know their status cannot be linked to treatment.
She said the survey provided Lagos with a clear and independent picture of the epidemic, showing who was living with HIV, receiving treatment and achieving viral suppression.
APIN Public Health Initiatives Chief Executive Officer, Dr Jay Osi Samuels, described the survey as a major achievement and called for more regular assessments to ensure that policymakers had timely information to guide interventions.
He also acknowledged the support of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (US CDC), commending Lagos State and other stakeholders for their cooperation.
US CDC Country Deputy Director, Dr Gbolahan Cole, said the United States Government had invested significantly in the survey, including training field personnel and strengthening laboratory capacity.
He reaffirmed the agency’s commitment to working with Lagos State and its partners to address the identified gaps and provide technical assistance.
Meanwhile, Lagos State AIDS Control Agency Chief Executive Officer, Dr Folakemi Animashaun, said the findings came at a critical time as the state moves towards greater domestic ownership of its HIV response.
She said the survey would guide planning, budgeting, accountability and funding priorities, stressing that its value depended on translating the findings into action.
The Network of People Living with HIV/AIDS in Nigeria, represented by its Strategy Manager, Inolode Emmanuel, urged stakeholders to keep community voices central to HIV interventions.
He described antiretroviral therapy as representing “hope, dignity, survival and the opportunity to live a healthy life.”
Director of Disease Control, Lagos State Ministry of Health, Dr Oladipupo Fisher, urged stakeholders to use the findings to strengthen interventions, reach people living with HIV who remain outside care and improve treatment outcomes.
The survey was supported by the United States Government in collaboration with federal and state health agencies, APIN/PHIS3, civil society organisations and community representatives. Stakeholders called for sustained investment and evidence-based action to advance efforts to end HIV as a public health threat by 2030.
The post HIV: Lagos survey reveals treatment gains, testing gap appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
…Jegede demands policy overhaul, AI integration, teacher training reform
By Joseph Erunke, Abuja
The Federal Government has designated the Nigerian Academy of Education (NAE) as the country’s apex national institution for digital literacy and leadership development, as part of efforts to align the education system with emerging technologies and future workforce demands.
However, the Academy has called for an urgent review of the National Policy on Education, a comprehensive overhaul of teacher education and professional development, and fundamental changes to classroom teaching and learning to achieve the objective.
The President of the Academy, Emeritus Professor Olugbemiro Jegede, disclosed the new national mandate at the opening of the NAE 2026 Annual Congress in Abuja, where he urged the government to move beyond piecemeal reforms and address structural weaknesses in the education sector.
The congress was attended by the Minister of Education, members of the National and State Assemblies, heads of educational parastatals and other stakeholders.
Under the new arrangement, the Academy is expected to spearhead the development of Nigeria’s national digital skills framework and provide intellectual leadership for policies aimed at preparing students and the future workforce for a technology-driven economy.
Its responsibilities will include promoting the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), emerging technologies, innovative teaching methods and evidence-based practices into education policies and classroom delivery.
Speaking at the event, Jegede warned that Nigeria could not build a competitive economy on an education system still dependent on outdated teaching methods and policies that no longer reflect contemporary realities.
“Nigeria stands at a volatile crossroads where obsolete educational paradigms collide with an unforgiving 21st-century reality. The era of comfortable, incremental reforms is over,” he declared.
Describing the Academy as the intellectual engine for Nigeria’s future-ready economy, Jegede said it would no longer restrict itself to issuing advisory recommendations while critical challenges confronting the education sector persisted.
“We are here to intentionally disrupt the archaic architectures holding our nation back,” he said.
The NAE president identified a comprehensive review of the National Policy on Education as one of the most urgent measures required to reposition the sector, arguing that changes in technology, the economy and society had made a reassessment imperative.
He also urged the Federal Government to enforce existing laws and regulations governing the composition of governing boards of educational institutions and parastatals, stressing the need for institutional accountability and compliance with established standards.
On teacher development, Jegede advocated a fundamental restructuring of teacher education and professional training to equip educators with the skills required to operate effectively in digital learning environments.
He said the transformation must extend beyond policy documents to actual classroom practices, calling for a comprehensive review of instructional methods to reflect contemporary educational demands.
The Academy president also advocated policies guaranteeing equitable access to digital technologies in schools across the country.
He warned against a situation in which students’ access to modern learning tools was determined by their geographical locations, stressing that learners in rural and underserved communities must not be excluded from the opportunities offered by emerging technologies.
According to him, achieving meaningful digital transformation would require coordinated action by the Federal Ministry of Education, state ministries of education, the legislature and other relevant institutions rather than isolated interventions by individual agencies.
Jegede further challenged members of the Academy, particularly newly inducted Fellows, to deploy their academic expertise in addressing the country’s educational challenges.
“The Academy has no room for sedentary scholars or armchair theoreticians. Nigeria requires your raw intellect and your immediate, unyielding involvement to reshape our pedagogical destiny,” he said.
He urged education experts to contribute actively to developing digital competencies, promoting emerging technologies and building an education system capable of producing graduates who can compete in the global labour market.
Jegede maintained that the Academy’s new mandate should be assessed not by the volume of policy recommendations it produces but by the measurable impact of its interventions on teaching, learning and national human-capital development.
The 2026 Annual Congress also featured the investiture of four distinguished academics as Fellows of the Academy.
Among those honoured was Professor Josiah Olusegun Ajiboye, the Academy’s First Vice-President, in recognition of his academic standing and contributions to education.
The congress also paid tribute to deceased members and relatives of Fellows, including Professor David Adamu Baikie, one of the Academy’s founding members, as well as the late Mrs Lassa and Mr Omotayo Olarinoye.
The Academy’s leadership reaffirmed its commitment to preserving the legacies of its departed members through continued dedication to academic excellence, educational advancement and national development.
With its new national responsibility, the NAE is expected to play a more prominent role in shaping Nigeria’s education sector, particularly as artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies increasingly influence employment requirements and economic growth.
Jegede said the ultimate measure of the initiative’s success would be the Academy’s ability to translate intellectual expertise and policy recommendations into practical reforms that prepare Nigerian learners for the demands of the future.
The post FG tasks education academy with digital skills revolution appeared first on Vanguard News.

Nigeria has called for stronger Pan-African partnerships, the exchange of proven practices, and greater alignment between continental commitments, national policies, and grassroots implementation.
Nigeria’s Minister of Women Affairs and Social Development, Hon. Imam Sulaiman-Ibrahim, made the call in her remarks at the 10th anniversary edition of the Africa Women Conference (AWC) currently holding in Accra, Ghana.
She said a significant milestone was the endorsement by Nigeria’s Federal Executive Council on 28 October 2026 of three important national instruments, namely, the National Action Plan on Ending Violence Against Children, the National Policy on Menstrual Health and Hygiene Management, 2026–2030, and the National Care Policy and Implementation Plan, 2026–2030.
Dr Jumai Ahmadu, Convener, Africa Women Conference (AWC), in her welcome address at the event, said the theme of the 10th Anniversary Edition is “A Decade of Impact: From Commitments to Action—Advancing Justice, Economic Power and Leadership for African Women and Girls”.
She said the purpose of the conference is to bring together women leaders, policymakers, development partners, entrepreneurs, academics, civil society organisations, traditional institutions and young people to develop practical solutions for the advancement of African women and girls.
Dr Ahmadu said AWC has consistently provided a platform for their voices to be heard, their experiences to shape policy conversations, their enterprises to gain visibility, and their leadership potential to be strengthened.
Speakers at the 2-day event include Princess Hauwa Tanimu Aduda, CEO of Phinada Group of Companies and Founder of PHPA Grassroot Girls STEM Alliance, who is Chairperson of the AWC 10th Anniversary Edition.
Others are Mrs Ngozi Oyewole, President of Commonwealth Business Women Africa, Ambassador Jacquelin Mohair from Atlanta, and Dr Cecilia Idika-Kalu, a Global Security and Gender scholar.
A Conference Sub-theme Paper will be delivered by Her Highness Hajiya Hawa Kulu Ibrahim, wife of His Royal Majesty Alhaji (Dr) Adamu Baba Yunusa, Ona of Abaji and Chairman, FCT Council of Chiefs.

Russia on Monday dropped several bombs on a building where residents of the Komyshuvakha village in the southern Zaporizhzhia region received humanitarian aid every week.

People are then seen in the shelter before the explosion cuts to black and silence.

items.author: Abubakar Adam Ibrahim
items.content:
The US has just held its mid-term elections, and America has been hit by a blue wave. Some have even called it a tsunami. It has left the country reeling, or euphoric, depending on one’s political alignment.
After voting on Tuesday, November 3, Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered a monumental defeat that saw them concede control of the US Congress and several key states to the Democrats. This defeat means that, while Trump remains president for the next two years until his tenure ends, he no longer has a compliant Congress to rubber-stamp his many controversial policies. In the Nigerian context, what happened in the US would be similar to President Bola Tinubu and the APC losing control of the National Assembly to a resolute opposition that could actually shut down his constant requests for foreign loans, which require NASS approval.
The key word here is a resolute opposition. And if anything has shown us the mettle of these Democrats, it is their resolve. They have challenged Trump’s excesses every step of the way and fought back from a disadvantaged position to now hold 54 of the country’s 100 Senate seats, leaving the Republicans with 44. The Democrats also claimed 237 seats in the House to the Republicans’ 139, thus giving the Democrats total control of both chambers of Congress.
To achieve this, they had to take at least seven Senate seats from the Republicans and flipped more than two dozen House districts. They made significant gains in states where Trump had total control in 2024 and defeated several incumbent Republican senators. Some of the most significant Senate victories were in Iowa, Texas, Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Maine, and Ohio. These have traditionally been Republican strongholds. They also flipped five Republican states by winning the governorships of these states, including Iowa and Texas.
The elections are a clear disapproval of Trump and how he has governed the US over the last two years. There is no sugar-coating it: Trump dreaded a Democratic win so much he hit the campaign trail and asked voters to imagine that he himself was on the ballot, even if after the defeat he proclaimed they lost because he was not on the ballot.
But in a way, he is. Trump’s biggest fear is a Democrat-controlled Congress that could impeach him before his tenure ends. At the very least, he feared a Democrat-controlled Congress that would put a greater check on his sweeping powers and policies that have created a lot of chaos not just in the US, but across the world.
While Trump might have admitted to his vice, JD Vance, that the Iran War might have cost him the elections, that is not the sole reason. Yes, the war Trump launched without congressional approval became an important issue during the campaign, with many Americans questioning its rationale, objective, and cost, but it is the consequence of that decision on Americans that proved most crucial. The decision to go to war with Iran drove up the cost of petrol and took a significant amount of money from the pockets of Americans.
This only compounded the economic dissatisfaction that Americans have, with many complaining about the rising cost of living, inflation, grocery prices, and household affordability. In addition, there has been overall dissatisfaction with Trump’s presidency. Polls have indicated Americans’ frustration with the administration and a desire for Congress to exercise greater checks on presidential power. But perhaps the biggest repudiation of Trump is that several Republican candidates he personally backed lost their races. Obviously, this will raise questions about the political consequences of his endorsements and the political baggage some candidates have to bear when they are forced to defend the unpopular policies of their party’s strongman.
Trump’s MAGA is a unit that exists within the Republican Party and has grafted itself to the party because the Republicans themselves subscribed to the essence of the phenomenon. However, the burden of MAGA may be too much for Republicans, if one can ever make a clear distinction between the two. These graftings delivered two Trump presidencies, and a strong power base.
It takes a statement victory by the Democrats to make the Republicans reconsider their parasitic relationship with MAGA. These elections delivered that. No Democrat had won a Kansas Senate seat since 1932. Adam Hamilton’s win is a historic shattering of a 94-year-old hold on that seat. There is a first Muslim Senator, Abdul El Sayed, one who was very openly anti-US support for Israel and one Trump was personally keen to see defeated. Deb Haaland, of New Mexico, became the first female Native American governor of a US state. Democrat Keisha Lance-Bottom becomes the first female black governor of any U.S. state, flipping Georgia for the first time in 20 years. James Talarico’s Senate win in Texas, the first for a Democrat in the last 50 years, is also a telling blow. Just as Senator Gina Hinajosa took the Texas governor’s seat from a three-time Republican incumbent. These are statement wins that built into a massive statement win across the country.
What the elections mean for the world is that perhaps we might not see the bullish, carefree, romping bull-in-a-China-shop Trump we have seen in the last two years. One who invaded Venezuela and kidnapped its president without fear or accountability to his electorate, or the one who goes to war with Iran without congressional approval, without fear of consequences for himself, or even the one who decides the way to make a point is to launch missile strikes on Nigerian farmlands and villages just because he wants to score some cheap political points with lobbyists.
Perhaps we would have a more considerate president who makes decisions with more deliberation because he knows Congress could now hold him accountable and move to impeach him if they believe he has abused his office. In total, the Republicans lost five governorship seats in key states that have now flipped and gone blue. All these set the scene for what will play out in the next two years when Americans vote for a new president to succeed Trump.
While Nigeria is gearing up for a general election next year, perhaps the country can learn lessons from the US’s elections. One of these is that democracy was instituted to install checks and balances for sweeping executive powers. Nigeria is leaning more towards a one-party state, with an opposition that barely carries any weight and states and a NASS that is entirely controlled by the President and his APC. Some of these states were won at the polls. The others were siphoned through incentivised defections. All of which have contributed to weakening the country’s democracy.
There are lessons in these elections for Republicans, Democrats, Nigerians, and the world. And for Trump especially. Democracy means nothing if it can’t regulate the excess power of its incumbents.

By Henry Ojelu & Deborah Oladeji
Former President of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), Professor Benedict Oramah, has urged African countries to take advantage of changing global realities and technological advancements to accelerate economic transformation.
Oramah made the call while delivering the keynote address at the 20th AELEX Annual Lecture in Lagos, with the theme, “Beyond Survival: Global Shocks, the Information Age and Africa’s Opportunity to Leapfrog.”
He said Africa must move beyond reacting to global disruptions and strategically position itself to benefit from emerging economic and technological opportunities.
According to him, geopolitical tensions, deglobalisation and rising protectionism are reshaping the global economy, creating an opportunity for African countries to rethink their development strategies.
He identified dependence on foreign capital, currencies and raw material exports as major constraints to the continent’s growth, stressing the need for African countries to take greater control of their resources and financial systems.
“Capital is our greatest constraint. Capital that we own but do not control is not ours,” he said, noting that between $350 billion and $500 billion in African foreign exchange reserves were held outside the continent.
Oramah called for the strengthening of indigenous financial institutions, increased local currency financing and investment in industries capable of processing the continent’s natural resources.
He also advocated the expansion of the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) and effective implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to boost intra-African trade.
Citing Kenya’s mobile money revolution, he said technology could enable African countries to leapfrog traditional stages of development.
He stressed the need for investment in energy infrastructure, data centres and critical minerals processing to prevent the continent from remaining dependent on technologies developed elsewhere.
The Chairman of the occasion and Chairman of Ecobank Nigeria Limited, Mrs Bola Adesola, said effective leadership, strong institutions and adequate preparation were critical for businesses and governments to withstand global shocks.
She emphasised investment in technology, business continuity planning and resilient supply chains, urging institutions to prepare for disruptions rather than wait for crises.
In his welcome remarks, a founding partner of AELEX, Mr Fubara Anga, SAN, described the annual lecture as a platform for discussing national issues, influencing public policy and strengthening institutions.
He called for greater involvement of state and local governments in attracting investments and driving economic development, rather than leaving the responsibility solely to the Federal Government.
The question-and-answer session, moderated by Mr Femi Ojumu, examined issues including artificial intelligence, digital sovereignty and Nigeria’s energy infrastructure.

items.content:
By Demola Akinyemi, Ilorin
Kwara State Governor, AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, on Wednesday laid the foundation for the conversion of the General Hospital, Omu-Aran, into the Thomas Adewumi University Teaching Hospital under a public-private partnership arrangement aimed at expanding access to specialised healthcare in Kwara South.
The project is expected to strengthen medical education, improve healthcare manpower development and reduce the burden on existing tertiary health facilities in the state.
Speaking at the foundation-laying ceremony, the governor, who was represented by his deputy, Kayode Alabi, described the initiative as a milestone in the development of healthcare infrastructure in Kwara South.
“Today marks another milestone as we witness the establishment of the first Teaching Hospital in Kwara South. This remarkable achievement, conceived and actualised through a strategic partnership with the Kwara State Government through the Ministry of Health, will deeply promote medical education, improve human resources in health and contribute significantly to increasing access to quality healthcare delivery for our people,” he said.
AbdulRazaq said establishing a tertiary healthcare facility in the southern part of the state would decentralise specialised medical services and reduce pressure on centrally located hospitals, which residents often find difficult to access.
He expressed confidence that the facility would contribute to reducing preventable deaths and improving healthcare outcomes across communities.
The governor said the project reflected his administration’s commitment to partnerships with private stakeholders to accelerate development, adding that upgrading the existing facility would bring medical services closer to residents of Omu-Aran and neighbouring communities.
He commended the founder, management, staff and students of Thomas Adewumi University for their commitment to medical education and development, while urging residents of Omu-Aran to support the project.
In his remarks, the Founder and Chancellor of Thomas Adewumi University, Engr. Johnson Bamidele Adewumi, said the former General Hospital, established on February 1, 1973, by the administration of the late General David Bamigboye, offered an opportunity to expand specialised healthcare services in Kwara South.
He said the university adopted the teaching hospital project as part of its vision to train medical doctors and other allied health professionals.
Adewumi explained that rather than establish an entirely new facility, the university approached the state government with a proposal to transform the existing hospital through a strategic partnership.
He clarified that the arrangement did not involve the sale or transfer of ownership of the hospital.
“Under the approved framework, ownership of the hospital remains firmly vested in the Government of Kwara State, while Thomas Adewumi University undertakes the construction and development of necessary academic infrastructure. For the avoidance of all doubt, the hospital was neither bought nor put on sale,” he said.
The chancellor, however, appealed to the state government to provide the necessary financial support for the extensive upgrading of the hospital’s infrastructure and engagement of specialist consultants.
He noted that the financial and technical requirements of a tertiary teaching hospital were beyond the capacity of a private individual or the host rural community.
Adewumi said the project was designed to be completed within 18 months, adding that a team led by Professor Kuranga, a former Chief Medical Director of the University of Ilorin Teaching Hospital, and 17 other professors had been involved in developing the initiative.
The ceremony was attended by government officials, traditional rulers and academics, including the Olupo of Ajase-Ipo, Oba Ismail Yahya Alebiosu; the Olomu of Omu-Aran, Oba Raheem Adeoti; the Commissioner for Health, Dr Amina Ahmed El-Imam; and a former Vice-Chancellor of the University of Ilorin, Professor Shuaib Oba Abdulraheem.
Also present were the APC senatorial candidate for Kwara South, Prince Lekan Adewoye, and Oloriewe Raheem Adedoyin, among other dignitaries.

By Edwin Philip, Lafia
The Nasarawa State Government has called on security agencies to investigate an incident that reportedly disrupted activities surrounding Vice-President Kashim Shettima’s visit to the Emir of Lafia during Wednesday’s All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rally.
The government made the call following reports of disturbances during the Vice-President’s visit to the traditional ruler and allegations of an incident involving Governor Abdullahi Sule at the rally held at Lafia Square.
The governor’s Personal Assistant on Social Media, Emmanuel Innocent Akwe, had raised concerns over the incident, alleging that the governor was pelted with objects suspected to be stones by some aggrieved party members.
In a statement, Akwe described the reported incident as unacceptable and called for respect for the office of the governor and the unity of the APC in the state.
The state government subsequently expressed concern over the reported disruption of the Vice-President’s visit to the Emir, urging security agencies to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.
The Secretary to the State Government, Labaran Magaji, who made the government’s position known in a statement, said Shettima had visited the traditional ruler as a mark of respect for the traditional institution.
He regretted that the visit was reportedly disrupted by actions he described as disrespectful to constituted authorities and the office of the Vice-President.
Magaji urged security agencies to conduct a thorough investigation, identify those responsible for any wrongdoing and ensure that anyone found culpable was dealt with in accordance with the law.
The development comes amid political disagreements within the state chapter of the APC following the party’s recent governorship primary.
However, the circumstances surrounding the reported disturbances and the identities of those responsible have yet to be independently established.
As of the time of filing this report, there had been no official clarification on the allegations surrounding the incidents.
The post Nasarawa APC crisis: Govt calls for probe of rally disruption appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
.partnership targets businesses, cross-border trade, access to global markets
By Udeme Akpan
The International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, and Access Holdings Plc have signed a partnership agreement to expand trade finance, support enterprise growth and improve African businesses’ access to regional and international markets.
The partnership is expected to strengthen Access Group’s capacity to finance businesses, facilitate cross-border trade and support sustainable economic growth across its markets.
The agreement, signed on the sidelines of the Africa Financial Industry Summit (AFIS) 2026 in Luanda, Angola, on November 4, 2026, also forms part of Access Holdings’ broader capital-raising programme aimed at attracting development finance institutions and other investors to support its growth.
The agreement was signed by Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede, Chairman, Access Holdings; Ethiopis Tafara, IFC Regional Vice President for Africa; and Roosevelt Ogbonna, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Access Bank Plc.
Under the partnership, IFC’s investment is expected to reinforce the Group’s capital base, enabling it to sustain and expand financing for businesses and trade activities that drive economic growth across Africa.
Commenting on the transaction, Aig-Imoukhuede said the partnership reflected a shared commitment to strengthening African financial institutions and supporting the continent’s economic development.
He said: “Our partnership with IFC has always been anchored on a shared belief that strong African financial institutions are essential to Africa’s growth. This investment is a vote of confidence in the institution we have built and, in the direction, we are taking it.
“Having built scale across Africa, our task now is to turn that scale into value: for the businesses we finance, the trade we facilitate and the communities we serve.
“Strengthening Access Group’s capital base deepens its role as a bridge between Africa and global markets, enabling us to mobilise more trade finance and investment for African enterprises.”
He added that the transaction was an important step in the Group’s efforts to attract long-term investment to support disciplined and sustainable growth.

“This partnership with Access Group will help channel more financing to businesses across the continent and translate Africa’s entrepreneurial potential into greater economic opportunity.”

items.content:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri
Dress code is a serious matter at the Nigerian Law School, where students are expected to present themselves in a manner befitting the legal profession.
However, the school’s dress policy has come under public scrutiny over alleged discriminatory treatment of Muslim candidates who wore the hijab to the ongoing Bar Final Examinations.
The examinations, which began on October 31, are scheduled to end on November 7, 2026.
The controversy stems from the school’s alleged refusal, particularly at its Bwari Campus in Abuja, to admit female candidates wearing long hijabs into the examination hall.
Reports of hijab-wearing students in tears after being restricted by school authorities prompted a range of reactions from different interest groups
While various Muslim groups insist that the hijab, which is already recognised under Part B, Rule 5 of the Nigerian Law School’s Code of Conduct for Students as acceptable attire for female students, must be retained even during examinations, the Association of Traditional Worshippers in Nigeria argues that its members should enjoy the same religious rights and be allowed to attend school activities in their traditional regalia, just as the hijab is permitted.
Reacting to the development at the Law School, the Muslim Students’ Society of Nigeria (MSSN), B-Zone, in an open letter on the first day of the exams, condemned the reported restrictions on the hijab, describing them as discriminatory.
It demanded an immediate review of the screening arrangements for candidates.
The body argued that Muslim candidates should be allowed to participate in the examinations without being compelled to compromise their religious convictions.
It argued that the wearing of the hijab is an expression of religious identity and should not be treated as an examination offence or an indication of academic misconduct.
Referencing Sections 38 and 42 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, which guarantee freedom of thought, conscience and religion as well as protection against discrimination, the students’ group argued against subjecting candidates to unequal treatment because of their faith.
Similarly, the Muslim Public Affairs Centre (MPAC) Nigeria, through its Executive Chairman, Disu Kamor, also flayed the reported treatment of hijab-wearing candidates, saying it had received complaints from the Bwari and Lagos campuses of the Law School.
For its part, the Muslim Rights Concern (MURIC) demanded a suspension of the examinations at all Nigerian Law School campuses over what it termed the harassment, intimidation and exclusion of female Muslim students wearing the hijab from examination halls.
The Islamic human rights organisation, in a press statement issued by its Founder and Executive Director, Professor Ishaq Akintola, also demanded an investigation into the incidents.
It vowed to mobilise parents, Muslim youths and other stakeholders for peaceful protests across Law School campuses nationwide if its demands were not met.
“Hijabites who came hoping to sit for their call-to-bar final examinations were disallowed from entering the examination halls.
“While this was going on, our office was inundated with telephone calls, text messages and chats.
“We heard the cries of traumatised candidates, the lamentations of distressed parents hundreds of kilometres away from the examination centres and the agitation of concerned Muslims around the country.
“MURIC strongly condemns the wanton disruption of the lawful educational pursuit of innocent Muslim ladies. It is crude, irrational and sadistic,” the body added.
Meanwhile, the Law School has denied any form of discrimination or harassment of the female Muslim candidates who were screened for the examinations.
The school, in a statement signed by its Secretary to Council and Director of Administration, A.O. Osho, said its examinations were conducted under established regulations designed to ensure proper identification, examination security and academic integrity.
It disclosed that a female student wearing a hijab was recently apprehended after she was found with electronic devices concealed on her body.
“On the 29th day of October 2026, a Bar Part I female student with her hijab on, was found with ear pod and a phone strapped to her thigh.
“This incident is still being investigated under the school rules and extant regulations,” the school added, saying the incident reinforced the need for strict examination security measures.
“The apprehension of the female student for examination malpractice during the Bar Part I examinations further underscores the necessity for strict and effective examination security measures.
“Such measures, however, must be applied fairly and without discrimination,” the school stated, even as it pledged commitment to protecting the constitutional rights and religious freedoms of all students.
It is worth noting that the intervention of critical stakeholders and the management of the school eventually led to an understanding that female Muslim students may wear only black, shoulder-length hijabs.
This has, however, not gone down well with the Association of Traditional Worshippers in Nigeria, which insists that what is good for the goose should also be good for the gander.
“Our position is founded on the inviolable principle of equality, religious freedom and non-discrimination.
“If Muslim students are permitted to wear hijabs during examinations on the basis of religious convictions, then students who practise traditional African religions must equally be permitted to manifest their religious identities and convictions without discrimination, marginalisation or institutional hostility,” the group insisted.
Remarkably, this is not the first time the hijab has sparked controversy over the dress code regulations for lawyers.
On June 23, 2022, senior lawyer and activist, Chief Malcolm Omirhobo caused a stir at the Supreme Court by appearing for a hearing in native doctor regalia.
Chief Omirhobo, who sauntered into the courtroom barefooted, wore his lawyer’s wig and black gown with a white shirt, though instead of black trousers and a suit, he wore a red wrapper with a mini-calabash amulet dangling from his neck.
The lawyer, who also wore amulets on his wrist and ankle, sat comfortably in a row of chairs reserved for legal practitioners while proceedings of the apex court lasted.
Although he was not accosted by security agents attached to the court, his bizarre appearance was not lost on a panel of justices of the Supreme Court, who quickly handled the case before them and retired to their chambers.
Speaking to journalists after he exited the courtroom, Chief Omirhobo said his decision was based on a judgement the apex court had just delivered, which permitted the use of the hijab in public primary and secondary schools in Lagos.
The Supreme Court, in a split decision of five to two justices, in an appeal marked SC/910/2016, which Lagos State, through its Attorney-General, filed against a minor, Miss Ayisat Abdukareem, and others, validated the use of the hijab in public schools.
Chief Omirhobo insisted the verdict enforced his right to include his traditional regalia, being his mode of worship, in what he wore to the court.
“You can see that I am not wearing shoes. Ifa has told me that if I wear shoes I’ll be dead. So I had no option; I had to obey the spirit.
“You see this eye (pointing at the calabash amulet on his chest), without it I can’t see the evil spirit coming to attack me. So with this I can see them,” Chief Omirhobo told journalists, referencing the Supreme Court judgment.
The case of Amasa Firdaus in 2017, when her hijab became the subject of controversy at the Call to Bar ceremony, also remains fresh in the memory.
Amasa’s refusal to remove her hijab led the Council of Legal Education to withdraw her from the list of those to be admitted into the Bar.
However, following high-level intervention, she was admitted into the Bar the following year.
The latest hijab controversy may be settled, but traditional worshippers’ push for similar accommodation will likely keep the issue alive.

By Daniel Kudayah
The Director-General of the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC), Prof. Mojisola Christianah Adeyeye, has received an Award of Excellent Performance from the Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (NACCIMA) in recognition of her contributions to industrial growth and the fight against fake and substandard drugs.
The award was presented at NACCIMA’s Breakfast Roundtable Meeting held at Providence Hotel, Lagos, where Adeyeye served as guest speaker.
The meeting brought together members of the association, captains of industry and key stakeholders from the organised private sector to discuss regulatory processes, business growth and public health protection.
In her keynote address, Adeyeye highlighted regulatory reforms introduced under her leadership, emphasising NAFDAC’s commitment to transparent, science-driven and business-friendly regulation.
She explained that the agency’s regulatory framework was designed to support industrial growth while ensuring that only safe, quality and wholesome products reach Nigerian consumers.
Industry leaders and other participants at the meeting commended the NAFDAC boss for her leadership, particularly her efforts to combat fake and substandard drugs and her contributions to creating a more supportive regulatory environment for businesses.
They praised her commitment to safeguarding public health while promoting the growth and development of industries in Nigeria.
The award, according to NACCIMA, recognised Adeyeye’s outstanding performance, hard work and contributions to industry and the fight against counterfeit and substandard products.
The presentation was greeted with applause from participants at the event.
NAFDAC, under Adeyeye’s leadership, has continued to pursue measures aimed at strengthening the regulation of food, drugs and other regulated products, with the dual objective of protecting consumers and supporting legitimate businesses.
The recognition by NACCIMA underscores the importance of collaboration between regulators and the organised private sector in promoting product quality, consumer safety and sustainable industrial development.
