Older devices will receive the update in December. This phase includes the Xiaomi 14 and 13 series, Xiaomi MIX Flip, Xiaomi 13T lineup, Redmi Note 14 family, and POCO F6 series.
However, these dates indicate the beginning of each rollout phase rather than fixed installation dates. Actual availability may vary depending on the region and device.
HyperOS 4 Brings a Redesigned Interface
HyperOS 4 introduces a refreshed user interface with a new design language called “Soft Light Glass.” Xiaomi has redesigned several interface elements to give the software a more modern appearance.
The update brings translucent panels, redesigned notifications, customizable lock screens, flexible app folders, and stacked widgets. It also improves floating-window support and introduces smoother animations to make everyday navigation more responsive.
Xiaomi Promises Better Performance
Apart from visual changes, Xiaomi has focused on improving system performance and responsiveness.
According to the company, HyperOS 4 reduces the time required to launch 30 applications after nine hours of usage from 40.3 seconds to 36.8 seconds. This represents an 8.7% improvement compared with HyperOS 3.
Camera performance is also expected to improve. Xiaomi claims that HDR photo processing time has dropped from 313.38 milliseconds to 240.16 milliseconds. The company also promises fewer dropped frames during video playback.
Super XiaoAi 2.0 Gets More AI Features
Artificial intelligence is another major part of HyperOS 4. Xiaomi is introducing Super XiaoAi 2.0, powered by its MiMo large language model.
The upgraded assistant will support more advanced tasks, including searching through photo libraries, organizing schedules, controlling compatible smart home devices, and identifying products displayed on the screen.
Xiaomi is also improving privacy protections. The system will ask users to confirm sensitive actions, such as deleting or sharing personal data, before proceeding.
Meanwhile, the company’s Super Island feature will support more than 130 services, providing users with additional ways to access information and manage activities.
Some AI features and other improvements may remain limited to specific devices and Chinese software versions. International users may not receive every feature included in the Chinese release.
Overall, HyperOS 4 appears to be a major upgrade for Xiaomi users, combining a redesigned interface, performance improvements, and expanded AI capabilities. The upcoming global rollout will reveal which features Xiaomi brings to its international devices.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Keeping hospital corridors clean or moving goods across factory floors involves repetitive, physically demanding work. For facility management companies, finding people to carry out these tasks is becoming harder.
This workforce gap is the opportunity behind Peppermint Robotics. Founded in 2019 and incubated at SINE, IIT Bombay, the Pune-based startup builds autonomous robots that scrub floors and move materials across commercial and industrial facilities.
Now, it has raised ₹100 Cr (about $10.5 Mn) in a Pre-Series B round to expand manufacturing, develop new robots, and strengthen its US and European businesses.
Led by pi Ventures and Crane Venture Partners, with participation from Asiana Fund, the round comprised primary capital and secondary share transactions. Founder Runal Dahiwade told Inc42 that the bulk of the investment was primary capital. The startup previously raised ₹34 Cr in a Series A round in April 2025.
Moving Beyond Floor Cleaning
Featured in Inc42’s June 2020 edition of ‘30 Startups To Watch’, Peppermint began with a floor-cleaning and sanitising robot. Its portfolio now spans scrubber-dryers, vacuuming and mopping robots, three material-handling models, and automated docking stations.
The startup says its cleanroom scrubber-dryer has passed qualification testing in an EU GMP Grade C cleanroom. Such controlled environments require strict limits on contamination, creating a specialised application beyond routine cleaning.
Dahiwade also claimed Peppermint is the world’s first cleanroom robotics company.
Over the next 12-15 months, Peppermint plans smaller and larger cleaning and material-handling robots, alongside upgrades. Outdoor cleaning robots are planned by 2028.
Its proprietary Peppermint OS powers navigation, while computer vision and LiDAR help machines map spaces and avoid obstacles. Customers can monitor operations through a cloud dashboard and mobile apps.
Selling Machines And Support
Peppermint sells robots primarily to facility management companies, earning additional revenue from spare parts, annual maintenance contracts, and software and hardware upgrades from the second year.
An average robot costs around ₹20 Lakh in India. US prices range from $35,000 to $40,000, depending on installation and other costs, Dahiwade said.
Its operating revenue rose from ₹2.71 Cr in FY23 to ₹6.26 Cr in FY24 and ₹21 Cr in FY25. The founder said revenue doubled last year and grew nearly sixfold between FY24 and FY26.
The US contributes nearly half its revenue, India close to 30%, and other markets the remainder. Peppermint is planning to set up an assembly line in North America, adding to its Pune manufacturing and R&D base.
It competes with China’s Gausium and Singapore’s LionsBot. Dahiwade claimed Peppermint commands over 65% of India’s floor-cleaning robotics market.
Inc42 Take: Can Peppermint Scale Without Stretching Its Service Network?
Selling through facility management companies offers a route to deployments across multiple customer locations. Expanding into material handling and cleanrooms could widen this opportunity.
The bigger test is servicing these machines across markets while funding a broader portfolio. According to Peppermint, its core business has operated profitably for several quarters, but R&D and international expansion have kept the company loss-making overall.
Converting fresh capital into reliable deployments and repeat business will matter more than portfolio breadth alone.

The Economic Times first reported the development.
Founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, Razorpay offers payment processing, business banking, payroll, and lending solutions. It filed its IPO papers through the confidential route in June, targeting a valuation of $5 Bn to $6 Bn, below the $7.5 Bn valuation it commanded in its last funding round in 2021.

Razorpay’s Growing AI Offerings
Alongside its IPO preparations, Razorpay has been expanding its AI offerings across payments, marketing, and business operations.
Last month, it announced an expanded partnership with OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT. Under the partnership, its growth marketing platform, Razorpay Engage, will enable brands to prepare product catalogues and launch and manage campaigns on ChatGPT Ads.
Razorpay has also launched Vulcan, a transformer-based AI foundation model for digital payments. The company claims the model can improve payment reliability and safety by scoring payment routes in real time and identifying fraud patterns across multiple merchants once deployed.
Built using NVIDIA and AWS technology, Vulcan combines Razorpay’s payments data with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AWS’ cloud infrastructure.
The fintech major has also been developing Agent Studio, a platform for deploying task-specific AI agents for businesses. Around 200 businesses were using the platform in beta as of August, with use cases spanning reconciliation, abandoned-cart recovery, subscription recovery, and finance operations.
Razorpay has raised over $800 Mn to date from investors including Y Combinator, Tiger Global Management, Ribbit Capital, and Lightspeed.

items.author: Ankush Das
items.content:
Can you trust a stranger with your login credentials, personal information, or private conversations? Of course not! Yet, we are increasingly trusting AI assistants with precisely this kind of information.
The rationale is simple: The more these assistants know about us, the more useful they become. However, this convenience comes with an uncomfortable question: Can we trust them?
The stakes are even higher for businesses, as AI assistants increasingly handle proprietary information, financial records and confidential legal documents. This growing tension has created an opening for privacy-focused AI products.
In October, Eternal announced Dark.ai, a privacy-focused AI assistant built around open-weight models and positioned around end-to-end encryption. Globally, products such as Brave Leo, Duck.ai and Proton Lumo are also attempting to address growing concerns over how AI systems handle sensitive information.
So, can it become the next big competitive advantage in AI? And, more importantly, what will it take for startups to turn that promise into a sustainable business?
Let’s explore in The AI Shift…
The Privacy Trade-Off
The more an AI assistant knows, the better it can do its job. But there is a catch. To deliver useful answers, it may need access to information that users and businesses would rather keep private.
Take a legal AI assistant, for instance. It may need to go through confidential case files to help lawyers with research. Similarly, an AI platform in financial services may need access to loan histories, transaction records and customer communications.
This puts AI startups in a tricky position. Without enough data and context, AI products may not be useful. On the flip side, how can these assistants be trusted if there is no guarantee that sensitive information will be handled safely.
Saakar Yadav, founder of legal research and workflow platform Lexlegis.ai, has seen this challenge firsthand. He said some organisations want to use AI to work with confidential legal documents but are unwilling to let that information leave their systems. For such customers, running AI locally on their own computers, even without an internet connection, could offer a solution.
The challenge is that there is no single way to make AI private. Some companies keep data on users’ devices, while others hide identifying details, encrypt conversations or restrict who can access the information. Each approach addresses a different risk, and what works for one AI product may not be enough for another.
For instance, AI-powered consumer assistant SuperLiving is working on protecting user information by masking conversations so that individual users cannot be easily identified. Cofounder Manavdeep Singh Grover said that the company is also working towards introducing encryption to strengthen its privacy safeguards.
However, masking alone cannot solve every privacy concern. Companies also need to consider where conversations are stored, who can access them and how the information is processed.
From Encrypted Chats To AI That Stays Offline
AI companies are approaching privacy through different technical choices, rather than relying on a single definition of a private assistant.
Brave Leo, from privacy-focused browser company Brave, has outlined protections that include encrypted conversations and confidential computing for supported inference. Duck.ai, from search engine DuckDuckGo, says it removes identifying information from requests before sending them to model providers. Proton Lumo, from privacy-focused technology company Proton, said it does not keep logs of conversations and does not use chats to train models without explicit permission.
Apple’s Private Cloud Compute takes another approach, using dedicated servers designed to process requests without retaining user data after they are handled. Apple has also said that independent researchers can inspect the system’s security properties.
The stakes are particularly high in financial services, where AI systems may need access to transaction histories, repayment behaviour and investment preferences to assist customers with financial decisions. But access to this information should not translate into unrestricted permission to use it.
Ashutosh Prakash Singh, cofounder and CEO at RevRag.ai, which works on AI solutions, argues that financial institutions need clear boundaries around what an in-app AI agent can access and infer, how long information is retained, and whether it can be used to train or improve models.
He believes stronger data protection will increasingly become a business necessity rather than just a compliance requirement. Financial institutions will assess AI not only on efficiency and cost, but also on governance, traceability and accountability. Losing customer confidence over how financial information is used can be as damaging as a data breach. As AI becomes more deeply embedded in financial services, trust will be central to whether customers are willing to use it.
This makes choosing architecture important. Some workflows may be served by masking and access controls, while others may require stricter retention policies, secure deployment environments or additional safeguards around where data is processed.
The opportunity for startups is therefore not simply to market an AI assistant as private but to build products whose privacy protections match the sensitivity of the work they are designed to handle.
Privacy As A Business Opportunity
Privacy can influence purchasing decisions, but it may not be enough to sustain an AI business on its own. Products still need to solve a meaningful problem and deliver an experience that customers are willing to pay for.
Kushal Bhagia, founding partner at All In Capital, believes privacy can be a strong differentiator when the underlying product is already compelling.
“Privacy becomes the reason someone chooses one product over another when the underlying utility is already compelling,” he said.
The distinction matters because not every customer will pay a premium for stronger privacy. A business using AI for routine internal tasks may have different requirements from one processing financial records, proprietary research or confidential customer information. For the latter, safeguards may be a basic condition for adoption rather than an optional add-on.
There are several possible opportunities here, including private AI infrastructure, secure deployment, data governance tools and specialised assistants built for sensitive workflows. But these products also bring costs. Security engineering, encryption, infrastructure and compliance can make development and deployment more expensive.
According to SuperLiving’s Grover, the company is working towards compliance with India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) framework, including considerations around data retention, encryption and the information shared with large language models.
The commercial challenge is to make such safeguards credible without making the product too expensive or cumbersome. Customers need to understand what protections are in place, how those protections work and what risks remain.
For businesses, the strongest opportunity may lie in enabling AI adoption in workflows that organisations would otherwise keep off public AI platforms. These could include legal research, financial analysis, customer data management and internal decision-making, where the risks of exposing sensitive information can outweigh the convenience of using a general-purpose assistant.
Building a more private AI business requires more than encryption or a promise not to train models on user data. Companies need clear data retention policies, access controls and safeguards that can be demonstrated in practice. They must also deliver enough value to justify the added costs of secure infrastructure and compliance.
Privacy, therefore, may be less of a standalone product feature and more of an enabler of AI adoption.
Top Stories From India & Around The World
Live2.ai Raises ₹130 Cr⁠: The startup raised ₹130 Cr to expand its AI-powered video marketing platform, which helps brands and ecommerce businesses turn product content into interactive shopping experiences and improve customer engagement.
Cognizant To Invest In Sarvam: IT services major Cognizant is reportedly in talks to invest in Sarvam AI at a valuation of $3.5 Bn-$4 Bn, signalling growing enterprise interest in India’s homegrown foundation model developer and its sovereign AI capabilities.
Innodata Cuts India Jobs: The US-based AI services company reportedly laid off nearly 550 employees in India, around 5% of its global workforce. The company cited a reduction in business assignments as workforce uncertainty grows.
India ChatGPT’s Largest Market: India has become ChatGPT’s largest market by weekly active users, with its user base doubling since January 2026, according to OpenAI India MD Prabhjeet Singh. The company is expanding Indian-language capabilities, local computing infrastructure and enterprise partnerships to support adoption.
MeitY’s New AI Framework: The IT ministry proposed a consent-based framework to help startups, businesses and researchers access India-specific datasets for AI training while protecting privacy. It includes secure data-sharing infrastructure and independent checks for bias, safety and fairness.
The Weekly Buzz: Google’s Suncatcher Runs AI From Orbit
Google reported this week that its experimental Suncatcher satellite successfully performed the first AI inference in orbit. The prototype carries Google’s own AI chips and runs the Gemma model, generating responses including a haiku while operating in space.
Suncatcher is an early test of whether data centres and inference workloads can eventually move off-planet, potentially easing terrestrial power and cooling constraints.
Only one chip runs at a time in the current design, and the project remains firmly in the research phase. Still, completing actual model inference outside Earth’s atmosphere marks a symbolic and technical milestone.
The demonstration arrives amid intensifying competition for energy and land for AI infrastructure on the ground. While practical orbital compute remains years away, Suncatcher shows Google exploring radical long-term options for scaling intelligence beyond conventional data-centre limits.
Startup In The Spotlight: Sitepace.ai
Founded in 2023, Mumbai-based SitePace.AI is building an AI-powered visual intelligence platform that helps construction teams monitor project progress remotely and coordinate work across multiple sites.
Project managers often rely on photographs, manual reports and physical site visits to track construction progress. These fragmented information sources can delay decisions, make it difficult to compare progress over time and stretch project timelines, particularly when teams oversee several sites simultaneously.
SitePace.AI uses 360-degree cameras, computer vision and AI to turn site walks into time-stamped, floor-linked visual records. Workers can mount cameras on their helmets to capture construction sites as they move through them, with the platform automatically organising the footage against floor plans and dates. Teams can remotely navigate sites, compare progress, add location-specific notes and collaborate through virtual walkthroughs.
The startup is expanding beyond visual documentation into AI-powered CCTV monitoring, drone intelligence and IntelliViz, a chatbot that lets users interact with site information. It is also developing computer-vision capabilities for automated progress tracking, defect detection and safety monitoring, moving towards more automated construction oversight.
Operating on a subscription-based SaaS model, SitePace.AI prices its plans according to project requirements. The company claims its technology can reduce inspection time by 48% and manual effort by 95%, positioning visual intelligence as a way to improve construction monitoring and reduce the need for repetitive on-site checks.
Prompt Of The Week
What prompts and hacks are CTOs, CEOs and cofounders using these days to streamline their work?
Here’s Kirti Prakash Mishra, founder and CEO of YoLearn.ai, with a prompt he uses to pressure-test any big, hard-to-reverse decision (a senior hire, a new market, a pricing change or a fundraise) before committing to it:
“You are a sharp, independent board advisor who has seen hundreds of startups make, and regret, big decisions.
Here is the decision I’m about to make: [Describe the decision, why now, the alternatives considered, the money and time involved, and what success looks like in 12 months.]
I need you to:
Restate the decision in one sentence, and the real problem it is meant to solve
Imagine it is 12 months later and this decision failed badly. Write the three most likely reasons why
Identify the assumption I am most confident about but have the least evidence for
Show me the strongest case for NOT doing this, or for waiting 90 days
Suggest a smaller, cheaper version I could test first
Define the early warning signals that should make me reverse course, and by when
Tell me who in my team, board or customer base I should talk to before deciding
Be direct and unsentimental. Don’t validate my thinking. Find the holes in it, and keep the output concise and decision-ready.”
Editor’s Note: Some prompts may need to be adjusted by users for best results or may not work as intended for certain users.

items.author: Zulker Naeen
items.content:
No justice for Bangladeshi workers who are recruited into Russia’s war
Originally published on Global Voices
War-wounded Bangladeshis in Russia plead to return home. Screenshot from a YouTube report by Ekhon TV. Fair use.
Maksudur Rahman was 31 when a labor recruiter arrived in his hometown in Lakshmipur district, southeastern Bangladesh, with a job offer: becoming a janitor in Russia. Nearly every family in the district has someone working overseas, so the pitch landed. According to an international investigation, he borrowed money and paid the broker BDT 1.2 million (about USD 9,800). For a household like his, that is a fortune, but the promised wages made the debt look manageable. He signed up and flew out.
What followed had nothing to do with brooms. Within weeks, he was on the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine. He and three other Bangladeshi workers were handed a paper written in Russian — a language they did not understand — and told to sign. Then came an army camp, where recruits were trained in drone tactics, medical evacuation, and heavy weapons. When Rahman protested, a Russian commander replied through a translation app that his own agent had sent him there. Workers in his group were threatened with ten-year jail terms and beaten, he said.
His story is a case study in how this insidious war pipeline operates: a local agent, a borrowed fortune, a contract nobody could read, and a war that was never part of the bargain. But to understand how a man from Lakshmipur ended up in that camp, it’s important to look at the realities in Russia and what is driving these recruitment traps.
A war that is running out of men
Russia has a manpower problem, and the figures are hard to wave away. Enlistment into contract service dropped about 20 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to international reporting relayed by Ukrainian outlets. This deficit persists even though Moscow is offering signing packages of up to USD 80,000 and debt write-offs of up to USD 140,000.
Meanwhile, BBC and Mediazona journalists estimate there have been at least 300,000 Russian deaths since the war began on February 24, 2022, based on local obituaries. Other Western intelligence estimates put Russian deaths near 500,000, with monthly casualties of 30,000 to 35,000.
One estimate says the country needs another 1.5 million workers to stabilize its labor market, and officials themselves expect a shortfall of 3.1 million people by 2030. Because stricter migration rules have also pushed out roughly a million temporary workers, the army and the factories now compete for the same shrinking labor pool.
While Russia has not dared to implement another full-scale military draft as it did in September 2022 — a move that was highly damaging to the regime and local support — officials are doing everything they can to buy recruits or force those who are vulnerable, elderly, or simply went to the draft station to register to go to the front lines.
Given these manpower challenges, Moscow has looked outward. It has already used tens of thousands of prisoners and three waves of North Korean troops, yet that wasn’t enough.
A UK defense assessment, summarized by a Ukrainian outlet, says the supply of convict recruits is probably exhausted, and Russia is widening its search across the Global South to avoid another mobilization at home.
Ukrainian data counts nearly 29,000 foreigners who have signed contracts since 2022. One report says the army wants at least 18,500 more in 2026, naming Bangladesh among its top targets.
Rights groups see a pattern behind these numbers. The International Federation for Human Rights described an organized pipeline aimed at undocumented migrants, detainees, precarious workers, and foreign students across three continents, and Amnesty International accused Moscow last month of deceptive, coercive, and exploitative recruitment.
Who is accepting this offer?
Within South Asia, this recruitment scheme goes beyond just Bangladesh. After Sri Lanka’s economic collapse in 2022 and Nepal’s recession, wages of at least USD 550 a month in Russia looked like a way out, according to analysis from the Observer Research Foundation (ORF). Nepal’s foreign minister admitted in early 2024 that more than 200 Nepali citizens had been recruited. Kathmandu later suspended work permits for Russia after numerous Nepali citizens died on the front lines in Ukraine. Sri Lanka, for its part, saw an estimated 600 to 700 former soldiers recruited.
Why, then, would anyone take the risk? Money comes first. One welder, according to a report on survivors’ accounts, was offered a USD 20,990 signing bonus, a salary of USD 2,664 per month, and a shot at citizenship. For families buried in debt, those numbers can drown out the danger.
But money isn’t the whole answer. Some Bangladeshis enlisted knowingly were misled about the role, the reporting noted, while others lost a visa-linked job and found a recruiter waiting with a better-sounding contract. Some never aimed for Russia at all: One prisoner said an Uzbek broker had promised him residence in Italy. Once inside, the choice largely disappears, as recruits were presented with contracts in Russian, with those who hesitated facing threats and violence, according to Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds. Another report described passports and phones seized on arrival.
The legal door and the missing agreement
Russia was never a typical destination for Bangladeshi workers. This labor force first entered the country via shipyards, where skilled hands were needed as the war strained the domestic labor supply. Initially, around 56 workers were sent there. Then the flow increased. According to the data of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), 993 Bangladeshis went in 2024 and 4,663 in 2025. The Bureau of Manpower Employment and Training (BMET) records 8,247 departures between 2024 and June 2026. The state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) sent just 426 among them, and those workers are reported safe; the private market carried the rest.
However, even with this sizable flow of workers, no signed labor agreement seems to exist between the two countries. During Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman’s June 2026 visit to Moscow, both sides merely urged early conclusion of pending accords, including a human resource agreement and a readmission agreement. Russia has agreed to fast-track a proposal for 100,000 Bangladeshi workers within a year. A state minister even spoke of 300,000 to 400,000 workers over five years. Meanwhile, Dhaka’s embassy in Moscow has asked Russia to bar Bangladeshis from military service.
The lack of a formal agreement leaves Bangladeshi workers exposed and vulnerable to scams and exploitation.
Fraud also shows up outside the war. In January 2026, 35 workers returned from Russia after being terminated, saying they had each paid about BDT 700,000 (roughly USD 5,651).
Agents, agencies, and the price of a seat
The route from village to barracks runs through ordinary offices. Bangladesh’s Special Response Battalion (SRB) said 30 men who flew to Russia in May 2026 went through three manpower firms, Jabal-e-Noor International, RS International, and TS Group. Officers arrested two alleged ringleaders in mid-October and say a Russian man and a Kyrgyz woman were part of the network, though these allegations remain unconfirmed. The expatriates’ welfare minister told Parliament that the men left with BMET clearance through licensed agencies, which shows that paperwork alone proves nothing.
Once the men landed, the script repeated. Their passports and phones were taken. After 21 days of training, they went to the front. Investigators said they were used as bait to expose enemy positions to drones.
Counting the dead without a count
Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds identified at least 104 Bangladeshis recruited as of February 2026 and at least 34 killed, based on Ukrainian information, and warned that the real toll is probably higher. But on October 14, 2026, the SRB said 20 of the same 30 were dead, with 17 killed by a drone strike on their first day at the front and six still fighting, local news reports said.
These figures can’t simply be added together, because the overlap is unknown and the sources differ: police, rights groups, and Kyiv. Those families, meanwhile, wait without bodies.
Rights groups have urged Dhaka to dismantle the networks and Ukraine to screen captured foreign fighters for signs of trafficking. Yet families still ask for rescue, and the same daily’s editors have pleaded with the government to start bringing the stranded men home.
No Justice for the victims
Back to Maksudur Rahman: He got out, and today he sits at home in Lakshmipur, holding up a Russian military dog tag as proof of where he has been. Others from the same corner of Bangladesh haven’t come home. Sajjad, 20, was killed after being taken to fight, and his father, Mohammed Siraj, now holds a photograph of where his son used to be. For Siraj, justice is not an abstraction. It is a name on a charge sheet, a body to bury, and an answer to the question of who sent his son to war.
In the village, families confronted the recruiting agents and demanded to know why their loved ones were being trained for war. Their questions belong in a courtroom, not only in a village courtyard. Until the agents who sold these jobs and the system that cleared their paperwork are made to answer, the families will keep carrying a debt that is more than money.
Rahman’s loan was real, the war was real, and the janitor’s job never existed. A man who left home to earn a living came back carrying a soldier’s dog tag. And no justice in sight.
Written by Zulker Naeen

items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
Microdrama platform Story TV’s parent EloElo Group has raised $80 Mn (nearly ₹756 Cr) in a Series C funding round led by global media and entertainment giant NBCUniversal and Hornbill Capital.
The round also saw participation from MIT Investment Co. and existing backers including Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures and Griffin Gaming Partners, among others.
The company will use the fresh capital to invest in premium original content across Indian languages, expand Story TV to international markets and strengthen its AI capabilities through Dolphin AI, its recently launched AI creative suite.
Founded in 2020 by former Flipkart executive Saurabh Pandey, EloElo Group operates four products — Story TV (microdrama platform), Master (microlearning platform) Dolphin AI (an AI-powered creative suite) and Voxy AI (an AI companion agent).
Story TV remains the company’s largest product, with over 5,000 microdramas across six languages. Across its portfolio of apps, EloElo Group claims to have over 40 Mn monthly active users and more than 300 Mn installs.
Speaking to Inc42, Pandey said the company plans to deepen its premium content slate by working with established production studios and experimenting with AI-generated and hybrid microdramas. It currently works with over 90 production studios, including Indian production house Balaji Telefilms.
The company also plans to take Story TV to international markets. Pandey further said the company would identify markets and work with local talent pools as part of the expansion.
Another focus area will be Dolphin AI, which allows users to generate videos, images and longer-form AI content, including films. EloElo currently has a team of around 200 people, of which 8-10 work on Dolphin AI. The fresh capital will support hiring across data science, generative AI, engineering and computer infrastructure teams.
Pandey said EloElo’s strategy is to control three layers of the entertainment value chain: intellectual property, AI-powered production infrastructure and content distribution.
With the latest fundraise, EloElo Group has raised $130 Mn to date.
The funding comes amid growing interest in the microdrama format. According to a report, the global microdrama industry is expected to generate $14 Bn in revenue by the end of 2026..

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
The Data Security Council of India (DSCI) has proposed an industry framework to determine liability when autonomous AI agents cause harm. It recommends assigning responsibility across the AI value chain based on the decisions each participant makes and the extent of its control over the system.
The discussion paper, titled ‘AI Liability: Industry Guidance for Agentic AI’, seeks to apply existing laws, contractual obligations and sectoral regulations to agentic AI systems rather than introduce a new regulatory framework.
It identifies five groups involved in enterprise AI deployment: end-user organisations, service providers and integrators, product companies and startups, tool and framework providers, and cloud and infrastructure providers. AI model providers are examined separately.
DSCI argues that liability should not rest solely with the company deploying an AI system or the technology provider supplying it. Instead, accountability should be determined by examining who controls key decisions, from model selection and system configuration to tool access, permissions and human oversight.
The paper highlights the risks posed by the shift from generative AI to agentic AI. While conventional AI systems primarily generate outputs for human review, AI agents can independently plan tasks, access tools, interact with application programming interfaces (APIs) and execute instructions with limited human intervention.
This raises the risk of unauthorised transactions, incorrect payments and data breaches, particularly when multiple agents interact or delegate tasks across organisations, potentially leading to cascading errors and wider disruptions.
DSCI identifies 12 areas of potential harm, including privacy breaches, security threats, discrimination, safety risks, inaccurate outputs, intellectual property violations, deepfakes, loss of control and AI-enabled cybercrime.
It also flags operational challenges that could complicate liability assessments such as changes in model behaviour, autonomous decision-making, human approval fatigue, delegation between agents and difficulties in reproducing how an AI system arrived at a particular action.
Liability To Depend On Control Across AI Value Chain
The framework draws on existing legal principles, including duty of care, product liability, causation and comparative negligence. It proposes an authority map to establish who controlled a particular decision and whether they could have prevented or limited the resulting harm.
Under this approach, companies deploying AI agents would be responsible for choosing use cases, setting permissions, assessing operational risks and deciding when human approval is required. Product companies could be held accountable for product claims, default settings and model versions, while system integrators would be responsible for system design, approval mechanisms and handling failures.
Tool and framework providers would be accountable for the orchestration, memory and safety features they supply. Cloud and infrastructure providers would have responsibilities around system isolation, identity management, data retention and platform logs.
The framework also links liability to the type of AI model and how it is deployed. Companies using open-source or open-weight models on their own infrastructure would take on greater responsibility for auditing, modifying and monitoring them.
Those using closed models through managed APIs could seek contractual recourse against model providers, although this would depend on the terms of their agreements and applicable liability caps.
DSCI said model providers should remain responsible for the capabilities they develop, safety measures, disclosures about known limitations and notifications of significant changes in model behaviour. However, their liability could reduce when other participants take control of how models are deployed and used.
DSCI Recommends Layered Safeguards For AI Agents
To limit these risks, the framework proposes six safeguards, including removing unnecessary capabilities, restricting system permissions, requiring human approval for significant or irreversible actions, monitoring AI behaviour, enabling systems to scale back operations safely and deploying kill switches with clearly defined ownership.
It also recommends that organisations assess risks before deploying AI agents, include liability provisions in procurement contracts and regularly review safeguards.
DSCI has also invited AI developers, industry members, policy think tanks and other stakeholders to submit feedback on the proposal. The council plans to publish further guidance on authority mapping, AI deployment in physical and biological systems, and agents operated by customers and business partners.
The proposed framework comes amid growing scrutiny of the risks posed by increasingly autonomous AI systems. Last month, MeitY proposed a consent-based framework to facilitate data sharing for AI model training in India.
Called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training, the framework aims to help startups, businesses and academic institutions access large-scale, India-specific datasets while protecting citizens’ privacy and ensuring compliance with the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act.
It also proposes a techno-legal architecture that would allow organisations to collaborate on AI model training without directly transferring the underlying datasets.
Separately, the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) released draft guidelines on the responsible use of AI in telecom networks and service delivery. The regulator has invited stakeholder comments on the proposals by November 27.

items.author: Team Inc42
items.content:
AI and advanced analytics company Fractal more than doubled (139%) its net profit to ₹79.2 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) from ₹33.2 Cr in the year ago quarter. Sequentially, the bottom line also rose 9.5% from ₹115.8 Cr in Q1 FY27.
Fractal attributed the growing profits to rising revenues, improving margins, increased spending by clients and broad-based growth across all its key verticals.
Revenue from operations rose nearly 20% to a record ₹956.5 Cr in the quarter under review as against ₹798.5 Cr in the preceding quarter. On a quarter-on-quarter (QoQ), the top line grew 4.8% from ₹912.5 Cr in Q4 FY26.
Including other income of ₹28.8 Cr, Fractal’s total income stood at ₹985.3 Cr during the quarter under review. In line with its top line, the company’s total expenses also rose 15% to ₹858.9 Cr in Q2 FY27 as against ₹746.6 Cr in the quarter ending September 2025.
In its investor presentation, Fractal also said that its adjusted EBITDA rose 30% YoY to ₹154.9 Cr during the quarter under review, while adjusted EBITDA margin improved by 123 bps YoY to 16.2%. The company attributed this to operating leverage; short-term impact in GM driven by investment in AI engineering talent.
Fractal also reported a loss of ₹23.2 Cr from an associate in the quarter, while its tax expenses stood at ₹24 Cr.
Giving a category-wise revenue split, the AI company claimed that its healthcare and life sciences (HLS) vertical clocked 79% YoY growth in revenues in Q2 FY27, while the banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) revenue rose 30% YoY. Consumer packaged goods and retail (CPGR), its biggest portfolio, saw 19% YoY top line jump.
However, Fractal’s revenues from telecom, media, and technology (TMT) clients declined 18% YoY in Q2 FY27.
Giving a geographical breakdown, Fractal said that Americas accounted for the bulk 67.3% of its total revenue during the quarter, while Europe and APAC (Asia Pacific), and other regions, contributed 21.5% and 11.2%, respectively.
In line with this, revenues from the Americas rose 22% YoY, while the top line from Europe and APAC and other regions jumped 20% and 7%, respectively.
The AI analytics company also said that its revenue per billable full-time equivalent (FTE) stood at ₹75 Lakh during the quarter under review, up 2% YoY. Billable FTE is an outsourcing-based billing model, where clients pay a fixed monthly rate for a dedicated employee’s time rather than per task.
Fractal also claimed that it increased its $20 Mn+ clients to four from six in Q2 FY26, while $1 Mn+ sized clients grew to 58 in Q2 FY27 from 52 in the year ago quarter.
In a filing with the exchanges, Fractal also said that its board approved the winding up of its step-down subsidiary, Analytics Vidhya Inc. The AI analytics company noted that this will lead to the simplification of the group’s corporate structure and reduce compliance, administrative overheads, and enhance operational efficiency.
Founded in 2000, Fractal generates revenue through analytics and consulting services as well as licensing and subscriptions for its AI platforms such as Cogentiq, Iqigai and Kalaido.ai. It serves global enterprises such as Google and Wells Fargo.
Shares of Fractal closed Tuesday’s trading session at ₹713.3 on the BSE.

Government of India (GoI) has announced the sale (re-issue) of two dated securities for a notified amount of ₹36,000 crore as per the following details:
Sr No Security Date of Repayment Notified Amount
(₹ Crore) GoI specific Notification Auction Date Settlement Date
1 7.06% GS 2041 Jul 27, 2041 23,000 F.No.4(1)-B(W&M)/2026 dated
November 02, 2026 November 06, 2026
(Friday) November 09, 2026
(Monday)
2 7.43% GS 2076 Jan 19, 2076 13,000
  Total   36,000      
2. GoI will have the option to retain additional subscription up to ₹2,000 crore against each security mentioned above.
3. The securities will be sold through Reserve Bank of India Mumbai Office, Fort, Mumbai – 400001. The sale will be subject to the terms and conditions spelt out in the ‘Specific Notification’ mentioned above and the General Notification F.No.4(2)–B(W&M)/2018, dated March 26, 2025.
4. The auction will be conducted using multiple price method. Both competitive and non-competitive bids for the auction should be submitted in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system) on November 06, 2026 (Friday). The non-competitive bids should be submitted between 10:30 a.m. and 11:00 a.m. and the competitive bids should be submitted between 10:30 a.m. and 11:30 a.m. The result will be announced on the same day and payment by successful bidders will have to be made on November 09, 2026 (Monday).
5. Bids for underwriting of the Additional Competitive Underwriting (ACU) portion can be submitted by ‘Primary Dealers’ from 09:00 a.m. up to 09:30 a.m. on November 06, 2026 (Friday) on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
6. The securities will be eligible for “When Issued” trading for a period commencing from November 03, 2026 – November 06, 2026.
7. Operational guidelines for Government of India dated securities auction and other details are given in the Annex.
Ajit Prasad          
Deputy General Manager
(Communications)    
Press Release: 2026-2027/1424
ANNEX
Type of Auction
1. For multiple price-based auction, successful bids will get accepted at the respective quoted yield/price for the security. For uniform price-based auction, bids will get accepted at the cut off yield/price accepted in the auction.
2. The auction will be yield based for new security and price based for securities which are re-issued.
3. In case of a Floating Rate Bonds (FRB), the auction will be spread-based for new security and price based for securities which are reissued. At the time of placing bids for new FRB, the spread should be quoted in percentage terms.
Minimum Bid Size
4. The securities will be issued for a minimum amount of ₹10,000/- (nominal) and in multiples of ₹10,000/- thereafter.
Non-Competitive Segment
5. In all the auctions, Government security up to 5% of the notified amount for sale of individual security will be allotted to the eligible individuals and institutions under the Scheme for Non-competitive Bidding Facility in the Auctions of Government Securities. Individual investors can also place bids as per the non-competitive scheme through the Retail Direct portal (https://rbiretaildirect.org.in).
6. Each bank or Primary Dealer (PD) on the basis of firm orders received from their constituents will submit a single consolidated non-competitive bid for individual security on behalf of its constituents in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
7. Allotment under the non-competitive segment will be at the weighted average rate of yield/price of the successful bids that will emerge in the auction on the basis of the competitive bidding.
Submission of Bids
8. Both competitive and non-competitive bids for the auction should be submitted in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
9. Bids in physical form will not be accepted except in extraordinary circumstances.
Business Continuity Plan (BCP)-IT failure
10. Only in the event of system failure, physical bids will be accepted. Such physical bids should be submitted to the Public Debt Office, Mumbai through (email; Phone no: 022-22603456, 022-22603457, 022-22603190) in the prescribed form which can be obtained from RBI website (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewForms.aspx) before the auction timing ends.
11. In case of technical difficulties, Core Banking Operations Team should be contacted (email; Phone no: 022-69870466, 022-69870415).
12. For other auction related difficulties, IDMD auction team can be contacted (email; Phone no: 022-22702431, 022-22705125).
Multiple Bids
13. An investor can submit more than one competitive bid in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
14. The aggregate amount of bids submitted by an investor in an auction should not exceed the notified amount of auction.
Decision Making Process
15. On the basis of bids received, the Reserve Bank will determine the minimum price/maximum yield up to which tenders for purchase of Government Security will be accepted at the auctions.
16. Bids quoted at rates lower than the minimum price/higher than the maximum yield determined by the Reserve Bank of India will be rejected.
17. Reserve Bank of India will have the full discretion to accept or reject any or all bids either wholly or partially without assigning any reason.
Issue of Securities
18. Issue of securities to the successful bidders will be by credit to Subsidiary General Ledger Account (SGL) or to Constituents’ Subsidiary General Ledger Account (CSGL), maintained with Reserve Bank of India.
Periodicity of Interest Payment
19. Interest on the Government Security will generally be paid half-yearly other than in case of securities with non-standard maturities. The exact periodicity of coupon payment is invariably mentioned in the specific notification for the issue of security.
Underwriting of the Government Securities
20. The underwriting of the Government Securities under auctions by the ‘Primary Dealers’ will be as per the “Revised Scheme of Underwriting Commitment and Liquidity Support” announced by the Reserve Bank vide circular RBI/2007-08/186 dated November 14, 2007 as amended from time to time.
Eligibility for Repurchase Transactions (Repo)
21. The securities will be eligible for Repurchase Transactions (Repo) as per the conditions mentioned in Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Repurchase Transactions (Repo)) Directions, 2025 as amended from time to time.
Eligibility for ‘When Issued’ Trading
22. The securities will be eligible for “When Issued” trading in accordance with the guidelines on ‘When Issued transactions in Central Government Securities’ issued by the Reserve Bank of India vide circular No. RBI/2018-19/25 dated July 24, 2018 as amended from time to time.
Investment by Non-Residents
23. Investments by Non-Residents are subject to the guidelines on ‘Fully Accessible Route’ for Investment by Non-residents in Government Securities and other related guidelines as issued by the Reserve Bank from time to time.

items.title: Decision Models Go Live, GIVA Nets $103 Mn & More
items.summary:
The Rise Of Decision Models
The AI race so far has largely been about models that can chat, code and reason. But a quieter shift is underway: decision models are emerging as an alternative to large models. As Indian startups and global giants enter the space, can decision models become AI’s next product layer?
What Are Decision Models? Unlike a conventional LLM, decision models do not generate prose. They return precise and structured outputs like probabilities and scores. items.content:
The Rise Of Decision Models
The AI race so far has largely been about models that can chat, code and reason. But a quieter shift is underway: decision models are emerging as an alternative to large models. As Indian startups and global giants enter the space, can decision models become AI’s next product layer?
What Are Decision Models? Unlike a conventional LLM, decision models do not generate prose. They return precise and structured outputs like probabilities and scores. Its approach is designed for bounded tasks and taking a decision – one that can be reviewed and governed later. General-purpose models can do this, but calling them at every step adds latency, cost and unpredictability.
The Growing Demand: Decision models are gaining more traction among enterprises as they are more affordable than LLMs. This is because they consume less tokens and bring strict output control, auditability and deep integration with proprietary internal data. While the momentum began with Jev, the first public model from TypeSafe AI, big giants like Cloudflare, Microsoft, AWS, OpenAI and Perplexity have also entered the space lately.
India Enters The Chat: Homegrown startups are also catering to this shift. PurpleTalk’s Sthānika lab recently launched Sieve, while ConvAI Innovations has also unveiled an open-weight model called Laya that developers can run locally on laptops or phones. Both target decisions rather than open-ended generation.
The Workflow Question: Industry insiders believe that the next commercial opportunity may lie in pairing decision models with proprietary data, feedback loops and a clearly defined customer problem. For India, the entry points include specialised models, routing infrastructure and applications built around high-volume enterprise workflows.
The challenge for local startups will be to prove measurable gains in accuracy, cost or speed, and not just benchmark scores. So, can Indian founders turn the early edge in the decision model space into a durable advantage? Let’s find out…
From The Editor’s Desk
GIVA Nets $103 Mn
The omnichannel jewellery brand has raised ₹975 Cr in a round led by Multiples Alternate Asset Management to accelerate its offline expansion, strengthen manufacturing capabilities and widen its product portfolio.
The transaction comprised a mix of primary and secondary capital. Early investors India Quotient and Sixth Sense Ventures partially exited through the deal while retaining some of their stakes. Multiples will also secure a board seat.
Founded in 2019 as an online-first silver jewellery brand, GIVA has since expanded into gold and lab-grown diamonds. It operates around 425 stores across India and plans to add 160 outlets in FY27. The brand closed FY26 with a revenue of ₹865 Cr.
Apple India’s Record Quarter
The smartphone maker claims to have reported an all-time revenue record in India in the September 2026 quarter. This came on the back of its iPhone business setting a quarterly revenue record, while Mac and services revenue reached new highs.
Globally, Apple’s revenue rose 12% YoY to $114.5 Bn during the quarter under review, while consolidated net profit increased 11.8% YoY to $30.7 Bn.
Going forward, the company expects its December 2026 quarter revenue to grow 7-10% YoY, projecting quarterly revenue at a new high.
Soket Debuts AI Model
Soket Labs, along with ZenteiQ, have launched indigenously-built AI models under the IndiaAI Mission. The models unveiled include EKA-1, developed by Soket Labs, and Dhir 2B and Dhir 5B, developed by ZenteiQ.
EKA-1 is a 26.3 Bn parameter AI model trained on nearly 7.5 Tn tokens across 22 scheduled Indian languages and English. The model claims to cater to use cases across mathematics, code, reasoning and agentic AI.
Meanwhile, ZenteiQ’s open-source models support English and 10 other Indian languages. It claims capabilities like document-grounded automation and knowledge even in low-connectivity or sensitive environments.
Nuuk Eyes ₹100 Cr
The D2C home appliances brand is raising around $10.5 Mn in a round led by Wipro Consumer Care Ventures and RPSG Capital Ventures. The potential fundraise will value the startup at about ₹500 Cr (about $53 Mn).
Founded in 2023, Nuuk sells design-focused home and kitchen appliances. Its portfolio spans vacuum cleaners, fans, heaters, garment care products, air fryers, juicers, and mixer grinders. The startup also operates an offline store in Delhi NCR.
Nuuk’s planned fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in home appliance startups. The investments point to VC interest in brands developing differentiated products, with in-house manufacturing and scalable distribution networks.
Top-Level Reshuffle At Porter
The logistics startup has named former Amazon executive Gaurav Jain as its new chief financial officer. Porter has also elevated Shubham Gupta and Mohit Rathi to the post of chief technology officer and chief marketing officer, respectively.
Jain joins Porter after over 11 years at Amazon India, where he headed finance and supply chain operations. His appointment comes nearly six months after the exit of his predecessor Anurag Jalori.
Founded in 2014, Porter offers logistics services, including B2B goods movements, packers and movers service for relocation, and intercity courier services. It claims to serve over 30 Lakh customers every month across 35 cities in India.
 
Inc42 Markets
Inc42 Startup Spotlight
How Balisto Is Building Electric Tillers For India’s Small Farmers
Farmers often need separate machines for tilling, weeding and puddling. This raises equipment costs, fuel expenses and reliance on manual labour. Balisto Agritech is building a multipurpose electric farm machine that can handle several field operations on one platform.
A Multi-Job Tiller: Founded in 2024, the startup has developed the Balisto 130 Pro, a 13 hp electric power tiller. It is designed for land preparation, weeding, inter-cultivation, puddling, rotavating, earthing up and trolley operations. It is also developing an autonomous version of its tractor using GPS, sensors and field coordinates.
The Electric Moat: The machine runs on detachable LFP batteries and three motors. It can be operated onboard or remotely, while IoT connectivity sends operating data to the cloud for monitoring and fault diagnosis. Balisto sells the single-battery version at ₹2.5 Lakh and the double-battery version at ₹3 Lakh.
Healthy Early Traction: The startup claims to have so far sold more than 30 machines, which have generated cumulative sales above ₹60 Lakh. It sells through 15 dealers in Maharashtra and also reaches farmers through rental agripreneurs. Its plant in Maharashtra can produce 60 machines a month, scalable to 150. It aims to sell over 200 machines by early-2027.
Operating in the Indian agricultural machinery market, which is projected to become a ₹2.72 Lakh Cr opportunity by 2034, can Balisto make electric farm machinery mainstream for India’s small farmers?

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
By Cynthia Alo
Agricultural experts have called for a shift from one-size-fits-all fertiliser recommendations to soil-based application, warning that farmers may be wasting money on nutrients their crops do not need.
They said differences in soil conditions and crop requirements meant that applying the same fertiliser rates across farming locations could result in poor nutrient use, higher production costs and lower productivity.
The experts spoke at the 2026 Nigeria Fertiliser Summit on Phosphorus and Food Security, organised by the Institute of Agricultural Research and Training (IAR&T), Obafemi Awolowo University and the Fertilizer Producers and Suppliers Association of Nigeria (FEPSAN), with the Fertilizer and Inputs Support Services Department of the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security as co-convener in Abuja.
Findings presented at the summit by the Regional Hub for Fertilizer and Soil Health for West Africa and the Sahel showed that phosphorus requirements for maize and rice in northern Nigeria ranged from zero to more than 60 kilogrammes of phosphorus pentoxide per hectare, depending on soil conditions.
Phosphorus is an essential plant nutrient that supports root development, crop growth and grain formation.
However, its availability to crops varies with soil properties and farming conditions.
A soil scientist and modelling expert at IAR&T, Prof. Vincent Aduramigba-Modupe, said improving agricultural productivity required more than increasing fertiliser application.
“Improving crop productivity is not only about applying fertiliser. It is about ensuring the right nutrient is applied in the right amount, at the right place, and under the right conditions,” he said.
The Minister of Agriculture and Food Security, Aliyu Abdullahi, represented by the Director of Agricultural Land and Climate Change Management Services, Oshadiya Olanipekun, emphasised soil data, testing and crop-specific fertiliser recommendations as important tools for improving farmers’ outcomes.
Also speaking, Prof. Jibrin Mohammed Jibrin, Visiting Scientist with the Regional Hub and Professor of Soil Science at Bayero University, Kano, described soil information as fundamental to food production.
Jibrin also called for better coordination among agricultural stakeholders, warning that fragmented interventions could undermine efforts to improve soil health.
“The basis of food production and food security is the soil. You need healthy soil to produce well and feed the nation with nutritious food. To do that, you need soil intelligence.
“Too many initiatives have been implemented in silos. Real progress will come when stakeholders align, collaborate and follow through on agreed actions,” he said.
Senior Agronomist at the Regional Hub, Dr. Bello Shehu, said improving phosphorus management was not about applying more fertiliser but understanding the nutrient requirements of different soils and crops.
The Vice-Chancellor of Obafemi Awolowo University, Prof. A.S. Bamire also stressed that agricultural productivity depended on responsible nutrient management, research, innovation and stronger partnerships.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
By Cynthia Alo
Lagos State Government is planning to establish between 50 and 100 small food-processing plants around its proposed food systems and logistics hub as part of efforts to promote local processing, add value to agricultural produce and strengthen the state’s food supply chain.
Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu disclosed this at the Executive Business Breakfast organised by the Nigerian-British Chamber of Commerce, where he outlined the state’s plans to develop an integrated system for food storage, processing and distribution.
He said the proposed processing plants would be located around the logistics hub and supplied with agricultural produce brought in from different parts of the country.
According to him, the arrangement is designed to create opportunities for value addition by ensuring that food commodities are not only stored and distributed but also processed within the state.
He stated: “The second part of that logistics hub is that it’s also going to feed about 50 to 100 small food processing plants.”
He added that the government had made provision for processing facilities around the hub as part of its master plan.
“We’ve created about 1,000 hectares all around that business, so we’re going to have layouts of small processing mills around it that can often do a lot of value addition,” he said.
The proposed hub is expected to receive food from different parts of Nigeria, with facilities for cold and dry storage, silos and a large trailer park to support the movement of commodities.
Sanwo-Olu said the facility was almost completed, describing it as one of the largest food systems and logistics hubs in Sub-Saharan Africa.

items.title: Osun lawyers urge Adeleke to avert collapse of court buildings
items.summary:
By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo
Lawyers in Osun State have raised the alarm over the deteriorating condition of court buildings across the state, urging Governor Ademola Adeleke to urgently intervene to prevent further decline in the administration of justice.
The lawyers, under the aegis of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA), representing the five branches in Osogbo, Ikirun, Iwo, Ile-Ife and Ilesa, said dilapidated buildings and inadequate facilities were disrupting court proceedings and undermining justice delivery.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo
Lawyers in Osun State have raised the alarm over the deteriorating condition of court buildings across the state, urging Governor Ademola Adeleke to urgently intervene to prevent further decline in the administration of justice.
The lawyers, under the aegis of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA), representing the five branches in Osogbo, Ikirun, Iwo, Ile-Ife and Ilesa, said dilapidated buildings and inadequate facilities were disrupting court proceedings and undermining justice delivery.
In a letter to the governor dated October 29, 2026, and received at the Governor’s Office on November 2, the association called for the comprehensive rehabilitation, renovation and modernisation of court buildings and facilities across the state.
The letter was signed by the chairmen of the five branches: Maruf Adediran (Osogbo), Abdulkareem Azeez (Ikirun), Emmanuel Gbadegesin (Iwo), Olawoye Festus (Ile-Ife) and Adefunso Esan (Ilesa).
According to the lawyers, several court buildings have deteriorated to the extent that they threaten the dignity of the judicial institution and expose judicial officers, legal practitioners, litigants and witnesses to avoidable hardship.
They identified leaking roofs, damaged ceilings, inadequate seating arrangements and other infrastructural deficiencies as major concerns.
The association said rainwater entering some courtrooms had forced proceedings to be interrupted or suspended, resulting in unnecessary adjournments and delays.
“It is unacceptable that court proceedings in a state governed by the rule of law should be dictated by the weather because the buildings in which justice is administered cannot adequately withstand rainfall,” the lawyers stated.
They said the problem extended beyond courtrooms to the office of the Chief Judge and the chambers of other judicial officers, raising concerns about the safety of court records, official documents, furniture and electronic equipment exposed to water leakage.
The association urged the state government to conduct a comprehensive audit of facilities across the High Court, Customary Court of Appeal, Magistrates’ Courts and District Customary Courts.
It said the exercise should cover affected locations, including Osogbo, Ikirun, Ilesa, Ile-Ife, Iwo and Ede.
Beyond structural repairs, the lawyers called for modern judicial equipment, including electronic case management systems, digital recording devices and computers, as well as adequate funding for maintenance and training of judicial and registry personnel.
They also urged the government to prioritise emergency repairs to buildings posing safety risks and involve the judiciary and NBA in identifying needs, setting project priorities and monitoring improvements, while respecting judicial independence.
“Our appeal is not merely about the physical appearance of court buildings; it concerns the ability of a critical institution of government to discharge its constitutional responsibilities effectively and the ability of the people of Osun State to access justice without avoidable hardship,” the letter stated.
The lawyers added that judicial officers should not be left to administer justice in buildings with leaking roofs, inadequate courtroom facilities or offices that expose personnel and court records to preventable risks.
They also stressed the need to equip courts with modern facilities and technology to improve efficiency and strengthen public confidence in the justice system, adding that the welfare of judicial officers was important to effective justice delivery.

items.content:
…PDP candidate’s supporters pledge grassroots mobilisation for ‘Ogun for Ogun’ agenda
By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta
Indigenes of Ogun State have reaffirmed their support for the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate, Oladipupo Adebutu, and his running mate, Yemi Sowunmi-Kolapo, pledging grassroots mobilisation for their ambition ahead of the 2027 governorship election.
The pledge was made during ward-to-ward engagements by the candidates across local government areas of the state, where residents expressed concerns about poor infrastructure, unemployment, inadequate agricultural support and the need for improved access to modern farming equipment.
The campaign tour is also aimed at presenting the candidates’ seven-point development agenda, tagged ITURA DE, to the electorate.
At the ward meetings, community leaders, market women, farmers and youths turned out to receive the candidates and discuss their expectations from the next administration.
Several stakeholders pledged support for the ‘Ogun for Ogun’ initiative, arguing that the state’s leadership should reflect the interests, heritage and aspirations of its indigenes.
At Alagada Ward in Obafemi Owode Local Government Area, a market leader, Mrs Folasade Ogunye, said her support for the movement was informed by the belief that indigenous leadership would better understand the challenges confronting grassroots communities.
She lamented the poor condition of roads leading to markets and the limited employment opportunities available to young people, pledging to mobilise women for door-to-door campaigns.
“We, the women of Obafemi Owode, have suffered neglect. Our roads to the markets are bad, and our children need jobs. We want someone who grew up here, who knows our language and understands our struggles,” she said.
At Alapakooni community, also in Obafemi Owode, some residents said to be former members of the All Progressives Congress (APC) publicly renounced their membership of the party.
The defectors reportedly set bunches of APC brooms ablaze to symbolise their departure, citing dissatisfaction with the party’s political leadership and questions surrounding the identity of its governorship candidate.
A community youth coordinator, Tunde Akinola, said their decision to align with Adebutu was motivated by their desire for leadership they could identify with and hold accountable.
He said the group wanted to support a candidate who understood the state’s challenges and could deliver on his promises.
Similarly, a community stakeholder and farmer at Onidunu Ward, Deji Bamidele, said farmers in the area wanted a government that would prioritise agricultural development through mechanisation and improved access to farming inputs.
He said a farmers’ cooperative with more than 300 members had pledged support for the ‘Ogun for Ogun’ initiative, following Adebutu’s presentation of his agricultural plans under the ITURA DE agenda.
At Owode Ward 3, a retired teacher, Alhaja Sariyu Bankole, described the movement as an opportunity to preserve the state’s political heritage.
She said residents should participate actively in the election to ensure that their voices counted in determining the state’s future.
In Sagamu Local Government Area, a youth leader, Comrade Bayo Oduwole, pledged to mobilise young people through voter education and door-to-door campaigns.
Speaking at Ward 10, Oduwole said the ‘Ogun for Ogun’ campaign should be driven by competence, accountability and an understanding of the state’s needs.
Responding to the expressions of support, Adebutu described the ward-to-ward engagements as an opportunity to understand the needs of communities and build a development agenda around them.
He said the ITURA DE agenda was designed to address the state’s socio-economic challenges, particularly in infrastructure, agriculture, employment generation and improved living standards.
“This tour has shown me that our people are yearning for homegrown leadership that understands their challenges and is prepared to address them.
“The ITURA DE agenda is not just a slogan; it is a social contract to restore dignity, fix our roads, empower our farmers, create jobs for our youths and return Ogun State to its rightful place,” Adebutu said.
He added that the campaign was not only about seeking votes but also about listening to residents and understanding their concerns.
His running mate, Kolapo, assured residents that a PDP administration would prioritise inclusive governance and ensure that grassroots communities were represented in policy decisions.
She highlighted the importance of women, children, education and primary healthcare in the proposed administration’s development plans.
Kolapo said the reception across the wards reflected residents’ desire for a government that would listen to them and address their needs.
The PDP candidates said their grassroots engagements would continue across the state as they seek to consolidate support and present their policy proposals ahead of the 2027 governorship election.
The post Ogun indigenes reaffirm support for Adebutu ahead of 2027 appeared first on Vanguard News.

“Enough is enough. For 20 years, we have had representation without results, or projects, and leadership without impact. It is time to change that narrative.

He called on members of the CWO to mobilise voters in support of his candidacy, describing women as an important grassroots political constituency capable of influencing electoral outcomes.
Ikonne also commended the organisation for its contributions to family life, the growth of the Catholic faith and community development.
In separate remarks, the CWO President in Aba Diocese, Lady Nneoma Florita Ngozi Anwuacha, and some parish presidents commended the candidate for what they described as his support for the diocese.
