items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
“The co-existence of several nations under the same State is a test, as well as the best security, of its freedom.” — Lord Acton
Nigeria’s convoluted debate on restructuring has endured for decades because it supposedly speaks to questions of power, identity, representation, resource distribution, security, federalism and belonging. Precisely because the debate has been driven largely by sectional advocates and habitual agitators, however, it has also become increasingly burdened and polarised by a tendency towards reductionism, or the habit of explaining the country’s many and complex difficulties through a single grievance, a single historical narrative, a single ethnic experience or a single constitutional remedy. It is here that the discourse on the so-called “national question” becomes difficult, protracted and, at times, almost futile. Nigeria undoubtedly has structural problems, just as other countries do. It also has governance challenges, adversarial politics, elite misconduct, civic indiscipline, institutional weakness, manufactured discontents and problems arising from deep historical memories. To collapse all these into one argument that Nigeria will work better only if one particular restructuring formula is adopted may be emotionally satisfying, but it is intellectually shallow and politically reactionary.
The central question, therefore, is no longer simply whether Nigeria should restructure. It is whether restructuring is being presented as a panacea, pursued as a genuine national project, or increasingly deployed as an instrument of demagoguery, a mockery of democracy and a vocabulary through which competing groups selfishly articulate accumulated grievances. That distinction is essential if an honest national discourse is to be undertaken. A federation is, by its nature, an arrangement for managing diversity. It seeks to reconcile unity with autonomy, common citizenship with regional identity, and national authority with sub-national self-government. Nigeria’s problem is not that diversity exists; that is an enduring fact. The more difficult question is whether the state has developed institutions capable of managing that diversity fairly, equitably, peacefully and productively.
Lord Acton’s dictum is instructive in this regard. The coexistence of several nations within one state is not necessarily evidence of political failure. It is, rather, a test of liberty and constitutional maturity. The challenge is whether institutions can make diversity compatible with freedom, equality and political order.
When those institutions are compromised and rendered incapable of delivering satisfactory governance, every disagreement acquires an ethnic or sectional interpretation. Administrative failures become evidence of domination. Economic inequalities are interpreted as deliberate marginalisation. Political defeat is transformed into collective humiliation. Historical assumptions become territorial claims. Every federal appointment, budgetary allocation, state boundary or constitutional provision is then subjected to ethnic or regional arithmetic. It is at this point that restructuring ceases to be merely a constitutional discussion and becomes part of the broader politics of grievance. There is nothing illegitimate about nursing a grievance or articulating it where it genuinely exists. Nations must allow legitimate grievances to be expressed freely and intelligently. Indeed, suppressing them may constitute a greater threat to national stability than openly debating them. But grievance must ultimately be converted into a constitutional proposition, not transformed into fuel for agitation and disunity. It must answer practical questions. What precisely is wrong with the country? What institution should be rearranged or changed? By what process? To whose benefit? At whose cost? And how will the rights of others be safeguarded?
Without this discipline, restructuring becomes an endlessly expanding concept into which every disappointment may be inserted. For some Nigerians, restructuring means a return to the regional arrangement of the First Republic. For others, it means fiscal federalism and greater resource control. Some understand it as devolution of powers from the Federal Government to the states. Others advocate state police, constitutional recognition of traditional institutions or the creation of additional states. Still others propose the consolidation of the present 36 states into larger regions. At the furthest end of the argument are those for whom restructuring is essentially a transitional language for confederation, self-determination or eventual separation. All these positions are described by the same word; however, they do not necessarily lead to the same destination. That is why the restructuring debate must first be rescued from ambiguity, inconsistency, shallowness and opportunism. Recent arguments surrounding the idea of autonomous regions illustrate the difficulty. One school of thought sees historical regions as natural foundations upon which a new federation may be reconstructed. Another insists that communities cannot simply be reassigned to reconstructed regions on the basis of historical maps, ethnic narratives or claims advanced on their behalf. Contemporary consent, according to this argument, must be central.
This raises one of the most profound questions in any future restructuring of Nigeria: who actually owns territory? Is territory inherited by historical regions? Does it belong to so-called ethnic nations? Is it defined by existing state boundaries? Or does ownership and political legitimacy ultimately rest with the communities presently inhabiting the territory? If so, when did such communities come into possession, and through what means — migration, conquest, displacement, allocation or settlement?
History unquestionably matters. No serious constitutional settlement can disregard it. Present identities, boundaries, conflicts and solidarities are themselves products of history. But history cannot be invoked selectively. Every part of Nigeria possesses multiple historical layers, shaped by the expansion and contraction of kingdoms, the movement of peoples, the emergence of emirates and chiefdoms, colonial boundaries, the rearrangement of older political communities, and the creation, merger and division of provinces.
So too did the establishment of regions, later abolished and succeeded by states in exercises beginning in 1967 and continuing through 1996, alter these historical arrangements. There is therefore no single pristine map to which Nigeria can simply be returned. This is precisely where reductionism becomes dangerous. Once history is reduced to one preferred narrative or period — whether 1914, 1960, 1963 or some earlier moment — that chosen point becomes a political entitlement. One group may point to the map of 1963, while another invokes the nineteenth century, pre-colonial kingdoms, colonial provinces or present administrative boundaries. A nation of more than two hundred million people, composed of hundreds of ethnic groups and subgroups, cannot build its constitutional future by allowing competing historical narratives and imaginary maps to become instruments of possession. Any restructuring that alters territorial relationships must therefore contain a strong element of consent. Communities should not simply be transferred from one political arrangement to another as though they were administrative property. But consent itself requires careful definition and a rational legal basis. 
If every village, ward, town, district or local government were independently entitled to choose its preferred region, the federation could become permanently fluid and unstable.
Territorial politics might descend into an endless series of claims, referenda and counterclaims. Economic viability, geographical contiguity and administrative coherence would become increasingly difficult to sustain. The principle of consent must therefore operate within an agreed national constitutional framework. It cannot mean an unlimited right of territorial fragmentation elasticity.
This is the essential balance Nigeria must find: historical identity without historical domination; community choice without permanent atomisation; and regional autonomy without national disintegration. The danger of the current discourse, driven increasingly by ethnic nationalism, is that too many actors approach restructuring from the standpoint of what their own group has lost or stands to gain rather than from the standpoint of what constitutional order all Nigerians can live under.
The language is revealing. One hears of stolen territories, denied access, lost political influence, historical ownership, strangers, domination, marginalisation and restitution. These are the vocabularies of discontent, grievance and, occasionally, unreason. They may describe apparently genuine experiences, but they cannot, by themselves, constitute a national federal constitution.
A constitution is necessarily a compromise and an accommodation among competing claims. The Kanuri, Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Fulani, Tiv, Ijaw, Ibibio, Nupe, Gbagyi, Jukun, Edo, Igala, Birom, Angas, Egbira, Idoma, Urhobo, Marghi, Itsekiri and Nigeria’s numerous other communities all possess historical narratives. None can reasonably expect its own narrative to become the overriding and exclusive organising principle of the federation.
The purpose of restructuring should therefore not be to transform historical recollections into territorial entitlement or grievance into constitutional ownership. History should inform the debate, certainly, but it should not imprison it. Any sustainable arrangement must recognise contemporary populations, existing communities, economic viability, constitutional order and, above all, the legitimacy of consent.
The real test is whether Nigerians are discussing restructuring in order to build a more workable and durable federation, or whether they are merely seeking a new constitutional vocabulary through which old disputes can be pursued. That is where the distinction between genuine and rational restructuring, on the one hand, and irrational grievance and reductionism, on the other, begins.
The post Reductionism and the national question: restructuring or grievance? (I), by Usman Sarki appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
The purpose of this series is to explain why the young people of Igbo extraction now reject the offer to join the Nigerian Army. In the first part, we saw how the Army that Igbo senior officers once led with distinction became the instrument for their subjugation, both during and long after the Biafra War, despite promises to the contrary. In the second part, we also saw how the military, as a political force, was used to prevent the Igbo resumption of their pride of place, not only in the political power arena but also in virtually every sector of Nigeria’s affairs. Each time the Igbo are poised to lead the country, the Establishment uses the Nigerian Army to stop them in preference for less-fancied options, which is why the country is dying, not growing. The straw that finally broke the camel’s back was the return of Muhammadu Buhari in 2015 as an elected president. Ndi Igbo had wholeheartedly thrown their support behind Dr Goodluck Jonathan in the 2011 presidential election. Jonathan obtained victory despite withering opposition from the North and South West, and he identified Ndi Igbo as the great, avuncular force behind his victory. He appointed Igbo sons and daughters into commanding positions in his government, giving them posts that had always been denied them by the military and its civilian agents. These included Secretary to the Government of the Federation. Jonathan even mandated Ndi Igbo to nominate a candidate of their choice.
He also brought back Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala to serve as Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister for the Economy. She commanded the power of a virtual Prime Minister and helped build the Nigerian economy to emerge as the largest in Africa in 2014 after a strategic rebasing, with a GDP value of $509.9bn. By contrast, our economy has currently slid to the third position, behind South Africa and Egypt, with a GDP value of $386.67bn, according to many authoritative sources, including Business Insider Africa. It was also during that era that Nigeria stood on the threshold of defeating Boko Haram, with the Nigerian Army under the supreme command of Igbo-born Chief of Army Staff, Lt-Gen Azubuike Ihejirika. The North and South West plotted the defeat of Jonathan in his re-election bid in 2015. Ndi Igbo felt the pain of Jonathan’s loss as if he were their ethnic kinsman. They were also made to pay for their support of him by the new All Progressives Congress (APC), whose candidate, Muhammadu Buhari, emerged victorious. Glowing in his victory, Buhari went to America, apparently to thank President Barack Obama for his support after three previous failures. At the US Institute of Peace on 25th July 2015 in Washington, DC, Buhari uttered a grossly irresponsible undertaking: that he would give his supporters 97 per cent and only 5 per cent to those who did not support him. To show he meant it, he loaded his cabinet’s juiciest positions and the military’s high commands with mostly Northern Muslims, with generous concessions to his South West partners.
He thus drove the Igbo nation, especially the youth, into the waiting hands of the Mazi Nnamdi Kanu-led Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB). Before Buhari’s unpatriotic utterance, the incendiary separatist broadcasts of Mazi Kanu, who had established Radio Biafra in London back in 2009, were generally ignored by most Igbo audiences, including this writer. He came strongly into the picture when he capitalised on the move for Brexit referendums to enable Britain to leave the European Union. Kanu argued that Nigeria’s amalgamation had expired in 2014, and that referendums should be staged to enable its indigenous people decide democratically and peacefully whether to stay on in Nigeria. He was very convinced that the people of the East, especially Ndi Igbo, would overwhelmingly vote for Biafra’s actualisation.
After Buhari’s hate declaration and subsequent hate actions to sideline Igbo people, Kanu’s messages started sounding like music, and many flocked to him. The Biafra agitation drew heavy traction, as youths joined the Biafra independence protests, leading to the proscription of IPOB and Kanu’s arrest and trial. Buhari used the Army, Police and security agencies to kill, harass, intimidate, arrest, detain and dehumanise Igbo youth and devastate communities suspected to be IPOB bases, especially in Abia, Imo and Anambra States. Worst of all, his regime funded armed Fulani herdsmen to set up ruga in no fewer than 350 forest bases in the South East alone. This was a strategic part of his evil Islamisation and Fulanisation agenda, with the military and security forces used to protect them. This led Kanu, who had escaped into exile, to establish the Eastern Security Network (ESN), specifically to protect Igboland from Fulani expansionism.
Till today, under President Bola Tinubu’s watch, IPOB and ESN remain proscribed, Kanu is in jail in Sokoto, and the Nigerian Army is sinisterly deployed in the South East. The Monday Sit-At-Home is passive resistance to protest Kanu’s unjust imprisonment and the siege of Igboland by the Nigerian Army. Igbo youth see the Nigerian Army as an oppressive, occupying force deployed to grease the wheel for armed Fulani conquest of their land. Secondly, the federal government’s suspicious handling of the war against terrorism (Boko Haram, bandits, ISWAP, Fulani herdsmen militias) and unconcerned attitude to Christian genocides aren’t helpful. Also, the unconfirmed general perception that “repented” Boko Haram terrorists are absorbed into the forces and sent to the East to kill people remains rife. The use of military and police checkpoints to harass and extort people in the South East is at a level not found anywhere else in the country.
Joining the military is the duty of all patriotic youths. But this is impossible when the armed forces are seen as oppressors; weapons fashioned against a particular ethnic group for no reason other than blind hatred and extreme bigotry.
CONCLUDED.

As he walked across the stage to address the gathering, the young MC joked on Monday morning that Prof. Joash Amupitan is one man nobody would really want to envy in Nigeria today. This was beyond a joke, which the INEC Chairman soaked in with some equanimity. In less than three months, his agency, which has struggled with a bout of image concerns, would be organizing some major elections which may give him a redeeming opportunity to change the calculus, to convince Nigerians that he can write a good story from a previously bad plot. It was the reason Amupitan was at the Continental Hotel in Abuja. Offered a platform at the National Summit on Electoral Information Integrity, jointly organized by the International Press Centre (IPC), the Centre for Media and Society (CEMESO) and DAI, with support from the European Union, he delivered a deeply troubling paper which could be summarized as follows: the fear of artificial intelligence (AI) is the beginning of good elections. “Today, elections can be undermined long before the first ballot is cast. The threat is no longer limited to physical interference (such as violent ballot snatching) at the polling unit; it takes shape within digital networks through synthetic media, automated misinformation/disinformation, deepfake fabrications, digital micro-targeting, and Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI). The troubling reality is that many democracies are not really prepared for these,” Amupitan said.
Addressing the Summit theme, Beyond the Ballot: AI, FIMI, and the Integrity of Nigeria’s 2027 Elections, Amupitan gave no room for fear but instead displayed a commanding grasp of the electoral ecosystem to rally stakeholders to the realization that the democratization of AI has unleashed more challenges for electoral managers to handle. We can help Amupitan tell his story from there. There was already AI in February 2023. But it was a computer glitch from the backend of the INEC setup that blemished the integrity of a national election which had gone well until that unfortunate intrusion. The exponential growth in AI technology, which even the promoters are beginning to be afraid of as they fear it can imperil life and other human activities, is creating a cluster of concerns globally, with Amupitan now having to call on the concerted efforts of stakeholders to rescue the 2027 elections from a technology which carries so much good and evil. Unfortunately for all of us, there are so many tech mavericks, the troubled cyber denizens who will always want to take advantage of the negative side of technology to create and extend damage just to satisfy their satanic instincts. This explains why the INEC boss alerted that the rapid democratisation of generative AI models has dramatically lowered the barrier to entry for malicious minds. 
So, there is so much to watch out for. This is the more reason Amupitan warned that as we prepare for the 2027 elections, the undeniable truth that we must confront is that public awareness alone is no longer an adequate defence against synthetic content and digital manipulation. Informing citizens that deepfakes exist or urging caution when consuming online news is useful, but it is insufficient against well-coordinated, highly funded, and hyper-targeted information operations designed to erode public trust in election administration. “What Nigeria urgently requires,” he suggested, “is a trusted, coordinated, and rights-respecting operational ecosystem – an institutional structure through which public authorities, security bodies, independent fact-checkers, media networks and platform operators can collectively anticipate emerging threats, verify evidence, escalate incidents without delay, communicate authoritatively, and institutionalize post-event lessons.”
Amupitan’s fears and expectations are not misplaced. He gave this illustration. In 2023, just two days before Slovakia went to the polls – during a mandatory 48-hour electoral blackout period when political parties and traditional news outlets were legally restricted from campaigning or broadcasting political responses – an AI audio recording went viral on local media. The cloned audio purported to capture a high-ranking political party leader actively discussing a scheme to buy votes and manipulate election results. It was a deliberate act, perfectly timed to coincide with the blackout period when campaigning was statutorily prohibited. Unfortunately, the sheer speed of digital dissemination, combined with the restricted response window, paralyzed institutional verification efforts. Amupitan observed that there are some vulnerable moments that some devious people would want to exploit, but, without throwing up his hands in the air in wanton helplessness, he declared very boldly that “our commitment to 2027 is rooted in technological resilience and transparency. To this end, Voter Education is moving beyond ‘how to vote’ to ‘how to verify,’ ensuring citizens can distinguish official INEC communication from AI-generated deepfakes. Furthermore, the electoral agency is also strengthening its digital infrastructure to withstand Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI), while establishing robust internal mechanisms to debunk viral misinformation within minutes of its emergence.” He informed that INEC was partnering with global social media platforms such as TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube, Facebook Messenger, Telegram and X (formerly Twitter). An MOU has already been signed with TikTok, he informed.
Amupitan is giving the assurance of INEC’s capacity to withstand everything thrown at it by perennially enraged cyber geeks. He appealed, however, that “as we construct this information defence system, we must proceed with strict institutional restraint. The legitimate threat of AI manipulation must never become a pretext for state overreach, digital censorship, or the suppression of political dissent.” It is gladdening that IPC, CEMESO and DAI have provided a platform to thrust the 2027 elections and AI onto the front burner, where they will now attract further interrogations from concerned citizens. While AI may have the good and the bad in equal measure, I want to observe that localizing the problems makes our situation significantly different. 
My deduction comes from the fact that Nigeria has a large digital army of very unhappy people, homogenized only by their misery and bitterness against a country that has placed them at the margins. This army, which comes under several names, is readily available to any willing buyer who is ready to pay a little cash. Apart from their desire to make money and take as much of it as possible from the politicians who have confined them to undeserved servitude, there is also the revenge instinct to pay the nation back for letting them down. They don’t need condemnation. The INEC boss is right. We all need to build trust and be educated about the electoral process and specifically know the roles ascribed to each of us as collective stakeholders in the destiny of our nation. The digital army must be made to feel a part of this nation and be assigned roles they can happily execute. You can’t live in a house and burn it over yourself. Putting AI to rogue use during the elections could be worse than burning a house over yourself. The effects could be too extensive to contemplate. Irrespective of how we feel, Nigeria demands from us that we make her a better nation, more able to provide good living conditions for the generations on their way here.
The post AI as election bogey, by Okoh Aihe appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
If one considers the unlikely calculus through which he emerged as the governor of Imo State in 2020, Chief Hope Uzodinma is one of the oddities of Nigeria’s adventure in democracy. Between him and Owelle Rochas Okorocha, with whom he has locked horns in a struggle over the senatorial ticket of Imo West, there is hardly anything to choose. He had been elected a senator and was in the middle of his second term representing Imo West at the National Assembly when he decided to throw his hat into the Imo governorship race in 2019. Owelle Rochas, whose jankara ideology of iberiberism signposts his fascination with statues and other monuments of dubious aesthetic value, at this time called the shots of Imo State politics. It was a peculiar political brand of domestic governance in which his family members had a firm grip on some of the prime aspects of Imo’s political estate. From his wife to his daughter, his daughter to his son-in-law, etc., all had a role to play.
Some of his antics in this regard prefigured the disdain with which he was held by people in the state and beyond. They were partly the reason some of his detractors misnamed him Okorohausa, a name that came from his long association with the north of the country, where he attained adulthood and made the economic fortune that he obviously leveraged into political mileage. It was in this political landscape, in which Okorocha was the godfather, that Hope Uzodinma emerged to carve a slice for himself as a senator. His vision did not at this time extend beyond part of the western corner of the much vaster space over which Chief Sam Mbakwe held court as the first executive governor between 1979 and 1983. His senatorial spell was halfway before ambition took the better part of him and he decided to be governor. With this, he appeared to have mistaken his political might and ended up biting off more than he could chew. For, in the election that was held in January of 2020, he was the clear underdog.
A former Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Emeka Ihedioha of the Peoples Democratic Party, was one of the two frontrunners. The other was Uche Nwosu, Rochas Okorocha’s favoured son-in-law. He was of Okorocha’s self-created Action Alliance. Emeka Ihedioha carried the day in the duel that had two other contestants, namely, Ifeanyi Ararume and, of course, Hope Uzodinma. They were respectively of APGA and the APC. Okorocha’s son-in-law emerged as the first runner-up, followed by Ararume and then Uzodinma, who took the rear position. Emeka Ihedioha was returned as the winner of the election and sworn in as governor, and the others headed to the election tribunal and later the Court of Appeal. But in a legal showdown that played out at the Supreme Court, Hope Uzodinma triumphed. It was a unanimous decision that was read by the current Chief Justice of the Federation, Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun. It was Uzodinma’s second victory through the courts. He became a senator through a Supreme Court decision. He probably knows the courts better than others. Which is why he may be headed in that direction again in his tango with Okorocha. He tripped last week in the Federal High Court of Justice Obiora Egwuatu.
Uzodinma’s main argument in the courts for his governorship contest rested on the simple claim that votes in 388 polling units had been excluded from his tally, which, if returned, would give him victory. The Supreme Court agreed. That was how, in a demonstration that lent political valence to a biblical declaration, the last, actually the fourth in this case, became first and the first became last. Emeka Ihedioha had to go home. The courts have given what the people did not give. It was a freak of a judicial pronouncement with a bizarre outcome that came straight out of the book of impossibilities. It normalised the abnormal. Under normal circumstances, Hope Uzodinma could not have had a cat in hell’s chance of emerging victorious. Nor was his joy diminished by the circumstances of his emergence. He walked into the office of the governor with every confidence he could muster, even as Imolites see him not as their choice but as an imposition of the courts. But dat one concern dem, concern dem papa, not Hope Uzodinma. A man with such a political background would not be fazed by anything. Not in life, much less in politics.
He would see himself as the divine beneficiary of what Nigerian Pentecostals call unmerited favour. If rules and laws could be divinely broken (which is what church people pray for) in order to make him governor, what would he consider sacrosanct? What could be held beyond the grasping fingers of his vaulting ambition? Is it any wonder that, after six and a half years of being in the saddle as governor and with nearly two years of his eight years left, Uzodinma has cleaned up his playbook to do gidigbo with Rochas Okorocha over a senatorial ticket? Without going into the details of the fight, which are as dirty as they could be and make both men look criminally liable notwithstanding their finger-pointing, it is reasonable to ask in which world this kind of thing happens? Just a year into his second term, Uzodinma decided to trade his senatorial ticket for that of a governor, and now, in his second term as governor, he thought it was time to jump ship and go for the same senatorial ticket he had voluntarily relinquished. He sure would have his cake and eat it.
Which section of our electoral law permits this brigand kpalongo? Assuming no section of the law explicitly forbids it, which political convention condones it? If a civil servant cannot hold two government-paid jobs simultaneously, how does an elected governor do that? Of course, Uzodinma has his eyes on something bigger than being governor, which is the rumoured seat of the President of the Senate that he hopes would go to the South-East in a post-2027 Bola Tinubu administration. But under what label or mechanism of governance would this happen while he is still a governor? And then, he chose to abuse his position as Chair of the Progressive Governors Forum, mobilising self-aggrandising governors like himself who claim to be working for the president’s re-election. But their goal was to thwart Nyesom Wike’s so-called Rainbow Coalition. Uzodinma is yet to demonstrate his might as a political heavyweight in an APC that is struggling to gain a foothold in a South-East awash with the separatist sentiments of an outlaw group. Which raises the question: what does Governor Hope Uzodinma bring to politics, to the APC table, beyond raw ambition?
The post What is the strange logic behind Hope Uzodinma’s political actions? By Rotimi Fasan appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
By DAVID OWENS
There was a common thread running through several of Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu’s engagements in the last week of October: the future of Lagos and the resources required to build it.
It was not immediately obvious from the variety of events he attended. Indeed, anyone following the governor’s activities from Monday, October 26, to Saturday, October 31, might have been struck first by their diversity. There was an economic summit, a women’s conference, an international business gathering, meetings with development partners, a political manifesto unveiling, a medical centenary, an education award ceremony, a bankers’ investiture and a fashion show. Yet, beneath the differences in setting and audience, several of these engagements raised essentially the same questions. How does Lagos attract investment? How does it translate infrastructure development into economic opportunity? How can public policy improve the conditions under which businesses and individuals operate? And how can a government prepare its institutions for the demands of a rapidly expanding metropolis?
These were among the questions that gave coherence to an otherwise unusually crowded week.
At the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit in Abuja on Monday, Sanwo-Olu approached Nigeria’s economic challenges from the standpoint of regional integration and trade. His contribution centred on the opportunities offered by the African Continental Free Trade Area, the importance of functioning trade corridors and the infrastructure necessary to facilitate commerce. For Lagos, these were not abstract economic propositions. A state with major ports, extensive commercial activity and growing industrial corridors has a direct interest in the efficiency of national transport infrastructure and cross-border trade. Sanwo-Olu argued that better roads, railways, electricity, broadband connectivity and logistics systems were essential to improving competitiveness. The significance of that position becomes clearer when considered alongside his activities two days later. At the Nigerian-British Chamber of Commerce executive business breakfast in Lekki on Wednesday, the governor returned to the subject of investment, this time with the future of Lagos itself as the centrepiece.
The gathering, themed The Future of Lagos: Business, Investment and Global Competitiveness, brought him into direct conversation with investors and private-sector operators. He spoke about the state’s long-term development plan, the expansion of rail transportation through the Blue and Red Lines, infrastructure improvements and the movement of certain government services onto digital platforms. These investments, he argued, formed part of the foundation for a more competitive economy. But the discussion also illustrated the distance between ambition and implementation.
Investors are concerned not only with major infrastructure projects but also with administrative efficiency, operating costs, land processes and the reliability of public services. For a state seeking to sustain its commercial position, those everyday concerns are as important as headline investment figures. The day’s subsequent engagements extended the conversation beyond domestic business interests.
At Lagos House, Marina, Sanwo-Olu met Christophe Lecourtier, Chief Executive Officer of the French Development Agency, to discuss continuing cooperation on transportation development. Among the projects under consideration was OMI-EKO, designed to improve water transportation and introduce modern electric ferries into the state’s transport network. The implications extend beyond the transportation sector. A city where workers and goods move more predictably has an economic advantage over one repeatedly constrained by congestion. The governor also received senior executives of international shipping company CMA CGM, whose operations are linked to the Lekki Deep Sea Port. He encouraged the company to deepen its investment and place greater emphasis on developing Nigerian talent. Such discussions are important because large infrastructure investments are not automatically synonymous with broad economic participation. Their wider benefits depend partly on employment, local capacity, supplier networks and the ability of smaller businesses to participate.
By Wednesday, the economic conversation begun in Abuja had moved through international trade, transportation, maritime investment and the practical concerns of local businesses. It would return on Saturday. At the Fellowship Investiture of the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria, Sanwo-Olu challenged financial institutions to put their enhanced capital positions to productive use. Against the background of banking recapitalisation, he argued that stronger financial institutions should translate into greater support for manufacturing, agriculture, industrial projects and small businesses. The governor identified affordable long-term credit as a major requirement for businesses seeking to acquire equipment, expand production or compete in wider markets.
The argument was particularly relevant to Lagos, where a substantial number of small and medium-sized enterprises coexist with large corporations and industrial operations. Investment promotion, after all, is incomplete without financing.
One can attract multinational companies and expand industrial infrastructure, but the wider economy also requires mechanisms through which local enterprises can obtain capital and participate in emerging opportunities. This was the point at which Sanwo-Olu’s conversations with economists, foreign investors and bankers began to look like different chapters of the same economic discussion.
The week also contained an important social policy component. On Tuesday, the governor launched the Lagos Private Health Plans and announced the enforcement timetable for mandatory health insurance. The policy is designed to improve access to medical care and reduce the burden of sudden healthcare expenses on households. With 21 Health Maintenance Organisations participating and the Health Equity Fund increased to N3 billion, the programme represented an attempt to expand the financial protection available to residents. Its success will depend on implementation, affordability, compliance and the quality of healthcare services delivered.
But its inclusion in the week’s events was significant: economic development concerns not only investment and infrastructure but also the ability of households to cope with illness without falling into financial difficulty. 
Another social dimension emerged at the 26th National Women’s Conference of COWLSO. The conference examined women’s economic participation, entrepreneurship, leadership and access to opportunities. It was also the setting for a more personal moment when Sanwo-Olu presented flowers to his wife, Dr Ibijoke Sanwo-Olu, before sharing a public kiss with her.
During the conference celebrations, a retiring teacher, Francisca Olaitan Lawal, won a three-bedroom apartment, while Lagos Ferry Services employee Mary Odofin received an SUV. The individual rewards were among the lighter aspects of a week otherwise dominated by discussions of larger institutions and investment. Friday brought the political and social dimensions of Lagos’ future into sharper focus. At the unveiling of Deputy Governor Kadri Obafemi Hamzat’s governorship manifesto, Sanwo-Olu spoke about continuity in government and the importance of experience accumulated through previous administrations. Hamzat’s proposals, grouped under The Lagos Promise, included commitments on transportation, healthcare, housing and employment. The event was political, but the subjects under discussion were closely related to those the governor had addressed throughout the week.
Later that Friday, Sanwo-Olu joined the Medical Guild’s centenary celebration, acknowledging the contributions of doctors and other medical professionals. The occasion also highlighted continuing debates about working conditions, professional allowances and the infrastructure required for effective healthcare delivery. At the Maltina Teacher of the Year Awards the same evening, Lagos-based Biology teacher Busayo Adeyemo emerged the national winner and received, among other prizes, a three-bedroom apartment announced by the governor. Education and healthcare provide the human foundations on which a productive economy depends. Skilled workers, healthy citizens and credible public institutions are all essential to sustaining investment. Even Saturday’s runway appearance at Lagos Fashion Week fitted, in a different way, into the week’s economic narrative. By walking for designer Ugo Monye, Sanwo-Olu drew attention to an industry whose business extends beyond the glamour of fashion shows. The creative sector involves designers, textile workers, manufacturers, photographers, event producers, retailers and countless supporting enterprises.
Like maritime logistics and manufacturing, it also requires financing, skilled labour and access to markets. The week, therefore, presented different faces of a single development challenge.
International trade must be supported by infrastructure. Infrastructure requires investment. Investment depends on finance and an enabling business environment. And economic expansion ultimately needs to benefit the people whose work sustains the system. Whether all these ambitions will translate into the desired outcomes remains a matter for assessment over time. What the governor’s engagements demonstrated, however, was the interconnected nature of the economic questions confronting Lagos. From Abuja’s economic discussions to the bankers’ gathering in Victoria Island, with health, education, maritime investment and creative enterprise in between, the week offered a broad view of the state’s development agenda. The venues changed. So did the audiences. But the underlying challenge remained remarkably consistent: how to turn Lagos’ considerable economic possibilities into lasting opportunities for its people.
The post Sanwo-Olu: One week and the different faces of a single development challenge appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
Nigeria’s electricity crisis indicts decades of failed planning. For a population approaching 240 million, the national grid remains unreliable, while millions lack access altogether. The World Bank’s access series put electricity access at 62.5 per cent in 2024; the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission (NIPC) says more than 85 million people remain without grid power. Installed capacity guarantees nothing when gas shortages, transmission bottlenecks and distribution failures keep power from consumers.
Successive administrations have promised relief through independent power projects, yet spending has delivered too little amid corruption allegations and poor accountability. Mambilla is the glaring cautionary tale. Conceived decades ago as a 3,050-megawatt hydroelectric project, it remains stalled by contractual disputes and litigation. In September 2026, an international tribunal rejected Sunrise Power’s claims against Nigeria and found settlement arrangements tainted by corruption. That ruling only removed a legal obstacle without switching on a single megawatt.
Solar offers a practical route to closing the gap. Nigeria receives average solar irradiation of about 5.5 kilowatt-hours per square metre daily and has a theoretical potential of 427 gigawatts, yet uses less than two per cent of it. Rooftop systems, mini-grids and solar home systems can reach off-grid communities, power clinics and schools, and help businesses escape costly generators. Solar with batteries cannot meet every round-the-clock industrial need, but it can complement hydro, gas and a reformed national grid.
President Bola Tinubu’s N10 billion solar project at Aso Rock, completed for testing in late 2025, is expected to reduce the Villa’s dependence on the grid. It demonstrates solar energy’s value and also the privilege gap: the Presidency is shielding itself from outages endured by ordinary Nigerians. The same determination must reach homes, markets, farms and public institutions.
Government should scale up the $750 million World Bank-backed DARES programme, provide affordable credit and pay-for-service plans, and prioritise solar mini-grids in underserved communities. States can use the Electricity Act 2023 to license intrastate markets, attract private developers and solarise hospitals, schools, water systems and industrial clusters. Federal agencies should set transparent targets, stable incentives and guarantees that attract investment.
India’s rooftop and agricultural solar programmes, alongside domestic panel manufacturing, show how finance, public procurement and clear standards can build markets. Nigeria should expand local panel assembly, then develop batteries, inverters, mounting structures and recycling through joint ventures and technology transfer. The Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) must enforce certification, traceability and installer competence, excluding counterfeits without using protectionism to inflate prices.
We need a national target for millions of new solar connections, an increase in local content and the publication of annual progress and audit spending. Solar must not become another slogan or procurement scandal. Properly financed, regulated and deployed, it can turn Nigeria’s sunshine into productive power—and make electricity access a common public amenity, not a presidential privilege.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
By Ndahi Marama, Maiduguri
The Borno State Police Command has arrested 103 suspected criminals during a week-long operation targeting substance abuse, violence, thuggery and other social vices in Maiduguri metropolis.
The arrests were made between October 29 and November 2, 2026, during township patrols and coordinated raids conducted by the command’s Rapid Response Squad (RRS) Social Vices Unit, with support from other security agencies.
The Police Public Relations Officer, ASP Keneth Daso, disclosed this in a statement issued on Tuesday.
He said the operation was carried out on the directive of the Commissioner of Police, CP Naziru Abdulmajid, and focused on identified crime-prone areas and security hotspots across the metropolis.
The areas included Gwange, Santiago, Texaco, Ajari, Gadan Zare, Budum, Shehuri, Bulabulin, Abbaganaram, Baga Road, Gidan Dambe, UNIMAID 202 Housing Estate, Mairi Kuwait, Bakari, Zanneri, Polo, Giwa Barrack Area, Kwanan Yobe, Jiddari, Kaleri, Damboa Road, Circular and Moduganari.
According to Daso, the suspects were arrested for alleged offences bordering on public nuisance, possession and sale of illicit drugs, and possession of dangerous weapons.
He said the suspects were undergoing preliminary screening and investigation, adding that those found culpable would be prosecuted in accordance with the law.
Items recovered during the operations included 889 wraps of Indian hemp, 104 wraps of Erinmo, seven packs of Colorado and two quantities of methamphetamine, popularly known as Ice.
The police also recovered eight bottles of codeine syrup, 266 tablets of D5, 13 tablets of diazepam, 11 tablets and seven capsules of tramadol, and 300 capsules of Exole.
Other items recovered were 12 tablets of Exole, four ice bunkers, a bottle of methylene chloride, popularly known as “Suck and Die”, four sharp knives, a cutlass, an axe and 11 rounds of live ammunition.
The command also said it recovered three sets of shisha pots and 11 pieces of ice bulbs.
Daso quoted the Commissioner of Police as commending the operatives and collaborating security agencies for their vigilance and commitment to maintaining public safety.
Abdulmajid reaffirmed the command’s resolve to sustain intelligence-led operations, intensify the fight against illicit drug activities and dismantle criminal hideouts and networks capable of threatening public peace and security.
The police urged residents to continue providing credible and timely information about suspicious activities, criminal hideouts and other security threats through established police communication channels.
The command reiterated its commitment to protecting lives and property and ensuring a safer environment for residents.

items.content:
By Cynthia Alo
High feed costs, fish mortality and inefficient water management are reducing the profitability of fish farming in Nigeria, prompting calls for wider adoption of technology that can help farmers improve production and cut losses.
One such innovation is Smart Pond, developed by Pysis Technologies, an agritech startup using Internet of Things (IoT) technology and artificial intelligence to help fish farmers make production decisions based on actual pond conditions rather than assumptions.
The technology monitors pond conditions and provides information to guide feeding and water management, addressing practices that often result in excessive feed use, poor water quality and avoidable fish deaths.
Chief Executive Officer and Co-founder of Pysis Technologies, Oluwatoyin Ogundeji, said fish farmers still rely largely on assumptions to determine when to feed their fish or change pond water, leading to unnecessary production costs.
He said: “Feed is already expensive, yet we still see about 15 to 20 per cent feed wastage, largely because farmers feed fish when their metabolism is low without knowing.”
According to Ogundeji, farmers using the solution could reduce fish mortality by up to 89 per cent, while operating costs can reduce by as much as 10 per cent.
He added that assessment of some farmers using the technology recorded profit margins of up to 55 per cent, compared with the 20 to 25 per cent he identified as the average for smallholder and mid-scale farmers.
The device has a built-in aerator that supplies oxygen to pond water, allowing farmers to extend the period between water changes and reduce energy costs associated with pumping and replacing water.
However, Ogundeji said the adoption of aquaculture technology also depends on addressing institutional challenges, particularly the policy classification of inland freshwater fish farming.
He called for a review of the policy that moved inland freshwater aquaculture from the Ministry of Agriculture to the Ministry of Blue Economy, stressing that the change has made it difficult for aquaculture-focused agritech businesses to access some agricultural interventions and support programmes.
According to him, more than 80 per cent of Nigerian fish farming takes place on land through freshwater ponds and tanks, making the subsector closely linked to agriculture through its dependence on land, agricultural feed inputs and local food production.
He noted that while marine capture fisheries and offshore mariculture fall under the Blue Economy, inland freshwater aquaculture should remain connected to agricultural policies and support systems.
To address farmers’ concerns about adopting unfamiliar technology, Pysis said it conducts demonstrations and refresher training through its Thriving Aquaculture Africa initiative.

items.content:
By Gabriel Ewepu and Cynthia Alo
A coalition of scientists, farmers, environmentalists, nutritionists and civil society organisations has called on the Lagos State House of Assembly to ban genetically modified organisms, GMOs, in the state, warning of potential threats to public health, biodiversity, farmers’ livelihoods and food sovereignty.
The coalition, under the GMO-Free Nigeria Alliance, made the demand during a mass awareness rally last week in Lagos, where it submitted a joint position paper to the state legislature, urging lawmakers to restrict the cultivation of genetically modified crops and strengthen regulations governing genetically engineered foods.
The GMO-Free Nigeria Alliance, which said its position was endorsed by more than 70 organisations, maintained that protecting indigenous seeds and promoting sustainable farming systems were critical to Nigeria’s long-term food security.
The coalition urged the Lagos State House of Assembly to consider its demands and take legislative action to protect consumers, farmers and the state’s agricultural environment.
Some of the stakeholder groups involved in the rally are Health of Mother Earth Foundation, HOMEF; Environmental Rights Action/Friends of the Earth Nigeria, ERA/FoEN; Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa, CAPPA; Kebetkache Women Development and Resource Centre; and the GMO-Free Nigeria Alliance.
The groups raised concerns about possible contamination of indigenous crop varieties through cross-pollination, soil degradation, health risks and increasing corporate control of seeds through patent rights, which they argued could undermine farmers’ traditional practice of saving and sharing seeds.
Speaking at the rally, HOMEF’s Director of Programmes, Joyce Brown, said opposition to GMOs was not peculiar to Nigeria, claiming that more than 30 countries had imposed partial or total restrictions on genetically modified crops.
She listed France, Germany, Austria, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Poland and other European countries, as well as countries in Asia, the Americas and Africa, including Algeria, Madagascar and Zimbabwe, among those that had adopted restrictions.
According to her, the Lagos Assembly has an opportunity to build on the motion moved by the House of Representatives in 2024 seeking the suspension of GMOs and an investigation into approvals already granted.
Also speaking, a Molecular Biologist and Public Health Policy Analyst, Dr. Ifeanyi Casmir, called for a precautionary, transparent and people-centred biotechnology policy, warning that Nigeria could face serious consequences if potential risks were not adequately investigated before the commercial deployment of genetically modified crops.
Casmir said a review of scientific literature published between 1995 and 2025 identified evidence, largely from animal and laboratory studies, pointing to possible allergenic, toxicological, reproductive and ecological concerns.
Similarly, Associate Director at CAPPA, Mr. Olamide Martins, questioned the adequacy of Nigeria’s biosafety regulatory framework, alleging that independent long-term risk assessments had not been sufficiently demonstrated despite the approval of more than 20 GMO products since 2016.
Matins said the approvals covered different purposes, including commercial cultivation and use in food, feed and processing.
He described the situation as unacceptable, insisting that the country’s food safety, environmental protection and food sovereignty should not be compromised.

The Zamfara State Ministry of Finance has presented the 2025 Budget Performance Report, highlighting how funds were utilised in the year under review.
The Commissioner for Finance, Muhammad Bello Auta, presented the report during the 2025 budget performance and accountability meeting held at the Finance Ministry Multipurpose Hall in Gusau.
Represented by the State Accountant General, Ali Akilu Muhammad Bungudu, the commissioner said that the 2025 Zamfara State Budget, tagged “Rescue Budget 2.0,” was approved at a total of N546,014,575,000.
He said the budget was designed to focus on key sectors, including security, education, healthcare and agriculture, among others.
Mr Auta maintained that approximately 72% of the total budget was allocated to capital expenditure, while about 28% was earmarked for recurrent expenditure.
He also said that the report captured the amount of revenue generated from various sources and the amount spent from the approved budgetary allocations.
He further explained that the ministries, departments and agencies that received funds, projects and programmes implemented with the allocated funds, and the level of implementation of major projects were all contained in the 2025 budget report.
The commissioner also said that in line with the government’s efforts to promote transparency and accountability in the management of public funds, the Q4 2025 Budget Performance Report was published on 28th January 2026, providing important information for assessing the implementation and performance of the 2025 budget at the end of the fiscal year.
He enumerated the projects and programmes identified by the government as beneficiaries of the 2025 budget, including the Gusau International Airport, Gusau-Magami-Dansadau Road, school projects, a modern medical research centre, Smart City, food production initiatives, hospitals, the Gusau International Conference Centre, the Gusau International Sports Centre, as well as road projects across various local government areas, adding that there was an important distinction between what was provided for in the budget and what was actually spent or implemented.

Governor Dauda Lawal of Zamfara State described the Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar III, as a humble leader who brings people together and provides stability.
On Monday, the governor attended the 13th Shaikh Usmanu Bin Fodiyo Week and the 20th anniversary of the coronation of Sultan Sa’ad, at the International Conference Centre in Sokoto.
This year’s ceremony, with the theme ‘Reviving Ethical Leadership and Social Harmony: Lessons from Sokoto Jihad Leaders’, brought together notable figures from Nigeria and beyond.
In his goodwill message, Governor Lawal said the government and people of Zamfara State have been greatly inspired by the Sultan’s wisdom, guidance, and steady leadership, especially during difficult social and security times.
He said, “With immense joy, respect, and gratitude to Almighty Allah (SWT), on behalf of the government and people of Zamfara State, I congratulate His Eminence Alhaji Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar III, 20th Sultan of Sokoto and leader of the Ummah, on the historic 20th anniversary of his coronation.
“We remain deeply grateful for your recent presence and support at our coronation and presentation of staff of office to our 19 Emirs in Gusau, which further underscores your commitment to strengthening the traditional institutions across our region.
“This year’s celebration reminds us that the Sokoto Caliphate’s legacy transcends borders. Its enduring values, knowledge, justice, moral discipline, responsible leadership and human dignity remain relevant to today’s challenges.
“Closer to home in Zamfara State, this legacy carries a particularly compelling message. At a time when insecurity, moral decline, poverty and youth vulnerability threaten our communities, we must draw inspiration from the teachings of Sheikh Usmanu Dan Fodiyo to promote peace, justice, education and social responsibility.”
Earlier, the Sultan thanked everyone who played a part and contributed during his 20 years as Sultan of Sokoto. He encouraged religious, traditional, and community leaders to work even harder to promote peace.

By Rotimi Ojomoyela
ADO-EKITI – The Association of Ekiti Traditional Chieftaincy Title Holders has pledged to mobilise one million votes for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid in the 2027 presidential election.
The association made the pledge at a gathering hosted by the Managing Director of the Federal Housing Authority (FHA), Hon. Oyetunde Ojo, where traditional title holders from across Ekiti State expressed support for Tinubu’s administration and called for sustained implementation of its policies.
The Chairman of the association, Chief Oluwole Ogunsakin, said the one-million-vote target represented its commitment to mobilising communities across the state ahead of the election.
He said the association’s network extended to towns, villages, families and grassroots organisations, adding that members would encourage eligible voters to participate peacefully and freely in the electoral process.
Ogunsakin also identified insecurity as one of the major concerns confronting residents, saying traditional rulers and chiefs were strategically positioned to contribute to grassroots security because of their closeness to the people.
He welcomed ongoing legislative discussions on the establishment of state police, expressing optimism that the proposal would eventually become law.
The association urged the government to consider involving traditional chiefs in screening and recommending credible candidates from their communities for recruitment into the proposed state police structure.
Ogunsakin said such involvement would strengthen public confidence in the security system, given traditional leaders’ knowledge of their communities and local security challenges, including activities around farmlands.
He said: “As custodians of our heritage and respected community leaders, we recognise the importance of peaceful democratic participation and constructive political engagement.
“On this occasion, the Association of Ekiti Traditional Chieftaincy Title Holders declares its commitment and aspiration to mobilise one million votes through our communities in support of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in the 2027 presidential election, while supporting your political mobilisation efforts.
“We shall encourage eligible voters to participate peacefully and make their choices freely at the ballot box.”
Speaking at the event, Ojo described the Tinubu administration’s infrastructure projects, particularly road construction, as unprecedented, comparing their scale to infrastructure development during the administration of former Head of State, General Yakubu Gowon.
He said the roads being constructed under Tinubu’s administration were designed to last between 30 and 40 years.
Ojo also commended the President’s appointments, saying they reflected fairness and representation across the country’s ethnic groups.
On security, he said the situation was gradually improving, citing the ongoing construction of a military barracks in Ikere-Ekiti as an intervention expected to strengthen security operations and create employment opportunities.
He said the project would stimulate economic activities and help address security challenges by providing more opportunities for productive engagement.
Ojo challenged critics of the President’s policies and programmes to explain what they would do differently if given the opportunity to govern.
Former Ekiti State Governor, Engr. Segun Oni, also called for collective support for Tinubu, saying the President’s second-term ambition required the commitment of political stakeholders.
Oni urged Nigerians seeking a prosperous future for the country to support the President while advocating political understanding and national unity across ethnic and regional lines.
A former member of the House of Representatives, Bimbo Daramola, expressed optimism about Tinubu’s electoral prospects in Ekiti State, saying the mobilisation target was to secure 90 per cent of the votes for the President.
He described traditional title holders as an important grassroots constituency in the mobilisation effort.
A highlight of the event was the conferment of the title of patron on Oyetunde Ojo in recognition of his contributions to community development, relationship with traditional institutions and philanthropic activities.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
…Govt promises standard facility
By Steve Oko
UMUAHIA — For pregnant women in Okuenyi community, Obingwa Local Government Area of Abia State, the journey to motherhood was often a painful test of endurance, one that began long before labour pains set in.
With no functional health facility to attend to them, expectant mothers had to trek approximately three miles to neighbouring communities in search of antenatal care and safe delivery. For some, the journey was a desperate race against time, with the lives of both mother and child hanging in the balance.
But one woman who grew up in the community could no longer bear the sight of her people enduring such hardship.
Moved by the plight of the women, Mrs Ebere Ulelu-Obiesie, an indigene of Okuenyi, stepped in to change the narrative, sponsoring the renovation and upgrading of the community’s dilapidated temporary health post and equipping it with essential medical facilities.
Her intervention, complemented by financial support from Rev. Friday Nnah, Proprietor of Abundant Living Christian School, Okuenyi, has brought renewed hope to a community whose women had for years faced the agonising prospect of travelling miles to access basic healthcare.
For the women of Okuenyi, the renovated facility which was inaugurated recently, represents much more than refurbished walls and newly acquired medical equipment. It offers the possibility of receiving medical attention closer to home and, perhaps, a safer journey into motherhood.
Painful reality that inspired intervention
Narrating the circumstances that prompted the intervention, Mrs. Ulelu-Obiesie told SEV that her attachment to Okuenyi, where she was born and raised before marriage, made it impossible for her to turn her back on the suffering of her people.
She disclosed that the decision to rehabilitate the health post was driven by her worry over the deplorable condition of the facility and the difficulties pregnant women in the area pass through to access healthcare.
According to her, a visit to the health post with her husband, Mr Ernest Obiesie, exposed the gravity of the situation and strengthened her resolve to intervene.
“I was born in Okuenyi before I got married. I could not stand by and watch my people continue to face these difficult challenges, especially in accessing healthcare services. Pregnant women, in particular, were exposed to enormous difficulties.
“After visiting the former health post in Okuenyi with my husband and seeing its deplorable condition, I resolved to liberate my people from these challenges by initiating the project through my husband, in collaboration with my co-sponsors,” she said.
Her husband, Ernest, revealed that he initially hesitated when she presented the proposal, citing financial constraints.
However, seeing the condition of the health post during a subsequent visit changed his perspective, as the couple resolved to respond to the community’s urgent healthcare needs.
Beneficiaries narrate ordeals
One of the beneficiaries of the medical outreach, Mrs Nwablessing Nwankudu, offered a poignant account of the ordeal residents had endured before the intervention.
She said pregnant women and other residents were often compelled to trek approximately three miles to neighbouring communities to access medical services, including antenatal care and delivery.
For expectant mothers, the distance was not merely an inconvenience. It was a potentially dangerous undertaking, particularly when labour commenced unexpectedly or complications arose.
Nwankudu expressed gratitude to the project sponsors, praying that God would continue to bless them for bringing relief to the community.
She, however, appealed to the Abia State Government to upgrade the facility into a standard health centre and rehabilitate the community’s access roads to make healthcare delivery more accessible.
Govt promises more intervention
Representing Governor Otti at the commissioning, Director, Office of the Special Adviser to the Governor on Health, Hon. Ukaegbu Ndubuisi said the intervention had drawn the state government’s attention to the absence of a standard health centre in Okuenyi and the deplorable condition of roads linking the community.
He assured the residents that their concerns would be conveyed to the governor for necessary action.
“We assure the people of Okuenyi that this message will get to the Governor, and he will swing into action in the coming months to ensure that the upgraded temporary health post is transformed into a standard health centre, the inaccessible roads are graded, and the people of Okuenyi receive their democratic dividends,” he said.
The inauguration ceremony was accompanied by a free medical outreach led by Dr Obioma Nwaogwugwu, Supervisor for Health, Obingwa LGA, and other healthcare professionals.
The outreach provided residents with access to medical consultations and other healthcare services, further extending the benefits of the intervention beyond the rehabilitation of the facility.
In a related humanitarian gesture, Mrs Precious Nnah, wife of Rev. Friday Nnah, distributed food items to women who attended the medical outreach.
In his remark, the Labour Party flagbearer for Obingwa East State Constituency in the 2027 Abia State House of Assembly election, Seth Kelechi Ebere, commended the benefactors for their contributions to the project.
He described the intervention as an exemplary act of community development worthy of emulation by other prominent indigenes.
Meanwhile, Ebere pledged continued support towards transforming the facility into a standard health centre and urged residents to support the continuity of the Otti administration in the 2027 general elections.
The inauguration attracted government officials, political stakeholders, traditional rulers, community leaders, healthcare professionals and other dignitaries.
For Mrs Ulelu-Obiesie, the intervention is a personal response to a longstanding communal challenge. But for the women of Okuenyi, it is a potential turning point in their healthcare experience.
But for pregnant women who once had to trek miles in search of a place to deliver their babies, the renovated health post simply means that motherhood should no longer begin with a hazardous journey in search of medical care.
However, with the facility still awaiting transformation into a standard health centre and the community’s access roads remaining a challenge, residents hope the government’s pledge will translate into concrete action.
For now, one daughter’s compassion has brought healthcare closer to homes. The agrarian community awaits the next chapter. Even though some health care facilities in Abia have received a facelift, some are still yearning for intervention.
Checks by SEV revealed that Otti’s administration has recorded significant progress in the health sector, renovating over 200 primary healthcare centres, six general hospitals and three tertiary health institutions across Abia State. The governor has also promised to sustain his health care transformation, assuring that other PHCs in dilapidated condition will receive government attention.
However, communities yet to benefit from the interventions are eagerly awaiting their turn.
The post Abia: How one woman ended Okuenyi mothers’ dangerous trek for childbirth appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Daily Trust
items.content:
Nigeria has been nominated in three of four female categories released for the 2026 Confederation of Africa (CAF) Awards.
Nigerian women were nominated in three categories including Team of the Year, Goalkeeper of the Year, and Young Player of the Year respectively.
Nigeria received nomination in the National team of the Year category on the back of a failed WAFCON 2026 title defence.
The Falconets also got knocked out of the U20 women’s World Cup at the quarter-final stage.
However, the Flamingos won the 2026 WAFU-B U-17 Girls Cup, and are currently semi-finalists of the U17 World Cup.
A shock nomination for goalkeeper of the year is Christiana Uzoma, Nigeria’s U20 shotstopper.
She makes the list ahead of upper Falcons’ Chiamaka Nnadozie who is conspicuously missing.
Uzoma won the NWFL title with Edo Queens, and starred for as the Falconets reached the quarter-finals at the World Cup.
Other breakout stars nominated are Seimeyeha Janet Akekoromowei and Oluwakemi Adegbuyi in the Young Footballer of the Year category.
While Akekoromowei’s goals and tenacity helped the Falconets reach World Cup quarter-final, Adegbuyi has been a revelation with the Flamingos.
The 16-year-old forward won the WAFU-B Girls Cup, was invited to the Falcons for Olympics qualifiers, and is currently starring at the U17 World Cup.
The CAF Awards is slated for December 7 at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts in Lagos.

items.author: Mohammed I. Yaba
items.content:
A pregnant woman, Jamila Muhammad, and seven other residents abducted by bandits in Kaduna State have regained their freedom after spending weeks in captivity.
The victims were rescued between October 31 and November 2 in a coordinated operation involving the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA), the Department of State Services (DSS), the Nigeria Police Force and the military, in collaboration with the Kaduna State Government.
Jamila, 27, was abducted on October 6 when bandits attacked Alrahus Estate in Millennium City, Chikun Local Government Area, and kidnapped her alongside Ahmad Zakka, his wife and their six-month-old daughter.
While Zakka, his wife and daughter regained their freedom on October 15, days after a video of them in captivity went viral on social media, Jamila remained with the kidnappers until the latest rescue operation.
Insecurity: How 98 cops were killed in 10 months
Access Holdings’ 9M profit rises to N667bn as Q3 earnings rebound
She reportedly lost her pregnancy while in captivity.
The other rescued victims were identified as Talatu Yakubu, 40; Yunana Bawa, 30; Calista Bishop, 27; Chidinma Onuwere, 36; Eucharia Obi, 41; Godiya Victor, 50; and Miracle Alex, an eight-year-old girl.
The Kaduna State Commissioner of Police, CP Muhammad Rabiu, announced the rescue during a press conference at the DSS Command headquarters in Kaduna.
Rabiu said the operation was part of sustained efforts to identify, disrupt and dismantle criminal networks responsible for recurring kidnappings in Millennium City and its environs.
He said the area had witnessed repeated abductions, raising concerns among residents and other stakeholders over their safety.
The commissioner said the latest breakthrough came barely weeks after security agencies rescued Zakka and members of his family from captivity.
He commended ONSA for its strategic coordination, the police for operational support, the DSS for intelligence-driven efforts and the military for its involvement in the rescue operations.
Rabiu also praised the Kaduna State Government, under Governor Uba Sani, for its continued support and cooperation with security agencies in tackling kidnapping and banditry.
He said the operations reflected President Bola Tinubu’s commitment to strengthening national security and protecting lives and property through effective coordination among security and intelligence institutions.
The police commissioner assured residents that security agencies were intensifying efforts to eliminate kidnapping and banditry across Kaduna State.
He said additional personnel and equipment, including 30 vans and eight armoured personnel carriers, would be deployed to improve security.
Rabiu noted that criminal groups often exploit the state’s difficult terrain to evade security forces, but assured residents that ongoing operations would be sustained and strengthened.
He urged residents to remain vigilant and provide credible and actionable intelligence on suspected kidnappers, bandits and other criminal elements.
He assured the public that information supplied to security agencies would be treated confidentially and acted upon appropriately.
The commissioner also called on traditional rulers, community leaders and other stakeholders to support efforts to restore peace, while urging media organisations to report responsibly and avoid publishing unverified information capable of undermining security operations or causing unnecessary panic.
He reaffirmed the commitment of security agencies and the Kaduna State Government to restoring lasting peace across the state.

items.title: Don’t consider critics as enemies, Sanusi tells FG
items.summary:

items.content:
Emir of Kano, Alhaji Muhammadu Sanusi II, has warned the Federal Government against treating every comment about as an attack on President Bola Tinubu.
Speaking virtually to the audience at the Oxford Global Think Tank Leadership Conference, organised by the Oxford Global Think Tank, on Tuesday, Sanusi advised the government to tolerate constructive criticisims.
“It’s not every time people talk about poverty or talk about difficulty that they’re just enemies of the government or making an attack on the president. That is not how to respond to economic distress,” he said.
The Emir also raised concerns about the size of government expenditure, saying Nigeria could not pursue fiscal consolidation while continuing to spend without restraint.
He said the World Bank had pointed out that in the first half of this year Nigeria’s debt service consumed 124 per cent of federal government revenue. BuyMaps
Sanusi warned that the country needed to urgently address the sustainability of its debt and pursue structural reforms that had not yet been made.
The monarch said reform must go beyond removing fuel subsidies and liberalising the exchange rate, describing it as a comprehensive package that needed to address many other areas.
He said government needed to make clear spending priorities, choosing between roads, electricity, agriculture, and technology based on available resources.
The former CBN boss said every $10 billion spent on roads was $10 billion taken away from electricity and agriculture, stressing the need for deliberate choices.
Sanusi acknowledged that Tinubu’s economic reforms had produced measurable progress, citing improvements in GDP growth, inflation, and foreign reserves.
Sanusi said GDP growth has risen from an average of 0.9 per cent under the previous administration to 4.5 per cent, describing the change as progress that deserved recognition.
“I think moving from an average growth rate of 0.9 per cent to 4.5 per cent is progress. Moving from inflation of over 30 per cent to 14.5 per cent is progress.”
“Moving from the point where in 2023 the central bank’s reserves were maybe negative to where we are now having reserves of $55 billion is progress.”
He, however, stressed that issues such as poverty, hunger, maternal mortality, malnutrition, education and healthcare remained serious concerns that the reforms has not yet addressed.
Sanusi said the government should have designed social safety net policies to soften the impact of reforms on vulnerable Nigerians from the beginning.
