items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Healthy snacking brand Troovy has raised ₹100 Cr ($10.5 Mn) in a Series B funding round led by existing investor Fireside Ventures, with participation from Sharrp Ventures.
The startup will use the fresh capital to expand its manufacturing capacity and fuel its research and development (R&D) for product development. The D2C brand will also strengthen its distribution across quick commerce and offline channels.
Besides, the startup plans to expand its portfolio into categories like namkeen, biscuits and cookies by January 2027, Baranwal said.
“We will also launch more products in existing categories and build our R&D capabilities. We’re planning to develop new products with parents, as well as innovators from across the country,” cofounder Mansi Baranwal told Inc42.
Founded in 2021 by husband-and-wife duo Mansi Baranwal and Aditya Mukherjee, Troovy initially entered the market with clean-label ketchup and later expanded into the healthy snacking category.
Its portfolio of products includes chips, puffs, sauces, spreads, millet-based pasta, cookies and milk mixes. Chips and puffs are Troovy’s hero categories, together accounting for around 60-70% of sales, as per Baranwal.
Troovy Doubles Down On Offline Expansion
Marketplaces and quick commerce account for roughly half of Troovy’s sales, while sales from its own website brings in about 30%. Offline retail, which the startup recently entered in Delhi NCR, accounts for close to 6% of revenue.
Troovy has begun building its offline distribution network, starting with Delhi NCR and neighbouring areas. It plans to expand into select metro and Tier I markets, initially focusing on Delhi NCR, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, with some presence planned in Punjab and Haryana.
Baranwal said the startup is taking a measured approach as it works out its distribution strategy for offline retail.
“We’re very much in learning mode. We’re trying to figure out the playbook and experiment with different things,” she said, adding that North India is an important market for chips.
The latest fundraise follows Troovy’s $5 Mn Series A round in January this year, led by Fireside Ventures.
“Troovy grew 5X in the eight months following our last investment, and that is what made us double down,” said Ankita Balotia, principal at Fireside Ventures.
The latest fundraise announcement comes months after the startup came under the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India’s (FSSAI) scrutiny over the use of the word “Healthy” in the names of its Veggie Chips, Ragi Chips and Moong Dal Chips.
The regulator said the product names could mislead consumers, despite the products containing other ingredients.
Responding to a question on the food regulator’s crackdown, Baranwal said stricter enforcement of food labelling rules could benefit brands that have invested in product formulation and ingredient transparency.
“I strongly think that this is great for the sector as well as for consumers and the country at large. These regulations exist for the benefit of the consumer, and tighter implementation is always better from a consumer perspective,” she said.
However, she said compliance could add to the costs and operational challenges faced by startups that lack adequate testing infrastructure.
“We do a lot of lab testing, and it puts a lot of pressure on startups like us that don’t have the correct infrastructure,” Baranwal said.
She added that Troovy was also working to reduce sodium levels in its products and limit the use of ingredients it considers undesirable.

items.author: Amiya Johar
items.content:
Microsoft is offering employees across several parts of its global operations the opportunity to take a voluntary exit deal, as it seeks to contain costs while ramping up investment in AI.
The offer being made is time-limited and includes financial support and career planning resources. Reuters reported the programme is targeting around 60,000 employees.
Microsoft’s FY26 annual report showed it had 223,000 full-time employees worldwide as of 30 June, putting the potential pool of eligible staff at more than a quarter of its global workforce.
In a statement, Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman explained the programme is available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the UK and the US at level 70 and below of its employee hierarchy.
Participation is limited to selected business units with eligibility varying according to “each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs”.
A source told Reuters the offer covers teams including Copilot, AI experiences, finance, human resources, Xbox and Windows + Devices. Marketing, commercial business and security are apparently excluded.
“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,” Coleman said, adding “these are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs” and that “we’ll learn from it”.
Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to around 9,000 US employees earlier this year and announced 4,800 job cuts in July, as it restructured its Xbox gaming business and planned to divest four studios.
The latest initiative comes as Microsoft commits substantial sums to AI infrastructure, including data centres and chips. The company forecast capital expenditure of $175 billion for calendar year 2026, drawing scrutiny over whether returns will justify the scale of spending.

items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
AI infrastructure startup Simplismart has raised $14 Mn (around ₹133 Cr) in a Series B funding round led by Dallas Venture Capital, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC, Micromax, and angel investors.
Dallas Venture Capital invested close to $5 Mn in the round, cofounder and CEO Amritanshu Jain told Inc42.
Simplismart plans to use the fresh capital to further develop its AI inference platform, deepen partnerships with cloud providers and sovereign AI players, and expand across North America and other global markets.
AI inference is the process of running trained models to generate responses or predictions.
Founded in 2022 by Jain and Devansh Ghatak, Simplismart builds the software layer between AI models and GPU infrastructure. Its inference engine lets businesses configure how models run based on their speed, cost, and performance requirements, while its orchestration platform manages deployment and scaling across cloud and on-premises infrastructure.
“We have spent four years building the software layer between the model and the GPU, helping customers optimise how their workloads are deployed and operated. This funding will allow us to take that platform to more enterprises and cloud providers globally,” Jain said.
The funding will also support the development of a dynamic GPU scheduling layer to match AI workloads with available computing capacity across regions and time zones, cofounder and CTO Ghatak said.
How Simplismart Makes Money
Jain said Simplismart offers three deployment and pricing models: shared endpoints, dedicated endpoints, and bring-your-own-compute deployments.
Under the shared endpoint model, customers pay based on token consumption, without a minimum fee. Dedicated endpoints allow customers to rent GPU infrastructure along with Simplismart’s optimisation software, with charges linked to GPU usage and runtime.
The bring-your-own-compute model caters to businesses that want to run workloads on their own infrastructure to meet data and regulatory requirements, particularly in sectors such as banking, financial services, and insurance.
For its cloud-provider offering, Simplismart works with NVIDIA to help providers deploy and manage AI infrastructure at scale. The startup does not own the computing infrastructure. Instead, its software enables cloud providers to offer managed AI services under their own brands using their existing GPUs.
The startup said this offering is already being used by Yotta, with Simplismart powering the serverless inference layer of its Shakti Studio platform. This allows customers to run AI models without managing the underlying inference infrastructure themselves.
Around 55% of Simplismart’s revenue comes from the US, with the remainder generated in India, Jain said.
Its customers include HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna, and Ema, which use its platform to run video, voice, multimodal, and enterprise AI workloads. Simplismart said its annualised revenue run rate grew 14X over the past six months.
Prior to this round, Simplismart raised $7 Mn in a Series A round led by Accel in October 2024.
The fundraise comes amid growing investment in India’s AI infrastructure ecosystem.
Tata Communications yesterday announced plans to invest $400 Mn to $450 Mn to build 10,000 km of AI-ready connectivity infrastructure across India. The proposed network will connect major data centres and AI hubs to support demand for high-speed, low-latency connectivity.

items.author: Bismah Malik
items.content:
Consider a kurta priced at ₹799 sold directly on Flipkart by a fashion brand such as Globus Fashion.
Since July, Flipkart stopped charging a commission on fashion products, so on paper the seller keeps more of each sale than it did a year ago.
But under Flipkart’s new penalty structure, effective August 23, the seller is penalised ₹30 the moment the kurta misses its dispatch-by date.
If the order is then cancelled, the seller is penalised another ₹60.
Flipkart now also counts three missed deadlines as a cancellation. But the flat penalty (a total of ₹90) means that sellers face a greater burden to clear low-value orders.
This is one example of how selling online has become costlier this festive season, and penalties are just one part of it. Besides this, there are fee surcharges that apply to every order, whether or not it is delayed or cancelled. And the cost of production and fulfilment have also gone up due to issues ranging from a crunch in raw material supply as well as high fuel prices due to the instability in West Asia.
No matter the seller, whether it is a brand or an Amazon-specific seller, these charges and surcharges are making it harder and costlier to sellers on ecommerce at a time when business is at its peak.
Third-party sellers usually operate on thinner margins than brands and have no control over the price listed on Amazon India, according to industry sources we spoke to.
Some brands take up the operations themselves, depending on the marketplace. Globus Fashion, for instance, sells directly on Flipkart but through Cocoblu Retail on Amazon.
Another brand, Ruhe India, which sells smart kitchen and smart home products, holds its own seller account and sells directly on the marketplaces. The approach is different but the charges will remain.
The changes coincide with the peak festive season sales on Amazon India and Flipkart. According to Redseer projections, festive ecommerce GMV will reach $15–16 Bn in 2026, up about 25% from roughly $12.5 Bn in 2025, with online festive shoppers rising to 180–185 Mn from 160 Mn.
But these estimates do not account for the higher cost that customers and sellers will have to pay for using the ecommerce platform. And that’s before we even account for the potential slowdown due to the merchant discount rate or MDR coming up in merchant UPI payments.
The New Penalty Structure
On August 17, months before its main festive season shopping window, Amazon changed how it charges cancellation fees for sellers on Easy Ship and Self Ship.
Under Easy Ship, Amazon picks up the order from the seller and delivers it; under Self Ship, the seller delivers it through its own courier.
The fee, earlier tied to flat category-based referral charges, is now a percentage of the order value, according to Amazon’s communication to sellers. Amazon now charges 10% of the order value on orders up to ₹10,000, 8% between ₹10,001 and ₹50,000, 5% between ₹50,001 and ₹1 lakh, and 2% above that, plus 18% GST.
A cancelled ₹30,000 order can end up costing the seller about ₹2,832 including the GST which is applicable on cancellation fee. Sellers of electronics, appliances and other big-ticket goods carry the most exposure per order.
“This fee is conditional and only applies in the rare event of a seller-initiated cancellation, which accounts for less than 1% of orders on Amazon.in. We have appropriate measures in place to ensure sellers are protected when cancellations are due to circumstances beyond their control,” Amazon told Inc42 in an emailed statement.
Electronics sellers are already under pressure due to expectations that the 2026 winter season will result in slower sales than 2025. This is largely due to the rising prices of mobile devices and electronics this year, but the extra charges will also play a role in whether sellers even offer some products for sale.
Flipkart did not respond to Inc42’s queries.
People familiar with the company’s operations said the penalties follow its zero-commission push, which has nearly doubled seller onboarding year-on-year. In July, Flipkart dropped commissions across its fashion catalogue, removing an earlier ₹1,000 price ceiling for the waiver.
Whose Fault Is A Delay?
The platforms’ position is that penalties apply only when sellers fail. Sellers, however, claim the line is not always clear.
Responding to Amazon’s notices on its seller forum, some sellers said cancellations were sometimes caused by delivery personnel failing to turn up for scheduled pickups, and asked why the fee should apply in such cases.
A founder of a snacking brand, who wished to be anonymous, told us when a logistics-side delay gets billed to the seller instead of the carrier, this becomes a source of friction and can disrupt many smaller sellers. “We have contested such cases with evidence of timely dispatch, but found the process cumbersome,” the founder added.
Kapil Gupta, founder of Ruhe India, whose catalogue runs from sub-₹500 to ₹3,000-plus, told Inc42 that Flipkart’s flat ₹90 penalty would land hardest on the brand’s value-tier catalogue.
Vinod Kumar, trustee of the Forum for Internet Resellers, Sellers and Traders (FIRST INDIA), said online sellers accept the need for timely fulfilment, but the increase in fees and penalties just before the festive season is a concern for MSMEs already dealing with thin margins and rising costs this year.
Unlike the penalties, these charges apply regardless of seller performance, which seems like a blanket rule meant to punish even those who have a very low proportion of cancellations or delays.
Deliveries Turn Costlier Too
What makes matters worse is that delivery fees and logistics costs have gone up across the industry, meaning no brand or seller is immune to this.
From September 7, Amazon raised its closing fee, a flat per-item charge separate from the commission, by ₹1 on products priced up to ₹500 and by ₹3 or higher-priced items. Amazon’s seller fee page attributes the increase to higher fuel and logistics costs.
Similarly, Flipkart’s logistics arm is mulling a revision in fulfillment fees for sellers, according to sources.
Logistics platform Delhivery added a surcharge on D2C shipments of ₹4 per express shipment and ₹2 per surface shipment, on top of contracted rates from September 1,. The company has reportedly attributed it to higher aviation turbine fuel prices, ground-staff costs and inflation across its network.
The new pricing structure affects a specific group: brands shipping orders from their own websites. Delhivery declined to comment to Inc42 related to queries on increase in the pricings.
Ruhe India’s Gupta said the surcharge would be a challenge for brands building native website sales, which rely on third-party logistics players such as Delhivery.
Globus Fashion, which sells directly and through marketplace sellers, said that logistics or fulfillment costs “can be renegotiated between the brand and marketplace”, but others say that this is not a standardised process.
The fashion brand expects festive logistics spending to rise with demand, but does not expect a big impact on revenue, because inventory placement and warehouse use have already been allocated ahead of time.
Large enterprises stock regional warehouses months in advance to lock in contracted freight rates and accept the holding costs. Other brands may not have these pieces in place.
But, freight operators see more and more brands responding to the festive rush ahead of time. Geetali Sunil Khare, founder of Rachana Speed Logistics, said brands and wholesalers are building inventory ahead of the rush rather than cutting order sizes to protect margins, to avoid stockouts and supply disruptions at peak demand.
In categories such as electronics and apparel, sellers need to retain minimal stock to avoid post-festive inventory risk, and absorb higher, fragmented spot freight costs instead. Truck rental rates in September held above year-ago levels, but month-on-month increases across most corridors have been relatively modest, Khare added.
The bigger festive challenge, she said, is meeting tighter service expectations with higher shipment volumes and heavier consignments.
“On the logistics side it is mostly the truck movement to warehouses that makes up for substantial expenses operation wise. With the deliveries now expanding to regional markets , it makes it harder to to fill vehicles on the way out and leaving return legs empty or under-used,” Aman Mahlawat, founder of Mahlawat Logistics, added.
On local runs, Mahlawat said, highway transit is smooth, but city entry restrictions and long queues at distribution hub docks cause major delays.
Quick commerce, according to the industry players we spoke to, has also added to the cost-strain. High-frequency replenishment of dark store inventory is changing how stock moves upstream from warehouses to the distribution endpoints.
Mahlawat said dark stores and retailers now prefer frequent, smaller drops to monthly bulk dispatches, which splits loads into smaller vehicles and leaves trucks spending more hours waiting at congested unloading docks than moving on the road. These frequent, fragmented dispatches need constant vehicle availability, squeezing truck turnaround times and load consolidation.
“More predictability, enough lead time on fee and policy changes to plan for them, rather than absorbing them mid-season is the only way sellers or brands can work around these changes,” Ruhe India’s Gupta added.’
Can Commission Cuts Offset Rising Costs?
While Flipkart, Amazon India and others have cut commissions for sellers this year, the rising logistics costs, the extra charges this year, and the growing dependency on advertising spending on marketplaces have eaten into the margins of sellers.
Amazon waived referral fees on products under ₹1,000 in March, and Flipkart extended zero commission to all fashion categories in July. Those cuts cover specific categories and price bands while closing fees, shipping charges and penalties apply across categories
Sellers are bemoaning the lack of clarity on when new charges are introduced or why they are applicable to all sellers regardless of their past performance. What sellers are asking for is more predictability from marketplaces and platforms, especially around the peak festive season.
 
The post Why This Festive Season Is Getting More Expensive For Ecommerce Sellers appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.title: Prince of Kalat, three guards kidnapped in Balochistan
items.summary:
Prince Muhammad Khan Ahmedzai, son of Khan of Kalat Mir Suleman Dawood Jan Ahmedzai, was reportedly abducted along with his three guards by unidentified suspects while travelling between Soorab and Kalat in Balochistan, sources said on Tuesday.
The incident reportedly took place last night when Prince Ahmedzai was travelling from Khuzdar to Kalat.
The armed men intercepted his vehicle during the journey and took him and his three security personnel away to an undisclosed location.
Official confirmation of the incident is awaited.
Read: Princely Liaisons: The Khan family controls politics in Kalat
Following the incident, police, security agencies and other law enforcement authorities have launched efforts to trace the abducted men and secure their safe recovery.
There was no immediate information about the whereabouts of the abducted individuals or the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi hinted on Tuesday that incarcerated PTI founder Imran Khan could be shifted to a new jail in Islamabad.
Imran has been imprisoned since August 2023, currently serving a sentence at Adiala Jail in a £190 million corruption case. He also faces pending trials under the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) related to the protests of May 9, 2023.
Speaking to the media during a visit to the Islamabad Model Jail facility, the interior minister informed that the project had been completed after being "pending for 17 years", further adding that the new jail would be inaugurated by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in the coming days.
While responding to a reporter’s question about how much time it would take to transfer prisoners from Adiala jail, Naqvi stated that all prisoners from Islamabad’s courts would be shifted to the jail.
Read: Imran to be moved to Islamabad jail
When asked if Imran would also be shifted to the jail, he replied: "My specific answer is that whosoever is a prisoner of Islamabad will be shifted here."
Naqvi noted that while work on the project had initially begun in 2009, construction work commenced in 2016, further adding that when he first visited the project in 2024, “only 40 to 50 per cent of it had been completed and the project had nearly been abandoned”.

The minister credited Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry and the team of the Capital Development Authority (CDA) for completing the project, working "day and night”, adding that Chaudhry had inspected every aspect of the facility.
“Now this project is ready. We are now waiting for the prime minister for the opening in the next few days, and then we will transfer the prisoners here,” he added.

They said Imran could be moved to the new facility between November 20 and 30. A special ward for him has reportedly been completed, while installation of its closed-circuit television surveillance system is in its final stages.
Naqvi had also indicated in February that  indicated that Imran may be shifted to the new jail. 
Speaking to the media after a visit to the under-construction prison, the interior minister was asked whether Imran would also be moved to the new facility, to which he had said, “If he has been sentenced by Islamabad, then he will come here. The people [sentenced in] Islamabad will be brought here.”
Background of Islamabad Model Jail
Located in Sector H-16 of the federal capital, the Islamabad Model Central Jail is spread over 90 acres and has been designed to accommodate 2,000 inmates. Once completed, it will become the first purpose-built prison for the federal capital, replacing the existing arrangement under which Islamabad's prisoners are housed at Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail.
The state-of-the-art correctional facility is being developed with modern security infrastructure and rehabilitation-focused amenities. The complex will include separate barracks for women and juvenile inmates, a fully equipped hospital, a mosque, a library, vocational training centres, courtrooms, administrative offices, residential accommodation for prison staff and a school for their children.
Officials say the facility has now entered its final phase of construction, although several key components still require completion before it can become operational.
At present, Islamabad has no functional prison of its own, forcing all undertrial and convicted prisoners from the capital to be lodged at Adiala Jail. Every day, hundreds of prisoners are transported between Rawalpindi and Islamabad courts for hearings, placing a significant burden on police manpower, security arrangements and traffic management.
Authorities believe the completion of the Islamabad Model Jail will substantially reduce these logistical challenges while improving security during prisoner transportation and providing a modern correctional environment.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Fintech startup Mochatrade, which offers US Stock tokens trading platform for Indian traders, announced the raise of $5.5 Mn (₹52.3 Cr) in a seed funding round led by CoinFund, with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Zero Knowledge Ventures, among others.
The startup will use the fresh capital to bolster its trading engine and risk infrastructure and expand its reach among active Indian traders.
Founded in 2026 by Utkarsh Sinha, Chetan Manda and Parth Maheshwari, Mochatrade is building a trading platform that allows Indian retail traders and global investors to trade perpetual futures and price-tracking contracts linked to US stocks, cryptocurrencies, commodities and major indices.
Its waitlist has crossed 25,000 sign-ups, although it is yet to announce a public launch date.
The platform is expected to allow users to fund their accounts through UPI and track balances, margins and profit and loss (P&L) in Indian rupees (INR).
The platform’s perpetual futures contracts will allow traders to take long or short positions based on their expectations of price movements, without owning the underlying assets. Unlike conventional futures contracts, these instruments have no fixed expiry date.
Mochatrade will also offer leveraged trading, allowing users to take larger positions with less upfront capital. However, leverage can amplify losses as well as gains. The startup plans to earn revenue through trading fees and eventually introduce contracts linked to select pre-IPO companies, US stock options and social trading features, subject to regulatory approvals.
“India traded $1.9 Tn in options premium turnover last year. The appetite to trade is already here. But when Indians want to trade the US market, the product still feels foreign,” said Sinha, CEO of Mochatrade.
Sinha previously cofounded crypto wallet Martian in 2022, which recorded more than 2 Mn installs and $2 Bn in transaction volume. Martian raised $3.6 Mn from Race Capital, Superscrypt and Jump Crypto before being acquired by Lightspeed-backed Pontem.
Manda became Sprinklr’s youngest director of product in 2025, while Maheshwari worked on Photoshop for the web at Adobe before leading payments and credit infrastructure at Navi.
Mochatrade is entering the market as Indian investors increasingly look overseas for exposure to global assets, particularly US stocks.
According to RBI data, Indian residents remitted $2.65 Bn overseas for equity and debt investments in FY26, up from $1.51 Bn in FY24. Remittances reached $1.4 Bn between April and July FY27, with July alone accounting for $344.6 Mn, a 121% year-on-year increase. These figures cover overseas equity and debt investments across markets, rather than US stocks alone.
At the same time, regulatory changes are reshaping India’s domestic trading market. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has tightened futures and options (F&O) rules to curb excessive speculation and protect retail investors.
Measures include limiting weekly expiries to one benchmark index per exchange, increasing contract sizes and tightening margin requirements. The changes have weighed on trading activity and revenue at several brokerage platforms, including Zerodha and Groww, during FY26.
Against this backdrop, Mochatrade is betting that demand for global market exposure will create an opportunity for a trading platform built around Indian users. Its ability to convert waitlist interest into active traders will depend on its product experience, risk controls and the regulatory framework governing the contracts it plans to offer.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Japanese tech investor SoftBank has sold another 1.2% stake in Ola Electric through a series of open market transactions between January 6 and October 22, reducing its holding in the electric two-wheeler maker to 11.7%.
Its investment vehicle, SVF II Ostrich (DE) LLC, sold 5.55 Cr shares during the period, leaving it with 54.15 Cr shares. The filing pegged its holding before the transactions at 12.9%, calculated using the company’s latest share capital.
The SoftBank entity also sold 1.12 Cr rights entitlements during the period, even as Ola Electric looks to raise nearly ₹1,000 Cr through a rights issue to repay debt and fund expansion.
SoftBank received 4.33 Cr rights entitlements against the 54.15 Cr shares it held on the October 13 record date, under the issue’s two-for-25 ratio. It sold approximately 25.9% of these entitlements, leaving it with 3.21 Cr as of October 22.
Rights entitlements allow eligible shareholders to subscribe to additional shares at the issue price. Shareholders can exercise these entitlements or transfer them to other investors. Selling an entitlement does not reduce their existing equity holding.
SoftBank first backed Ola Electric in July 2019 with a $250 Mn investment that valued the EV maker at around $1 Bn. It participated in a subsequent funding round in September 2021, when Ola Electric’s valuation rose to $3 Bn.
The Japanese investor has progressively reduced its holding since the company went public in August 2024.
In January this year, SoftBank disclosed the sale of 9.46 Cr shares, or a 2.15% stake, through open market transactions between September 3, 2025, and January 5. That disclosure put its holding after the sales at 13.53%. The latest filing calculates the pre-sale holding using Ola Electric’s expanded share capital.
Before that, the investor sold another 9.4 Cr shares, representing a 2.15% stake, between July and September 2025.
Another Round Of Fundraising
Ola Electric is seeking additional capital to stabilise its core electric scooter business while investing in battery manufacturing and energy storage.
Its ₹999.74 Cr rights issue opened on October 22 and will close on October 30. It comprises up to 37.03 Cr partly paid-up equity shares priced at ₹27 apiece.
Investors must pay ₹16.20 per share on application, with the remaining ₹10.80 payable through a subsequent call.
In June, Ola Electric raised ₹780.24 Cr through a qualified institutional placement (QIP), exceeding its initial target of ₹500 Cr. It had earmarked ₹225 Cr from the net proceeds for debt repayment, ₹335 Cr for organic growth, and the remainder for general corporate purposes.
Meanwhile, Motilal Oswal Financial Services and Calliope Capital Advisors applied for a combined 2.39 Cr shares on the opening day of the rights issue.
Motilal Oswal applied for approximately 1.28 Cr shares against entitlements transferred by ANI Technologies, an Ola Electric promoter-group entity. Calliope applied for another 1.1 Cr shares against entitlements transferred by Indus Trust, another promoter-group entity.
Revenue Decline Adds Pressure
The fundraise comes as Ola Electric steps up investments in battery cell manufacturing and battery energy storage systems while pursuing a broader business reset. This includes shifting towards dealer-operated stores and rolling out more affordable electric scooters.
The company’s consolidated operating revenue fell 45% to ₹455 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹828 Cr in the corresponding quarter of the previous fiscal year. Its net loss, however, narrowed 21.5% to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr. It is yet to announce its Q2 FY27 results.
Ola Electric is also battling to regain ground in the electric two-wheeler market. Its market share fell to 6.5% in September from 7.6% in August.
Earlier this month, Goldman Sachs downgraded its recommendation on the stock to ‘Sell’ from ‘Neutral’ and cut its target price to ₹23 per share.
Shares of Ola Electric ended today’s trading session 16.775 higher at ₹34.95 on the BSE.

items.author: Anadolu Agency
items.content:
The Turkish parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee on Tuesday approved a bill to ratify the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
The bill was approved following deliberations during which Deputy Foreign Minister Levent Gumrukcu answered lawmakers' questions about the agreement.
Speaking at the committee meeting, Gumrukcu said the agreement aimed to strengthen regional security through cooperation and collective defence.
“The Makkah agreement is not only an extension of the special friendly relations between the three countries, but also a concrete product of the regional ownership increasingly needed in our region,” Gumrukcu said.
Read: Pakistan condemns 'reprehensible' Houthi attacks in Makkah, Madinah regions
He recalled that the agreement was signed in Makkah on August 7 by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman, and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
He said Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had completed their domestic ratification procedures and submitted the required official notifications.
Gumrukcu said the agreement marked an initial step toward establishing a regional security framework based on cooperation and collective defence, adding that the three countries aimed to take responsibility for addressing regional challenges rather than waiting for solutions from outside the region.
He said the framework was intended to contribute not only to the security of the three signatories but also to that of the wider region by strengthening dialogue and cooperation based on mutual trust and promoting lasting stability.
Deal ‘envisions integration rather than bloc-building in region’
Gumrukcu stressed that the agreement was entirely defensive in nature and did not target any country.
He said it was open to all regional countries that respect international law, including the principles of state sovereignty and territorial integrity, the prohibition of the use of force except in self-defense, the peaceful settlement of disputes and non-interference in internal affairs.
"The agreement envisions integration rather than bloc-building in the region, embracing an inclusive rather than divisive vision," he added.
Defence cooperation and NATO commitments
Gumrukcu said the agreement envisaged strengthening collective deterrence, holding regular consultations on international security issues, and improving interoperability between the countries' armed forces through personnel exchanges, joint training programs, and military exercises.
It also provides for closer defence industry cooperation, including joint production and technology sharing, stronger joint counterterrorism efforts, and logistical support between the parties in implementing the agreement, he said.
The deputy foreign minister emphasised that the agreement would neither replace nor undermine Türkiye's obligations under its existing alliances and agreements.
He said the initiative was expected to complement Türkiye's participation in multilateral platforms, particularly NATO, by contributing to security and stability across the broader Middle East and supporting European security in light of the interconnected nature of the two regions.
Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Fuat Oktay also dismissed concerns that the pact could constitute an alternative to NATO.
"There were questions about whether an alternative to NATO was being created. Absolutely not," Oktay told reporters.
"This agreement will not undermine the territorial integrity or sovereignty of the three countries, nor any agreements they have concluded to date," he added.
Oktay said the pact would not alter the countries' legal standing, sovereignty or foreign and defense policies, stressing that it would not disrupt the coherence of Türkiye's foreign policy.

Opener Marques Ackerman struck a career-best 95 and Aiden Markram made 78 as South Africa reached 221-4 at tea on the opening day of the third Test against Australia at Newlands on Tuesday.
Ackerman and Markram shared a commanding 158-run opening partnership in 31.4 overs, putting the hosts in a strong position after Australia captain Pat Cummins won the toss and elected to bowl.
Ackerman, 30, playing only his second Test, looked set for a maiden century before falling five runs short when he charged spinner Nathan Lyon and was stumped attempting to clear the boundary.
Markram also fell after a productive innings, caught by Mitchell Starc on the boundary off Josh Hazlewood.
Australia then struck twice more to contain South Africa's progress, with Lyon bowling captain Temba Bavuma for a duck before left-arm spinner Cooper Connolly trapped Matthew Breetzke lbw for two.
David Bedingham was unbeaten on 41 at the interval, with Ryan Rickelton on two as South Africa looked to rebuild in the final session.
Cummins opted to bowl in sunny conditions, citing moisture in the pitch. It was only the 12th time a team had chosen to field first in a Test at Newlands since 1889, with five of the previous 11 matches won by the side making that decision.
Earlier, Australia made four changes after their innings and 31-run defeat in the second Test at Gqeberha, bringing in Cameron Green, wicket-keeper Josh Inglis, Connolly and Lyon.
Steve Smith was ruled out with a neck injury after failing to recover in time, while Nic Maddinson, Beau Webster and Scott Boland were also omitted. Boland had taken five wickets in the previous Test and scored 40 as a night-watchman.
Marnus Labuschagne retained his place despite going 47 international innings without a century, equalling Australia's record for the longest such drought.
South Africa made one change, with fast bowler Gerald Coetzee replacing the injured Anrich Nortje.
The three-match Test series is level at 1-1 after Australia won the opening Test in Durban by 214 runs before South Africa responded emphatically in Gqeberha.

items.author: Faran Khan
items.content:
Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari on Tuesday said the Sindh Assembly had already made its decision on the issue of further administrative units in the province and the debate should now be put to rest.
Speaking to reporters after inaugurating the expansion of the public-private project to uplift the Dr Kaikhusrow Nanabhoy Spencer's Eye Hospital, established in 1938, in Karachi, Bilawal reiterated the PPP's stance against division of Sindh.
“The party and the Sindh Assembly have repeatedly made their position clear [against division of Sindh],” Bilawal said, adding that the province's elected representatives had reflected the will of its people.
He maintained that only the people of Sindh could decide the province's future and that no one else had the right to determine the fate of its cities. The PPP scion also called for an end to the debate, saying the people had already settled the matter.
لائیو: پاکستان پیپلزپارٹی کے چیئرمین بلاول بھٹو زرداری لیاری ٹاؤن میں تاریخی ڈاکٹر کیخسرو نانابھائے اسپینسرز آئی اسپتال کے دورے کے بعد میڈیا سے گفتگو کررہے ہیں۔ https://t.co/OBEICH2O0l
— PPP (@MediaCellPPP) October 27, 2026
During the media briefing, the Bhutto scion reponded in negative, when asked whether the federal government or its coalition partners had discussed proposals to amend the 18th Amendment through a proposed 28th Constitutional Amendment.
The PPP chairman lambasted “certain” political representatives for promoting division and hatred among people instead of addressing the people’s issues.
He also took to task the federal government for stifling Karachi's rightful share.
“Karachi is Pakistan's economic hub and requires strong cooperation among federal, provincial and local authorities,” he stated, stressing, “Its administrative structure is such that public services could be improved only if all institutions worked together.”
Read: MQM-P calls for new administrative units to address urban Sindh’s woes
He then asserted that the federal government and other institutions needed to pay attention to the provincial capital's development.
Turning to the issues hampering the city's progress, Bilawal expressed concern over the worsening electricity crisis and said electricity was either unavailable or too expensive for consumers. He said the electricity crisis was affecting people across Sindh and the country, while the prevailing economic circumstances had made the situation even more difficult for people.
Therefore, he said Spencer Eye Hospital had been upgraded to use solar power to avoid grid electricity woes. Bilawal also expressed a desire to extend similar arrangements across Lyari to provide residents with electricity at affordable rates.
The PPP chairman said he was pleased to see Spencer Eye Hospital operational and providing free treatment to the public.
“Healthcare was a sector in which people constantly needed assistance,” he said, while acknowledging that treatment at private hospitals remained prohibitively expensive.
Read more: Mpox claims another child's life in Sindh, this year's death toll rises to 12
“With people facing mounting economic difficulties, the Sindh government and Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) are making efforts to ease the financial burden on citizens,” he stated during the media briefing. He also appreciated Karachi Mayor Barrister Murtaza Wahab for undertaking development projects for the betterment of the city.
Speaking at the inauguration ceremony, the Karachi mayor said the foundation stone of Spencer Eye Hospital was laid in 1938, and the facility became operational in 1940. Describing it as part of Karachi’s historic heritage, he said the hospital had remained closed for a period before the authorities began work on its restoration.
“Under a public-private partnership, the facility had been equipped with modern amenities and is now providing free medical examinations and outpatient department services,” he outlined.
The hospital’s operation theatre had also been made functional, while medicines and spectacles were being provided at discounted rates, Mayor Wahab added.
The mayor concluded his speech saying that further steps would be taken to improve the hospital’s facilities under Bilawal’s guidance.
Debate over new administrative units in Sindh
The debate over new administrative units in Sindh centres on whether creating smaller, empowered units would improve governance or threaten the province’s territorial integrity.
The MQM-P is the principal advocate of the new administrative units. Party leaders Mustafa Kamal, Farooq Sattar and chairman Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui argue that Pakistan’s growing population requires a new administrative structure with stronger local governments. The party also demands greater control over the resources and public services of Karachi, Hyderabad and other urban areas.
Federal Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has also backed the creation of additional provinces or administrative units, asserting that the existing governance system had failed to deliver justice and opportunities.
He maintained that restructuring would improve accountability and ensure a fairer distribution of resources, highlighting that the move would strengthen governance and not target any ethnic community.
The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) strongly opposes any move to divide Sindh or alter its territorial boundaries. The party argues that Sindh has a distinct historical, cultural and constitutional identity that must be protected. On September 3, the Sindh Assembly unanimously passed a resolution rejecting proposals to divide the province or detach any of its districts.
The disagreement remains unresolved.
The constitutional framework is also central to the dispute: Article 239 (4) of the constitution requires a two-thirds majority of the provincial assembly’s total membership before a constitutional amendment altering a province’s boundaries can be presented for presidential assent.
Furthermore, the 18th constitutional amendment has also allowed provinces to exercise greater control over localised decisions, and some quarters within the coalition government are deliberating on another amendment to trim certain powers of the provincial government.
The debate therefore involves not only governance but also constitutional authority, political representation and the future structure of the federation.

items.content:
Luxury watch brand Rotoris has raised $8.5 Mn (₹80.9 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures. The round also saw participation from 100Unicorns, Centricity, Diwakar Goel’s family office, Atul Singh’s family office, Adhiraj Burman’s family office, and Rannvijay Singha.
The D2C startup said it would deploy the fresh capital towards research and development, expanding production capacity, and growing its Rotoris House retail footprint in India and overseas, including Mumbai and New York.
Founded in 2025 by Bella Vita’s founder Aakash Anand, Wolfpack Labs’ founding partner Prerna Gupta, and Drink Free Advertising Media’s cofounders Anant Narula and Kunal Kapania, Rotoris aims to build “India’s first global watch brand”. It operates as a luxury watch brand, selling limited-edition watches through an invitation-only membership programme called the Rotoris Registry.
Rotoris assembles and tests its watches at its Rotoris Atelier in Gurugram, using machinery sourced from Switzerland. The startup said its assembly processes were established with guidance from Swiss horologists with experience at watchmakers and luxury brands such as Patek Philippe, IWC and Tiffany & Co.
“The design creates the desire, but the engineering, assembly and attention to detail earn the trust. We are building both sides of Rotoris with the same level of intention,” Gupta said.
The startup launched its first collection of 2,100 numbered watches in February 2026, which it claims sold out within days. Since then, nearly 1 Lakh people have registered for access to its collections, with around 40% of demand coming from international markets, including the US, Dubai and Australia.
Prior to this round, Rotoris bagged $3 Mn in a seed funding round co-led by Zerodha’s Nikhil Kamath, VC firms Venture Catalysts and 100Unicorns as well as actor Vivek Oberoi and content creator Tanmay Bhat, in December last year.
The country’s luxury watch market size is expected to grow at a 5.7% CAGR from $1.8 Bn in 2025 to $2.9 Bn by 2034. In this growing market, the analog watch segment holds the leading type share at 62.4% in 2025, while the men’s segment leads end user demand at 48.9%.
Rotoris bids to challenge the legacy luxury watch brands like Seiko, Tissot, Citizen, and Rado, who have established a strong foothold in the segment. Beside the Aakash Anand-led startup, Bangalore Watch Company and Jaipur Watch Company are also emerging contenders in the premium watch category.

An Indian court allowed Bollywood actor Imran Khan ‌to remain in the country until at least November 2, local media said on Tuesday, pausing a government order that asked him to leave for breaching immigration laws by allegedly participating in a protest.
Khan, 43, is a US ​citizen and was asked to leave the country by October 28 after he was accused of ​joining protests in Mumbai against the country's election chief this month.
 
Under Indian law, ⁠the participation of foreigners in political protests can be treated as a violation of immigration and ​visa rules.
Khan appealed against the order in the Bombay High Court, saying it was unconstitutional and arbitrary, ​local media reported.
There was no evidence to show that Khan participated in the protest and mobilised a crowd, his lawyer said in the appeal, legal website Live Law reported.
On Tuesday, the Bombay High Court postponed the hearing to November ​2 due to technical reasons and said that the order Khan had challenged would remain on ​hold until then, legal website Bar and Bench posted on X.
There has been no official statement from Mumbai Police ‌on ⁠Khan’s case. The city's police chief did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
A nephew of actor Aamir Khan, Imran belongs to a prominent film family. He acted in several hit Bollywood films from 2008 to 2015, before suddenly retiring.
His partner, Lekha Washington, said in a post on her Instagram ​page on October 12 ​that she, Khan, his ⁠mother and a cousin walked toward the protest site to ask about a friend who had been detained by police and were immediately surrounded by ​media representatives.
"He (Imran) responded to the questions of the media, saying we have ​no demands, ⁠we are not part of an organisation," Washington said in the post.
Both Khan and Washington posted pictures from inside what appeared to be a police van on the day of the protests, smiling into the ⁠camera.
The rally ​in Mumbai was one of several protests across the country ​demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over what opposition parties and activists say is a revision of voter lists that ​benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party.

items.author: Life And Style Desk
items.content:
Humayun Saeed believes Pakistani dramas deserve greater international visibility, including on streaming platforms such as Netflix, but says the country needs to develop its own over-the-top (OTT) platform to help local productions reach wider audiences.
In an interview with Ali Salman, the actor and producer discussed the distinctive style of Pakistani television, the challenges facing the local streaming industry, the role of social media in discovering new talent and the lessons he learnt while working on the international series The Crown.
Speaking about the possibility of Pakistani dramas reaching Netflix, Saeed said local productions had a distinct identity, particularly in their writing, dialogue delivery and use of Urdu. “Our dramas have a specific style. The writing also has its own style. When we deliver our lines, there is a way of speaking because of the way our Urdu is delivered,” he said.
Acknowledging that OTT productions often adopt a different, edgier approach, Saeed maintained that existing Pakistani dramas could still find an audience on international streaming platforms. “If you are saying the dramas we have already made should go on Netflix, then yes. We do have our own style,” he said.
Saeed suggested that political considerations might influence Netflix’s approach to Pakistan, although he admitted he was unsure when local productions might become available on the platform. 
Rather than relying solely on international streaming services, the actor stressed the importance of establishing a local OTT platform where Pakistani filmmakers and actors could showcase their work.
“Where there will be a platform, things will be made. Pakistani OTT will be made and once people show their work, then there will be Netflix,” he said, pointing to India’s experience as an example. “Even in India, these OTT platforms came first,” he added.
Saeed also called on the government to give the entertainment industry greater attention and support. “I think the government should do something about it and give importance to it,” he said.
Social media is opening doors for new talent
Beyond streaming platforms, Saeed discussed how social media had changed the way aspiring actors entered the entertainment industry.
He recalled a time when newcomers had to audition, meet directors, learn from experienced professionals and rehearse before securing roles. Platforms such as TikTok now allow people to showcase their skills directly, creating new opportunities while making it more difficult to distinguish acting ability from online popularity.
Citing Hania Aamir as an example, Saeed recalled discovering the actor through Dubsmash before casting her in a drama. “The thing is that even I saw Hania on Dubsmash and then we took her in a drama so there is potential,” he said.
However, he cautioned that performing well in short social media videos did not necessarily translate into the ability to handle a scripted role. An actor’s skills became clearer when they were given proper dialogue and scenes to perform, he suggested.
Saeed also reflected on his own unconventional entry into showbiz, revealing that he had been working in a factory before an opportunity led him towards acting.
He said Nadeem Ahmad, whose factories he helped manage, had an interest in modelling and encouraged him to attend an audition after enjoying a celebratory show Saeed had organised.
“One day, I held a celebratory show with performances and he really enjoyed it. He used to be called for interviews and auditions and one day, he told me to go for one,” Saeed recalled. “When I went, I got a drama,” he added.
What The Crown taught him about discipline
Saeed also spoke about his experience working on the Netflix series The Crown, in which he portrayed Dr Hasnat Khan. He said one of the most important lessons he took away from the international production was the value of discipline, organisation and professionalism.
He described the production’s carefully planned arrangements, from transport and make-up timings to meals and call times, contrasting them with what he considered less structured practices in Pakistan’s entertainment industry.
“I wanted to learn discipline,” he said, recalling how his co-star Elizabeth Debicki remained focused on her work and followed a strict schedule.
“The actor, Elizabeth who was with me. She was so involved in her work. When she had lunch at 1pm, she knew exactly when she had to be back. She also focused so much on her work so that that the scene could be what it was. Here, we just think about having fun while filming,” he said.
Saeed added that international productions communicated schedules clearly, ensuring cast members knew when to have breakfast and report to the set. “We here are not as organised as producers here, so it would take time for actors to be as well,” he confessed.
Does not consider himself a star
Despite his success as an actor and producer, he rejected the idea that his profession automatically made him a star.
“I do not see myself as a star. This is just my work. You are not a star for doing it. I think Fahad Mustafa and Fawad Khan must be stars,” he said.
Saeed added that he preferred to work in his own way, enjoyed producing projects and kept his social circle small.
His latest released film is Love Guru (2025), a romantic comedy directed by Nadeem Baig and co-starring Mahira Khan. On television, he appeared in Main Manto Nahi Hoon in 2025. He has also been associated with the Jawani Phir Nahi Ani franchise, with Jawani Phir Nahi Ani 3 reportedly in development.

items.author: Leocadia Bongben
items.content:
Oil rigs threaten biodiversity and compromise the well-being of coastal and Indigenous communities
Originally published on Global Voices
Offshore platform from Garand-Batanga Beach, Kribi South region of Cameroon. Photo by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.
This story by Leocadia Bongben was produced with the support of Internews’ Earth Journalism Network.
Dede Sluk, 35, a father of three, sits pensively in front of his plank house, fishing nets hanging at the corner, wondering how to fish for his family and prepare his children for school. Sluk lives in the village of Grand-Batanga 2 in Kribi, in southern Cameroon. Like many fishermen there, Sluk is annoyed by the lack of access to fish beyond the offshore platforms. He states,
We don’t have access to areas with high fish stock; the Battaillon D’intervention Rapid (BIR), a special army unit guarding the petroleum platform, prohibits passage.
According to the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative’s (EITI) 2023 report, oil and gas contributed FCFA 774.51 billion (USD 1.3 million) to Cameroon’s budget. However, these oil rigs threaten biodiversity and compromise the well-being of coastal and Indigenous communities.
Offshore oil and gas platforms are massive marine structures used to explore, drill, extract, and process petroleum and natural gas from rocky layers beneath the ocean floor; some require the laying of pipes. The yellow flames and smoke from the Ebome Marine Terminal, a petroleum rig operated by Perenco and SNH west of Grand Batanga, are visible 6.5 kilometers (4.04 miles) from the Kribi coastline.
Two other platforms are the Sanaga 2 offshore facility around Kribi, connected via undersea pipelines from onshore in Bipaga. West of the Kribi Port is the Kome-Kribi 1 Terminal (FSO), built in 2003, operated by Cameroon Oil Transport Company — the Chad-Cameroon pipeline. Meanwhile, the Hilli Episeyo, operated by Golar LNG, Perenco, and the National Hydrocarbons Corporation (SNH), departed in July 2026, after eight years.
Among the platforms of concern are those operated by Perenco, a Franco-British company and a prominent player in the oil and gas sector, tagged as an opaque multinational by Friends of the Earth for oil spills, wastewater discharges, gas flaring, and old pipelines crossing rivers. An Info Congo investigation indicted Perenco for flaring and environmental hazards, endangering the coastal ecosystem and the health of local communities.
Tar balls found in a marine protected area, dolphin and whale strandings, and fish scarcity are hidden costs of offshore oil and gas exploitation, which seems to stall Cameroon’s progress towards the 30×30 marine target under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Fish scarcity linked to petroleum platforms
Laure Ndingue, 50, a mother of five who worked as a fish roaster along Grand Batanga beach for over 10 years, knows that, opposite her charcoal braise, an oil and gas platform sits in the ocean. She recalls,
Growing up, six barfish were sold for FCFA 500 (USD 0.85); the price jumped to FCFA 1,000 (USD 1.70) and now is FCFA 5000 (USD 8.54) per kilogram. Even frozen fish is now expensive. Before, we were not suffering; fish stocks have declined.
Petroleum exploitation is done when the platform is planted on a rock, and most times, the rocks are marine ecosystems that breed fish. Now, the rocks are occupied by offshore installations, contributing to reduced fish stocks, explains Divine Francois Xavier Mbunje, a fisherman, geologist, and president of the 150-fishermen union at the Grand Batanga beach.
He suggests the government can demarcate platforms and areas of high fish concentration. About a kilometer or two from the beach, there is no fish, and three kilometers deep, we can have around forty kilograms of fish. Sluk proposes that oil and gas platforms should help the local population with activities like fish farming, loans to make up for the fish scarcity, recommending that the government provide a loan scheme and subsidize the purchase of motorized equipment, as this will help the fishers go further into the ocean.
He estimates the required nylon fishing gear for a fisherman at FCFA 1 million (USD 1,720) and FCFA 1,500,000 (USD 2,572) for an engine. Sluk explains,
Motorised gear will help us fish towards Ntem, Lokonje, and Douala away from the offshore platforms. We now rely on crabs to feed the family, with fish becoming rare.
Smelly, oily nets and tar balls
Early in 2026, fishermen reported oil on their nets smelling like crude. “I was fishing and witnessed this strange phenomenon, which lasted for more than three weeks and gradually disappeared,” says Ebodje Emile, a fisherman in Ebodje village, where the marine protected area is situated, 50 kilometers (31.1 miles) from Kribi. Leon Kisito Bekwale, who has fished for about 35 years, still has nets his fishermen used, colored by oil. Still looking worried, he turns the nets dumped at the corner of the house to reveal the dark, oily parts.
Leon Kisito holding oily nets in Ebodje, Cameroon. Photo by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.
“I don’t know if this is linked to the offshore gas and oil,” Bekwale says, explaining that the wooden local boats only go for about three kilometers, suggesting the substance was inside the marine protected area, far from the petroleum platforms. Fishermen reported the phenomenon to the park conservator and NGOs.
A Perenco spokesperson told Global Voices via email:
We are not aware of any issues in the field across our sites, whether at the Northern or Southern sites. The comment may be referring to the northern coast of Cameroon, bordering Nigeria, where we have witnessed oil slicks drifting from Nigeria to Cameroon over recent years (possibly related to tanker discharge of oily waste or activities in Nigerian oil fields). This does not relate to any Perenco activity. Cameroon security forces are patrolling our sites and have also not reported any incidents.
Dr Jean Kenfack, focal point for seas and oceans at the Ministry of Environment, Nature Protection and Sustainable Development, MINEPDED, also doubts the incident, outlining the procedure to inform the ministry of the incident: “In case of an incident, the departmental delegate sends the information to the ministry. In case of a spillage, an inspection mission is deployed to identify the author for sanctions if confirmed, and there is a pumping station in Kribi managed by the ministry with SNH and the Marines.”
Meanwhile, marine biologist Joel Wanba, Megafauna Officer at Tube Awu in Ebodje, who links the oily substance to activities along the coast, says, “But we do not have the means to analyze the substance given the small NGO budget; it is difficult to conduct such research.
Tar balls linked to offshore platforms form when crude oil spills into water. They are frequent along the coast and in the Manyange Na Elombo Campo marine protected area”, says Wamba. “This area is noted for sea turtles that may mistake tar balls for food, leading to indigestion and death. When we see residues, it indicates a malfunction. Contaminants build up in fish and other marine life over time when exposed to polluted water. When we eat contaminated fish, those toxins build up in our own bodies too, ” Wanba states. By obstructing sunlight, hurting living tissue, and harming the surrounding ocean environment, oil and gas spills damage seagrass beds and coral reefs, he adds.
Tar-Balls-in-Ebodje-Kribi-Cameroon by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.
Tube Awu surveyed eight sites using bioindicators (living plants, animals, and microbes whose presence or absence suggests environmental health), which were not found at all sites, revealing an unhealthy environment and dying corals, according to Wamba.
Whales and dolphins stranding
The African Marine Mammal Organization (AMCO), Cedric Fogwan, a marine biologist, reveals how offshore exploitation affects marine biodiversity. “Offshore exploitation impacts mostly whales, dolphins, and marine turtles, as their activities disrupt animal freedom. The sharks and whales no longer have any space for their nesting activity and the possibility of feeding on coral reefs,” he states. “Whales and dolphins that live in shallow waters use echolocation to communicate. Offshore activities’ noise interferes with echolocation behavior, leading to strandings — whales or dolphins washing up on the shore — because they are disoriented and lose direction getting to areas too shallow for them to survive or get entangled in a net they couldn’t locate,” Fogwan says.
Experts say installing pipes destroys coral balance, the most important marine biodiversity habitats that support animals like dolphins, sharks, turtles, and whales. Consequently, platforms reduce bottom diversity, killing everything underneath when the structure is placed over their habitat. However, for those platforms that stay for only a short time, the ecosystem can restore itself, Fogwan states.
Citing model nations like the Seychelles and Zanzibar Island, growing tourism based on the conservation of their natural resources, he laments that development is frequently perceived as building harbors and exploiting oil, activities that are not sustainable.
Management of marine environmental hazards
MINEPDED oversees environmental protection, including offshore exploitation. The Petroleum Code and the Abidjan Convention set out rules to combat marine pollution in West and Central Africa, while SNH oversees the National Oil Spillage Contingency Plan. Cameroon adopted its National Environmental Management Plan (NEMP) in 1996, which incorporates pollution control, risk mitigation, and environmental impact assessments (EIAs) before starting development projects. However, it is not clear how regulations are respected.
According to J. Folack, a researcher at IRAD RHSM, budgetary constraints, a lack of target-oriented research, and competing responsibilities of the ministries involved in coastal zone management hinder NEMP implementation.
MINEPDED's yearly inspections verify if environmental impact studies on potential hazards are updated, and semester environmental management plans for offshore platforms are checked for grey areas; however, the results are not public.
“With demarcation and good fishing gear, we can get enough to feed our families, and sell some to change our standard of living,” Sluk concludes.
Fisherman with a wooden boat at Ebodje Beach in Cameroon. Photo by Leocadia Bongben. Used with permission.
Written by Leocadia Bongben

items.summary:

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Healthtech startup Cent, launched by Practo cofounder Shashank ND earlier this year, announced the raise of $15 Mn (about ₹143 Cr) in a Series A round led by Blume Ventures and existing investor South Park Commons (SPC), with participation from individual investors including former Vodafone CEO Arun Sarin and former OpenAI B2B CTO Srinivas Narayanan, among others.
The fresh capital will be deployed to strengthen the preventive healthcare startup’s R&D function. Besides, the startup also intends to expand its AI, engineering and clinical teams.
Apart from the fundraise, Cent also announced the acquisition of Medsee, an AI-powered radiology reporting workflow platform, to help it deliver faster and more consistent reporting as scan volumes increase.
Cent was launched by Shashank, along with ex-Ola Electric CMO Anshul Khandelwal and former Lenskart product head Arpit Garg earlier this year. It last raised a $5 Mn seed funding round back then from OneFlow Holdings and South Park Commons.
Bidding to build a positioning of helping users live a hundred years, Cent combines precision radiology, AI, and biomarkers to screen asymptomatic patients for over 300 conditions like cardiac disease, cancer, and neurological disorders.
Its flagship offering, Cent Check, combines full-body MRI, low-dose CT, DEXA scans, ECG, echocardiography in a single visit lasting around two hours. Its proprietary CCNM protocol is designed to assess cancer, cardiac, neurological and metabolic health risks.
It uses AI to consolidate findings from different diagnostic modalities and generate organ-level risk assessments, while AI-assisted imaging helps reduce MRI scan times, with an aim to identify serious conditions before symptoms begin to surface.
Its comprehensive health screening package is priced at ₹27,500, positioning itself as an alternative to conventional preventive health checkups that largely rely on blood tests and limited imaging.
The startup said it has completed 10,000 preventive whole-body scans across Bengaluru, Mumbai and Delhi NCR since inception. It aims to scale this to 1 Cr scans by 2035.
Cent plans to use the data generated through its scans to establish health baselines for asymptomatic Indians, train models to identify disease risks earlier and support clinical research.

items.summary:

The company was preparing to obtain the financing to strengthen its financial resources amid ongoing military tensions in the Middle East, risks to oil exports and an uncertain economic outlook.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco is close to securing a $10 billion loan from a large group of international banks, according to a special report published by Bloomberg on Monday.
The company was preparing to obtain the financing to strengthen its financial resources amid ongoing military tensions in the Middle East, risks to oil exports and an uncertain economic outlook.
The report said Saudi Aramco could sign an agreement with global banks for a new loan of around $10b in the coming weeks, adding that talks with US, British, Chinese and Japanese banks had reached their final stages.
Sources familiar with the development, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the company was seeking a credit facility that would let it draw funds up to a specified limit as needed. The facility would be revolving credit, meaning Aramco would not have to take the entire amount at once.
Read: Aramco halts October crude deliveries to some European refiners after pipeline attack: report
Saudi Arabian state-backed oil company Aramco is nearing agreement with international banks on a $10 billion loan that would bolster its finances as conflicts in the Middle East threaten crude exports https://t.co/J8WYQJisYx
— Bloomberg (@business) October 26, 2026
It could use the funds when needed and, after repayment, draw them again under the agreed terms.
Major banks from US, UK, China and Japan to provide loan
According to Bloomberg, several major global banks were expected to participate in the proposed loan for Saudi Aramco. They include JPMorgan Chase and Citigroup of the United States, HSBC of the United Kingdom, Bank of China and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, and Japan’s Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group.
The participation of financial institutions from several countries indicates that major international banks remain interested in providing financial facilities to Saudi Aramco despite ongoing military tensions in the region. Sources said the proposed interest rate could be 60 basis points above SOFR, the benchmark rate used for US dollar financing.
In financial terms, 60 basis points equal 0.60%. Thus, the applicable interest rate would be 0.60% above the relevant benchmark, although the final cost would depend on the agreement’s terms and any other potential fees.
Bloomberg reported that Saudi Aramco and some of the major banks involved declined to comment, while an immediate response could not be obtained from the Chinese banks. Therefore, the loan amount and terms are being viewed as details of ongoing negotiations rather than a finalised agreement.
أرامكو تقترب من توقيع اتفاقية قرض بـ10 مليارات دولار مع بنوك عالمية بحسب بلومبرغ #العربيةـBusiness
— العربية Business (@AlArabiya_Bn) October 26, 2026
Important decision amid Iran war and risks to oil exports
Saudi Aramco’s plan comes as ongoing military tensions in the Middle East have affected global energy markets and oil shipments from Gulf countries. The war with Iran has pushed up crude oil prices in global markets, increasing the possibility of higher revenue for Saudi Aramco.
At the same time, military attacks, disruptions to maritime routes and threats to oil facilities have created new challenges for the company. In recent weeks, Yemen’s Houthi group has claimed attacks on Saudi oil facilities, refineries and key facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.
Read More: Houthis hit Aramco HQ, vow more attacks
These actions, along with disruption to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, have increased uncertainty surrounding oil exports and transportation costs. In these circumstances, securing a $10b credit facility from banks could provide Aramco with additional financial flexibility, allowing it to access capital quickly when needed and continue its business activities.
Saudi Aramco previously arranged a $10b revolving credit facility in 2024, according to Bloomberg. Of this, $7b was provided through international banks, while an additional $3b was obtained from regional banks under Islamic murabaha financing.
Murabaha is a method used in Islamic finance in which capital is provided under specific commercial and financial terms instead of a conventional interest-bearing loan. The new agreement would give Aramco another important facility to meet its financial needs.
However, it is unclear whether the company will replace or renew the existing facility under the new arrangement, or use it as additional financial capacity. It is also important not to equate the $10b credit facility immediately with an equal increase in the company’s debt, as a revolving facility allows the company to use funds according to its needs, while undrawn funds do not necessarily become payable debt.
Gulf energy companies increasing reliance on global debt markets
Amid the ongoing war and trade disruptions in the Middle East, major Gulf energy and power companies have also increasingly sought financial resources from banks. Bloomberg reported that QatarEnergy, Qatar’s state-owned energy company, obtained a $3b loan this month with significant participation from Chinese banks.
Saudi Electricity Company arranged Islamic murabaha financing worth 15.8b riyals, or approximately $4.1b, in July. Seven Gulf banks participated in that agreement.
These financial arrangements indicate that major companies in the region are trying to diversify their sources of funding amid uncertain global conditions, reducing reliance on any single market or financing method.
Saudi Aramco is considered one of the world’s largest oil-producing companies and plays a fundamental role in Saudi government revenues and the national economy. Changes in the company’s financial position, oil production and exports are important not only for Saudi Arabia but also for global energy markets.
According to Bloomberg, the proposed $10b loan could be signed in the coming weeks. However, the company or the relevant banks have not yet formally announced a finalised agreement.

items.author: Debarghya Sil
items.content:
VerSe Innovation, the parent of news aggregator Dailyhunt and short-video platform Josh, has seen two investment funds managed by Baillie Gifford mark down the value of their holdings by around 80% over different periods.
Pacific Horizon Investment Trust valued its holding in VerSe at £4.08 Mn as of July 2026, down 51.4% from £8.39 Mn a year earlier. The holding’s value has fallen 80.3% from £20.69 Mn ($27.7 Mn) in July 2024.
Separately, The Schiehallion Fund valued its VerSe holding at $7.47 Mn as of August 2026, down 78.2% from $34.31 Mn in January 2025.
ET reported that Schiehallion’s investment represented a 1.3% stake in VerSe, implying a company valuation of about $576 Mn – nearly 90% below its $5 Bn valuation in 2022.
The implied valuation reflects the fund’s assessment of its investment, rather than a price established through a fresh funding round.
VerSe’s $5 Bn Valuation Under Pressure
VerSe last raised a major funding round in April 2022, when it secured $805 Mn at a reported valuation of $5 Bn.
In August 2024, TechCrunch reported that investor 360 ONE had valued VerSe at around $2.9 Bn, about 42% below its 2022 valuation.
VerSe disputed that interpretation, saying the assessment did not represent its overall valuation and that other investors continued to value it at around $5 Bn. At the time, the company also said it had not conducted a price-discovery funding round since April 2022.
The latest portfolio disclosures show that investors continue to reassess the value of their holdings. However, they do not establish a definitive company-wide valuation.
Founded in 2007 by Virendra Gupta and later joined by cofounder Umang Bedi, VerSe Innovation operates news aggregator Dailyhunt and short-video platform Josh. The company has raised nearly $1.7 Bn across funding rounds from investors including Google, Microsoft, Peak XV Partners, Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, and Luxor Capital.
Revenue Growth, Lower Burn
Schiehallion had flagged concerns about VerSe’s performance in its interim report for the six months ended July 2025. The fund cited a deterioration in the company’s trajectory, including declining revenue, as the reason for a substantial downward revaluation during that period.
VerSe subsequently reported an improvement in its FY25 financial performance. According to the company, operating revenue rose 88% to ₹1,930 Cr from ₹1,029 Cr in FY24. Excluding acquisitions, operating revenue grew 33% to ₹1,373 Cr.
Its EBITDA burn, excluding non-cash expenses, narrowed 20% to ₹738 Cr from ₹920 Cr.
VerSe has been betting on acquisitions and adtech to diversify revenue. Its 2024 acquisition of Valueleaf was intended to strengthen advertiser targeting through NexVerse.ai, while Magzter expanded its subscription content business beyond advertising.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Ugandan startup XenFi is helping internet service providers (ISPs) and Wi-Fi hotspot operators sell internet access, manage customers and collect payments via mobile money from a single platform.
Founded in 2025, XenFi has built a hotspot billing and management platform that also lets operators monitor transactions and manage multiple MikroTik routers from a centralised dashboard.
“Many hotspot operators need to manage customer access, sell vouchers, collect payments, monitor revenue and administer multiple routers. Handling these processes through disconnected tools or manual systems can make it difficult to track transactions, maintain operational efficiency and scale,” said Charles Wasswa, XenFi’s CEO.
“XenFi brings these functions together through a centralised platform that supports mobile money payments and simplifies the management of hotspot businesses.”
The startup is self-funded by its founders, which Wasswa said forced discipline from the start.
“Starting without relying on external investors required us to be disciplined in how we allocated resources, developed our technology and acquired customers,” he said.
That approach has paid off. XenFi is already profitable and employs more than 100 people.
“Rather than treating profitability as the end goal, we are using it to strengthen our technology, expand our operations and reach more customers,” Wasswa said.
The platform serves approximately 6,000 active users in Uganda and has customers in close to 15 African countries, including Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi and Gabon. XenFi has also set up a physical presence in Kenya.
“Uptake has been encouraging,” said Wasswa. “Beyond Uganda, we are seeing adoption across other African markets, with businesses welcoming our system as a solution for managing their hotspot operations and payments.”
XenFi makes money through platform charges and billing and transaction fees, which vary by service and market.
“As our customers grow and process more activity through our platform, we have opportunities to grow our revenue alongside them,” Wasswa said.
The startup competes with international hotspot billing platforms, regional providers, locally developed billing tools and operators still relying on manual systems. Wasswa said XenFi stands out through its focus on African market needs, payment integration and ease of use.
Expansion has brought its own challenges.
“Payment systems, customer expectations, connectivity infrastructure and regulatory requirements differ from country to country, making international expansion a continuous learning process,” Wasswa said.
“Customers need reliable systems that support their businesses consistently, so we place considerable importance on product reliability, customer support and continuous improvement.”
XenFi now plans to deepen its presence in existing markets, strengthen local partnerships and move into more African countries.
“We are proud of how far we have come, but we see this as the beginning of a much larger journey,” said Wasswa.
