items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
We should begin where we must. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has his virtues. For one, he is not given to petty vindictiveness as former President Obasanjo too often was. Tinubu has not been involved in any open political fights with governors or lawmakers as Obasanjo did. Instead, he appears generally forgiving and conciliatory, having brought several of his fiercest political critics into his government. Also, unlike many of Nigeria’s previous leaders, Tinubu did not come to office by accident, nor was he enthroned by anyone. He arrived in office by sheer personal grit, itself an unusual thing in Nigerian political leadership at that level.
Now, the average Nigerian president is a very powerful person. How they wield that power, however, is the key difference between one president and another. Tinubu is no average Nigerian president. He sits above his party and the nation, in a way that no president has done since 1999. Nigerian ruling parties are characterised by internal dissent, factionalism, and opposition, which serve as a check on a president’s power, often better than can be expected from the official opposition parties. There is no such thing under Tinubu. By removing Senator Abdullahi Adamu as Chairman of the APC within weeks of assuming office, Tinubu made that point clear early on. Now, a personal anthem, “On your mandate we shall stand”, rings out at the mention of his name among officials and party faithful because everyone gets the message.
The President also has an iron grip on his cabinet, the National Assembly, the governors, the security agencies, anti-corruption agencies, and, as the rumours go, the courts, and perhaps INEC too. From 1960 to date, the National Assembly, particularly, has never been this pliant to a president, often passing executive bills in less than 48 hours, even before some members had a chance to read them. By removing officials without cause or notice, he has signalled that even the most favoured appointees can get the sack. He has induced the defection of all but one or two governors to his party, in name or at least in function. Criticism from the media, civil society, or labour has been blunted, if not outright buried, save for a few notable exceptions.
All of this leaves no one in doubt that Tinubu is the lion in Nigeria’s political jungle. Yet, Tinubu’s power is not backed by authority in that specific Weberian sense. Behind this image of an all-powerful president still lies something cosmetic. Obasanjo came to office with the charisma of a former head of state and national hero at multiple points in the country’s history. Buhari was the face of a political movement with more than 10 million loyal votes each election for nearly 20 years. Jonathan came to office by accident, but once there, he commanded the unflinching loyalty of nearly as many Nigerians as Buhari.
Tinubu has none of these. His personal anthem may ring out loud, but it rings hollow still because the President’s political coalition is held together not by popular admiration or ideological belief in his programme, but by the depth of his pocket or the fear of losing one’s job in a Nigeria that has grown much harsher economically for nearly all but those in government. Tinubu is quite possibly the most politically vulnerable president facing re-election since 1999. But the opposition lacks money, and the mass public lacks food. A clear majority of Nigerians may well not be happy with the current conditions in the country, but they lack the energy—or the hope—to put up a sustained fight.
And then there is the not-so-small matter of the incompetence of the government, although in a different sense than Nigerians are used to in their government. Few governments in Nigerian history have initiated as many far-reaching economic reforms from the start as the Tinubu administration: complete fuel subsidy removal, wholesale naira devaluation, free university tuition converted to loans, high electricity tariffs, tax reforms, and so on. Yet, the government clearly appears to lack the capacity to make a genuine success out of its own reforms, and by the end of the first year, all the swagger Tinubu came into office with had gone.
Far-reaching economic reforms generate costs and benefits, and thus, winners and losers. Who are the winners and losers of the fuel subsidy removal policy, for example? How can the policy be tweaked to spread the gains or mitigate the pains? How can we build a genuine political coalition strong enough to sustain the reforms beyond this administration? These are the questions that would engage a more competent reformer, and they would answer them with evidence-based policy adjustment, rather than a shouting match with Catholic bishops. Yet, beyond infographics that have little bearing on reality, you would struggle to find a serious policy paper or further policy actions produced by this government since 2023.
But it is in foreign policy that the real character of the current government is laid bare. Tinubu may be a lion at home, but he is a lamb on the world stage. As Daily Trust reported two weeks ago, Nigeria has agreed to a U.S. “America First Global Health Strategy” framework that effectively amounts to signing off our sovereignty for transactional aid. Under this agreement, Nigeria would provide U.S. companies with our health data on short notice. The companies manufacture drugs and vaccines they will resell back to us at huge profits, effectively turning Nigerian sickness into a cash cow for America. And all of this under a health minister who has talked the most about developing local manufacturing capacity in the healthcare sector.
Mortgaging Nigerian sovereignty—for a pittance or for free—is the norm under this government. Virtually every single foreign policy action this government has taken since 2023 has been either on behalf of or to the benefit of foreign countries, principally France, Britain, the United States, Israel, or Saudi Arabia. Nigeria itself gets almost nothing out of its foreign policy engagements. Under Tinubu, Nigeria has sparred with two neighbours on behalf of France; sold our tax administration to the same country without any receipts; accepted a controversial asylum-seeker deportation deal with Britain; joined a Red Sea Alliance with Saudi Arabia that has no discernible benefit for us; and watched almost helplessly as the United States promotes a narrative that directly threatens our fragile peace.
A bolder government has several countermeasures for each of these foreign policy engagements. France can train our tax officials, rather than hand over our entire system to them. A more strategic government should be capitalising on the current conflict in Europe and the Gulf to do deals that would pump out more of our oil and gas reserves. An Obasanjo or Yar’Adua would have more forcefully rejected the narrative of Christian genocide the U.S. is self-servingly imposing on us to fleece our resources like rare minerals and colonial healthcare deals. A bolder and more sovereignty-inclined Tinubu would at least get the nation to convene an open hearing on this issue, at least to take matters into our own hands.
For Tinubu’s foreign policy, however, the problem is not just the decisions or actions, but the approach and the attitude behind it. The government’s foreign policy actions are almost always conducted in complete secrecy. This means that the President may well be entangling Nigeria in unfavourable or unnecessary foreign arrangements that might be difficult for future leaders to repair. At a time when many countries on the continent are flexing self-determination muscles, the so-called Giant of Africa is crouched on the ground licking foreign what-not. Most disturbing of all, President Tinubu appears to believe that once an idea, policy, or agreement has the approving stamp of a Western government or Western-aligned international institutions like the World Bank and IMF, then such a policy or idea is automatically good for Nigeria. Our government appears unable or unwilling to go against any foreign governments or institutions. This is perhaps the sole reason the government has stuck to a punitive fuel subsidy removal that no one in the administration can point to the gains of with any confidence.
The government may yet be returned in this election. But some things cannot be left unsaid.
The post Tinubu: Lion at home, lamb abroad? By Suleiman A. Suleiman appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru
PRESIDENT Bola Tinubu has extended his heartfelt condolences to the Okonjo royal family of Ogwashi-Uku, Delta State, on the passing of Prof. Kamene Okonjo, who died at the age of 96.
Prof. Okonjo was a distinguished scholar, a champion of women’s empowerment, and a revered matriarch.
The President particularly commiserated with her daughter, Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Director-General of the World Trade Organisation, other family members, and the people of Ogwashi-Uku over the loss of their beloved mother, matriarch, and community leader.
President Tinubu described Prof. Okonjo’s passing as the loss of an accomplished academic whose life was defined by intellectual distinction, service to humanity, and an enduring commitment to advancing women and society.
He acknowledged her contributions to scholarship and her inspiring example as a woman who combined professional excellence with dedication to family, community, and the preservation of traditional institutions.
The President prayed that Almighty God will grant the departed eternal rest and comfort the family and all who mourn her passing.
Vanguard reports that Kamene Okonjo, a professor of sociology and advocate for women’s rights, died on Friday, according to reports citing a statement issued by the Umu Obi Obahai royal family of Ogwashi-Uku kingdom in Delta state.
Okonjo-Iweala, in a post on X on Sunday, thanked friends and followers for their messages of condolence and support to her family.
“Today, I have been overwhelmed with messages of condolences and tributes to my wonderful mother.
“I just want to thank all my friends and followers and let you know how appreciative my entire family and I are of your support.
“My mother lived a quality life till the end and we are very grateful we had her for so long. May her soul rest in perfect peace.” She wrote

items.title: Soldiers earn peanuts, APC youth leader flaunts billion-naira SUVs  —  Utomi
items.summary:
Professor Pat Utomi has criticised the All Progressives Congress (APC) over the distribution of luxury sport utility vehicles (SUVs) to selected youth leaders, contrasting the expenditure with what he described as poor salaries paid to Nigerian soldiers.
Utomi, a chieftain of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), said it was troubling that an APC youth leader could display expensive vehicles at a time Nigerians had been told that government funds were limited.

items.author: Akinbayo Wahab
items.content:
Professor Pat Utomi has criticised the All Progressives Congress (APC) over the distribution of luxury sport utility vehicles (SUVs) to selected youth leaders, contrasting the expenditure with what he described as poor salaries paid to Nigerian soldiers.
Utomi, a chieftain of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), said it was troubling that an APC youth leader could display expensive vehicles at a time Nigerians had been told that government funds were limited.
In a post on X on Sunday, Utomi wrote: “Nigerian soldiers are being paid peanuts as salaries, yet an APC youth leader is flaunting SUVs worth billions of naira. This is the same government that told Nigerians there was no longer money in the treasury. At this point, they must think we are fools!”
In another post, the professor questioned whether the money spent on the vehicles could have been put to better use, particularly in the health sector.
“Each of the SUVs in this video costs more than ₦100 million. I wonder how many world-class ambulances the millions being spent on these vehicles could buy. What a pity!” he wrote.
The comments followed a video posted by APC National Youth Leader, Dayo Israel, showing brand-new 2026 Toyota Prado SUVs he said were presented to selected youth leaders to support election mobilisation ahead of the 2027 general elections.
“Today, I presented brand new 2026 Prado to my committed selected youth leaders to aid their election mobilisation activities,” Israel wrote.
He also expressed gratitude to First Lady Oluremi Tinubu for what he described as her continued support for the party’s structure under his leadership.
“The party is supreme and that supremacy will show in our action in this election period — we will deliver polling unit by polling unit,” he added.
The video, which has since been deleted, drew criticism from Nigerians on social media, with some questioning the timing of the vehicle distribution amid the economic hardship associated with the Tinubu administration’s reforms.
Utomi’s remarks add to the criticism surrounding the display, with the NDC chieftain raising questions about public spending priorities and the cost of the vehicles.

items.author: efosataiwo@vanguardngr.com
items.content:
Kylian Mbappe struck twice to earn Jose Mourinho’s Real Madrid a 2-1 Clasico victory over La Liga leaders Barcelona on Sunday at Camp Nou, cutting the gap to three points.
French superstar Mbappe opened the scoring before the interval and then slotted home late on to inflict Barca’s first domestic defeat of the campaign after Raphinha had equalised for the champions.
Real Madrid remain third, behind Atletico Madrid and Hansi Flick’s Barca, who had won their first nine games before a chastening week.
The Catalans suffered a second straight defeat after losing on Tuesday against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League.
Barca had won six of the seven previous Clasicos since the German arrived but were surprisingly subdued against Mourinho’s side.
Los Blancos, without suspended winger Vinicius Junior, won their fifth straight game across all competitions and are finding their footing under veteran Portuguese coach Mourinho.
The opening period of the game was cagey, with few opportunities.
Barca defender Pau Cubarsi twice reacted well to shut down Mbappe, while Real Madrid’s Marc Cucurella took a rapid liking for Lamine Yamal’s shirt, constantly grabbing at the 19-year-old winger.
Anthony Gordon, playing in his first Clasico since joining Barcelona from Newcastle, backheeled the ball to Raphinha, who fired narrowly wide as Barca threatened.
The hosts were dealt a setback when young defender Xavi Espart pulled up hurt and needed to be replaced by Alejandro Balde before the half-hour mark.
Andriy Lunin, playing in goal for Madrid after Thibaut Courtois pulled out of the squad with flu, saved at his near post from Gordon before the visitors took the lead.
Mbappe scored his 10th league goal of the season and also his easiest, with Barca’s Gerard Martin clearing a cross straight at the Frenchman, who deflected it into the net.
Barca responded by carving out a glorious chance for an equaliser but teenage sensation Yamal for once miscued in front of goal, firing wide when poised to level.
The game opened up and Yan Diomande came close to doubling Madrid’s lead before half-time, drilling into the side-netting.
– Sting in the tail –
Martin redeemed himself early in the second half as he held off Jude Bellingham, who could neither beat the defender nor find a free Mbappe.
Raphinha, who had a quiet first half, pulled Barcelona level just after the hour mark.
Pedri fed the Brazilian, La Liga’s top goalscorer with 13, who fired through Bellingham’s legs and Lunin could not keep the shot out.
The Ukrainian goalkeeper did make a superb save to deny Martin at a corner, as Barcelona flowed forward with the wind finally in their sails.
Yamal bent an effort wide with Lunin at full stretch and Barca substitute Frenkie de Jong had a shot desperately blocked by Dean Huijsen.
There was a sting in the tail for the Catalans though as substitute Gabriel Jesus lost possession and Madrid raced through on goal.
Eduardo Camavinga beat Cubarsi and unselfishly cut the ball back for Mbappe to tuck home his second of the night into an empty net with Joan Garcia drawn out of position.

items.author: efosataiwo@vanguardngr.com
items.content:
The Lagos State Government has reiterated its readiness to prevent, detect and respond to potential Ebola threats, urging residents to remain calm and vigilant.
The state Commissioner for Health, Prof. Akin Abayomi, in a statement on Sunday assured residents that there was no Ebola case in Lagos.
Abayomi’s reassurance followed the confirmation of an imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus in Abuja.
He disclosed that the state Ministry of Health, through its Directorate of Epidemiology, Biosecurity and Global Health, was strengthening disease surveillance, risk communication and community engagement.
According to him, the state is also collaborating with agencies at points of entry, including the Murtala Muhammed International Airport (MMIA), to enhance early detection and response to suspected cases.
“As part of its preparedness efforts, the State has conducted a strategic engagement and assessment at MMIA with airport management, Port Health Services and other aviation and public health stakeholders.
“The engagement focused on passenger screening, information sharing, infection prevention and control, and coordination of emergency response measures.
“The ministry is also intensifying public enlightenment through educational materials on Ebola, its symptoms, transmission and prevention,” Abayomi said.
Ebola Virus Disease is a severe illness that can be fatal.
It spreads primarily through direct contact with the blood and other body fluids of an infected person who is showing symptoms, contaminated materials, or the bodies of people who have died from the disease.
Infection may also occur through contact with infected animals.
The commissioner advised residents to avoid contact with potentially infectious materials and rely on verified information rather than rumours or speculation.
He explained that Ebola symptoms might develop between two and 21 days after exposure and included fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain.
The commissioner added that unexplained bleeding or bruising might occur in some cases.
He said, “As early symptoms can resemble malaria and other common illnesses.
“Residents who become unwell, particularly after possible exposure or travel from an area with active transmission, should seek prompt medical assessment.”
In line with Lagos State’s fever-management policy, Abayomi advised anyone with a fever to undergo a malaria rapid diagnostic test before taking antimalarial medicines.
“Where the test is negative, a healthcare professional should assess other possible causes and determine appropriate treatment.”
Abayomi also advised residents to wash their hands regularly, avoid contact with the body fluids of sick persons, refrain from handling potentially contaminated materials and avoid contact with sick or dead wild animals.
He appealed to travellers arriving in Nigeria, particularly from areas reporting Ebola transmission, to cooperate with Port Health Services and other authorised officials.
The commissioner urged them to provide accurate travel and health information when requested, and comply with applicable public health guidance.
“Anyone who develops symptoms during travel or after arrival should promptly notify the appropriate health personnel and seek guidance before visiting a healthcare facility.”
He emphasised that airlines and airport operators should sustain established public health protocols, while travellers should consult official advisories from the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention.
The commissioner also urged travellers to consult the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority and the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) for current guidance.
“Anyone who suspects exposure to Ebola, especially following contact with a suspected or confirmed case, should promptly contact public health authorities for guidance before visiting a healthcare facility.
“Suspected cases or relevant exposure concerns in Lagos may be reported through the State’s emergency numbers, 112 or 767.”
He added that exposures could also be reported to the Directorate of Epidemiology, Biosecurity and Global Health, Lagos State Ministry of Health, on 08023169485.
“Early detection and prompt reporting save lives.”
The commissioner stated that the Lagos government would continue to monitor developments, strengthen surveillance and response readiness, coordinate with relevant stakeholders and provide verified updates as necessary.

items.content:
Bayern Munich reclaimed top spot in the Bundesliga with a 3-1 win at Freiburg on Sunday, days after coach Vincent Kompany was hospitalised when he collapsed at training.
Bayern were missing several first-team players and Kompany, but cruised to a two-goal lead at half-time with Dayot Upamecano and Serge Gnabry scoring.
Freiburg pulled one back and were pushing for a point in stoppage time when goalkeeper Mio Backhaus was caught out up the field, allowing Michael Olise to slide the ball into an empty net.
Kompany remains in hospital and is being treated for a mystery virus, with Bayern saying Saturday the coach is likely to be out for “days, not weeks”.
“I just opened my phone to a message from Vince saying ‘well done’ and he was happy,” assistant coach Aaron Danks told DAZN.
“I just replied saying ‘brilliant — now go rest’. I sent him a kissing emoji, so hopefully he rests up.”
Bayern sporting director Max Eberl gave an update on Kompany’s condition.
“He’s stable. He no longer has a headache. He’s now undergoing a thorough examination. Everything is being handled,” he said.
“There’s no diagnosis, nothing final yet.”
With victory Bayern leapfrogged Borussia Dortmund to top the table ahead of the duo’s clash in Munich next week.
Harry Kane had a close-range effort saved late in the second half but failed to find the net a day before the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London, with the England captain among the favourites.
Bayern arrived in the Black Forest after a tumultuous few days which left them lacking leaders. With coach Kompany still in hospital after collapsing on Friday, Englishman Danks was in the dugout.
The visitors were also without injured captain Manuel Neuer, Luis Diaz, Jamal Musiala, Aleksandar Pavlovic and Kim Min-jae, while midfielder and Germany captain Joshua Kimmich was on bereavement leave due to the sudden death of his father.
Bayern were in the unusual position of sitting back and absorbing pressure as Freiburg pushed, but took the lead after 16 minutes when Upamecano started and finished a length-of-the-field counter.
The France defender won possession near his own box, played a one-two with Olise before thundering goalwards and sending a cool shot past Backhaus.
Bayern doubled up just before the break when Gnabry latched onto a Nathaniel Brown pass and nutmegged Backhaus to score.
With 10 minutes remaining, Kane stung Backhaus’s palms from close range and the hosts went on an immediate counter, forcing Tom Bischof into conceding an own goal.
The goal sparked Freiburg to life and Bayern ‘keeper Jonas Urbig needed to make crucial saves from Igor Matanovic in the dying moments.
With Freiburg and Backhaus pushing high, Olise won possession and scored to wrap up the victory.
– Hoffenheim hit 1,000 mark –
Hoffenheim scored three goals in the final 11 minutes, including the 1,000th league goal in their history, as they snapped Bayer Leverkusen’s six-game winning streak with a 3-0 home victory.
Hoffenheim, who beat Lyon by the same scoreline in the Europa League on Thursday, have now won three in a row.
The best chance of the opening half fell to former Leverkusen forward Adam Hlozek when he rattled the post with 38 minutes gone.
With the match looking headed for a scoreless draw, Leverkusen captain Edmond Tapsoba swept Fisnik Asllani’s ankle while defending a cross, with the referee pointing to the spot after a VAR review.
Andrej Kramaric’s 79th-minute penalty was the milestone goal and put Hoffenheim on track for victory.
With Leverkusen pushing for an equaliser, Hoffenheim broke on the counter and Alexander Prass scored, but he picked up a second yellow for removing his shirt in celebration, before leaving the pitch slapping himself on the forehead in dismay.
Max Moerstedt added a third despite the one-man disadvantage in the sixth minute of stoppage time.

The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has criticised the All Progressives Congress (APC) after its National Youth Leader, Dayo Israel, announced the distribution of brand-new 2026 Toyota Prado SUVs to selected youth leaders for election mobilisation.
The NDC said the seven vehicles shown in a video posted by Israel were worth about ₦1.015bn, accusing the ruling party of spending taxpayers’ money on the lavish lifestyles of politicians while Nigerians grapple with economic hardship.
The average cost of a brand-new 2026 Toyota Prado is ₦145,000,000.
In this video, we counted seven such vehicles, and the number could be even higher. The total cost of these seven vehicles alone amounts to ₦1,015,000,000.
While the rudderless, clueless, and ruinous… https://t.co/QYeB7UU21y— Nigeria Democratic Congress (@NigeriaNDCHQ) October 25, 2026
In a post on X reacting to Israel’s video, the opposition party said the estimated cost of the vehicles reflected what it described as wasteful spending by the President Bola Tinubu-led administration.
“The average cost of a brand-new 2026 Toyota Prado is ₦145,000,000. In this video, we counted seven such vehicles, and the number could be even higher,” the NDC said.
“The total cost of these seven vehicles alone amounts to ₦1,015,000,000.”
The party criticised the government’s economic policies, saying Nigerians had been asked to endure hardship while political leaders continued to enjoy expensive benefits.
“While the rudderless, clueless, and ruinous administration of President Bola Tinubu has been asking Nigerians to endure the pains of its wicked and cruel reforms, this is how taxpayers’ money is being spent,” it said.
“The wasteful APC-led administration is funding the lavish lifestyles of politicians while ordinary Nigerians wallow in poverty.”
The NDC called on Nigerians to vote the ruling party out in the 2027 general election, describing opposition to the administration as a civic responsibility.
“We cannot continue like this. We owe Nigerians and the unborn generation the civic duty to vote the ruinous administration of President Bola Tinubu out of power,” the party said.
It also used the controversy to promote its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, pledging that his administration would reduce the cost of governance.
“Our presidential candidate is strongly committed to cutting the cost of governance,” the NDC said, urging voters to support Obi for what it described as “a new and working Nigeria for all, and not for a corrupt few”.
Israel had earlier posted a video showing the vehicles, saying they were presented to selected youth leaders to support their election mobilisation activities.
“Today, I presented brand new 2026 Prado to my committed selected youth leaders to aid their election mobilisation activities,” he wrote.
He also thanked First Lady Oluremi Tinubu for her support for the party’s structure under his leadership.
“I am grateful to my Mummy, H.E Mrs Oluremi Tinubu for her continuous support to the party structure under my leadership,” Israel said.
He added that the APC would focus on grassroots mobilisation ahead of the election, saying the party would “deliver polling unit by polling unit”.
The NDC’s valuation is based on its estimate of the vehicles’ average price and its count of seven SUVs in the video.

items.content:
Flights resumed at Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday following a series of deadly attacks on the facility that saw it closed for two weeks, even as Yemen’s Houthis targeted the country with strikes.
King Khalid International Airport’s website showed several domestic and international flights scheduled on Sunday, including arrivals to the kingdom from Dubai, Paris and Cairo.
The renewed operations at the airport came as explosions rattled Riyadh early Sunday, after a text message was sent to residents warning of a hostile threat targeting the city.
The airport closure was a major blow for Saudi Arabia, with the kingdom’s flagship investment conference postponed until 2027 as residents scrambled to find alternatives to enter and exit the country.
The prestigious motor sport race, the Dakar Rally, also added its name to a long list of events to be cancelled, postponed or relocated amid the fallout from the war.
Saudi officials did not provide additional information when asked by AFP about the scope of the renewed operations at the airport.
But the tracking website Flightradar24 showed a small number of flights had departed, though the vast majority were cancelled.
The Houthis have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree earlier warned that Riyadh airport was still “unsafe” and a “military target”.
“The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines — as well as staff and travellers — against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces,” he said.
“The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport.”
– ‘Everything is shaking’ –
Later on Sunday, Saree said Saudi Arabia had struck Yemen dozens of times over the previous 24 hours.
“During the past 24 hours, Saudi warplanes launched 56 airstrikes and missiles targeting civilian objects in the governorates of Hajjah, Lahj, Amran, Saada, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Ibb using F-15 and “Typhoon” planes that took off from the bases of Khamis Mushait and Taif, and missiles from Najran,” he said on X.
As operations at the airport restarted, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis arrived in Riyadh and met with Saudi de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
During the meeting, Mitsotakis “responded favourably to the kingdom’s request to keep the Patriot system in Saudi Arabia, given the current challenging circumstances”, his office said.
Greece has deployed a battery to operate the US-made Patriot air defence system in Yanbu, a major oil export hub on the Red Sea coast.
The SPA news agency added that the two leaders “underscored the critical importance of safeguarding the security and integrity of international maritime corridors and ensuring the safe and continuous flow of energy supplies to global markets”.
Earlier, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles.
The fighting erupted after a years-long truce between the Houthis and Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government fell apart.
“The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning — may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions,” one resident in Khamis Mushait told AFP on Sunday on condition of anonymity.
The kingdom’s civil defence agency later said two people were injured in the south by falling debris, also reporting damage to several buildings and vehicles.
Images released by the official Saudi Press Agency showed a building with part of its upper facade destroyed, exposing metal rods. Another image captured large windows shattered, with shards of glass strewn across the pavement and part of the road.
– Attack warning –
AFP journalists in Riyadh heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday, with residents receiving alert messages for a “hostile aerial threat” and urging them to stay in a safe place.
The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards the capital, as well as two drones in the Riyadh area.
“Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh,” the coalition posted on X.
Later Sunday morning, the coalition said its forces intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Houthis at the kingdom’s southern city of Khamis Mushait.
Attacks appeared to target areas across the south, with warnings also issued for Abha city along with areas in Taif, Namas and Jazan.
The attacks came after the Houthis said they targeted three Saudi airports, including in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base within 24 hours.

By Dickson Omobola
President Bola Tinubu has appointed Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, to head the Directorate of Air Mobilisation of the All Progressives Congress, APC, 2027 re-election campaign
Keyamo would serve as Director of the Directorate of Air Mobilisation, with the Managing Director of the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria, FAAN, Mrs Olubunmi Kuku, appointed Deputy Director 1, while Engr Farouk Ahmed Umar would serve as Deputy Director II.

“Keyamo’s appointment brings to the campaign structure the experience of a serving aviation minister who has been at the forefront of policy initiatives aimed at strengthening Nigeria’s aviation sector, improving its international standing and positioning the country as a major aviation hub in Africa.
“His familiarity with the operational demands of the aviation industry is expected to provide useful leadership in coordinating the directorate’s activities and establishing an effective framework for air-mobilisation planning.
“The appointment of Mrs. Olubunmi Kuku and Umar as Deputy Directors also brings aviation-sector leadership and technical experience into the directorate, strengthening its capacity to address the planning and coordination demands associated with nationwide campaign movements.”

items.author: ProPK Staff
items.content:
Traffic fines on Lahore Ring Road have been significantly increased as authorities step up enforcement against road safety violations.
According to Punjab Ring Road Authority, the revised penalties apply to a wide range of offences, including overspeeding, driving without a licence, wrong overtaking, lane violations and underage driving.
Motorists caught driving without a valid licence will now face a fine of Rs. 5,000, up from Rs. 500.
The fine for overspeeding has also been increased. Vehicles with engines up to 2,000cc will face a Rs. 5,000 penalty, while vehicles above 2,000cc may be fined Rs. 10,000.
Wrong overtaking will carry a similar penalty structure, with fines of Rs. 5,000 for smaller vehicles and Rs. 10,000 for vehicles above 2,000cc.
Authorities have also fixed a Rs. 2,000 fine for improper lane use and Rs. 5,000 for driving in the wrong direction or violating one-way restrictions.
The penalty for overloading has increased from Rs. 2,000 to Rs. 7,000, while wrong parking will now result in a Rs. 2,000 fine instead of Rs. 1,000.
Underage driving will carry one of the highest penalties at Rs. 10,000.
Motorists using black or tinted windows will face a Rs. 5,000 fine. Vehicles without number plates or with non-standard registration plates will also be fined Rs. 5,000.
Motorcycles entering Lahore Ring Road, where their movement is restricted, will face a Rs. 5,000 penalty.
The fine for pedestrian crossing violations has been increased from Rs. 200 to Rs. 1,000.
Meanwhile, motorists caught using a mobile phone while driving or failing to wear a seat belt will now face a Rs. 3,000 fine, up from Rs. 500.

The revised fine structure is part of a broader effort by the Punjab Ring Road Authority to improve road discipline, reduce dangerous driving and strengthen traffic enforcement on Lahore Ring Road.

items.content:
NADRA has explained how married citizens can update their marital status in official records using a computerized marriage certificate and the Pak ID mobile app.
According to NADRA, citizens must first obtain a computerized marriage certificate from the relevant Union Council, Cantonment Board, or Municipal Committee. The certificate provides a Civil Registration Management System (CRMS) number, which is required to process the marital status update.
After obtaining the certificate, applicants can update their marital status either by visiting a nearby NADRA Registration Centre or by using the Pak ID mobile application.
The process links the marriage record registered with the relevant local authority to NADRA’s database. The CRMS system records major civil events, including births, marriages, divorces, and deaths, through authorized local government bodies across Pakistan.
Get a Computerized Marriage Certificate
The first step is to make sure the marriage has been officially registered with the relevant local authority.
Applicants should obtain a computerized marriage certificate from their Union Council, Cantonment Board, Municipal Committee, or other competent registration authority, depending on where the marriage was registered.
Citizens should ensure that the details on the certificate are correct before using it for the NADRA update.
Keep Your CRMS Number Ready
The computerized marriage certificate includes information linked with the Civil Registration Management System (CRMS).
Applicants should keep the relevant CRMS number available when updating their marital status.
NADRA’s CRMS infrastructure is used by local authorities to register vital events, including births, deaths, marriages, and divorces. NADRA says the system is deployed across more than 11,000 Union Councils and supports the issuance of civil registration certificates.
How to Update Marital Status Through the Pak ID App
Citizens who want to complete the process online can use NADRA’s Pak ID mobile application.
Applicants should download the official Pak ID app, create an account or sign in to an existing account, and select the relevant CNIC modification or non-printable information update service.
They can then enter the required information and provide the supporting documents requested by the application.
NADRA confirms that Pak ID supports CNIC modification and updates to non-printable fields. The platform also allows applicants to upload documents, pay applicable fees online, and track their applications.
Applicants should follow the instructions shown in the app, as additional verification may be required depending on the individual case.
How to Update Marital Status at a NADRA Registration Centre
Citizens who prefer an in-person process can visit their nearest NADRA Registration Centre.
They should take their computerized marriage certificate and other required identity documents with them and request an update to their marital status.
NADRA may ask applicants to complete identity or biometric verification as part of the process.
Citizens should make sure their marriage information matches the details already registered with the relevant local authority.
What If the Marriage Record Is Not Updated?
Applicants should first confirm that their marriage has been properly registered with the concerned local authority.
NADRA’s registration ecosystem relies on civil registration information generated through provincial and local government systems. Its policy framework also provides for marriage registration data to be linked with NADRA records to improve verification and accuracy.
If the marriage record or CRMS information contains an error, applicants may need to have the issue corrected by the authority that registered the marriage before completing the NADRA update.

items.author: Danial Saigra
items.content:
Parents in Pakistan can now register their child’s birth with the relevant local authority from home through NADRA’s Pak ID mobile application, removing the need to complete the entire process through physical visits.
The facility is available through the Provincial Civil Registration Services section of the Pak ID app and connects users with the relevant Union Council, Municipal Committee, Town Committee, or other participating local registration authority.
NADRA officially lists birth registration among the provincial civil registration services available through Pak ID. The app also supports online payments and digital document services.
Download and Log In to the Pak ID App
Parents should first download the official Pak ID mobile application on their smartphone.
New users need to create an account and complete the registration process, while existing users can sign in using their registered credentials.
NADRA provides the Pak ID app for both Android and iOS users. The platform allows citizens to access identity and registration services directly from their phones.
Open Provincial Civil Registration Services
After logging in, users should open the Provincial Civil Registration Services section.
They must select the relevant province and then choose Birth from the available civil registration options.
The app may display children already linked to the applicant’s family record. Parents should select the child whose birth they want to register.
If the child does not appear in the list, users can select the option indicating that the child is not listed and continue to the next stage.
Select District, Tehsil and Union Council
The application will then ask for details relating to the registering authority.
Parents should select the relevant district, tehsil, and Union Council or other applicable local authority.
They will also have to choose the relevant application category and provide the child’s date of birth.
These details help determine which local authority will process the birth registration.
Check the Applicable Birth Registration Fee
The app provides a Calculate Fee option before users begin the full application.
Parents can select this option to see the amount payable for their application.
The applicable fee may vary depending on provincial rules and the type or timing of registration. Applicants should rely on the amount calculated by the app for their particular case rather than assuming a fixed nationwide fee.
After reviewing the fee, users can select Start Application to continue.
Enter the Child’s Details
The next stage asks parents to provide information about the child.
If the child’s details are already recorded with NADRA, applicants can select Yes and enter the child’s B-Form or identity document number. The system will then retrieve available information.
Parents should review the displayed details and provide any additional information requested by the application.
If the child is not already registered in NADRA’s records, applicants can select No and manually enter the required information before proceeding.
Provide Parents’ Information
The Pak ID app will then display the Parent Details section.
Applicants must enter the required information about the child’s parents and make sure the details match their official identity records.
After completing this section, users can proceed to the additional information required for civil registration.
Enter Additional Family and Birth Details
The application may also request additional information concerning family members and the circumstances of the birth.
According to NADRA’s instructional process, users should complete all fields shown on the screen before moving to the next stage.
Parents should review the information carefully because mistakes can delay verification by the relevant registering authority.
Photograph and Biometric Requirements Depend on the Child’s Age
The Pak ID process applies different identity requirements according to the child’s age.
For children under three years of age, fingerprints are not required. NADRA’s current child-registration rules state that children aged three to 10 years require a photograph and iris data, while children aged 10 to 18 years require a photograph, fingerprints, and iris data for relevant child identity registration.
In the birth-registration workflow demonstrated by NADRA, the app does not show a child-photo capture option for children below three. For children over three and under 10, the process requires a photograph, while applicants aged above 10 and below 18 are also prompted for fingerprint capture.
Users should follow the requirements displayed in the app for the child’s age and application type.
How to Capture the Child’s Photograph
If the application requires a photograph, users should select Capture Photo.
The app allows parents to use the front or rear camera of their smartphone.
The child’s face should remain inside the guide shown on the camera screen. Parents should make sure the image is clear before confirming and saving it.
NADRA’s Pak ID platform supports live photo capture as part of its digital identity services.
How to Scan Fingerprints
If fingerprint verification is required, the app will display the Capture Fingerprints section.
Users should select Start Scan, continue to the scanning process, and capture the required fingers according to the instructions displayed on screen.
NADRA’s biometric policy does not require fingerprints from children below 10 years of age.
Applicants should complete every required scan before proceeding.
Select the Address for the Birth Certificate
The app will then ask which address should appear on the child’s birth certificate.
Parents can select the available permanent or current address, depending on the information shown in their application.
They should check the selected address carefully because it will form part of the civil registration record.
Pay the Birth Registration Fee Online
After completing the required information, users will reach the payment section.
According to NADRA, Pak ID supports online payments through credit and debit cards, Raast, JazzCash, EasyPaisa, and e-Sahulat, subject to the service being used.
Applicants should complete the payment using one of the available methods and then continue to the next step.
Review the Application Before Submission
The app will display a review screen before final submission.
Parents should select Review Your Data and carefully check the complete form.
They should verify the child’s name, date of birth, parents’ details, address, and other information before proceeding.
After checking the information, applicants must accept the required acknowledgements and select Submit.
The app will display a confirmation message once the application has been successfully submitted.
What Happens After You Submit the Application?
After submission, NADRA processes the digital application and forwards the relevant information through the civil registration system.
The appropriate registering authority then processes the child’s birth registration according to the applicable provincial and local rules.
NADRA’s Civil Registration and Management System supports registration of vital events, including births, through thousands of Union Councils and other local registration bodies across Pakistan.
How to Download the Birth Certificate
Once the registration process has been completed and the certificate becomes available, users can return to the Applications section of the Pak ID app.
They can select the relevant application and tap the download option.
According to NADRA’s instructional process, the birth certificate will then become available through the user’s ID Vault.
NADRA describes Pak ID Vault as a digital space where citizens can securely keep and access supported official documents and certificates.
Parents should keep in mind that the exact requirements, fees, and processing conditions may depend on the province, local authority, and circumstances of the birth registration. Users should follow the instructions displayed in the official Pak ID app for their individual application.
The post How to Register Your Child’s Birth Online Using NADRA Pak ID App appeared first on ProPakistani.

items.author: ProPK Staff
items.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is likely to inaugurate the Pak-China Friendship Hospital in Islamabad on October 27.
The 250-bed facility in Chak Shahzad was originally built as an isolation hospital during the COVID-19 pandemic. It has now been renamed and will reopen as a general hospital serving residents of the area.
Renamed on PM’s Directions
The hospital was renamed the Pak-China Friendship Hospital on the instructions of the Prime Minister.
According to sources, the Ministry of National Health Services and the Isolation Hospital and Infectious Treatment Centre (IHITC) had initially decided to name it Margalla Hospital.
Federal Health Minister Syed Mustafa Kamal told The News that the name was changed in recognition of China’s contribution. “The hospital was built with Chinese assistance, and the prime minister has directed that it should be named Pak-China Friendship Hospital,” he said.
General Hospital Under PPP Model
The health ministry and the IHITC have decided to run the facility as a general hospital. Its isolation facility will be operated under a public-private partnership (PPP).
The health ministry had earlier signed an agreement with the Indus Hospital & Health Network (IHHN) for the management of the isolation facility.
The development comes weeks after plans were announced for a new 167-bed hospital in Islamabad offering free treatment.
Built With Chinese Grant During COVID-19
The hospital was set up in 2020 during the first wave of COVID-19. China donated $4 million for the project.
It was built by the Frontier Works Organisation (FWO) in collaboration with the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and the National Institute of Health (NIH) in 40 days. The total construction cost was reported at around Rs. 980 million.
Then prime minister Imran Khan inaugurated the facility on July 9, 2020. However, after the pandemic ended, the hospital was deactivated due to operational challenges, including a shortage of medical staff.
Earlier, PM Shehbaz Sharif inaugurated a modern cancer hospital in Azad Kashmir.
Source: ARY News

Pakistan has turned down a $490 million commercial loan offered by the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) Group because the lender’s interest rate was too high, even as the country’s gross financing needs remain at around 20 percent of GDP.
The one-year facility was offered by the International Islamic Trade Finance Corporation (ITFC), the IsDB Group’s trade finance arm.
The Debt Management Office (DMO) of the Finance Ministry rejected it last week.
Why the Loan Was Rejected
Finance Division was hoping for an interest cost of around 6 percent. The ITFC’s all-in cost of about 8 percent was also higher than Pakistan’s December 2027 bond, which was trading at 6.1 percent.
The government has now asked the Economic Affairs Division to find a new facility at competitive rates, either from the ITFC or another lender.
Financing Needs Stay High
The decision comes a couple of months after Pakistan took a $300 million loan from United Bank Limited in August. The government granted an income tax exemption on the bank’s profit to secure it.
Under the Finance Ministry’s borrowing plan for FY2026-27, total gross financing needs are projected at Rs. 28.647 trillion, or about 20 percent of GDP.
Net external financing is estimated at Rs. 813 billion ($2.8 billion), with multilateral lenders expected to provide most of it.
Meanwhile, the IMF’s latest report projects the current account deficit at 1 percent of GDP, or nearly $4.5 billion. That is at least $1.5 billion more than the $2.5 billion to $3 billion estimated by Pakistani authorities.
Borrowing has also become costlier. In September, Pakistan raised $3 billion through Eurobonds, including a five-and-a-half-year bond at 7.5 percent and a 10-year bond at 7.9 percent.
Earlier this year, the country also signed three loan agreements worth $603 million with the IsDB.

items.author: SYED HARIS AHMED
items.content:
The world's power sector is entering a period in which the availability of electricity will depend not only on generation capacity but also on the ability to secure the equipment, materials and services needed to build and maintain the electricity network. Transformers, cables, switchgear, turbines, solar modules and batteries are increasingly becoming strategic inputs rather than routine procurement items.
Electricity demand is rising rapidly as industries electrify, data centres expand and countries add renewable-energy capacity. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that annual grid investment must increase by around 50%, from about $400 billion today to roughly $600 billion by 2030, to keep pace with electrification and climate goals.
Yet factories producing critical equipment are already under pressure. Long lead times for large power transformers, high-voltage cables and other grid equipment can delay projects even when financing and generation capacity are available. According to the IEA's Building the Future Transmission Grid report, lead times for large power transformers have almost doubled since 2021, reaching up to four years for the largest units. High-voltage cables now take two to three years, while direct-current cables for long-distance transmission can exceed five years.
The Utilities for Net Zero Alliance (UNEZA) estimates its members alone will need close to 90,000 kilometres of transmission cable by 2030 – more than twice the Earth's circumference – and over 270 high-voltage transformers, with waiting times now exceeding three years. A country may therefore have sufficient investment capital, plans for new generation and growing electricity demand, yet still find that its grid cannot expand at the required pace because critical components are unavailable.
Manufacturing and mineral processing are heavily concentrated. China accounts for around 60% of global mined production of magnet rare earths, more than 90% of refining and nearly 95% of permanent magnet production, according to IEA data. In solar manufacturing, China produces roughly 80% of global PV modules and over 90% of polysilicon and wafers. Lithium, copper, cobalt, nickel, graphite and rare-earth elements are increasingly viewed not simply as commodities but as strategic inputs into the energy transition. Over half of strategic energy minerals are now subject to some form of export control, making diversification a security imperative rather than a procurement preference.
Renewable energy adds another layer of complexity. Solar and wind generation are variable, requiring stronger transmission networks, storage, flexible generation and more sophisticated grid-management systems. The supply chain must therefore support not just additional generation but an increasingly complex electricity system. The rapid growth of data centres and AI applications is adding to this pressure. The IEA projects that data-centre electricity consumption could rise from about 415 TWh in 2024 to roughly 945 TWh by 2030, with the US and China accounting for almost 80% of the increase. Large computing facilities require reliable and continuous electricity supplies, often in locations where existing grids have limited spare capacity.
A modern power supply chain is also an information system. Utilities need visibility across several tiers of suppliers to know where critical components are manufactured, what raw materials they depend upon and how quickly alternative sources can be activated. Digital technologies can help. Internet-connected sensors, AI, advanced forecasting and digital twins can improve inventory management, predict equipment failures and provide earlier warnings of potential disruptions. Better data-sharing between utilities and manufacturers can also help suppliers plan production instead of responding only when orders arrive. But technology alone cannot solve a supply shortage. If several utilities place orders for the same specialised equipment at the same time, better software cannot manufacture transformers or high-voltage cables faster. Procurement strategy therefore matters. Utilities need to move beyond the lowest-bid approach and consider quality, delivery reliability, technical capability, supplier concentration, cybersecurity and geopolitical exposure when selecting suppliers.
Long-term contracts can give manufacturers greater confidence to invest in production capacity, while utilities obtain greater assurance of future supplies. Collaborative procurement could become particularly important. Utilities and governments can provide manufacturers with clearer multi-year demand forecasts while standardising equipment specifications where technically possible. This can reduce unnecessary customisation, shorten procurement cycles and allow manufacturers to benefit from larger production runs.
Diversification is equally important. A resilient supply chain does not mean abandoning global trade or producing everything domestically. It means avoiding excessive dependence on a single supplier, country or transport route for a critical component. Strategic inventories can also have a role. Maintaining stocks of every item would be prohibitively expensive, but selected critical components, particularly those with long manufacturing lead times, can be held to reduce the consequences of unexpected failures or supply disruptions.
The same principle applies upstream to critical minerals. Greater investment in mining, processing, recycling and alternative materials can reduce dependence on concentrated sources. International partnerships and regional supply arrangements can complement domestic production. The circular economy offers another opportunity. Power-sector companies do not always need to respond to rising demand by buying entirely new equipment. Transformers and other assets can sometimes be refurbished and kept in service longer. Copper, aluminium and steel can be recovered from retired equipment, while batteries and solar technologies offer increasing opportunities for recycling and second-life applications.
Cybersecurity is becoming another essential element of supply-chain management. Power systems increasingly depend on digital technologies and connected equipment, making suppliers themselves part of the security perimeter. IBM's 2024 Cost of a Data Breach report put the global average cost of a data breach at $4.88 million, a 10% rise in a year. Procurement decisions therefore have to consider not only technical specifications but also the security of associated software, communications systems and vendors.
The shortage of skilled labour and manufacturing capacity adds to the challenge. Expanding production of specialised grid equipment requires engineers, technicians, factory workers and testing facilities. Building such capacity can take years. Governments and utilities therefore need to provide manufacturers with enough visibility of future demand to justify long-term investment.
For developing economies such as Pakistan, these global changes carry special significance. Pakistan's power sector remains heavily exposed to imported fuel, equipment, technology and capital goods. Cumulative solar imports have exceeded $3 billion in recent years, with the overwhelming majority sourced from China, according to trade data. A weakening currency can raise the local cost of imported equipment, while procurement delays can postpone projects and increase financing costs. Dependence on external suppliers also means that international disruptions can quickly become domestic problems.
This makes supply-chain resilience relevant not only to new generation capacity but also to the reliability of the existing transmission and distribution system. Maintaining adequate stocks of critical components, developing reliable local suppliers where economically viable, improving demand forecasting and establishing longer-term relationships with strategic manufacturers could reduce some of these vulnerabilities. Localisation, however, should not become an excuse for inefficient production. Domestic manufacturing makes economic sense where Pakistan has the skills, market size and cost advantages to compete. In other areas, diversified international sourcing may remain more efficient. The objective should be supply security at a competitive cost, rather than self-sufficiency for its own sake.
The writer is a mechanical engineer

items.author: newsdesk.
items.content:
Karachi floods during the monsoon and chokes under summer pollution. Both crises have multiple causes, but waste management connects them in ways the city can no longer afford to ignore.
Cleaner air could add an estimated 2.7 years to the average Karachi resident's life. Industry and transport are the largest contributors, but waste is part of the same crisis. Uncollected garbage accumulates in drains, on vacant plots and at open dumpsites, and when burned adds black carbon and other pollutants to air that met the World Health Organisation's (WHO) daily guideline on only three days in 2024, according to PAQI's 2025 national report.
An official of the Sindh Solid Waste Management Board (SSWMB) said Karachi generates more than 14,800 tonnes of waste daily, including over 3,000 tonnes in District Central alone. Around 42% is organic. Karachi is also reported to account for 25% of Pakistan's recyclable plastic waste. PAQI's 2025 source inventory attributes 7% of Karachi's PM2.5 emissions to open waste burning.
Waste as economic value
A 2014 World Economic Forum report estimated the circular economy at over $1 trillion per year in material savings globally, with recycling in Europe alone already supporting 500,000 jobs. Pakistan imported virgin plastic resin worth $3 billion in 2022, compared with $707 million in tea imports. Better collection and sorting could reduce dependence on some virgin resin imports.
Pakistani businesses are already showing what recovery can look like. Concept Loop converts difficult-to-recycle multilayer plastic packaging into construction products such as pavers, blocks and tiles, turning material that would otherwise clog a drain or burn on a roadside into a product with a market price. The company has received support through Karandaaz's GreenFin Innovations programme and reports that its pavers were used in a Mari Petroleum project at Daharki in Sindh, diverting over 7,000 kg of low-value plastic waste.
The Sindh Enterprise Incubation Centre reports that Concept Loop has recycled over 1,300 tonnes of plastic and produced more than 100,000 square feet of building materials. However, Karachi needs a system to recover recycled waste.
Regulation can shift behaviour when it is enforced consistently. Rwanda banned plastic bags in 2008, one of the first countries in the world to do so, and later expanded the ban to cover single-use plastics. According to the Global Green Growth Institute, enforcement included border inspections to prevent smuggling, strict penalties for violations and government support to help businesses transition to alternatives. Karachi does not need to replicate the ban. It needs what made it work: enforcement, alternatives and businesses brought in from the start.
Organic waste should become a product
Lahore's Mehmood Booti composting project shows that waste recovery and carbon finance are not theoretical possibilities in Pakistan. Lahore Compost Limited began operating there in 2006 under an arrangement with the City District Government, processing municipal waste into compost while pursuing carbon revenue from methane reductions. The proposed carbon finance project also received $5.524 million in World Bank funding. The original operation ran until 2016. It is a historical example, but the lesson applies: composting requires clean organic inputs, a reliable market and sustained management.
The potential of carbon finance is demonstrated by the World Bank's account of the Monterrey Waste Management and Carbon Offset Project in Mexico, which generated and sold more than one million metric tonnes of certified emissions reductions between 2005 and 2017. Carbon revenue should supplement, not replace, reliable funding for basic waste collection and disposal services. Karachi's Bagh Ibne Qasim biogas plant shows what this looks like in practice. The facility converts organic and livestock waste into biogas, with reported processing of around two tonnes of organic waste daily and production capacity of 150 cubic metres of gas. The project was designed to supply subsidised cooking fuel to 70 to 80 households in Clifton at Rs2,000 per month.
Fixing the system: accountability, financing
It was reported in July 2026 that the World Bank had downgraded Karachi's $100 million Solid Waste Emergency and Efficiency Project to "Moderately Unsatisfactory". Delays to four transfer stations, contract management problems and no measurable waste disposed through a sanitary landfill were among the concerns. Investment without functioning management and public accountability does not deliver.
Karachi's informal recyclers are already turning waste into economic value, yet remain excluded from formal waste-management planning. A 2023 study estimated that they recover 4,100 tonnes of waste daily, valuing Karachi's informal recycling economy at Rs1.2 billion annually. Yet workers remain vulnerable, with the Fair Circularity Initiative estimating monthly earnings at around Rs42,500 to Rs43,300, below the Rs60,434 monthly living-wage benchmark calculated using the Anker methodology.
Pune in India offers a practical model through its SWaCH cooperative, which integrates over 3,900 waste pickers, diverts approximately 80,000 tonnes annually and has been associated with estimated municipal transport savings of Rs16 million a year. Karachi can build on its existing recycling economy by giving registered kabariwalas access to sorting facilities, protective equipment, working capital and fair municipal contracts.
Financing waste services through user charges has a record. Worcester in Massachusetts introduced a Pay As You Throw programme in which households pay per bag of waste they discard, reducing volumes and increasing recycling rates. Closer to home, Punjab under the Suthra Punjab programme introduced a sanitation fee ranging from Rs300 per month for smaller urban households to Rs5,000 for the largest properties, collected alongside property tax. A fee without reliable service is a tax with no corresponding benefit. Any comparable charge in Karachi must be tied to published service standards and transparent expenditure.
From waste crisis to circular economy
Karachi's waste is an economic opportunity sitting in plain sight. The city already has businesses converting plastic into products, informal workers recovering materials at scale, and local projects demonstrating the potential of biogas and composting. What is missing is enforcement, accountability and money tied to results. Progress should be measured not by projects inaugurated but by waste recovered, pollution reduced and a formal, transparent system that works.
THE WRITER IS AN ASSISTANT PROFESSOR AT THE SCHOOL OF ECONOMICS AND SOCIAL SCIENCES, IBA. SHE HOLDS A PHD IN ECONOMICS FROM CLARK UNIVERSITY

items.author: Dr Fahd Rehman
items.content:
In the era of financial globalisation, most of the business firms follow a shareholder orientation strategy. Shareholder orientation means that business firms intend to show high profitability. They usually show this profitability by downsizing the workforce and then distributing higher profits among shareholders to satisfy them.
This shareholder orientation strategy at the micro level disappoints in terms of profit rate at the macro level. In other words, the financial gains enjoyed by business firms at the micro level cannot be realised at the macro level.
A shareholder-oriented business firm focuses on higher profitability. Their Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) are incentivised through stock options, which means that higher dividend payouts will increase their salary/compensation packages. These CEOs outsource certain functions to minimise their labour force.
They also hire contractual workforce in order to lessen their wage bills. Since these managers have short-term contracts, they intend to increase profitability in order to raise their compensation.
Business firms, which focus on shareholder value orientation, also resort to share buybacks. As these firms do not retain profits, they have to either borrow from banks or issue bonds. Such borrowings increase their corporate debt-to-equity ratio. Hence, these firms become highly leveraged in the course of time and their dependence on debt increases.
A leveraged firm intends to have easy access to credit. Credit access is easier when circumstances are normal. As the circumstances are far from normal, credit access becomes difficult. Under these circumstances, these business firms become financially constrained. Such situations may be a prelude to a firm-creditor conflict.
Business firms are meant to invest in real capital ie, investment in machines, men and materials. The realisation of real investment is uncertain. Shareholder value orientation does not allow business firms to invest in risky ventures.
These firms become selective in their investment projects as they tend to choose less risky projects. This selection of investment projects does not increase aggregate demand, as and when required. Specially, selection and continuation of risky investments are necessary during the phase of recession.
Many business firms listed on the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) have adopted a shareholder orientation strategy. Firms from cement, banking, insurance, textile and pharmaceutical sub-sectors have bought back their shares in the last four years as they held excessive cash in their balance sheets. Few of them have bought their shares twice in the last couple of years.
Similarly, financialised households are involved in debt-financed consumption. These households buy and consume durable and luxury products and services through borrowings. Such borrowings increase the debt-to-income ratio of consumers. If access to credit is easy, consumers will increase their consumption.
In an economy, a small percentage of high-net-worth consumers are bondholders while a large percentage of low-income individuals are consumers. High-net-worth individuals have a low propensity to consume while low-income individuals have a high propensity to consume. Debt-financed consumption transfers income from low-income consumers to high-income ones which, in turn, reduces aggregate demand.
Access to credit entices consumers to increase consumption in the short run. Debt-financed consumption increases the debt burden on consumers. Owing to debt servicing and repayment obligations, consumption decreases in the long run.
In short, shareholder value orientation increases the level of debt in the economy. Moreover, it decreases the level of real investment which, in turn, reduces aggregate demand. The decline in the level of aggregate demand has contractive effects on the macroeconomy. This situation does not bode well for the aspiring millions.
The writer is an independent economist who authored a book: Pakistan's Structural Economic Problems in the era of Financial Globalization

items.author: Asad Hayat
items.content:
Pakistan's automobile industry stands at a critical crossroads as the government prepares to introduce the Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026-31. The proposed framework aims to transform a largely assembly-based sector into a competitive, export-oriented manufacturing industry.
For years, manufacturers have sought policy consistency, lower production costs, protection for local vendors and incentives for technological development. Consumers, meanwhile, expect affordable vehicles, better quality, improved safety and greater market competition. The challenge for policymakers is to balance these competing expectations without repeating the weaknesses of earlier automotive policies.
The draft policy has set an ambitious direction, including an export target of $6 billion over five years, gradual tariff reductions and greater adoption of electric vehicles. According to details reported after the prime minister approved the draft on October 20, 2026, the document is expected to move to the federal cabinet for in-principle approval before further legislative consideration. It proposes reducing tariffs on completely built-up vehicles and completely knocked-down kits to as low as 15% by 2030-31. This represents a significant shift from the protection-oriented approach that has historically shaped Pakistan's automobile market.
The industry's expectations, however, are more complicated than the policy's headline targets suggest. Local assemblers and parts manufacturers want a predictable tariff structure that allows them to plan investment and compete with imported vehicles. Parts manufacturers are particularly concerned that rapid tariff reductions could expose domestic vendors to cheaper imported components before they have achieved economies of scale or technological competitiveness. The Pakistan Association of Automotive Parts and Accessories Manufacturers has warned that tariff cuts on imported parts to 15% without addressing domestic cost disadvantages could weaken local manufacturing and turn Pakistan into an import-dependent market.
The concern is rooted in the structure of the industry. Pakistan has attracted several new automobile brands over the past decade, increasing competition and expanding consumer choice. However, additional assembly capacity has not automatically translated into higher production, deeper localisation or significant exports. The Pakistan Institute of Development Economics notes that the number of automobile manufacturing and assembling firms has increased to more than 15, while production capacity has more than doubled over the last decade. Yet sales have remained relatively stagnant and the industry continues to depend heavily on imported CKD kits and high-value components. This indicates that increasing the number of assemblers is not the same as building a strong manufacturing base.
Official production figures also highlight the gap between capacity and actual market demand. The Pakistan Economic Survey 2024-25 reported car production of 76,339 units during July-March FY2025, compared with 55,678 in the corresponding period of FY2024, an increase of 37.1%. Production of jeeps, SUVs, pickups and light commercial vehicles rose by 79.8% to 26,147 units. Although the recovery was encouraging, it followed a period of weak demand, high financing costs, inflation and exchange rate instability. The figures demonstrate that the sector remains sensitive to macroeconomic conditions and cannot achieve sustained expansion through policy incentives alone.
The proposed export target is another major test. The draft envisages combined vehicle and parts exports of $6.01 billion over five years, with annual targets rising from $256.6 million in 2026-27 to $2.19 billion in 2030-31. It also proposes export-linked incentives and penalties for manufacturers that repeatedly fail to meet their obligations. The direction is positive because Pakistan cannot continue treating the domestic market as the industry's principal destination. However, exports require internationally competitive prices, consistent quality, economies of scale, reliable supply chains and compliance with global safety and environmental standards. These capabilities cannot be created simply by setting targets.
Localisation must therefore become a practical industrial strategy rather than a numerical requirement. Pakistan has spent decades encouraging local production, yet many technologically advanced components are imported. Domestic vendors need access to modern machinery, technical training, research facilities and partnerships with international manufacturers. Small suppliers also require affordable financing and predictable orders to justify investment. If tariff reductions are introduced before local firms become competitive, the result could be industrial contraction rather than modernisation. Conversely, indefinite protection would weaken incentives to improve productivity and quality. A gradual, evidence-based transition is essential.
EVs provide another opportunity, but affordability and infrastructure remain major constraints. The draft proposes a 1% sales tax on battery electric vehicles, with different rates for range-extended and plug-in hybrid vehicles. It also proposes increasing the financing limit for EV purchases from Rs3 million to Rs10 million and extending repayment from three to five years. These measures could encourage adoption, but consumers also need accessible charging facilities, reliable electricity, battery warranties, maintenance networks and clarity about battery replacement costs. EV incentives should support mass-market mobility rather than primarily benefiting buyers of expensive vehicles.
The proposed establishment of the Pakistan Automotive Testing Institute is an important step towards improving vehicle safety, certification and export readiness. Pakistan needs enforceable standards for crash protection, emissions, durability and manufacturing quality. Consumers should also benefit from transparent pricing, realistic delivery commitments and effective after-sales services. The new policy's success should ultimately be measured not only by investment announcements or the number of assembly plants, but by whether vehicles become safer, more affordable and technologically advanced.
The government has also stated its intention to use an Automotive Development Levy to support export incentives and industrial development. The draft estimates collections exceeding Rs232 billion over five years. Such funds must be managed transparently, with measurable outcomes and independent oversight. Support should reach productive investment, technology upgrading, vendor development and research rather than becoming another permanent subsidy for established players.
Pakistan's draft auto policy offers an opportunity to move beyond an assembly-led model towards genuine industrial competitiveness. But the gap between industry hopes and policy realities will remain unless tariff reform is matched by lower production costs, stronger local suppliers, consistent regulation and export capability. The government must protect neither inefficient manufacturers nor consumers from competition; instead, it must create conditions in which efficient producers can compete and buyers receive better value. The real achievement will be a sustainable automobile industry that earns foreign exchange, creates skilled employment and delivers affordable, safe and reliable vehicles to the Pakistani market.
THE WRITER IS A MEMBER OF PEC AND HOLDS A MASTER'S DEGREE IN ENGINEERING

items.title: The model that fuels Europe's protests
