items.author: Ankush Das
items.content:
PHP, a programming language used to build websites, is at the centre of a major security concern after researchers uncovered two critical flaws that could let hackers take control of vulnerable servers.
Called PHP2Shell, the vulnerabilities could let attackers run malicious code on affected systems without needing to log in. Since the vulnerabilities lie in PHP itself rather than individual websites built on it, businesses cannot rely on website-level security measures alone to stay protected.
The vulnerabilities affect specific PHP versions, and fixes were released on October 21, 2026. Businesses must now check whether they are running affected versions, install the updates and investigate whether hackers exploited the flaws before the fixes were applied.
The discovery story involves both independent research and AI-assisted security work. Security firm Calif credited pseudonymous researcher LCFR with first discovering PHP2Shell and developing a working exploit. Separately, AI company OpenAI said security research firm Calif identified a critical flaw using its GPT-5.6 Sol model, while cybersecurity firm Wiz independently discovered and reported both vulnerabilities. OpenAI’s disclosure describes the collaboration that helped prepare fixes before public disclosure.
The episode also highlights a growing cybersecurity concern: AI tools are helping researchers uncover complex security flaws, but organisations must be equally agile to fix them.
Which Businesses Face The Risk?
PHP powers around 70% of websites globally. This highlights the language’s reach, but does not mean that 70% of websites are vulnerable. The actual risk depends on the PHP version, server configuration and exposure to attack. The vulnerabilities can allow attackers to run code remotely on affected servers without authentication.
Amruta Moktali, chief product officer at Skyflow, a data privacy and security platform, said initial industry reports cited millions of potentially exposed instances because PHP is widely used across websites, content management systems, hosting environments and enterprise applications.
For Indian businesses, Moktali said the immediate priority should be internet-facing PHP systems that handle sensitive information. These include systems connected to payment services, customer databases and identity and authentication tools.
Small businesses and website operators may face additional challenges if they depend on third-party hosting providers or lack dedicated security teams. They may not know which PHP version their websites use or whether their provider has installed the relevant updates.
Sooraj Sathyanarayanan, a cybersecurity researcher and program manager at privacy-focused web browser Brave, said successful exploitation could allow attackers to execute code without logging in or requiring user interaction. Depending on the server’s permissions, this could expose customer data and credentials, enable website changes or allow malware to be installed.
However, the level of risk depends on the PHP build and server configuration, so not all installations are equally vulnerable.
Legacy systems are another concern, as the flaw occurs within PHP’s core engine before an application’s own code runs.
“One thing organisations must keep in mind with PHP2Shell is that because this flaw triggers inside the core PHP engine before any application code executes, traditional application-level safeguards won’t stop it,” said Niv Lanyado, security research team lead for PHP at JFrog, a software supply chain security company.
He stressed that organisations need visibility into all their systems, particularly older PHP installations that may no longer receive security updates, so they can be patched or isolated.
Fixing The Software Is Not Enough
The PHP team released fixed versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 on October 21. Its official security advisory says there are no complete mitigations and urges users to update.
Organisations should first identify where PHP is running across their servers, cloud environments and third-party hosting arrangements. They should then check which installations are affected and confirm that the updated software is active.
According to Aditya Narayana K, the cofounder of cybersecurity company focused on AI security, Mirror Security, organisations need a repeatable process to identify vulnerabilities, fix them and verify that the fixes work. He pointed to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 as a useful guide for managing this process.
“Organisations must confirm that patches are active and the vulnerability is no longer reproducible, rather than assuming that applying a patch resolves the risk,” Narayana said.
Where immediate patching is not possible, businesses should follow official guidance from PHP and their hosting or software providers. Temporary measures may reduce exposure, but they are not a substitute for a complete fix. Unsupported installations may need to be upgraded or isolated until they can be secured.
The incident has also raised questions about whether businesses can keep pace with AI-assisted vulnerability discovery.
Sriram Krishnan, a technology investor and former general partner at venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), wrote on X that the PHP disclosure will make the ecosystem safer by finding long-lurking issues. “However, the entire software supply chain will need the muscles to rapidly build and deploy fixes. We might need a lot more public + private partnerships to secure infrastructure across the country.”
How Can Businesses Check For A Breach?
Patching closes a known vulnerability, but it does not establish whether hackers exploited it before the update was installed. Businesses must investigate their past exposure alongside fixing their systems.
According to Narayana of Mirror Security, investigators should identify which systems were exposed and review activity from before patching. This includes checking server logs, unusual system behaviour, unauthorised file changes and suspicious network connections.
Organisations should also look for unexpected programs running on their servers or unexplained changes to files and configurations. Security teams can use monitoring tools to bring together information from different systems and identify patterns that may indicate an attack.
Sathyanarayanan recommended reviewing activity from at least a week before the October 21 patch release, given that exploitation attempts were reported before public disclosure. Businesses should not assume that installing a fix eliminates the risk of an earlier compromise.
If investigators find signs of an attack, they should preserve logs and other evidence, involve their hosting provider or an incident response specialist, and assess whether credentials need to be replaced. Patching alone may not remove malicious software or unauthorised access established before the fix.
An attempted attack does not necessarily mean hackers gained access. Equally, the absence of security alerts does not guarantee that a system is safe.
Timely patching must go hand in hand with continuous security monitoring, as attackers can move quickly once vulnerability details become public. The PHP2Shell disclosure demonstrates why cybersecurity cannot end with a software update. Businesses need to know what technology they run, fix vulnerabilities quickly and establish whether attackers gained access before the fix was applied.
As AI tools make it easier to uncover complex flaws, the ability to investigate, patch and verify systems quickly will become just as important as discovering the vulnerabilities themselves.
[Edited by: Shishir Parasher]
[Creatives by: Abhyam Gusai]

items.title: Child safety concerns mount as unregistered shelter homes escape oversight in Punjab
items.summary:
For hundreds of orphaned, abandoned, and vulnerable children in Punjab, a shelter home is meant to be a place of safety. Yet many of the private institutions housing these children remain outside the government’s full oversight, leaving authorities without a clear and up-to-date picture of how many children are living there, under what conditions, and whether they are safe.
According to the Child Protection and Welfare Bureau (CPWB), only 14 shelter homes have been licensed, while more than 50 remain unregistered. A 2021-22 CPWB mapping study, conducted with UNICEF Pakistan, identified 105 residential care institutions in Punjab — 41 government-run and 64 private — with 5,762 children. Four years later, however, the government still lacks updated data on these institutions and the children living in them.

A 2021-22 CPWB mapping study, conducted with UNICEF Pakistan, identified 105 residential care institutions in Punjab — 41 government-run and 64 private — with 5,762 children. Four years later, however, the government still lacks updated data on these institutions and the children living in them.
The CPWB said applications from another four to five facilities were under review. Before licensing, officials inspect buildings, staff, facilities and child-care arrangements, followed by periodic inspections.
Read: Teenager allegedly run over by employer after work dispute
Private shelter homes provide accommodation, food, education and other basic facilities to children at a time when capacity in government institutions remains limited. However, the lack of effective oversight of unregistered facilities has raised concerns about child protection. In the past, several incidents have also raised questions about the living conditions and treatment of children in unregistered institutions.
The recent killing of 15-year-old orphan Waseem Abbas in Multan has renewed concerns about the protection of children living in institutional care. Waseem, who had been living at an NGO-run orphanage, was allegedly chased and run over by a contractor after being sent to work with him to learn electrical work. Police registered a murder case, while the CPWB rejected the orphanage’s registration application on October 20, citing concerns about arrangements for the protection and supervision of children. The case has raised questions about how children are supervised and safeguarded after leaving the institutions responsible for their care.
In April 2024, 32 children were recovered from an unregistered orphanage in Gajjumata, Lahore. According to the CPWB, the children were living in two small rooms. A case was registered against the head of the institution under the Punjab Destitute and Neglected Children Act, although medical examinations did not confirm sexual abuse.
In September 2025, 18 children were taken into protective custody after a video showing children being subjected to violence at an unregistered institution in Chichawatni surfaced on social media. Police said the children had been physically abused. One caretaker was arrested, while cases were also registered against the institution's administrators.
Child protection experts say the existing system for registering and regularly monitoring private shelter homes needs to be strengthened. Iftikhar Mubarak, head of Search for Justice, said registration with the CPWB could improve the quality of services provided to children as well as the monitoring system.
He suggested that shelter homes should also be required to produce a CPWB registration certificate when registering with the Punjab Charity Commission or renewing their registration annually.
Child rights activist Rashida Qureshi said it was alarming that some institutions did not even have clear legal authority to keep children in their custody. She called for the registration and regular inspection of all shelter homes, along with uniform standards for children's accommodation, food, education and healthcare.
Also Read: Waseem Abbas case: HRCP calls for independent probe after alleged extrajudicial killing of prime suspect
Sahil Legal Aid Coordinator Imtiaz Soomro, advocate, said effective monitoring was necessary to ensure the safety of children in shelter homes, religious seminaries and boarding schools. However, he said it remained unclear which institution was responsible for monitoring these facilities under the existing system.
He called for the CPWB and other child rights institutions to establish an effective and regular monitoring mechanism to prevent the exploitation of children.
According to Soomro, incidents of sexual and physical abuse and other forms of exploitation in shelter homes, seminaries and boarding schools often go unreported. He further added that media access to some of these institutions was also limited, making it difficult for incidents involving children to come to light.
The CPWB said 11 Child Protection Institutes were currently operational in Punjab, while 25 Child Protection Units had been established across the province, of which only six were functional.
With more private than government institutions providing residential care to vulnerable children, the lack of an updated government record raises a fundamental question: if authorities do not know the current number of private shelter homes or the children living in them, how can the safety, rights and welfare of those children be effectively monitored?

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) has arrested 42 people during raids on three companies in Karachi’s Rabia City over alleged involvement in producing and selling sexually explicit digital content.
The agency’s Karachi Zone conducted the operation against businesses suspected of creating, promoting and selling pornographic cartoon animations and other digital content to foreign customers. Officials also seized 41 mobile phones for technical examination and digital forensic analysis.
Preliminary findings suggest the companies allegedly operated through organized teams that contacted international customers via social media platforms, including Instagram and X (formerly Twitter).
NCCIA Raids 3 Karachi Companies, Arrests 42 Suspects Over Alleged Sexually Explicit Content
Investigators suspect that the teams created and managed multiple social media accounts using fake identities, women’s names and misleading profiles to attract foreign clients. These accounts reportedly promoted services such as logo design, banner creation, digital illustrations and animations, alongside sexually explicit cartoon content.
Officials are investigating whether the suspects used these identities to approach international customers and obtain orders for pornographic animations.
See Also: Naqvi Urges Women to Avoid Sharing Photos Amid Rising Cybercrime
Details of the Three Companies
According to officials, one company was owned by Fida Hussain and had operated for about two years. The business provided logo design, banner creation, and other digital artwork services to international clients. Investigators seized 19 mobile phones from its premises.
The second company allegedly belonged to a man named Danish and had four employees. It mainly promoted logo and banner design services to foreign customers through online platforms. The agency recovered five mobile phones during the raid.
The third company was allegedly operated by Mohsin and Ehsan and employed 17 people. It offered digital design, animation and other online content services to international markets. Officers seized 17 mobile phones from the premises.
NCCIA Examines Digital Evidence
The NCCIA has taken the seized devices into custody to determine the nature and extent of the alleged activities. Investigators are examining social media accounts, digital communications, suspected explicit animations and other electronic evidence linked to the companies.
The forensic examination is expected to help investigators establish how the businesses operated, how they communicated with foreign customers and whether the suspected activities violated applicable laws.
The investigation is ongoing, and the allegations against the arrested individuals have not yet been established in court.

items.content:
China aims to largely complete its national blockchain network by 2030 and speed up the rollout of an intelligent internet, according to a plan outlining the country's digital development over the next five years.
The document, issued by the Central Cyberspace Affairs Commission, also proposes the commercial launch of sixth-generation (6G) mobile services at an appropriate time.
It sets a broader goal of making significant progress in informatization by 2030, with digital technologies playing a greater role in advancing Chinese modernization.
China's internet penetration rate is expected to rise to 85 percent by 2030, up from 80.1 percent in 2025, while the number of 5G base stations per 10,000 people is projected to increase from 34 to 50, according to the document.
The plan calls for stronger basic research in computational mathematics, communication networks and data science, and expects breakthroughs in core technologies in key sectors, such as deeper integration of AI with operating systems and software development toolchains.
Read More: Bill Gates warns of 20 years of turmoil from artificial intelligence
As AI continues to advance rapidly, the plan calls for expanding AI education across all levels of schooling, promoting AI literacy across society and accelerating the development of a vocational education system for digital talent.
The plan also aims to further open up the telecommunications and internet sectors in an orderly manner.
China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology projects that the country's information and communications industry revenue will reach 4.1 trillion yuan (about 615 billion US dollars) by 2030.
It also stresses the need to strengthen data security and protect personal information.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Moonshot ​AI has reduced the cyber-offensive capabilities of its newest model, the Chinese startup said ‌on Saturday, as fears grow that increasingly autonomous AI could turbocharge hacking.
Beijing-based Moonshot announced the curbs while introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, which it describes as its most capable 3-trillion-parameter-class open-weight model. The company plans to publish the model's ​weights — files allowing outside developers to run and modify it on their own systems — by ​November 4.
Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments ⁠used to develop the model, while retaining general coding skills.
"We aim not to release open weights ​that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability," the company said.
Governments, technology companies and security researchers ​are growing increasingly concerned that AI could make sophisticated hacking easier and cheaper. Models that can write code, operate software tools and complete long, multi-step tasks may help users identify weaknesses in programs and automate parts of cyberattacks.
China proposed ​export controls last week that would ban exports of AI-driven malware-generation and mutation technology and restrict AI-assisted ​vulnerability-discovery tools. The draft measures, which remain open for public comment, cite the risk that such capabilities could be ‌used ⁠against critical infrastructure, defence-industrial and core government systems, or to bypass security protections.
Read More: Bill Gates warns of 20 years of turmoil from artificial intelligence
Moonshot said open-weight models can improve security by helping more organisations inspect and secure their own software, including older systems that receive little attention.
Unlike proprietary, closed-weight AI systems, however, open-weight releases make central oversight more difficult. Once the files ​are widely distributed, the ​original developer has less ⁠ability to restrict access, monitor use or update safeguards than with a hosted service.
K3.1 Pro scored 81.0% on its internal cyber benchmark, compared with 90.5% ​for a similar version without the risk-reduction measures, the company said. The ​test involved finding ⁠and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. Moonshot said the comparison showed that filtering cyber-related data reduced the model's offensive cyber performance, although it still outperformed its predecessor. The results have not been independently verified.
K3.1 ⁠Pro has ​a 1-million-token context window, allowing it to process very large ​amounts of text at once. Moonshot also released a faster version, K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which it said runs at two to ​three times the speed of the standard model.

items.title: AI-Discovered Software Flaws May Trigger More Global Disruptions, Experts Warn
items.summary:

Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are helping cybersecurity researchers discover software flaws that could lead to further global internet disruptions, experts have warned. The growing number of identified flaws is forcing companies and government organisations to strengthen their security systems to prevent cyberattacks.
According to seven cybersecurity professionals who spoke to Reuters, AI-driven vulnerability detection is likely to expose more weaknesses in widely used software. While finding these flaws can help developers improve security, it also creates pressure to fix them before cybercriminals exploit them.
Matthew Prince, chief executive of internet infrastructure company Cloudflare, said several serious vulnerabilities had already been identified in other critical software systems. While finding these flaws can help developers improve security, it also creates pressure to fix them before cybercriminals exploit them.
Matthew Prince, chief executive of internet infrastructure company Cloudflare, said several serious vulnerabilities had already been identified in other critical software systems. He expects the coming months and years to bring more security challenges as AI uncovers weaknesses that have remained hidden for a long time.
Prince warned that organisations could face repeated security emergencies as developers discover and work to fix these problems.
PHP Vulnerabilities Cause Website Disruptions
The warning follows recent disruptions affecting government websites in Europe and other regions. The incidents came after researchers discovered vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used programming language that powers a large number of websites.
Following the disclosures, website operators rushed to update their systems and address the security risks. Some organisations temporarily took their websites offline because they feared attackers could exploit the flaws before patches became available.
The incidents highlight the challenges organisations face when vulnerabilities affect widely used technologies. Even when security updates are available, applying them across complex systems can take time. Taking websites offline may become a temporary option when administrators believe they cannot secure their systems quickly enough.
AI Is Helping Researchers Find More Bugs
Research from Massachusetts-based cybersecurity intelligence firm VulnCheck indicates that the number of discovered software vulnerabilities has doubled year-on-year. The company attributes part of this increase to advances in AI and was preparing to publish its findings in the coming days, according to Reuters.
AI tools can help researchers examine software code, identify weaknesses and detect security problems that might otherwise remain unnoticed. This can allow developers to identify and fix flaws more quickly.
However, the same developments may also increase the workload for security teams. Organisations must assess newly discovered vulnerabilities, determine which systems are affected and apply appropriate fixes before attackers can take advantage of them.
Cybersecurity professionals expect this process to create more urgent patching efforts and operational challenges for businesses and public institutions.
Experts Divided Over the Risk of More Cyberattacks
Although experts agree that AI is helping uncover more software weaknesses, they do not share the same view on whether this will automatically result in more successful cyberattacks.
Finding a vulnerability does not necessarily mean that attackers can exploit it. The actual risk depends on factors such as the nature of the flaw, whether vulnerable systems are exposed to the internet and how quickly organisations apply security updates.
At the same time, the growing number of discoveries could give security teams less time to respond to each issue. If attackers learn about a vulnerability before an organisation fixes it, the chances of exploitation may increase.
The situation presents both an opportunity and a challenge for the cybersecurity industry. AI can strengthen digital security by helping researchers uncover weaknesses, but organisations must also respond to a faster flow of security threats.

Organisations Face Growing Pressure to Improve Security
The latest developments underline the importance of regular software updates, vulnerability monitoring and effective incident response plans. Companies and government departments that rely on widely used software may need to review their systems more frequently as new flaws emerge.
Security teams will also need to prioritise vulnerabilities based on their severity and the potential damage they could cause. Promptly installing patches and monitoring systems for suspicious activity can help reduce the risk of exploitation.
As AI tools continue to improve, cybersecurity experts expect software developers and organisations to face increasing pressure to identify and address vulnerabilities before they cause widespread disruption.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan on Saturday issued a notification stating that the party’s provincial organisation in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) would continue to function under the presidency of Junaid Akbar, highlighting no changes to the provincial cabinet or organisational structure until further orders.
The government and opposition failed to reach an agreement, and emergency and governor’s rule were declared on October 11 after talks failed, following a PTI long march towards Islamabad that began on October 4. On the same day, police arrested 59 PTI workers in Swabi and six others in Khyber district, while reports emerged that ousted chief minister Sohail Afridi and Akbar had also been taken into custody. Since then, intraparty rifts reportedly emerged, leading to PTI leaders exchanging barbs online.
According to a notification issued today and shared on X, Senator Noorul Haq Qadri, identified as the party’s senior vice-president in K-P, would preside over meetings of the provincial cabinet in the absence of Junaid.
The notification further assigned PTI K-P General Secretary Ali Asghar the responsibility of chairing meetings in the absence of the senior vice-president. He was also authorised to convene and chair meetings of other tiers of the provincial organisation.
چیئرمین پی ٹی آئی بیرسٹر گوہر خان کا خیبر پختونخوا میں پارٹی کے تنظیمی امور سے متعلق اہم نوٹیفکیشن جاری۔
خیبر پختونخوا کی موجودہ صورتحال کے پیشِ نظر جاری کردہ نوٹیفکیشن کے مطابق جنید اکبر خان بدستور صوبائی صدر رہیں گے۔ ان کی عدم موجودگی میں سینیٹر نورالحق قادری پارٹی اجلاسوں کی… pic.twitter.com/EP9z4MfAod
— Barrister Gohar Khan (@BarristerGohar) October 24, 2026
According to the document, Asghar would oversee the organisation’s administration, coordination and supervision across its various tiers and wings to ensure the implementation of party policies, strategies and decisions.
The notification was signed by Barrister Gohar in his capacity as chairman of PTI.
The notification comes amid an internal rift within the PTI, with differences over the party’s leadership and political strategy in K-P spilling into the public domain. On October 21, The Express Tribune reported that former K-P chief minister Ali Amin Gandapur and PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja had exchanged criticism over allegations of internal divisions, the provincial leadership and the handling of the party’s political affairs.
Raja warned of attempts by what he described as “undemocratic decision-makers” to undermine internal consensus, while Gandapur demanded that the party secretary general substantiate his allegations and apologise.
The dispute intensified following a purported audio recording in which Gandapur allegedly blamed Raja’s “mismanagement and flawed planning” for the provincial government’s dismissal and the party’s current predicament. The Express Tribune said it could not independently verify the recording.
Read more: Opposition leaders criticise govt over stalled talks, restrictions on parliamentarians
Gandapur also challenged claims that provincial lawmakers were attempting to decide the party’s leadership and the next chief minister without the approval of PTI founder Imran Khan and the party’s political committee. Raja, meanwhile, maintained that Afridi remained the lawful chief minister and that Akbar continued as provincial party president, with Asghar acting in Akbar’s absence.
Barrister Gohar sought to contain the fallout, telling the media that he had spoken to the leaders involved and urged them to stop issuing statements against one another.
He maintained that the party’s provincial lawmakers remained united and that Afridi continued to be the party’s choice for chief minister. Against this backdrop, the October 24 notification formalises the arrangements for the PTI’s K-P organisation, specifying who will preside over meetings in the absence of senior office-bearers.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Federal Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has urged women to be cautious when sharing their photographs online as complaints of cybercrime, harassment and blackmailing continue to rise in Pakistan.
Speaking to journalists during an open court at the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) zonal headquarters in Lahore on October 23, Naqvi said the agency was receiving a large number of complaints involving the harassment of women and girls.
He urged women to avoid sharing their photographs under any circumstances, warning that online activity could expose them to different forms of cybercrime.
Naqvi Urges Women to Avoid Sharing Photos Amid Rising Cybercrime
The minister also advised the public not to transfer money to strangers who make financial requests through social media or other online platforms. He cautioned that fraudsters often pretend to be ill or face an emergency to convince people to send money.
Naqvi said people should verify such requests before taking any action and avoid falling for emotional appeals used to obtain money through deception.
Warning Against Fake Accounts and Online Scams
The interior minister also warned citizens about fake social media accounts that criminals use to deceive people and collect money. He urged the public to remain alert when dealing with unfamiliar accounts and online requests.
He further cautioned against schemes that promise to double money within a short period. Such offers attract victims and steal their savings.
Naqvi also highlighted the risks of sharing passwords over the phone. He questioned how people could keep their money safe if they disclosed sensitive account information to others.
The minister said authorities had taken hundreds of people into custody during operations against illegal call centres. These centres are among the targets of efforts to curb online fraud and related criminal activities.
NCCIA Faces Shortage of Staff
Naqvi said the NCCIA had only 61 officers across Punjab, despite receiving a substantial number of complaints from citizens.
He acknowledged the difficulties faced by people seeking help from the agency and said the government was working to ensure adequate staffing to handle complaints more effectively.
The minister added that he would raise the staffing issue with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to seek further support for the agency.
He also said many women had approached the NCCIA with complaints about online harassment and cyber-blackmailing, highlighting the need for stronger measures to address such cases.
Awareness Campaign Planned
The interior minister said the government planned to launch an awareness campaign for women, girls and the general public to help them recognise online threats and avoid falling victim to cybercriminals.
The campaign is intended to encourage safer online behaviour and improve public awareness of common fraud tactics.
As online scams and harassment remain a concern, citizens are advised to avoid sharing passwords, verify requests for money, and report suspicious accounts and threatening messages to the relevant authorities.
Naqvi’s remarks highlight the need for greater public awareness and stronger institutional capacity to tackle cybercrime and protect people from online exploitation.

Key Startup Funding Highlights Of The Week
AI startups continued to see the highest investor interest for a second consecutive week, raising $93.9 Mn across six deals. Ajeet Sing-led AI powered martech startup Different emerged from stealth and raised $48 Mn, the biggest cheque for an AI startup this week.
Healthtech was the second-most funded sector, attracting $60.6 Mn across two deals. The funding number was largely driven by Even Healthcare’s $50 Mn Series B round, while CureBay raised $10.6 Mn in a mix of equity and debt.
Venture debt firm Trifecta Capital and early-stage focused VC Blume Ventures backed two startups apiece, becoming the most active investors this week.
In a relatively dull funding week, seed stage startups were more sought after by investors. Five startups at this stage lapped up $51.4 Mn, making up about 28% of the overall funding pie.
Startup IPO Updates Of The Week
Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging closed its ₹852 Cr IPO with a whopping 135.9X subscription and listed on the bourses on Friday at a 66% premium.
On the other hand, B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk’s ₹5,012.3 Cr IPO closed with an 3.06X oversubscription and made its debut with a premium of 5.5%.
Hunger Pangs, the parent of restaurant chain Burma Burma, has filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) for an IPO comprising a fresh issue of up to ₹150 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 2.8 Cr shares
Other Developments Of The Week
Mygate is set to amalgamate with adtech startup AdOnMo by December 5. AdOnMo backer and Zomato-parent Eternal will hold 4.4% stake in the merged entity worth ₹156 Cr.
Peak XV doubled down on San Francisco-based AI startup Blacksmith, backing the startup’s $66 Mn Series C round. Blacksmith entered the unicorn club post the round.

items.author: Oboh
items.content:
The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began Friday, the head of the World Health Organization said.
Read Also: Return of Ebola: Triumph of 2014, test of 2026
The DR Congo’s worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
The trial began with the first shot of Ervebo being administered in Bunia, the capital of the DRC’s northeastern Ituri province, which is the epicentre of the outbreak.
“Science gives us hope. Today, in Bunia DRC, the first participants were vaccinated in a new Ebola vaccine trial called Tumaini, which means ‘hope’ in Swahili,” WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X.
“This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work,” he said, adding that in the meantime, the existing Ervebo vaccine would be tested.
“WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives.”
Two vaccines in the pipeline
The so-called Tumaini trial is a single trial framework that can test the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of multiple vaccines.
The trial will use a ring vaccination approach: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection.
It is gearing up to incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are currently advancing through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.
Both have received funding from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, and are expected to enter the trial “shortly”, CEPI said in a statement.
“Tumaini will work closely with affected communities, health authorities and outbreak response partners to generate robust evidence on vaccine performance that could contribute to curtailing the epidemic, saving lives, and strengthening preparedness for future Bundibugyo outbreaks,” said CEPI.
The trial will include pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials.
‘Important step’
WHO emergencies director Chikwe Ihekweazu said the trial was set up to generate the rigorous evidence needed to determine whether the participating vaccines could protect people at risk.
“If successful, this would be the first time we have clear evidence of vaccine efficacy against Bundibugyo virus — a major advance that could transform how we respond to this outbreak and prepare for future outbreaks and help save lives,” he said.
Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
“Bringing this trial into the Ebola response is an important step towards addressing the urgent needs of affected communities,” said Steve Ahuka-Mundeke, the DRC Ebola response incident manager.
The DRC declared its 17th outbreak of Ebola on May 15, and the WHO two days later triggered a public health emergency of international concern, its second-highest alert level.

items.author: Oboh
items.content:
By Chief Handel Okoli
As Nigeria inches towards another general election, against a backdrop of political tension, growing anxiety, and genuine national security concerns, certain aspects of the life and times of one of our finest statesmen have assumed renewed significance. The ideas, convictions, and political philosophy of Dr. Alex Ifeanyichukwu Ekwueme, GCON, former Vice-President of Nigeria, deserve serious reflection as we consider the kind of country we wish to build.
Dr. Ekwueme was born on 21 October 1932. Had he not passed away on 19 November 2017, he would have celebrated his 94th birthday on Wednesday, 21 October 2026. His death elicited an avalanche of tributes and encomiums from across Nigeria, reflecting the profound respect he commanded among people of different ethnic, religious, and political backgrounds.
Even before his death, the late Professor Ben Nwabueze, SAN, had drawn national attention to Ekwueme’s enduring contributions in his 2013 book, The Legacies of Dr. Alex Ekwueme to Government and to Political and Social Development of Nigeria. Among the legacies highlighted were his formidable intellectual credentials as an asset in governance; his commitment to a strong multiparty system, constitutionalism, and the rule of law; his advocacy for the restructuring of the Nigerian federation; his proposal for the equitable distribution of political offices among the six geopolitical zones; and his remarkable public-spiritedness and philanthropy, which I once described as Ekwueme’s extravagant philanthropy.
Yet, perhaps the most compelling of his legacies, and certainly one of the most relevant to Nigeria’s present political circumstances, was his altruistic and pragmatic approach to national integration.
This is one of the fundamental challenges the Buhari administration failed woefully to address. Rather than build upon the emerging spirit of national reconciliation and integration, the administration, in my view, took the country in the opposite direction. President Jonathan had handed over the report of the National Conference to President Buhari, but the latter apparently had other priorities. An important opportunity to confront Nigeria’s unresolved national questions and build a more inclusive federation was consequently lost.
Ekwueme understood that the survival of Nigeria as a united nation depended, to a considerable extent, on addressing the fears of domination, exclusion, and marginalisation among its constituent ethnic and regional groups.
THE QUEST FOR NATIONAL INTEGRATION
Following the end of the Nigerian Civil War in 1970, the urgent questions of national reconstruction, reconciliation, and the restoration of confidence among the country’s diverse peoples occupied a central place in political discourse. These concerns became particularly prominent during the formation of political parties in 1978, as Nigeria prepared for a return to civilian rule.
The political parties recognised, to varying degrees, the need to accommodate the country’s complex ethnic and regional composition. The National Party of Nigeria (NPN), which eventually won the presidential election, adopted a political arrangement that reflected the importance of balancing interests across the North and the South in the distribution of key political offices.
It was within this political atmosphere that Dr. Alex Ekwueme emerged as the NPN’s vice-presidential candidate, alongside Alhaji Shehu Shagari as its presidential candidate.
The significance of the Igbo presence in the vice-presidential calculations of the major political parties of the period deserves particular attention. With the exception of the Nigerian People’s Party (NPP), whose presidential candidate, Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe, chose Professor Ishaya Audu as his running mate, the other major parties also featured Igbo politicians as their vice-presidential candidates.
These choices were politically significant. At the very least, they reflected an awareness of the need to broaden the political coalitions upon which the Nigerian federation rested and to reassure the Igbo people that, despite the devastation of the Civil War, they remained an integral part of the Nigerian project.
It would, however, be a mistake to regard these political arrangements as merely symbolic. They raised a fundamental question about the future of Nigeria: could the country achieve genuine reconciliation and lasting unity without creating a political environment in which every major ethnic and regional group had a fair opportunity to participate in national leadership?
The prospect of an Igbo man ascending to the presidency subsequently became a subject of considerable political sensitivity. It has been suggested that apprehensions about Dr. Ekwueme’s possible emergence as President, particularly in the context of political succession under the Shagari administration, formed part of the considerations surrounding the military coup of December 1983.
While such claims require careful examination against the available historical record, they underscore a larger and more enduring problem: the difficulty Nigeria has faced in separating the legitimate pursuit of political power from fears about the ethnic or regional identity of those who might exercise it.
The lesson is unmistakable. National unity cannot be sustained by rhetoric alone. It requires deliberate political arrangements, mutual trust, and a willingness to accommodate the legitimate aspirations of all sections of the country.
FROM MILITARY RULE TO THE QUEST FOR A NEW NIGERIA
The military coup that terminated the Second Republic in December 1983 abruptly ended the democratic experiment in which Dr. Ekwueme had played such a prominent role. 
He was subsequently detained by the military authorities and subjected to imprisonment.
Yet, in a remarkable demonstration of intellectual resilience, that period of confinement provided him with an opportunity to reflect more deeply on the Nigerian condition and to nurture his ideas about the kind of country Nigeria ought to become.
Rather than seize the opportunity to address the structural problems that had contributed to political instability, mutual suspicion, and the struggle for power, successive military administrations introduced institutional changes that, in my view, further complicated Nigeria’s national question.
The creation of additional states and local government areas, the delineation of electoral constituencies, and the conduct and interpretation of population censuses became contentious issues in the struggle over political representation and the distribution of national resources.
The consequences were particularly troubling for what is today the South-East geopolitical zone, whose concerns about representation and its relative position within the federation have remained important elements of the national debate.
The point is not that every administrative or political change undertaken under military rule was necessarily designed to disadvantage a particular region. Rather, it is that institutional arrangements introduced without sufficient regard for fairness, transparency, and the confidence of all constituent groups can deepen existing grievances and undermine national cohesion.
The failure of the Babangida administration to complete a credible transition to democratic rule, culminating in the annulment of the 12 June 1993 presidential election, further aggravated the national crisis and deepened public distrust of the political process.
It was against this background of political uncertainty, institutional distrust, and unresolved questions of national identity that Dr. Ekwueme, having endured detention and imprisonment, began to engage more actively with like-minded Nigerians on the need to reconstruct the Nigerian federation on a more equitable foundation.
His concern was not simply who would occupy the presidency at any given time. It was how Nigeria could evolve a political system in which the struggle for power would no longer be perceived as an existential contest among ethnic and regional groups.
THE 1994/95 CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE: A DEFINING MOMENT
Dr. Ekwueme played a leading role in articulating the structural and constitutional issues confronting Nigeria. In this endeavour, he worked alongside other prominent Igbo leaders, including the Ikemba Nnewi, Chief Emeka Odumegwu-Ojukwu.
The challenge before the South-East was not merely to secure immediate political concessions. It was to participate meaningfully in the reorganisation of the Nigerian state and advance constitutional arrangements capable of protecting the interests of all regions over the long term.
Dr. Ekwueme’s contribution to the 1994/95 Constitutional Conference reflected his characteristic preference for altruistic intellectual engagement over political theatrics. He served on the Committee on the Structure and Framework of the Constitution, where he made significant contributions to debates on the institutional foundations of the federation.
His performance earned him recognition as one of the outstanding delegates. Among the honours he received was an award from The Punch newspaper as its Most Distinguished Delegate.
His approach demonstrated an important lesson in public leadership: political influence is not determined solely by the prominence of the office one occupies. It can also derive from the quality of one’s ideas, the depth of one’s preparation, the clarity of one’s vision, and the ability to persuade others through reasoned argument.
Ekwueme understood that the national question could not be resolved by political slogans or temporary compromises. It required a serious examination of the structures through which power was distributed, resources allocated, and the constituent peoples of Nigeria represented.
RESTRUCTURING AND THE SIX GEOPOLITICAL ZONES
Among Dr. Ekwueme’s most consequential contributions to Nigeria’s constitutional discourse was his advocacy for restructuring the federation and organising the country around six geopolitical zones.
The proposal was rooted in a practical understanding of Nigeria’s political realities. A federation as diverse as Nigeria could not achieve lasting stability if access to its highest political offices and the benefits of national development were persistently perceived as the exclusive preserve of particular regions or groups.
It is important to appreciate the deeper logic of Ekwueme’s proposal. He was not simply advocating a convenient formula for distributing political offices. His vision was to reduce the desperation associated with political power by assuring every part of the country that it had a legitimate place in the national leadership structure.
Where groups believe that political exclusion will permanently deny them access to influence, resources, and opportunities, competition for power can become bitter and destabilising. Conversely, where credible constitutional arrangements provide assurances of inclusion, political competition is more likely to take place within an atmosphere of mutual confidence.
The six geopolitical zones were therefore more than geographical classifications. In Ekwueme’s conception, they offered a framework for promoting national integration, political accommodation, and unity.
The proposal was understandably controversial. Any arrangement that seeks to alter an established distribution of political power will encounter resistance from those who benefit from the existing order. Yet resistance to such proposals does not diminish the importance of the questions they raise.
Indeed, the continuing debate over restructuring demonstrates that the fundamental issues Ekwueme sought to address remain unresolved.
His vision challenged Nigerians to look beyond the immediate question of who should occupy the presidency and confront the more consequential issue of how the Nigerian state could be organised to inspire confidence among its constituent peoples.
ROTATION OF THE PRESIDENCY AND THE UNFINISHED PROJECT
The constitutional deliberations of the Abacha era gave considerable attention to questions of political inclusion, the distribution of power, and the restructuring of the federation. Dr. Ekwueme was among the prominent advocates of arrangements designed to make the Nigerian political system more equitable and inclusive.
The broader principle behind his six-zonal approach was straightforward: if the presidency rotated among the six geopolitical zones in an agreed sequence, every zone would have a reasonable expectation of producing a President within a defined period.
Such an arrangement could also have a practical political benefit. By giving every zone a credible expectation of access to the presidency, it could reduce the incentive for political actors to treat every election as a final opportunity to secure power for their own region.
However, an important distinction must be drawn between a constitutional proposal, a political understanding, and an enforceable constitutional provision. The six geopolitical zones have not been constitutionally entrenched as the exclusive units for rotating the presidency.
This omission is significant.
Nigerian politicians have often demonstrated a willingness to embrace the principle of zoning when it serves their immediate interests, only to abandon or reinterpret it when its consistent application would require sacrifice or accommodation in the broader national interest.
The result is a political culture in which the language of fairness is frequently invoked, but the discipline required to sustain equitable arrangements is often lacking.
Otherwise, why should a country that has repeatedly acknowledged the importance of geographical balance in political leadership continue to treat the six-zone principle as a matter of political convenience rather than a serious framework for national integration?
Nevertheless, the principle underlying Ekwueme’s argument remains compelling. Had Nigeria adopted and consistently implemented an effective constitutional arrangement for equitable regional participation in the presidency, it might have reduced some of the recurring grievances associated with political exclusion and the distribution of national power.
It would, of course, be an overstatement to suggest that rotational presidency alone would have eliminated every complaint about marginalisation, infrastructure, or the distribution of public resources. These challenges are influenced by many factors, including fiscal federalism, the distribution of federal institutions, the allocation of public investment, the quality of governance, and the independence of constitutional institutions.
Yet a credible power-sharing arrangement could have made an important contribution to national confidence by demonstrating that Nigeria’s political system was designed to accommodate all its constituent parts.
This, in my view, is the enduring significance of Dr. Ekwueme’s vision: to transform national integration from a political slogan into a practical constitutional commitment.
AN UNFINISHED LEGACY
As Nigeria approaches another general election, it is worth asking whether the country has sufficiently embraced the lessons of Dr. Alex Ekwueme’s political philosophy.
Have we built a federation in which every region feels a genuine sense of belonging?
Have we developed institutions that command the confidence of citizens, irrespective of ethnicity, religion, or political affiliation?
Have we created a political culture in which the distribution of power is governed by fairness and mutual accommodation rather than by the fear of domination?
These questions are particularly important for the South-East, whose concerns about political representation and equitable participation in national leadership remain central to the wider debate about restructuring and national integration.
Nevertheless, the significance of Ekwueme’s vision extends far beyond the South-East. It is a vision for Nigeria as a whole: a country in which no ethnic group needs to fear another, no region should feel permanently excluded, and no citizen should be made to feel that national leadership belongs exclusively to a privileged section of the federation.
True egalitarianism does not mean that every region must be identical in population, resources, or political influence. It means that differences should not become instruments of permanent exclusion or domination.
It requires a constitutional order that recognises diversity while guaranteeing fairness, dignity, and equal citizenship.
It also requires political leaders who understand that the long-term stability of the federation is more important than the immediate advantages that may accrue to one region, one political party, or one group of individuals.
Ekwueme’s legacy challenges contemporary Nigerian leaders to look beyond the immediate calculations of electoral advantage and ask a more fundamental question: what kind of political system will leave the country more united, more stable, and more confident in its collective future?
NORTH–SOUTH ZONING OF THE PRESIDENCY: A DISTORTION OF THE SIX-ZONAL VISION
Let me state clearly, for the avoidance of doubt, that the current practice of zoning or rotating the presidency between the North and the South does not adequately reflect the essence and significance of Dr. Ekwueme’s six-geopolitical-zone approach.
A North–South arrangement, in my view, falls short of the more inclusive vision underpinning the six-zonal framework. By reducing Nigeria’s complex geopolitical structure to two broad blocs, it risks overlooking the distinct identities, interests, and aspirations of the six geopolitical zones.
The North and the South are not homogeneous political entities. Each comprises distinct geopolitical zones with their own histories, interests, concerns, and expectations. A system that recognises only two broad blocs may provide a measure of regional balance, but it does not necessarily guarantee equitable participation by all six zones.
Most unfortunately, those who appear to have acquiesced in this arrangement include some of the very people for whose protection and political inclusion Dr. Ekwueme’s prescriptions were designed.
His vision was not intended to replace one form of exclusion with another. It was intended to create a fairer political order in which every geopolitical zone would have a credible opportunity to participate in national leadership.
The North–South formula, therefore, cannot be regarded as an adequate substitute for a genuine six-zonal framework. It may address the immediate question of balancing power between two broad regions, but it leaves unresolved the more fundamental question of equity among the six geopolitical zones.
If Nigeria is genuinely committed to national integration, political equity, and a more inclusive federation, it must give serious consideration to the broader and more purposeful framework represented by six-zone rotation.
This does not mean that zoning alone will solve Nigeria’s national question. Nor does it mean that the presidency should become a substitute for the wider constitutional reforms that the country requires. Rather, it means that equitable access to national leadership should form part of a comprehensive effort to build a federation in which every constituent part has a genuine sense of belonging.
The objective should not be to confer permanent political advantages on any region. It should be to establish a credible framework of fairness, mutual accommodation, and shared national responsibility.
That, in my understanding, is the enduring message of Ekwueme’s egalitarian philosophy.
CONCLUSION: BEYOND TRIBUTES TO IMPLEMENTATION
As we remember Dr. Alex Ifeanyichukwu Ekwueme, Ide Oko, on what would have been his 94th birthday, we should do more than celebrate his achievements. We should revisit his ideas, examine their continuing relevance, and summon the political courage to implement those that can help build a truly united and egalitarian country.
Ekwueme’s life reminds us that patriotism is not merely about occupying public office, winning elections, or enjoying the privileges of political power. It is also about the willingness to challenge an unjust status quo, advance ideas that may not yield immediate personal benefits, and work towards a political order that gives every citizen and every region a fair opportunity to thrive.
His legacy calls for a Nigeria in which national integration is not merely proclaimed but practised; in which constitutional arrangements inspire confidence rather than suspicion; and in which the pursuit of political power is moderated by a genuine commitment to fairness and the common good.
The greatest tribute we can pay this distinguished statesman is not the eloquence of our birthday tributes but the seriousness with which we engage his ideas and the determination with which we pursue the national transformation he envisioned.
May his enduring legacy continue to inspire the quest for a more united, equitable, and egalitarian Nigeria.
Chief Handel Okoli is Former Special Assistant to Former President Dr. Alex Ekwueme; Former Special Assistant to Former President Olusegun Obasanjo on Special Duties.

items.author: Oboh
items.content:
When Nigerians discuss election preparedness, attention often turns to the chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, its national commissioners and the technology the commission plans to deploy.
Read Also: 2027: Violence threatening polls
But former INEC National Commissioner Mike Igini says the decisive test may lie further down the chain – with the temporary workers who manage voting and counting at polling units.
“The people that are going to conduct these elections are not the regular permanent staff of INEC,” Igini said during a television interview. “Nigeria needs to focus on the people that are going to conduct this election.”
These workers, including presiding officers, handle key tasks on election day. They verify voters, manage election materials and record results. If their identities or impartiality are in doubt, Igini argued, public confidence in the process could suffer before the results are even announced.
He urged agencies that supply temporary election workers to ensure their lists are accurate and that those recruited are properly verified. He also called on INEC to check the lists it receives rather than rely solely on the agencies that submit them.
The issue, he said, is that political interests could find ways to influence recruitment lists. He recalled an incident in Akwa Ibom State during his time as a commissioner, when he said officials found people on a list who were not staff of the university expected to provide workers for the exercise.
“We discovered that mercenaries were sent in on that list,” Igini said. He added that a market woman told officials her name had been included and that she had come to attend training.
Igini said the discovery prompted him to stop the training while the list was examined. The episode, in his account, showed how a process intended to draw qualified workers from established institutions could be vulnerable to interference.
His concerns also extend to the recruitment of members of the National Youth Service Corps, NYSC, whom he identified as a key source of polling-unit officials. He called on the corps to protect the integrity of the names it submits to INEC and on the commission to verify the people assigned to election duties.
“The list is infiltrated,” he said, describing what he believes can happen when recruitment is not sufficiently checked. He warned that a compromised list could put people at polling units who have not been properly vetted or trained.
Igini cited a separate controversy from the 2023 elections in Rivers State, alleging that an ad-hoc worker who announced results in one local government area had claimed to be a lecturer at a college. He said journalists who checked with the institution could not find the person on its payroll.
The claim, as presented in the interview, was not independently verified. Igini used it to argue that election authorities should be able to explain who is recruited, where the workers come from and how their identities and qualifications are confirmed.
He said the problem was not simply whether a temporary worker had completed training. The commission, he argued, must also be confident that the person attending the training is the same person who will serve at the polling unit.
That concern places responsibility on several institutions. Agencies that provide personnel must keep reliable records and protect their recruitment processes. INEC must scrutinise the names it receives, verify identities and supervise workers on election day. Political parties and their agents, meanwhile, have a role in observing the process and raising concerns through proper channels.
Igini said INEC’s senior officials would not be present at every polling unit on election day. The work would be carried out by temporary staff under the commission’s supervision, making the quality of that supervision central to the process.
He also noted that party agents and voters could help monitor what happens at polling units. He encouraged agents to audit election materials and document the process, including by taking a clear image or video of the original Form EC8A after results are recorded.
“The power of the people at the polling unit is awesome,” he said, adding that voters would normally outnumber election officials there.
His argument is that accountability should not end with the recruitment of workers. The public needs confidence that the people managing the vote are the people selected for the job, that they have been properly trained and that their actions can be checked.
For the 2027 elections, that requires clear answers to basic questions: Which institutions will provide the ad-hoc staff? What checks will be used to verify their names and identities? How will INEC prevent political interference in recruitment? And what happens when an irregularity is discovered?
Igini’s warning is that the credibility of an election can be weakened by decisions made long before ballots are cast. If the people entrusted with the polling-unit process are not properly recruited and supervised, he said, the result may be an election in which citizens struggle to trust the process.
He advised: “The most important staff that Nigeria should focus on will be the presiding officers.”

items.author: Oboh
items.content:
By Sola Ogundipe
October 20 has acquired an unsettling significance in Nigeria’s public health history. 12 years ago, on that date, the World Health Organisation (WHO) declared Nigeria free of Ebola after a painstaking campaign halted an outbreak that threatened to overwhelm the country’s fragile health system. On October 20, 2026, the confirmation of an imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in Abuja reopened an uncomfortable question: how prepared is Nigeria to confront the virus again?
The coincidence is striking, but the lesson is more important than the date. The 2014 victory demonstrated what decisive leadership, vigilant surveillance, contact tracing and coordinated action could achieve. The new case tests whether those hard won lessons have translated into lasting capacity.
The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare confirmed the case on October 20 following laboratory testing. He said the patient, a woman with a recent travel history to Uganda, reportedly developed symptoms on October 7, sought care at a private health facility in Abuja on October 11 and tested positive on October 20. 
She was isolated and receiving medical care, while investigations continued to establish the likely source of infection and reconstruct her travel and exposure history. The ministry reported that 44 contacts had been identified for monitoring.
The warning hidden in a victory
Nigeria’s 2014 experience remains one of Africa’s most cited examples of successful Ebola containment. The outbreak began after Liberian-American Patrick Sawyer arrived in Lagos in July 2014 while infected with the virus. His illness exposed health workers and others to a disease that many facilities had limited experience managing.
Nigeria recorded 20 cases, including eight deaths, before the outbreak was contained. The response required the identification and monitoring of hundreds of contacts, the isolation of suspected cases, rapid investigation and sustained public communication. On October 20, 2014, the World Health Organisation (WHO) formally declared Nigeria Ebola-free after 42 days without a new case following the discharge of the last confirmed patient.
Dr Rui Gama Vaz, then WHO representative in Nigeria, captured the significance of the achievement while warning against complacency.
“It shows that Ebola can be contained, but we must be clear that we have only won a battle, the war will only end when West Africa and other affected countries are also declared free of Ebola,” he said at the declaration ceremony.
His words have acquired fresh relevance. Nigeria won that battle through a combination of epidemiological investigation, disciplined contact tracing, isolation, laboratory support and cooperation between public authorities and private institutions. The achievement was not simply a declaration. It was the result of work carried out by public health teams, clinicians, laboratory personnel and communities under considerable pressure.
But victories in public health can breed a dangerous illusion: that because a country defeats a threat once, it will necessarily defeat it again.
Ebola has returned in a different form, under different circumstances and against a public health system facing its own constraints. The anniversary should therefore be less a celebration of past success than an examination of what has endured since 2014.
New strain, different challenges
The virus responsible for the Abuja case is Bundibugyo, a species of Ebola virus distinct from the Zaire ebolavirus associated with the 2014 Nigerian outbreak. That distinction is clinically important because vaccines and treatments developed for one Ebola species cannot automatically be assumed to work against another.
According to WHO, there is currently no approved vaccine or specific antiviral treatment for Bundibugyo Ebola, but that does not mean the disease is untreatable. Prompt diagnosis, isolation, careful supportive care and management of complications can be critical to a patient’s survival and to preventing further transmission.
Professor Oyewale Tomori, virologist and chairman of the West African National Academy of Scientists, has warned against treating the strain’s comparatively lower historical fatality rates as grounds for complacency.
“When we say Bundibugyo is less severe, however, that does not mean it is harmless or that it cannot kill people,” he said. The distinction also exposes a potential weakness in preparedness. 
Equipment, diagnostic protocols and clinical experience acquired during an earlier outbreak cannot simply be assumed to provide everything required for a different strain.
Diagnosis gap
One of the most consequential questions concerns the interval between the patient’s first symptoms and laboratory confirmation.
The reported timeline places the onset of symptoms on October 7, the first medical consultation on October 11 and laboratory confirmation on October 20. 
Tomori has questioned whether the diagnosis could have been made sooner, particularly given the patient’s travel history and the outbreak already under way elsewhere in Africa. “We need to improve on that,” he said, referring to the time taken to confirm the case.
His concern goes to the heart of outbreak control. Early Ebola symptoms can resemble common illnesses, including malaria. But when a patient has recently travelled from a region affected by an outbreak, that history must change the clinical assessment.  
 The 44 contacts identified by the Federal Ministry of Health represent an important starting point, not the end of the investigation.
Nigeria’s 2014 response showed the value of rapidly identifying contacts and following them systematically. The present outbreak demands the same discipline, supported by reliable data and a clear chain of command.
No fragmented responses
The Abuja case is part of a wider regional emergency. The Bundibugyo outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in May 2026, and infections have subsequently been detected in other countries, including Kenya.
On October 20, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Director-General Dr Jean Kaseya called for urgent international support following Nigeria’s confirmation. He described the outbreak as the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak in history and appealed for financing, medical supplies, diagnostics, trained responders and stronger community surveillance.
“My appeal to the international community is urgent: act now,” Kaseya said.
His appeal reflects a basic reality of epidemic control: viruses do not respect national borders, and no country can manage a cross-border outbreak effectively in isolation.
The WHO has called for sustained readiness across the region, including laboratory capacity, rapid-response teams, infection prevention measures, essential supplies and community engagement. 
It has also advised against restrictions on travel or trade with affected countries.
For Nigeria, the challenge is to translate these recommendations into dependable systems that function outside emergency press briefings.
What October 20 should now mean
Nigeria’s 2014 Ebola victory remains a defining moment. It showed what swift action, sound coordination and the courage of health workers and communities could achieve in the face of a deadly outbreak. But winning that battle then is no guarantee of winning the next one. The coincidence of October 20, 12 years apart, brings that lesson into sharp focus. 
“Preparedness cannot be switched on when an outbreak strikes and forgotten when it passes.”
 Surveillance must continue, laboratories must be ready to investigate unusual infections, and health workers need regular training. Private hospitals and clinics, often the first point of contact for sick patients, must also be part of the national response. Essential supplies, isolation facilities and reliable communication systems must be in place before they’re needed.
On October 20, 2014, Nigeria celebrated a hard won victory. On the same date in 2026, it was reminded that such victories are never permanent. The date has come full circle, but the outcome isn’t predetermined. Whether this episode becomes another story of successful containment or exposes the cost of neglected preparedness will depend on the decisions Nigeria makes no
Prevention tips: What you should do
1. Avoid contact with the blood and other bodily fluids of anyone who is ill with suspected Ebola.
2. Do not touch the body or bodily fluids of someone who has died from suspected Ebola
3. Wash hands regularly with soap and water.
4. Seek urgent medical assessment if symptoms develop after a possible exposure, and call ahead so the facility can prepare for safe assessment
5. Follow instructions from public health authorities if identified as a contact

items.title: EES, ETIAS and €20 Fee: How confusion over Europe’s new border systems fuels visa scam
items.author: Oboh
items.content:
By Vera Anyagafu
A new digital stamp at Europe’s airports is free. The €20 travel authorisation some Nigerians are talking about does not apply to Nigerian visa applicants to Europe. 
Yet from Instagram vendors in Surulere to travel plazas in Onitsha, agents are charging Nigerian travellers up to N250,000 for both.
Since 10 April 2026, every Nigerian arriving in Paris or Frankfurt on a short-stay Schengen visa no longer gets an ink stamp. 
A camera and fingerprint scanner logs you into Europe’s Entry/Exit System (EES) automatically, at no cost.
The other system, the European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS), is the source of the rumour. 
It will eventually cost €20, valid for three years, but it is only for travellers who do not need a visa to enter Europe, like Americans, British, Australians and Canadians. For Nigerians, who still need a Schengen visa, ETIAS is never required. If someone in Nigeria is charging you for it, you are paying for something you do not need.
That gap is where the exploitation happens.
The EES became fully operational on 10 April 2026 across all 29 Schengen countries. You do not apply for it in advance. When you land in Paris or Frankfurt, you look at a camera, place your fingers on a scanner, and your entry is recorded digitally, replacing the old ink stamp. It applies to all non-European nationals on short stays, which includes every Nigerian travelling on a Schengen visa, and it automatically calculates your period of stay.
ETIAS is different. It is a pre-travel check only for visa-exempt travellers, people who do not need a Schengen visa to visit Europe.
For Nigerians who need a visa, ETIAS is never required. If you need a Schengen visa today, you will continue to use the visa process through VFS Global or TLSContact in Lagos and Abuja.
The official fee for ETIAS, when it eventually launches, will be €20 for travellers aged 18 to 70, free for under 18 and over 70, and any additional charges will go to commercial intermediaries. 
The only official website where the application will be available once launched is the European Union’s official ETIAS portal, and the information portal for both systems is the official Travel Europe portal managed by the European Union.
And for travellers who will eventually need it, the system is not yet open. The official portal has made it clear that no action is required at this time, and any website currently offering to process an application is not legitimate.
HOW THE SCAM WORKS
Consular Hub gathered that the European authorities have already identified over a hundred unofficial websites providing information on ETIAS. These sites use convincing designs and domain names to mimic legitimate portals.
Since the programme is on hold, any site requesting a €20 fee today is considered fraudulent. Travellers are warned to be very cautious because it is not currently possible to apply for an official ETIAS authorisation since the system is not operational yet. Many of these third-party sites charge inflated fees or steal personal information.
In Nigeria the pattern is now familiar.
Take Sola, a 28-year-old applicant in Surulere. A travel agent on Instagram operating as Travel with Tayo told her she needed to pay N65,000 naira for mandatory ETIAS registration before her Schengen visa appointment at VFS Global. She paid and was given a receipt that looked official with a European Union logo. At her appointment, VFS Global told her ETIAS does not apply to Nigerians and the paper was worthless.
Or Emeka, a trader in Onitsha who wanted to visit his brother in Milan. An agent in his local plaza operating as Blessed Travels collected tens of thousands of naira, for EES biometric pre-registration and ETIAS approval, promising fast-track entry. He arrived in Rome to find his entry under EES was recorded fresh at the border anyway and the extra papers meant nothing.
TO STAY SAFE
To stay safe as a Nigerian passport holder, remember three things; You do not pay €20 for ETIAS, you pay about €90 for the Schengen visa itself at VFS Global or TLSContact. The Entry/Exit System costs nothing and you do not pre-register for it. And only use the official portals for information, as the protection of your personal data cannot be guaranteed if you use another website.
Vanguard News
The post EES, ETIAS and €20 Fee: How confusion over Europe’s new border systems fuels visa scam appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.title: GIDEON OLAJIDE (1930-2026): A tribute to a beloved church father
items.summary:
By Prof. Jacob Kehinde Olupona
The passing of the Rt. Revd. Gideon Isaac Oladipo Olajide, retired Bishop of the Diocese of Ibadan (Anglican Communion), marks the end of an era for the Church of Nigeria. I extend my heartfelt condolences to his family and to the whole Anglican Communion in Nigeria. Baba, as many of us lovingly called him, was a towering figure in the Church. In many respects, he was perhaps the last bishop of his generation. His passing calls us to two things: to celebrate a life well lived and to reflect solemnly on what he gave to the Anglican Church we hold so dear. Above all, it calls us to remember the movement he quietly championed, which many regard as a clarion call for a holiness church and true evangelism, if not for a reform of the Church itself.
