items.author: Anirudh Trivedi
items.content:
Getting an acquisition across the finish line can take months of negotiations, due diligence, paperwork and financial scrutiny. But closing the deal is only half the battle. The real challenge comes when you integrate the business, unlock synergies, and deliver the value that justified the deal in the first place.
Much of this heavy lifting falls on CFOs, who are expected to go beyond balancing the books to evaluate acquisition targets, assess financial risks, structure deals and ensure the business derives long-term value from the transaction.
This is part of a broader shift in the CFO’s role, from financial oversight to strategic decision-making. Whether determining how to extract value from an acquisition or assessing if an investment in AI will deliver adequate returns, finance leaders are making critical capital-allocation decisions while ensuring the business stays on track to meet its growth ambitions.
At Perfios, a B2B SaaS fintech serving more than 1,000 financial institutions across multiple geographies, Group CFO Prashant Mahagaonkar sits at the heart of these decisions.
With more than 25 years of experience across traditional finance, multinational companies, M&A and venture-backed businesses, Mahagaonkar’s career has given him a front-row seat to the changing nature of the finance function.
For the concluding edition of The CFO Code series, Inc42 caught up with Mahagaonkar to discuss his experiences and learnings from decades of building finance systems, integrating acquisitions and working alongside founders and CEOs.
Speaking with Inc42, Mahagaonkar broke down how his role has evolved, what he has learnt from acquisitions, why CFOs need to question technology spending, and what he believes will define the next generation of finance leaders.
Walking The Tightrope Between Risk and Reward
Mahagaonkar’s career began in 1999 at Tata Motors, but he soon realised traditional audit and compliance work wasn’t where he wanted to build his career.
In 2022, Mahagaonkar joined Givaudan India, a Swiss flavour and fragrance major where he got his first real exposure to what a well-built financial system looked like. For Mahagaonkar, the experience became an education in how large organisations build systems and roll them out across markets.
Mahagaonkar then shifted to Essilor India, a spectacle lens manufacturing company, where he was exposed to acquisitions and moved from traditional finance to a more M&A- and business-oriented role.
He later joined venture-backed Amba Research, where he raised capital, worked with investors across geographies and eventually managed an exit. Moody’s acquired the company. Mahagaonkar moved to CitiusTech, where he became the company’s first CFO and worked closely with the founder-CEO to scale revenue from roughly $60 Mn to $500 Mn.
“Working with the founders to scale the team was a great learning experience for me. I realised how different a founder’s mindset is from that of a professional CEO. Their risk-taking appetite is very different, and they bring perspectives that a traditional professional may find difficult to act on,” said Mahagaonkar.
As Mahagaonkar puts it, the experience taught him how to keep the company business-friendly while also protecting it financially. According to him, while founders may be willing to offer more flexibility to win a customer, the finance leader’s job is to ensure the company is adequately protected.
“But the solution was not always to take the most conservative position. Instead, the finance team had to establish a playbook that clearly defined what it would agree to and where it would draw the line,” said Mahagaonkar.
He added that finding “the art of the possible” within an accepted compliance framework is one of the most important skills he has developed over time.
Making Acquisitions Work Beyond The Deal
Mahagaonkar’s M&A experience proved valuable when he joined Perfios in July 2025. By then, the company had completed three acquisitions, and his mandate was to integrate the acquired businesses into a cohesive organisation.
Perfios acquired an eFRM (Enterprise Fraud Risk Management) business, a segment it had not historically operated in. In another acquisition, it added a collections company, adjacent to its existing loan origination, approval, and credit underwriting businesses. Each acquisition required a different integration strategy.
Mahagaonkar shared that his task was to determine what should be fully integrated into Perfios, what should retain its independence and how each business could contribute to the broader ecosystem. All this had to be done while ensuring that every entity remained compliant with the applicable regulatory and reporting requirements.
Smaller companies often lack the same level of compliance infrastructure as a private equity-backed or larger organisation. “Therefore, the integration process involved bringing acquired businesses up to Perfios’ standards across areas such as information security, contracts, insurance, risk and statutory compliance,” the CFO said.
However, amid all the finance and integration of compliance functions, what generally gets understated and undermined is the integration of people and cultures.
Mahagaonkar argues that people integration is also a finance responsibility because acquisitions can easily leave redundant roles and overlapping functions in place.
“You need to put it together and be part of those discussions to help and make sure that we build that one organisation which is required,” he said.
AI Spend Under CFO’s Scanner
The expanding role of the CFO is particularly evident in capital allocation, where Mahagaonkar believes AI has fundamentally changed how technology investments are evaluated and prioritised.
“Today, product life cycles have shortened so much that companies may have just six months, rather than two years, to get ahead of competitors before they develop similar products,” he said.
For the CFO, this means asking harder questions about whether the company is deploying its capital into the right assets and whether its innovation engine is moving quickly enough to match the pace of competitors.
But in this chase, increasing AI spend may seem like the obvious choice for almost every problem, and Mahagaonkar believes companies need to look before they leap.
“Not every problem needs AI, particularly when a simple automation can do the job,” Mahagaonkar said.
At Perfios, the company has built an ROI matrix around its usage that monitors productivity gains, potential changes in hiring requirements and whether a particular use case should use AI at all, instead of automation or machine learning.
Becoming The CEO’s Co-Pilot
With the changing relationship between finance and technology, Mahagaonkar believes the CFO has moved from being a backroom player to becoming a co-pilot to the CEO or founder. He also mentioned that being a co-pilot to the CEO does not mean becoming the de facto CEO.
Mahagaonkar estimates that around 40% of a CFO’s decisions today require forward-looking judgement rather than relying solely on historical financial data.
When asked about the skill sets that will matter most for the next generation of CFOs, he said, “We must accept that today’s young people often know more than we do. They have greater access to information, and they can process and apply it much faster. The real test for the next generation of leaders, not just CFOs, will be managing such high-calibre talent, helping them find meaning in their work and creating an environment where they can succeed.”
According to Mahagaonkar, finance leaders of the past could succeed by knowing the numbers better than everyone else, but CFOs of the future will have to understand the numbers, the business, the technology and, increasingly, the people behind the decisions.
[Edited By Shishir Parasher]

items.author: Anne Florentyna
items.content:
Update | October 23, 16:55 IST
Shares of Ola Electric ended the day 6.39% lower at ₹29.90 apiece on the BSE today, while its market capitalisation stood at ₹14,946.06 Cr ($1.58 Bn). The company’s shares are now trading 61% below its listing price of ₹76.
Original | October 23, 14:31 IST
Shares of electric two-wheeler maker Ola Electric crashed as much as 7.6% to hit an intraday low about ₹29 on the BSE today (October 23) after a bearish outlook from Goldman Sachs.
A day after the company opened its ₹1,000 Cr rights issue, Goldman Sachs downgraded its outlook on Ola Electric to “Sell”. The brokerage slashed the stock’s price target to ₹23.
It foresees a challenging path for Ola Electric to become cash flow positive given the relatively high interest cost and capex needs of the cell and E2W business.
It also cut the EV maker’s top line growth projections by up to 10% for the period FY27-29.
The bearish momentum comes a day after Ola Electric opened its rights issue for bidding. Within hours of opening the issue, Motilal Oswal and Calliope Capital Advisors applied for a combined 2.39 Cr shares against entitlements transferred by two promoter group entities — ANI Technologies and Indus Trust.
Founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal pledged a 4.32% stake in the electric two-wheeler maker to fund his participation in the company’s proposed rights issue of up to ₹1,000 Cr.
Ola Electric plans to use the proceeds from its ₹1,000 Cr rights issue primarily to reduce debt and fund business expansion as it looks to strengthen its financial position and move towards cash-flow breakeven.
Of the total proceeds, ₹350 Cr has been earmarked for the repayment or prepayment of borrowings, including accrued interest and applicable penalties, while ₹400 Cr will be invested in organic growth across its electric mobility and energy storage businesses.
Ola Electric is yet to report its second quarter earnings results. As of Q1 FY27, the company trimmed its net loss by 22% to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Operating revenue declined 45% to ₹455 Cr from ₹828 Cr in Q1 FY26.
As of 13:52 IST, the stock was down 6.57% at ₹29.87 per share on the BSE, while its market capitalisation stood at ₹14,931.06 Cr ($1.57 Bn).
If losses hold, this would be the sixth straight session of the stock ending in red. In the past one month, the stock has lost over 20% in value.

items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
Chennai-based dronetech startup Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹25.9 Cr in FY26, growing 41.1% from ₹18.4 Cr from the previous fiscal year.
In terms of operational profitability, the drone maker’s EBITA for the fiscal year jumped 31.8% to ₹35.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹26.6 Cr in the FY25.
Operating revenue surged 66.8% YoY to ₹206 Cr during the fiscal under review from ₹123.5 Cr in the previous year. Sales of drones and drone parts brought in ₹99.4 Cr to the top line while the remaining ₹106.5 Cr via sale of services. Another ₹15 Lakh was earned from delivery charges.
Including other income of ₹26.5 Lakh, total income for the fiscal stood at ₹206.2 Cr.
“During the year, we continued to strengthen our manufacturing capabilities, expand our Drone-as-a-Service (DaaS) operations, deepen our investment in indigenous research and development, and build strategic partnerships in India and international markets. We also advanced our capabilities in artificial intelligence, autonomous flight, data analytics, defence systems and specialised mission platforms,” cofounder and whole-time director Agnishwar Jayaprakash noted in a message to shareholders.
The improvement in the financial performance comes as Garuda’s proposed public listing plans take shape. The startup took the pre-filing route to confidentially submit its draft IPO papers with the SEBI earlier in April. The IPO was greenlit by the markets regulator in August.
While the startup is yet to file its updated DRHP for public access, its board approved plans to raise up to ₹750 Cr via the fresh issue component of the proposed IPO back in March. As per reports, the OFS component could result in investors offloading shares worth as much as ₹250 Cr.
In its annual report for FY26, the startup disclosed that its board of directors had approved a private placement of equity shares worth ₹57.2 Cr back in August. Investors who backed the startup were Umasankar Nistala, Rakesh Pillai, Jitendra Rana, Vimaan Innovators LLP and Aditum Management.
The proceeds of the issue would fuel business growth, working capital requirements, and be used for loan repayments.
The startup claims to have become India’s largest drone maker, having manufactured and sold over 3000 drones. It also claimed to be the first drone company to partner with three defence PSUs.
It has raised a total funding of over $37 Mn to date from investors like Venture Catalysts, We Founder Circle, cricketer Mahendra Singh Dhoni, among others. It was last valued at $250 Mn after raising a $11 Mn Series B funding round led by Venture Catalysts.
Where Did Garuda Aerospace Spend In FY26?
Garuda Aerospace’s total expenses in FY26 rose 73.2% YoY to ₹172.2 Cr from ₹99.4 Cr in FY25. It reported no exceptional items during the fiscal but bore ₹8.2 Cr tax expenses.
Here are the main operational expenses of the startup:
Cost of Materials Consumed: Representing the largest operational expense, raw material costs surged 61.5% YoY to ₹116.8 Cr from ₹72.3 Cr in FY25.
Impairment Losses on Financial Assets: Impairment losses amounted to ₹11.1 Cr in FY26, compared to ₹6.5 Lakh in the year-ago period.
Employee Benefit Expenses: Garuda Aerospace’s personnel-related costs decreased 16.7% YoY to ₹8 Cr in FY26 from ₹9.6 Cr in the previous year.
Depreciation And Amortisation Expenses: The cost recorded under this line item increased 13.3% YoY to ₹4.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹3.6 Cr in FY25.
Other Expenses: Spending on items like professional expenses, travel, maintenance, rent, and other corporate overheads stayed nearly flat at ₹29.2 Cr.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Messaging platforms including WhatsApp and Telegram are reportedly set to implement the Department of Telecommunications’ (DoT) SIM-binding mandate from January 1, 2027, requiring their services to remain linked to the active SIM associated with a user’s registered mobile number.
According to a Times of India report, platforms must complete implementation by December 31, 2026, ahead of the reported operational start date the following day. The requirement could affect users who access messaging apps on phones without the associated SIM.
The mandate stems from directions issued by the DoT in November last year under the Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024. The original directions named WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, Snapchat, Arattai, ShareChat, Josh, and JioChat.
The department said some app-based communication services continued to function without the SIM associated with the registered mobile number being present in the device. According to the DoT, this allowed fraudsters operating from outside India to misuse Indian mobile numbers.
SIM binding requires covered services to remain continuously linked to the associated active SIM, rather than relying solely on verification when an account is first set up. The government said the measure was intended to improve traceability and curb phishing, digital arrest, impersonation, and investment scams.
The original directions gave platforms 90 days to implement the measures and 120 days to submit compliance reports. However, the government subsequently specified December 31, 2026, as the compliance deadline for SIM binding.
Platforms Prepare For Compliance
According to a CNBC report, Apple has updated its iOS software to support the SIM-binding requirements ahead of the implementation deadline.
WhatsApp and Arattai have confirmed that they are working to comply with the rules. Telegram is yet to clarify on its compliance status, while Signal has not responded to government notices, CNBC reported.
Snapchat has reportedly maintained that the mandate does not apply to its service because it does not use phone numbers to identify users.
Questions also remain about how individual platforms will support eSIM users. CNBC reported that WhatsApp and Telegram would require a physical SIM card to function, although the precise requirements for eSIM users have not been clarified.
The mandate could affect users who access messaging apps over Wi-Fi on phones without their registered SIM, as well as those who frequently switch SIMs. Its impact on access across multiple devices will depend on individual platforms’ implementation.
However, the DoT has clarified that international roaming will not be affected as long as the associated SIM remains in the handset.
The implementation push comes amid concerns over cyber fraud in India. According to data sourced from the home ministry, Indians lost ₹22,495 Cr to cyber fraud in 2025 compared with ₹22,845 Cr in 2024.
In June, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) said Indians had lost around ₹52,976 Cr to cyber-enabled fraud over the past six years, with nearly 8% of the losses linked to digital arrest scams.
Speaking at the India Mobile Congress 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi called on global technology companies, financial institutions, and telecom operators to work together to build a comprehensive framework to tackle cyber fraud and deepfakes.
“At a time when telecom and digital technology have become so important, it is equally important to make the security framework associated with it ironclad. It is our priority to secure mobile phones and networks,” Modi said, adding that trust was crucial for people using phones to communicate and make payments.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The government has allocated Rs352.5 million for the Prime Minister’s SPARK and ELEVATE technology programmes for FY2026-27, with grants of up to Rs200 million per project aimed at turning research into marketable products and accelerating technology commercialisation in Pakistan.
According to documents, the programmes will fund up to 60 research and innovation projects annually, including 30 projects under each initiative, through competitive selection.
The allocation was approved by the Board of Ignite – National Technology Fund and will be financed through the Research and Development (R&D) Fund, without any allocation from the federal budget or the Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP).
Government Allocates Rs352.5 Million for Technology Research Programmes
Under the programme, SPARK (Strategic Program for Advanced Research and Knowledge) will finance research projects aimed at developing functional prototypes, while ELEVATE (Empowering Latest age Engineering, Validation, and Accelerated Technology) will support the validation and commercialisation of technologies that already have functional prototypes.
The Prime Minister announced the initiatives on July 22, 2026, at the Indus RAS Expo 2026. They are being implemented under the amended Research and Development Rules, 2006, through Ignite.
The first call for proposals is open until October 26, 2026, for project concepts, while full proposals are due by the end of November 2026.
Under the funding framework, SPARK offers grants of up to Rs100 million per project, while ELEVATE provides up to Rs200 million per project. Both programmes will support projects for a period of up to 18 months, with funds released in milestone-linked tranches.
See Also: Pakistan Clears Rs 40.8 Billion PakSat-2 and Geo-AI Projects Under Uraan Pakistan
Ignite has envisaged two cohorts of grants every six months, with up to 30 projects under each programme annually.
The government has identified nine priority areas, including digital industry and advanced manufacturing, agriculture and water systems, energy efficiency, digital healthcare, smart cities, connectivity and digital infrastructure, cybersecurity and trust systems, education, and smart mobility.
However, the programmes are sector-agnostic, allowing proposals from different technology fields to compete for funding based on their merits.
The first two years will primarily cover project selection, grant awards and milestone delivery, with final outputs expected upon completion of projects.
Each SPARK-funded project will be required to deliver a functional prototype supported by verifiable real-world results, such as pilot deployment, validation in an operational environment or evidence of industry uptake.
Similarly, ELEVATE projects will be required to convert existing prototypes into market-ready products, supported by a confirmed pilot site or first customer. The programmes envisage up to 30 prototypes and 30 market-ready products per cycle, subject to the number of grants awarded.
The framework also encourages intellectual property protection, allowing funded projects to file patent applications in Pakistan or internationally through the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), with patent filing costs admissible under the grants.
The minister clarified that startup incubation is not part of SPARK and ELEVATE, as this function is performed through Ignite’s National Incubation Centers, which have hosted more than 2,250 startups. Startups and small and medium enterprises (SMEs), however, can lead projects under the two programmes.
See Also: CDWP Clears Seven Projects Worth Rs116 Billion Under Uraan Pakistan Initiative
Separately, the government expects the proposed $20 million Pakistan Venture Fund (PVF) to help address financing constraints faced by high-potential technology startups by mobilising private investment through professionally managed venture funds.
The fund will focus on technology-driven businesses, including artificial intelligence, robotics, augmented and virtual reality, deep technology, defence technologies, cybersecurity, financial technology, healthcare technology and agricultural technology.
The government expects the initiative to help startups expand product development, commercialise innovations, enter international markets and attract domestic and foreign capital.
No university or research centre has been designated as a primary implementation partner for SPARK and ELEVATE. The minister said eligible public and private universities, research organisations, startups and SMEs could compete through an open, nationwide selection process.
Successful applicants will be selected through Ignite’s Project Evaluation Ranking Matrix and approved by its board. ELEVATE projects will be industry-led, with universities and research centres participating as consortium partners.
The post Government Allocates Rs352.5 Million for Technology Research Programmes appeared first on PhoneWorld.

The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) has recovered only 12.9 percent of Rs4.27 billion in penalties imposed on four cellular mobile operators over the last five years for non-compliance, while 58 cases remain sub judice.
According to official information, the PTA recovered Rs551.35 million against total penalties of Rs4.270 billion, while Rs537.75 million was pledged, and 58 cases were pending before courts. The authority also issued 22 warning letters during the period.
PTA Recovers only 12.9pc of Rs4.27bn Penalties from Cellular Operators
PTML (Ufone) faced the highest penalties of Rs1.873 billion through 31 show-cause notices, followed by Jazz World Pakistan with Rs1.401 billion through 27 notices, CMPak (Zong) with Rs590.95 million through 17 notices, and Telenor Pakistan with Rs404.95 million through 21 notices.
The PTA has also taken measures to address disruptions in cellular services caused by power outages, requiring operators to restore affected network sites and services within prescribed timelines and maintain adequate backup power arrangements to ensure continuity of telecom services.
The regulator monitors compliance with applicable quality-of-service requirements and takes up service interruptions with the concerned operators for corrective measures.
The PTA has coordinated with the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (NEPRA), the Power Division and distribution companies through a joint task force constituted under the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication to mitigate the impact of power interruptions on telecom services.
The proposed measures include dedicated feeders, smart-grid solutions and appropriate tariff arrangements to improve the reliability of electricity supplies to telecom infrastructure.
Corrective measures also include redundant backhaul and connectivity arrangements, enhanced network resilience, improved restoration mechanisms and adequate backup power facilities to minimise service interruptions.
The PTA monitors implementation of these measures and, where necessary, conducts re-verification testing to assess whether identified deficiencies have been rectified.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) has blocked 229,157 government employees or their spouses from receiving financial assistance after identifying them through audits, while recovering Rs712.4 million from ineligible recipients, the government has informed Parliament.
Minister for Poverty Alleviation and Social Safety Syed Imran Ahmad Shah, in a written reply to a parliamentary question, said the recovery comprised Rs545.784 million through the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), Rs21.550 million from BISP employees and Rs145.066 million from other government departments.
The minister said recovery proceedings had also been initiated against 236 BISP employees, with disciplinary action taken against delinquent officials.
BISP Blocked 229,157 Government Employees, Spouses as Beneficiaries
He added that updated data of government employees and pensioners had been obtained from the Controller General of Accounts (CGA), ministries, autonomous bodies and state-owned enterprises (SOEs), while more than six million records had been forwarded for profiling and further action.
According to the reply, 32,971 of the 229,157 blocked cases involving government employees or their spouses had been exempted from recovery because their monthly pension was Rs29,000 or below, in accordance with a decision of the BISP Board.
The minister said the process of data updating, profiling, blocking and recovery was continuing, adding that the number of irregular or ineligible beneficiaries and the recoverable amount could change as the exercise progressed.
Responding to concerns over illegal deductions, unauthorised charges, fraudulent biometric verification and other malpractices in BISP payments, the minister said complaints were examined individually and action was taken under the applicable rules.
Cases involving banks and payment service providers were referred to the relevant institutions for investigation and resolution. Depending on the findings, corrective measures could include penalties, recovery of irregular amounts and other action against those responsible.
The minister said legal or disciplinary proceedings were also initiated where fraud or serious malpractice warranted such action to safeguard beneficiaries’ payments.
BISP currently disburses financial assistance through the retail networks of six partner financial institutions (PFIs). The minister said these networks were monitored through field visits, beneficiary complaints, system-based controls, inspections and audits.
Where irregularities were detected, action could include suspension or blacklisting of agents, recovery of amounts and penalties under contractual provisions.
However, the reply did not provide the consolidated number of bank branches, campsites, agents, point-of-sale (POS) agents and ATMs involved in disbursement, or the total number of agents suspended, blacklisted or proceeded against. The bank-wise and province-wise details were referred to an annexure.
See Also: SBP Clarifies BISP Digital Wallet Charges, Says Online Transfers Will Remain Free
The government said BISP was gradually shifting towards digital and direct payment mechanisms through Social Protection Wallets (SPWs) to reduce human intervention and beneficiaries’ dependence on intermediaries.
The initiative aims to provide beneficiaries with greater choice, transparency, convenience and security while ensuring they receive the full amount sanctioned under the programme.
The minister said BISP had also developed and implemented an Integrated Grievance Management System (IGMS), integrated with partner financial institutions to streamline complaint handling and improve transparency and payment security within the State Bank of Pakistan’s regulatory framework.
Further development of the grievance management system would be undertaken gradually according to need, he added.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) has rescued a 13-year-old girl in Karachi who was allegedly targeted by an online network linked to the dark web. The group reportedly instructed the girl to carry out acts of animal cruelty and self-harm, raising concerns about the growing risks of online exploitation involving children.
The incident highlights how cybercriminals can use social media platforms, messaging applications and concealed online identities to approach young people, manipulate them and pressure them into harmful activities.
Dark Web Exploitation in Pakistan: NCCIA Rescues 13-Year-Old Girl in Karachi
According to NCCIA Additional Director Tariq Nawaz, the agency launched an investigation after receiving information from a foreign intelligence agency about suspicious online activities linked to a group allegedly involved in child exploitation.
The agency received a tip-off containing an email address associated with the suspected group and relevant internet protocol (IP) addresses. Investigators traced the digital activity to Karachi and discovered that the person linked to the suspicious activity was a victim rather than a perpetrator. The agency then rescued the girl.
How Online Networks Target Children
According to Nawaz, individuals allegedly linked to the network contacted the girl through social media platforms and messaging applications. They reportedly used concealed online identities to communicate with her and assign tasks involving animal cruelty and self-injury.
Such cases demonstrate how online predators can exploit children’s trust and vulnerability. Offenders may use manipulation, intimidation or threats to pressure victims into following instructions. They may also attempt to isolate children from their families or discourage them from seeking help.
Not every case of online exploitation involves the dark web. Criminals can approach victims through mainstream platforms before moving conversations to private channels or hidden online services. This can make it difficult for parents to recognise the warning signs before a situation becomes serious.
What Is the Dark Web?
The dark web is a part of the internet that requires specialised software or configurations to access. While it has legitimate uses, criminals can also misuse hidden online services to conceal their identities, communicate privately and facilitate illegal activities.
Some online networks exploit these features to target vulnerable people or distribute illegal material. However, anonymity does not make users completely untraceable. Investigators can analyse digital evidence, IP addresses, online communications and other records to identify suspects and locate victims.
The Karachi case demonstrates the importance of digital investigations and cooperation between agencies. Information received from a foreign intelligence agency helped investigators trace suspicious online activity and identify a child who needed protection.
Online Blackmail and the Misuse of Private Photographs
Online exploitation can take several forms, including cyber blackmail, harassment, grooming and the non-consensual sharing of private photographs. Criminals may build trust with victims before using personal information or images to threaten them.
In some cases, offenders demand money, additional photographs, or compliance with other instructions. Others may threaten to share private material with family members or publish it online. Once such material spreads across multiple accounts and platforms, removing every copy can become difficult.
A recent court case in Islamabad has also highlighted the seriousness of online exploitation. Two men reportedly received 10-year prison sentences each for blackmailing a 12-year-old girl using objectionable photographs. The case underlines the legal consequences of exploiting children through digital platforms.
Although these incidents involve different alleged methods of abuse, they highlight a common concern: criminals can use digital tools to manipulate, threaten, and harm children.
How Parents and Siblings Can Protect Children
Parents, siblings and guardians have an important role in helping children stay safe online. Open communication can make it easier for children to report suspicious messages, uncomfortable interactions or threats without fearing punishment or blame.
Families should teach children not to share private photographs, personal information or account details with strangers. They should also encourage them to question requests from unknown online contacts, especially when someone demands secrecy or pressures them to complete disturbing tasks.
Privacy settings, strong passwords, two-factor authentication and age-appropriate parental controls can provide additional protection. Parents should also remain aware of the platforms and messaging applications their children use.
Most importantly, children must understand that they can seek help if someone threatens or manipulates them. Families should support victims rather than blame them for the actions of offenders.
How Victims Can Seek Help
If a child receives threatening messages or is pressured into harmful activities, families should preserve relevant evidence, including screenshots, usernames, account links and messages. They should report abusive accounts to the relevant platform and contact the appropriate authorities.
In Pakistan, suspected cybercrime can be reported to the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency. Families should avoid confronting suspected offenders directly, as doing so could increase risks or interfere with an investigation.
The rescue of the 13-year-old girl in Karachi highlights the need for stronger awareness of online exploitation and closer cooperation between families, technology platforms and law enforcement agencies.
As children’s lives become increasingly connected to the internet, protecting them requires more than monitoring their screen time. Families must help them recognise manipulation, feel safe reporting abuse and understand that support is available when someone targets them online.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistan’s 5G rollout is gaining momentum, with 1,782 5G sites deployed across 24 cities, according to details shared by Federal Minister for Information Technology and Telecommunication Shaza Fatima Khawaja.
Jazz is leading the deployment with 1,015 sites, followed by Zong with 640 and Ufone with 127. The figures reflect the operators’ reported network infrastructure as Pakistan gradually expands next-generation mobile connectivity.
The minister said 5G services were introduced after the country’s multiband 5G spectrum auction, with Next Generation Mobile Services (NGMS) licences signed on March 19, 2026. The four-phase rollout started on March 20, 2026, under a plan approved by the federal government.
The licensing obligations seek to improve existing 4G services alongside the phased introduction of 5G. All cellular mobile operators conducted technical 5G trials between 2020 and 2025, the minister added.
Which Cities Have the Most 5G Sites in Pakistan?
According to the minister’s reply, 5G services have been launched or are being consolidated in Islamabad, Karachi, Lahore, Rawalpindi, Faisalabad, Peshawar, Quetta, Multan, Gujranwala, Sialkot, Sheikhupura, Hyderabad, Abbottabad, Attock, Jhelum, Kasur, Kohat, Mardan, Rahim Yar Khan, Sahiwal, Sukkur, Swabi, Chitral and Gujrat.
Karachi has the highest reported number of deployed sites at 385, followed by Lahore with 373 and Islamabad with 276. Faisalabad has 144 sites, Peshawar 122, Rawalpindi 108, Multan 103, Sialkot 87, Quetta 65 and Sheikhupura 55.
Jazz leads deployment in Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad and Multan, while Zong has a stronger presence in Peshawar, Quetta, Sheikhupura and Sialkot. Ufone’s footprint remains comparatively limited at 127 sites across the reported rollout cities.
Under the first phase of the NGMS licence obligations, deployment in federal and provincial capitals is mandatory. Operators may expand into additional cities according to their respective business models.
However, deployed sites do not necessarily mean citywide 5G availability. Real-world network experience may vary by location and operator, as highlighted in PhoneWorld’s earlier coverage of 5G coverage and mobile network performance.
Affordable 5G Smartphones Remain a Major Challenge
While network deployment is expanding, the cost of compatible devices remains a barrier for many users. According to the minister, the cheapest locally available 5G-capable handset currently costs approximately Rs. 36,000.
The government reported that 607,093 5G-compatible handsets were locally assembled between January and August 2026. Local manufacturing could help improve access to more affordable devices, although the pace of adoption will also depend on consumer budgets and coverage.
PhoneWorld has previously reported on the country’s local mobile phone assembly trends and 5G production, underscoring the importance of device availability as networks expand.
The minister clarified that existing 4G SIM cards do not need to be replaced to access 5G. Consumers will still need a compatible handset and an active 5G signal from their mobile operator.
Although the rollout represents an important step for Pakistan’s digital connectivity, the government did not specify a definitive timeline for making 5G affordable for ordinary consumers. Wider coverage and the availability of lower-cost handsets will remain key factors as the next generation of mobile broadband reaches more users.

Pakistan has stopped issuing Machine-Readable Passports (MRPs) from October 23, 2026, and will now issue only electronic passports, also known as e-passports, to new applicants across the country.
According to the Directorate General of Immigration and Passports, the new policy applies to passport offices throughout Pakistan and Pakistani embassies abroad. The government had initially set October 15 as the deadline to discontinue MRPs but later extended it.
Pakistan to Issue Only E-Passports from October 23, 2026
Authorities continued issuing and renewing machine-readable passports until October 22. From October 23, applicants seeking new passports will receive only e-passports under the updated policy.
Existing Passports Will Remain Valid
The authorities have clarified that people who already hold machine-readable passports do not need to replace them immediately. Existing MRPs will remain valid until their expiry dates.
This means citizens can continue using their current passports for international travel as long as they remain valid. The new policy does not require existing passport holders to apply for e-passports solely because the government has changed the issuance system.
However, applicants seeking new passports will need to follow the updated policy and apply for an electronic passport.
What Is an E-Passport?
An e-passport is a travel document that contains an electronic chip. The chip stores the passport holder’s personal and biometric information, helping authorities verify the holder’s identity more securely.
This technology can improve passport security and make identity verification more reliable. It also helps reduce the risk of passport fraud by adding an electronic layer of protection to the travel document.
With this change, Pakistan is moving towards a fully electronic passport issuance system for new applicants. The policy aims to strengthen the security of travel documents while bringing the country’s passport system in line with modern international practices.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistan’s National Computer Emergency Response Team (National CERT) has issued an urgent cybersecurity advisory warning government departments, financial institutions, and private organizations about two critical security vulnerabilities affecting PHP-based systems.
According to the advisory, both vulnerabilities carry a severity score of 9.2 out of 10, indicating serious security risks for organizations operating vulnerable web applications and online services.
National CERT has circulated the warning to federal ministries, government departments, regulators, public-sector companies, financial institutions, and ICT service providers, urging them to implement immediate security measures.
The vulnerabilities could potentially allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely without requiring user authentication or prior authorization. Attackers may exploit the weaknesses by sending specially crafted HTTP requests to vulnerable systems.
This raises concerns for government web portals, financial platforms, business applications, and other critical information systems that rely on affected PHP environments.
The advisory also highlights reports of early exploitation-related activity internationally, suggesting that organizations should not delay preventive action.
How Could These PHP Vulnerabilities Affect Pakistani Websites?
PHP is a widely used programming language that powers numerous websites, online portals, and web-based applications. Security weaknesses affecting vulnerable PHP deployments can therefore have implications for organizations that depend on these systems.
According to National CERT, the identified vulnerabilities could allow attackers to execute unauthorized commands on affected servers, potentially compromising sensitive information and disrupting essential digital services.
Government websites, financial institutions, and business applications could be particularly vulnerable where affected systems are exposed to the internet and appropriate security measures have not been implemented.
The advisory warns that malicious HTTP requests could be used to exploit the weaknesses remotely, making internet-facing systems an important priority for security teams.
However, the presence of PHP on a website does not automatically mean the website is vulnerable. Actual exposure depends on the affected software versions, server configurations, and whether appropriate security fixes have been applied.
National CERT Calls for Immediate Security Measures
To reduce the risk of potential cyberattacks, National CERT has directed organizations to identify all internet-facing PHP systems and assess their exposure to the reported vulnerabilities.
The advisory recommends deploying available security patches and updates for affected systems as soon as possible. Where immediate fixes are unavailable, technical teams should prepare emergency updates and apply appropriate temporary protections.
National CERT has also advised organizations to strengthen their defenses through Web Application Firewalls (WAFs), which can help detect and block suspicious web requests.
Security teams have been instructed to closely monitor system logs, investigate unusual activity, and look for signs of unauthorized access or suspicious web shells that could indicate a compromised server.
Any suspected intrusion or malicious web shell activity should be reported immediately to National CERT Pakistan to support timely investigation and coordinated incident response.
The advisory underscores the importance of regularly updating web infrastructure, monitoring critical applications, and maintaining effective cybersecurity controls. With government services, financial transactions, and business operations increasingly dependent on online platforms, weaknesses in widely used web technologies could create serious risks if affected systems are left unpatched.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Kenyan electric mobility company Spiro has launched its first 100 electric motorcycles in Ghana, introducing its Ekon 450 M1 V3 model and battery-swapping network to the West African market.
Spiro is Africa’s largest electric mobility company, operating the continent’s most extensive and fastest growing network of battery-swapping for electric two-wheel vehicles. It has operational assembling facilities in Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda, Togo, Cameroon and Benin.
The company is positioning the Ekon 450 M1 V3 as an alternative to petrol-powered motorcycles for everyday riders, particularly commercial riders and delivery fleets whose earnings depend on fuel costs and time on the road. It is paired with Spiro’s battery-swapping technology, which lets riders exchange a depleted battery for a charged one at a swap station in around two minutes instead of waiting to recharge.
The Ghana rollout comes as Spiro accelerates its continental expansion off the back of a US$270 million equity funding round, as well as US$18 million in debt financing from the Africa Go Green Fund.
“Ghana represents a major opportunity for electric mobility, with a rapidly growing two-wheeler market and increasing demand from commercial riders and delivery fleets,” said Kaushik Burman, CEO of Spiro.
“With the launch of the Ekon 450 M1 V3, we are bringing a solution that addresses two key barriers to adoption: operating costs and access to charging infrastructure. Our first 100 motorcycles mark the beginning of our ambition to make electric mobility accessible at scale across Ghana.”
Spiro currently operates in seven countries, with more than 156,000 electric motorcycles on the road and over 2,500 battery-swapping stations, including 11 mega swap stations in Kenya and Rwanda. It has facilitated more than 57 million battery swaps to date, covering over 3.1 billion kilometres. It aims to be present in 20 African markets, and is preparing to enter Ethiopia, Malawi, Mali and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Nigerian business banking platform Nomba has extended its Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) payments corridor into Zambia, allowing Congolese businesses to pay Zambian suppliers instantly.
Founded by Yinka Adewale and Pelumi Aboluwarin in 2016, and formerly known as Kudi, Nomba has evolved over the years into a profitable, omnichannel payment service provider.
Across its DRC operations and Canadian-licensed money service business, Nomba – which raised a US$30 million pre-Series B funding round in 2023 – processes more than US$480 million a month.
Disrupt Africa reported last month the startup had secured a US$ 3 million debt facility to scale that figure to US$1 billion monthly, starting with DRC, where businesses on its platform collect and pay in both US dollars and Congolese francs (CDF).
Working with licensed local partners, Nomba now enables these businesses to make payments in CDF and USD to suppliers in Zambia, with funds landing instantly in bank accounts or mobile wallets.
The move targets one of the continent’s fastest-growing trade routes. Zambia’s goods exports to the DRC hit US$1.6 billion in 2025, up roughly a third year-on-year, according to the Bank of Zambia. However, businesses trading along the corridor in sectors such as agriculture, retail and wholesale still contend with slow cross-border payments, cash-management burdens and foreign exchange shortages, which tie up working capital.
“The ambition to grow intra-African trade has outpaced the financial infrastructure needed to support it. Many of the continent’s busiest trade corridors remain underserved by payment solutions that help businesses move money efficiently and scale,” said Adewale.
“We’ve spent the past decade building solutions to address these challenges, and we’re now extending that infrastructure to the heart of Africa along the DRC–Zambia corridor. This is part of our own ambition to build a business banking platform that enables African businesses to trade, scale and compete beyond their home markets.”
Nomba plans to raise a further funding round to support its expansion. Over time, it aims to offer businesses on the corridor a wider range of services, including deposits, foreign exchange and credit.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The federal government collected more than Rs. 66 billion in super tax from Pakistan’s telecom sector between FY2015-16 and FY2025-26, according to figures submitted by the Ministry of Finance to the Senate.
The figures were presented alongside information on sales tax applicable to mobile SIM activation, imported smartphones, and locally supplied mobile phones.
The ministry’s sector-wise statement records approximately Rs. 66.08 billion in telecom-sector super tax collections over the reporting period. Collections reached around Rs. 11.41 billion in FY2024-25 and Rs. 29.80 billion in FY2025-26, according to the submitted table.
How Much Sales Tax Applies to Mobile Phones in Pakistan?
The information presented to the Senate outlined different sales tax treatment depending on a mobile phone’s import value and whether it is imported or supplied locally.
According to the submitted briefing, fully assembled imported mobile phones valued at up to $500 attract an 18% sales tax, while those valued above $500 fall into the 25% sales tax category. The general sales tax rate for locally supplied mobile phones is stated as 18%.
The briefing also stated that a Rs. 250 sales tax is charged on activation of each mobile SIM. However, the current legal applicability of this charge requires confirmation against the relevant provisions and effective dates in the Sales Tax Act.
These sales tax rates do not necessarily represent the total amount a consumer pays to import or register a smartphone. Depending on the device and applicable rules, other duties, levies, and withholding taxes may affect the final cost.
Telecom Super Tax Collections Rise Sharply
The ministry’s figures show that telecom-sector super tax receipts increased substantially during the later years of the reporting period. Collections were approximately Rs. 281 million in FY2015-16, Rs. 6.16 billion in FY2022-23, Rs. 6.33 billion in FY2023-24, Rs. 11.41 billion in FY2024-25 and Rs. 29.80 billion in FY2025-26.
The data indicates that FY2025-26 accounted for a considerable portion of the sector’s cumulative super tax collections. However, the sector-level figures alone do not establish the amounts paid by individual telecom operators or the causes of year-to-year changes.
The disclosures come amid continued discussion about smartphone affordability and taxation in Pakistan. For consumers, the distinction between sales tax categories is relevant because taxation can affect the final cost of imported and locally supplied mobile phones.

items.author: Inc42 BrandLabs
items.content:
India’s baby care market is growing, and so is the challenge of finding products parents can genuinely trust. When it comes to baby care, Indian parents often look for the same thing: products that are made well, priced for the value they deliver, and worth bringing home.
Ahmedabad-based Kunal and Kinjal Popat found themselves at the centre of this dilemma when they became parents in 2011. The couple began searching for a safer alternative, but that search opened another can of worms: finding a product that was safe, well-designed and priced right.
Their hunt for safer alternatives soon hit a snag. While there was no shortage of baby products in the market, very few offered the combination of safety, thoughtful design and transparent pricing the couple was looking for.
Instead of compromising, the Popats decided to build what they could not find. Kunal brought over a decade of experience across engineering, marketing and sales, while Kinjal, trained in design, brought a different lens to the problem. Together, they set out to make baby products that put safety first with the right price tag. And that is how R for Rabbit came into being in 2014.
The couple started with around ₹40 Lakh of their own savings, designing products in-house and working with established, safety-certified manufacturers.
“I used to visit factories before finalising any partnerships to ensure quality control, testing and certification standards remain as we want for the brand,” said Kinjal.
Initially, R for Rabbit started with three baby-gear products, led by strollers. From there, the company began expanding its portfolio and distribution. Today, the brand controls more than 450 SKUs across categories such as car seats, baby apparel, personal care, feeding ranges, and ride-on toys.
R for Rabbit expanded into kids’ personal care by launching the Biomimic baby skin care range in August this year and entered the baby clothing segment with its apparel range in September.
As it continues to grow its product portfolio and distribution, getting products to customers efficiently became an increasingly important part of its growth strategy. The company’s partnership with Shadowfax in 2026 reflects this shift, with last-mile delivery becoming a key consideration as the brand scales across markets.
Building A Full-Stack Baby Care Brand
At the outset, R for Rabbit relied heavily on word of mouth to build trust. Mothers who discovered the brand began recommending its products through WhatsApp groups and personal networks because of the brand’s focus on quality and international standards of safety.
This grassroots buzz helped the duo build early sales without leaning heavily on traditional advertising. Thanks to this organic growth, the brand’s portfolio grew to around 25 products by 2016.
“Over time, as our range grew, we put a much clearer framework around how we developed our products. We built everything around four pillars: safety, quality, innovation and customer support. For us, the highest quality and international standards are the floor, rather than the ceiling,” Kunal told Inc42.
The founders’ focus was clear: the brand’s products should be designed around everyday realities of Indian parents. Strollers, for instance, were designed to fold with one hand, making them easier to manoeuvre in India’s often cramped lifts and busy urban spaces. Similarly, the founders focused on plug-and-play assemblies for parents to set up products without a complicated installation process. They also designed convertible high chairs that could double up as toddler desks.
R for Rabbit also began developing and patenting more of its own products instead of selling products already available in the market. This helped the brand carve out a space between expensive imported brands and cheaper local alternatives.
By 2019, R for Rabbit built a base of nearly 1.5 Mn parents.
From Growth To A More Complex Fulfilment Model
The key change for R for Rabbit came when it moved beyond products that parents bought only occasionally. It entered toys with ‘Orapple Toys’ in 2020 and then launched Feather Diapers in 2022.
The expansion into new categories also began to show up in R for Rabbit’s business numbers.
The company raised its first institutional round in October 2021, and by FY23, its revenue reached ₹128 Cr. It crossed ₹250 Cr in FY25, helped by a wider product portfolio that grew by more than 100 products during this period.
Diapers, in particular, emerged as one of the company’s fastest-growing categories, giving the business a more consistent revenue stream.
The 2025-26 phase brought further expansion. In August 2025, R for Rabbit raised $27 Mn in Series B funding, led by Filter Capital and 3one4 Capital. In the following year, the company added BioMimic, a biomimicry-based kids’ personal care range, and launched its first apparel line.
In 2026, R for Rabbit’s offline reach crossed 3,000 retail touchpoints, while quick commerce emerged as another important channel. As the company added more products, repeat purchases and customers across more markets, fulfilment became a bigger part of the equation.
The challenge was no longer just having the right products, but getting them to customers quickly while keeping delivery costs in check. This also meant rethinking how it stored and moved inventory.
R for Rabbit eventually moved from a single warehouse to a regional third-party logistics model, bringing inventory closer to customers across different markets. The company partnered with Shadowfax in 2026 to strengthen its last-mile network and offer same-day and next-day deliveries.
The primary aim of the partnership was to improve delivery speed and coverage as the brand continues to grow across categories and markets.
“We wanted to build a logistics network that could keep pace with our growth and get products to customers faster. As we expand across categories and markets, being closer to the customer becomes increasingly important. Our partnership with Shadowfax helps us strengthen that last-mile capability and improve both delivery speed and coverage,” says Kunal.
Shadowfax’s same-day and next-day delivery capabilities have helped the brand reach more pincodes and improve delivery timelines. According to Kunal, the partnership has brought tangible improvement in its turnaround times and greater operational flexibility.
As volumes increase, the company expects better logistics efficiency and wider coverage to help it grow revenue while keeping fulfilment costs and operational inefficiencies under control. Faster delivery and broader coverage could also help reduce delivery-related drop-offs and improve the customer experience.
Scaling The Next Mile
For R for Rabbit, the next stage of growth will extend beyond its existing footprint. The company is looking to deepen its presence in Tier II, Tier III and other emerging markets while continuing to grow in metros.
This expansion will bring more customers, higher order volumes and greater demand for faster deliveries, making fulfilment an increasingly important part of the customer experience.
“As we work towards becoming a ₹1,000 Cr business, we know that our ability to serve customers across more locations will be critical. Partnering with Shadowfax lets us hold that promise on delivery too, with faster, more reliable fulfilment as we reach deeper into Tier II and Tier III India,” said Kunal.
That makes logistics more than just an operational function. Faster same-day and next-day deliveries can improve the customer experience, while better reverse logistics can make returns and exchanges easier.
R for Rabbit maintains an overall NPS of 80+, reflecting the word-of-mouth loyalty that has helped build the brand. As the company expands, maintaining that trust will depend on delivering a consistent experience beyond the product itself.
By partnering with Shadowfax, R for Rabbit is strengthening its last-mile capabilities to support faster deliveries and wider coverage as it expands into new markets.
At the same time, expanding into new markets means R for Rabbit needs to bring inventory closer to customers without allowing fulfilment costs and operational inefficiencies to rise.
From three baby-gear products in 2014 to a portfolio spanning everyday parenting needs, R for Rabbit has come a long way. But as the company enters its next phase, the challenge now is to make sure that its products reach customers quickly, reliably and efficiently.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
vivo is reportedly preparing to introduce its latest Y-series smartphone, the vivo Y32, in Pakistan following its recent debut in international markets. The handset brings a massive 8,000mAh battery, improved durability and a smoother 120Hz display, making it an interesting option for consumers who prioritize battery life over flagship-level performance.
According to recent market reports, the vivo Y32 could arrive in Pakistan as early as the final week of October 2026. Although the company has yet to announce an official local launch date, the handset is already available in select international markets, suggesting that its Pakistani debut may not be far away.
The new vivo Y32 revives a smartphone name originally introduced in 2021. However, the 2026 model brings several upgrades, particularly in battery capacity, display refresh rate and water resistance.
Massive 8,000mAh Battery and Improved Durability
The biggest highlight of the new vivo Y32 is its 8,000mAh battery, which is considerably larger than the batteries found in many conventional mid-range smartphones.
The phone also supports 44W wired fast charging. With such a large battery, users could potentially get up to two days of usage on a single charge, depending on their activities, network conditions, and display settings.
Another notable improvement is the handset’s reported IP68 and IP69 ratings for dust and water resistance. These ratings indicate protection under specified testing conditions and should not be taken as a guarantee against all water damage.
The device also reportedly carries a five-star SGS drop-resistance rating, making durability another major selling point.
On the front, the vivo Y32 features a 6.87-inch IPS LCD with HD+ resolution, a 120 Hz refresh rate, and up to 1,300 nits of claimed peak brightness. Although an AMOLED panel would have been welcome, the higher refresh rate should offer smoother scrolling and animations than the original model’s 60Hz display.
Performance, Cameras and Software
Under the hood, the vivo Y32 is reportedly powered by the Unisoc T7300 processor, built on a 6 nm process. The chipset is designed for everyday use, including social media, video streaming, multitasking, and casual gaming.
The handset runs Android 16 with OriginOS 6 and supports 4G LTE rather than 5G. International memory configurations are reported to include 6GB RAM with 128GB or 256GB storage, although Pakistan variants are not yet confirmed.
For photography, the phone features a reported 50MP main rear camera and an 8MP selfie camera. Overall, the handset appears positioned around endurance, durability, and everyday usability rather than high-end gaming or photography.
vivo Y32 Expected Price and Release Date in Pakistan
vivo Pakistan has not officially announced local pricing or a launch date. However, a credible source has confirmed the price around Rs 99,000.
These figures are unofficial estimates, not confirmed retail prices. Final pricing will depend on the storage configuration offered locally and vivo’s distribution and pricing decisions.
Reports point to a possible launch during the final week of October 2026, but preliminary listings vary, so the actual timeline remains uncertain until vivo issues an announcement.
If the company introduces the Y32 in the expected price bracket, its large battery and reported resistance ratings could appeal to consumers seeking extended daily use. Buyers should wait for official Pakistan availability, variants, and prices before making a purchase decision.

items.content:
Swiggy’s Sweet And Sour Q2
Swiggy had a mixed quarter in Q2 FY27. While its food delivery business delivered record profits and margins, rising investments in Instamart and newer businesses continued to stifle its bottom line.
Here’s a quick glance at the foodtech major’s Q2 FY27 numbers:
Net loss narrowed 16% YoY to ₹922 Cr but widened 16% QoQ
Operating revenue climbed 36% YoY to ₹7,571 Cr
Adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹760 Cr from ₹695 Cr a year earlier
Gross order value (GOV) rose 25% YoY to ₹20,793 Cr
Instamart’s Burn Continues: Swiggy’s quick commerce expansion continued to put pressure on its bottom line despite its operating revenue jumping 33% YoY to ₹1,306 Cr. However, its adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹895 Cr, as Swiggy continued to invest in customer acquisition and store expansion. The company believes that Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA losses peaked in Q2 FY27.
The Inventory-Led Shift: The company is eyeing pivoting Instamart to an inventory-led model by mid-Q3 FY27, with the transition expected to take two to three quarters. This will uplift the vertical’s contribution margin by 80 basis points once fully implemented while shortening the working capital cycle by 8-10 days.
Food Delivery Leads Charts: Swiggy’s food delivery business reported its highest-ever profits and margins in Q2 FY27, with revenue rising 22% YoY to ₹2,338 Cr and operating profit jumping 39% to ₹349 Cr. The company is also pushing into affordable meals through Toing, its standalone app, which it says has seen encouraging early adoption, with 2 out of 3 users being either new to Swiggy or long inactive on the platform.
As Swiggy continues to scale its quick commerce operations and newer offerings such as Toing, here is a closer look at how the foodtech giant fared in Q2 FY27.
From The Editor’s Desk
CYBERSECURITY
eMudhra To Exit Global Certificate Business
eMudhra will voluntarily wind down its global SSL/TLS certificate business after a security flaw involving eight intermediate certificate authorities prompted Google and Mozilla to distrust its certificates, triggering fallout for its global TLS operations.
The company said it revoked the affected CAs within 14 hours, with no end-entity certificates issued by them and no data breach. It will transition existing customers to alternative providers free of charge over the next month.
The SSL/TLS business contributes around 1% of eMudhra’s global revenue. The company plans to focus on core digital trust solutions, including AI and quantum computing.
HEALTHTECH
CureBay Bags ₹100 Cr
The healthtech startup has raised ₹100 Cr ($10.6 Mn) in a Pre-Series C round, with over ₹69 Cr in equity led by IvyCap Ventures and around ₹30 Cr in debt from Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital and VentureSoul Partners.
The startup will use the funds to expand its geographical presence, strengthen its delivery network and invest in AI and technology capabilities.
Founded in 2021, CureBay connects patients in underserved areas with healthcare providers through rural clinics, community health workers and a digital platform linking them to doctors, hospitals, diagnostic labs and pharmacies.
Electric Vehicle
Ola Electric Rights Issue Gets Moving
Motilal Oswal Financial Services and Calliope Capital Advisors have applied for a combined 2.39 Cr shares in Ola Electric’s ₹1,000 Cr rights issue against entitlements transferred by promoter group entities — ANI Technologies Pvt Ltd and Indus Trust.
The rights issue comprises up to 37.03 Cr partly paid-up shares priced at ₹27 apiece. Ola Electric plans to use ₹350 Cr to repay borrowings and ₹400 Cr for organic growth.
The fundraise follows Ola Electric’s ₹780.24 Cr QIP in June, with ₹190.77 Cr of QIP proceeds and ₹139.21 Cr of IPO proceeds still unutilised as of September 20, 2026. The company’s Q1 FY27 revenue fell 45% YoY to ₹455 Cr, while its net loss narrowed 22% to ₹336 Cr.
Defence Tech
Tonbo Imaging IPO: Founders Pocket ₹137 Cr
Tonbo Imaging’s cofounders and early investors sold shares worth hundreds of crores in the defence tech company’s ₹852 Cr IPO, which closed with 136X subscription. The company is set to make its stock market debut today.
The three cofounders collectively pocketed ₹137.2 Cr through the offer for sale (OFS). CEO Arvind Lakshmikumar sold shares worth ₹80.5 Cr, while CBO Ankit Kumar and chief commercial officer Cecilia D’Souza offloaded shares worth ₹40.6 Cr and ₹16.1 Cr, respectively.
Related entities CEAQ Technologies and CEAQ Technologies Pte Ltd were the largest selling shareholders, offloading shares worth ₹350 Cr and ₹291 Cr, respectively. Early investor Artiman and promoter group entity Vinimaya Advisory LLP also sold shares in the IPO.
Ecommerce
BlueStone Swings To ₹4.4 Cr Loss In Q2
BlueStone reported a consolidated net loss of ₹4.4 Cr in Q2 FY27, against a net profit of ₹6 Cr in Q1 FY27. Revenue rose 45% YoY to ₹745 Cr, while losses narrowed 92% YoY.
The jewellery retailer added 27 stores in Q2, taking its network to 379 stores across 146 cities. Its customer base grew 19.3% YoY to 10.24 Lakh.
BlueStone reported an adjusted PAT of ₹19.6 Cr and pre-IndAS EBITDA of ₹53.5 Cr. Repeat customers contributed 56.3% of quarterly revenue, while the company approved raising up to ₹300 Cr through NCDs to refinance debt and fund business requirements.
Inc42 Markets
Building A Distinct Technology Stack For Electric Motorcycles?
Building an electric motorcycle involves more than replacing a petrol engine with an electric motor. Manufacturers must engineer the powertrain, battery architecture and vehicle controls to deliver the performance riders expect. Bengaluru-based Magron Novus is developing its own technology stack to bring these elements together.
Two-Wheel Ambition: Founded in 2022, Magron Novus is developing two electric motorcycle platforms — the C-20, designed for everyday riding, and the H-35, aimed at the performance segment. According to the company’s published specifications, the C-20 features a 22.5 kW motor, while the H-35 packs a 35 kW motor.
Under The Hood: The startup’s proprietary technology stack includes the Apex Drive system, battery architecture and vehicle intelligence features. It is also developing wireless power transfer technology and a virtual assistant to enhance the charging and riding experience.
A Growing Market: India’s electric vehicle market is projected to reach $132.2 Bn by 2030, according to Inc42’s India’s Electric Vehicle Startup Landscape Report. Electric two-wheeler sales rose 12.2% month-on-month to 2.07 Lakh units in September, up from 1.84 Lakh units in August, reflecting the scale of the opportunity.
As competition intensifies, can Magron Novus turn its in-house technology into reliable, commercially viable electric motorcycles that stand out in India’s two-wheeler market?

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Update | October 23, 2026, 18:07 IST
B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk’s shares closed their debut session at ₹138.30 on the BSE, down 8.4% from the issue price of ₹151 and 13% from the listing price of ₹159.
On the NSE, the stock closed at ₹138.25, down 8.4% from the issue price and 13.2% from the listing price of ₹159.25.
The shares touched intraday highs of ₹160.50 on the BSE and ₹161 on the NSE, before falling to lows of ₹127.20 and ₹127.40, respectively.
At the BSE closing price, Zetwerk’s market capitalisation stood at ₹23,431.54 Cr ($2.4 Bn).
Original | October 23, 2026, 10:00 IST
B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk made its stock market debut at a 5.46% premium on the NSE at ₹159.25 against its issue price of ₹151. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹159, up 5.3% from the issue price.
The listing followed Zetwerk’s ₹5,012.3 Cr IPO, which opened for subscription on October 15 and closed on October 19. The company had set a price band of ₹143-₹151 per share.
Ahead of the public issue, Zetwerk raised ₹2,251.2 Cr from anchor investors by allotting 14.91 Cr equity shares at ₹151 apiece on October 14.
The IPO comprised a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of 14.45 Cr shares worth ₹2,182.3 Cr. At the issue price, Zetwerk’s post-issue valuation stood at around ₹25,583 Cr.
Zetwerk increased the fresh issue from the ₹2,600 Cr proposed in its updated draft red herring prospectus (UDRHP). The OFS component also rose 49.2% from around 9.7 Cr shares.
Promoters and cofounders Amrit Pratik Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan each offered to sell up to 1.42 Cr shares. Other selling shareholders included promoter group entity Creovate Innovation and funds associated with Peak XV Partners, Accel India, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Kae Capital.
Kae Capital Fund II and Kalysta Capital Fund II bagged 38.3X returns on shares sold through the OFS, pocketing ₹196.3 Cr and ₹63.3 Cr, respectively. Lightspeed’s funds collectively received around ₹440 Cr, while Peak XV’s funds realised ₹359.3 Cr from their share sales.
Zetwerk has earmarked ₹2,160 Cr from the fresh issue to repay or prepay borrowings of the company and certain subsidiaries, with the remaining proceeds allocated to acquisitions and general corporate purposes.
The company confidentially filed its draft IPO papers in March and submitted its UDRHP in August.
Revenue Rises, Loss Widens
Zetwerk’s operating revenue grew 40.4% to ₹15,913.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹11,331.9 Cr in the previous year. However, its net loss, including discontinued operations, widened to ₹1,606.2 Cr from ₹370.7 Cr in FY25.
The FY26 loss included a ₹796.4 Cr exceptional charge linked to changes in share conversion ratios and a ₹453 Cr impairment charge in its discontinued civil infrastructure business.
In Q1 FY27, operating revenue from continuing operations rose 55.4% to ₹4,117.9 Cr from ₹2,649.4 Cr. Its total net loss narrowed 46.4% to ₹733 Cr from ₹1,368.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter.
Of the latest quarterly loss, ₹668.9 Cr came from discontinued operations, while continuing operations accounted for ₹64.1 Cr.
Founded in 2018, Zetwerk operates a manufacturing platform serving businesses across industrial and consumer goods categories. It combines capacity from third-party suppliers and its own facilities to fulfil orders across renewable energy, consumer electronics, aerospace, defence, oil and gas, and industrial automation.
Its customers include Siemens Gamesa, Acer India, boAt, NTPC Renewable Energy, CG Power and Industrial Solutions, and the Indian Air Force. As of June 30, 2026, Zetwerk operated 26 manufacturing facilities across India, the US, Germany, and Spain.
The company entered the unicorn club in 2021 after raising $150 Mn. Before its IPO, it had raised over $900 Mn from investors including Peak XV Partners, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Accel India, Greenoaks Capital Partners, and D1 Capital Partners.

items.title: DoT’s SIM Binding Rules Set to Take Effect Beginning January 1 to Curb Cyber Fraud: Here’s What Changes
items.summary: The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) has directed messaging and communication apps to comply with SIM-binding rules from January 1, 2027. The compliance directive mandates that such apps implement a SIM-based login verification process in an attempt to keep user accounts linked to the active SIM cards associated with their registered Indian mobile numbers. DoT says the move is aimed at curbing fraud and safeguarding the digital ecosystem. The rules could change how users access services such as WhatsApp, Telegram and Signal on their devices.

items.content:
It is hereby notified for information of the public that in exercise of powers vested in it under sub section (1) of Section 35 A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) vide Directive Ref. No. CHN.DoS.UCBs.No.S336/16-05-847/2026-2027 dated October 19, 2026, has issued certain Directions to ‘Puducherry Co-operative Urban Bank Ltd’, (“the bank”), whereby, as from the close of business on October 21, 2026, the bank shall not, without prior approval of RBI in writing, grant or renew any loans and advances, make any investment, incur any liability including borrowal of funds and acceptance of fresh deposits, disburse or agree to disburse any payment whether in discharge of its liabilities and obligations or otherwise, enter into any compromise or arrangement and sell, transfer or otherwise dispose of any of its properties or assets except as notified in the RBI Direction dated October 19, 2026, a copy of which has been directed to be displayed on the bank's website / premises for perusal by interested members of the public. Considering the bank's present liquidity position, the bank has been directed to permit withdrawal of an amount not exceeding ₹5,000/- (Rupees Five Thousand only) from savings bank or current accounts or any other account of a depositor but is allowed to set off loans against deposits subject to the conditions stated in the above RBI Directions. The bank may incur expenditure in respect of certain essential items such as salaries of employees, rent, electricity bills, etc., as specified in the said Directions.
2. RBI has in the recent past engaged with the Board and Senior Management of the bank for improvement in its functioning. However, lack of concrete efforts taken by the bank to address the supervisory concerns and protection of the interest of depositors of the bank have necessitated issuance of these Directions.
3. The eligible depositors would be entitled to receive deposit insurance claim amount of their deposits upto a monetary ceiling of ₹5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakh only) in the same capacity and in the same right, from the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC), as applicable under the provisions of the DICGC Act, 1961, based on submission of willingness by the depositors concerned and after due verification. The depositors may contact the bank officials for further information. Details may also be accessed on the DICGC website: www.dicgc.org.in.
4. The issue of the above Directions by the RBI should not per se be construed as cancellation of the banking license by RBI. The bank will continue to undertake banking business subject to restrictions specified in the said Directions till its financial position improves. The RBI continues to monitor the position of the bank and will take necessary actions including modifications of these Directions, as warranted, depending upon circumstances and in the interest of the depositors.
5. These Directions shall remain in force for a period of six months from the close of business on October 21, 2026 and are subject to review.
(Brij Raj)           
Chief General Manager
Press Release: 2026-2027/1362
