items.content:
[Under Section 45ZL of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934]
The sixty third meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), constituted under Section 45ZB of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, was held during October 5 to 7, 2026.
2. The meeting was chaired by Shri Sanjay Malhotra, Governor and was attended by all the members – Dr. Nagesh Kumar, Director and Chief Executive, Institute for Studies in Industrial Development, New Delhi; Shri Saugata Bhattacharya, Economist, Mumbai; Professor Ram Singh, Director, Delhi School of Economics, Delhi; Dr. Poonam Gupta, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy and Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya, Executive Director (the officer of the Reserve Bank nominated by the Central Board under Section 45ZB(2)(c) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934).
3. According to Section 45ZL of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Reserve Bank shall publish, on the fourteenth day after every meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee, the minutes of the proceedings of the meeting which shall include the following, namely:
the resolution adopted at the meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee;
the vote of each member of the Monetary Policy Committee, ascribed to such member, on the resolution adopted in the said meeting; and
the statement of each member of the Monetary Policy Committee under sub-section (11) of section 45ZI on the resolution adopted in the said meeting.
4. In the light of evolving developments on the global and domestic front, the MPC reviewed in detail the staff’s macroeconomic projections that included inputs from survey results and stakeholder consultations. The MPC also reviewed alternative scenarios around various risks to the outlook. Drawing on the above and after extensive discussions on the stance of monetary policy, the MPC adopted the resolution that is set out below.
Resolution
5. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) held its 63rd meeting from October 5 to 7, 2026, under the chairmanship of Shri Sanjay Malhotra, Governor, Reserve Bank of India. The MPC members Dr. Nagesh Kumar, Shri Saugata Bhattacharya, Prof. Ram Singh, Dr. Poonam Gupta and Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya attended the meeting.
6. After a detailed assessment of the evolving macroeconomic and financial developments and the outlook, the MPC voted unanimously to increase the policy repo rate under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) by 25 bps to 5.50 per cent. Consequently, the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate stands adjusted at 5.25 per cent and the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate and the Bank Rate at 5.75 per cent. The MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening.
Growth and Inflation Outlook
Global Outlook
7. Since the last MPC meeting in August 2026, the re-escalation of the conflict in West Asia and the consequent sharp volatility in crude oil prices has kept the global economy in a state of flux. Global growth has remained resilient. Acceleration of inflation in key economies has prompted a shift towards hawkish monetary policy. The US Fed hiked by 25 bps in September. The Fed commentary thereafter along with rate tightening by major systemically important central banks have reinforced expectations of higher global policy rates. Tighter global financial market conditions coupled with fiscal sustainability concerns in major economies are keeping global bond yields at record high levels. With a resolution of the West Asia conflict remaining elusive, significant downside risks to the global outlook remain, including further tightening of global financial conditions, continuing elevated AI-related asset valuations and high public debt.
Domestic Outlook
8. Notwithstanding these persisting global headwinds, the Indian economy has remained resilient. As per National Statistics Office (NSO) estimates, real GDP growth in Q1:2026-27 at 7.8 per cent was higher than expected. Strong private consumption and fixed investment, rebound in merchandise exports and sustained buoyancy in services exports supported growth. On the supply side, the manufacturing sector grew at a robust pace. Services sector activity strengthened further, owing to buoyant domestic and external demand.
9. In Q2, available high frequency indicators for July-August suggest sustained momentum in domestic economic activity. Domestic demand remains resilient and is well supported by robust external demand with merchandise exports registering double-digit growth.
10. Looking ahead, global economic uncertainty will continue to have some bearing on domestic economic activity. While energy prices and supply chain pressures have continued, their near-term trajectory remains uncertain amidst the lingering West Asia conflict. Their adverse impact is being contained with active diversification of supply sources. Deficient south-west monsoon and strong El Niño conditions pose risks to agriculture sector’s outlook and rural demand, although healthy buffer of foodgrains and proactive policy interventions by the government are expected to mitigate the impact. Furthermore, continuing momentum in services and broadly stable employment conditions are likely to support urban demand. Strong capacity utilisation, robust credit flows and the government’s thrust on infrastructure are expected to sustain investment activity. While services exports are expected to remain buoyant, bilateral trade agreements should boost merchandise exports.
11. Taking all these factors into consideration, real GDP growth for 2026-27 is projected at 7.1 per cent, with Q2 at 7.2 per cent; Q3 at 6.9 per cent and Q4 at 6.8 per cent. Real GDP growth for Q1:2027-28 is projected at 7.1 per cent. The risks are evenly balanced (Chart 1).
12. CPI inflation increased to 4.8 per cent in August 2026 from 4.5 per cent in July. While the increase has been predominantly on account of higher inflation in food and fuel groups, core inflation has also picked up indicating some signs of widening price pressures. Food price increases have become more broad based along with notable spikes in certain items such as sugar and onion. The uptick in fuel inflation in August largely reflected unfavourable base effects. Core inflation increased to 4.2 per cent and core inflation, excluding precious metals, increased to 2.9 per cent in August. The weighted share of items in headline CPI recording inflation above 4 per cent increased steadily to about 37 per cent in August.
13. The near-term outlook on inflation points towards continued pressures from supply side on account of the deficient monsoon, ongoing El Niño conditions and high energy and other commodity prices, the pass through of which is still continuing. Considering all factors, CPI inflation is projected to be 5.2 per cent for 2026-27 with Q2 at 4.9 per cent; Q3 at 6.0 per cent; and Q4 at 5.7 per cent (Chart 2). Inflation for Q1:2027-28 is projected at 5.6 per cent with risks being evenly balanced. Core inflation is projected at 4.4 per cent for 2026-27.
Rationale for Monetary Policy Decisions
14. The MPC noted that the global context on account of geopolitical developments remains challenging. Nonetheless, the Indian economy has been strong. The economic momentum remains broad-based. The economy is expected to remain resilient.
15. In the light of available data, it is clear that inflation and its outlook are not benign as they were last year with headline CPI inflation expected to average almost 5.8 per cent in the next three quarters and core inflation projected at 4.4 per cent this year. In this milieu, recalibrating the policy rate is imperative.
16. As regards supply side inflation, monetary policy primarily acts by curtailing second round effects (inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, etc.), which take time to manifest and are difficult to extract from available data. Apart from data related to inflation expectations and firm level pricing behaviour, indicators of generalisation of inflation like core inflation and diffusion indices are used for this purpose. It may, however, be kept in mind that it is difficult to distinguish between the second-round effects and the indirect impact of supply side pressures (in production cost through energy and other inputs) as both are present in these indicators. While there is some evidence of elevated inflation expectations and generalisation of inflation, there are only limited signs of supply side pressures getting embedded in pricing behaviour.
17. Similarly, while there is limited evidence of demand side pressures, risks in view of strong growth in monetary and credit aggregates exist.
18. Considering all these factors, the MPC unanimously voted to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent. The MPC also decided to change the stance to calibrated tightening. It only signals that given the current conditions, rate cuts are off the table in the near term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on the evolving conditions and the outlook. The duration and extent of rate hike cycle would be contingent on the actual growth-inflation developments and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, the extent of broadening of price pressures and second round effects of the supply shock, as also the impact of demand impulses.
19. Two members - Dr. Nagesh Kumar and Prof. Ram Singh - were of the view that the stance be retained at neutral.
20. The MPC remains committed to its price stability mandate and will endeavour to progressively align inflation with its target.
21. The minutes of the MPC’s meeting will be published on October 21, 2026.
22. The next meeting of the MPC is scheduled for December 2 to 4, 2026.
Voting on the Resolution to increase policy repo rate by 25 bps to 5.50 per cent
Member Vote
Dr. Nagesh Kumar Yes
Shri Saugata Bhattacharya Yes
Prof. Ram Singh Yes
Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya Yes
Dr. Poonam Gupta Yes
Shri Sanjay Malhotra Yes
Statement by Dr. Nagesh Kumar
23. The 7.8% GDP growth logged by the Indian economy in Q1:FY2027, coming as it does against the backdrop of the West Asia conflict and continued trade policy uncertainties, is impressive, highlighting its resilience. The Q1 growth was underpinned by robust manufacturing growth of 9.2%, which is encouraging because of its direct and indirect job-creating effects. There are indications that the growth momentum is being carried through into Q2, as borne out by a healthy rate of gross fixed capital formation (GFCF), which was 34.3% in Q1:FY27 compared to 31.4% in Q1:FY26. If this 290-basis-point jump sustains, it would be very good for the economy, paving the way for the private investment cycle to gain momentum and drive industrial growth. The expansion of industrial credit also supports the view that the private investment cycle may finally be taking off. Similarly, the capital goods sector has been posting double-digit growth for the past 4 months, which is consistent with the robust GFCF and credit growth. A number of big investment proposals for data centres are coming up from big IT majors/global tech companies, and GCCs are augmenting their presence in the country. Hence, the projected growth for FY2026-27 has been raised to 7.1% from 6.7% at the time of the previous policy.
24. Merchandise exports have also shown robust growth in spite of global trade policy uncertainties, along with those of services exports, helping to keep the current account deficit in a manageable range of around 1% of GDP. The FCNR(B) scheme of RBI has helped to bring substantial inflows of NRI deposits which, besides helping to stabilise the exchange rate of the rupee, will lead to a significant balance of payments surplus in 2026-27. Going forward, the India-EU FTA, among others, which is likely to come into force towards the beginning of 2027, is likely to boost India’s exports, especially of labour-intensive goods, by giving Indian products a level playing field vis-à-vis peers such as Vietnam and Bangladesh, for the first time.
25. The inflationary outlook, on the other hand, remains challenging due to a combination of factors, including the deficient monsoon, rising crude oil prices, precious metals prices remaining at elevated levels, and exchange rate depreciation, leading to a revision of the forecast for headline inflation for 2026-27 by 20 basis points from 5.0% at the last policy to 5.2% and core inflation by 10 basis points to 4.4%. While inflation is driven largely by supply-side factors and does not show any signs of overheating of the economy nor of generalisation, it is important to manage inflationary expectations.
26. Keeping in mind the need to manage the inflationary outlook, I vote for a 25-basis-point increase in the repo rate. In view of the continued geopolitical and trade policy uncertainties, I feel that a neutral stance remains appropriate.
Statement by Shri Saugata Bhattacharya
27. Since the August ‘26 review, global financial conditions have tightened significantly. Energy prices have again risen. El Niño led weather disruptions have resulted in an increase in prices of many agricultural commodities, particularly of edible oils, sugar and, to an extent, cereals.
28. Most major central banks, responding to global macro-financial conditions, have adjusted their policy rates upwards. Benchmark yields have risen sharply across multiple G20 countries, and research reports suggest this is partly a result of rising term premia now sought by investors.1
29. In India, since the August 2026 review, some of the upside risks to inflation have started materialising. Data increasingly suggests that price pressures are getting entrenched into the economic system. Input prices, recorded in Wholesale Price Indices, have been printing close to 9% yoy. Media reports and enterprise surveys suggest that these input costs are being passed on to consumer prices. While ‘underlying inflation’ has thus far remained more subdued, and might implicitly be a signal of some residual demand weakness, trends in CPI inflation components indicate that a presumed slack relative to the potential output – if a slack at all even exists at present – appears to be closing.
30. MPC growth forecasts and official estimates reinforce current data, market reports, media news and forward-looking surveys suggesting that economic activity is – and will remain – resilient. High bank credit growth, earlier mostly restricted to the retail segment and to an extent MSMEs, have now dispersed into virtually all sectors and segments.
31. India’s external balance, however, remains a concern. The balance of payments shows some vulnerabilities, particularly given the tight global financial environment. At the very least, maintaining a certain gap between India and G7 interest rates is important for attracting debt capital flows. At the same time, too rapid a policy rate adjustment risks constricting growth and hence growth-led capital flows.
32. In this context, might the broad monetary policy environment in India now be too accommodative? Inflation risks and financial markets suggest it is. Growth is resilient enough to permit a closer focus on an incipient inflation persistence. The current and forecast level of real interest rates do not seem consistent with levels required for ensuring price stability. The real natural rate of interest (pertaining to Q4 of FY23-24) estimated this to be 1.4-1.9%. It is very likely that the slack of current output from potential will have shrunk, compared to the immediate post-COVID period.
33. Hence, the totality of information indicates a strong economic case at this time for tightening monetary policy, to bring inflation closer to the target sooner rather than later and anchor inflation expectations.
34. Domestic financial conditions have tightened significantly. This, to an extent, mitigates the need for large domestic monetary policy actions. Hence, the magnitude and pace of monetary policy adjustment needs to be carefully calibrated to balance the multiple trade-offs from these actions – inflation vs growth, credit vs deposits, domestic vs external and more. A data dependent approach is best to deal with the broad range of possible outcomes in this uncertain economic environment.
35. Hence, I vote to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points. Given the upside risks to inflation, it is also appropriate to change the stance to calibrated tightening.
Statement by Prof. Ram Singh
36. Since the last MPC meeting, inflationary pressures have hardened in most leading economies, prompting their monetary authorities to adopt a hawkish stance. Domestic inflation and its near-term trajectory have also turned less benign. Evidence suggests inflation has generalised beyond the direct effects of fuel, energy, and commodity prices since the onset of the West Asia conflict. Emerging evidence points to indirect effects (firms passing these cost increases onto the prices of the goods and services they provide). Diffusion indices and the core inflation trajectory provide some evidence. The number of items in the CPI basket rising above 4% has increased. The core is projected at 4.4 per cent this financial year. Non-food, non-fuel core inflation also climbed to 4.2% in August 2026, at least in part because producers raised their selling prices. Furthermore, the RBI’s September household survey showed the 3-month median inflation expectation jumped to 9.9%, reflecting households' anticipation of a higher cost of living.
37. These effects and their impact on headline CPI have been moderate so far. However, combined with possible demand-side pressures, driven by strong credit growth, the economy faces the risk of supply-side pressures becoming more widespread in the coming months. Headline CPI inflation is expected to remain elevated, averaging almost 5.8 per cent over the next three quarters, nudging the upper limit of the FIT tolerance band. Additionally, at the current repo rate level, the projected inflation trajectory will render the real rate negative, generating perverse saving-consumption trade-offs.
38. To realign the inflation trajectory towards the target, and from the real repo rate perspective, a calibrated increase in the repo rate is needed. The duration and magnitude of the rate hike required to meet these objectives would depend on the emerging growth-inflation outlook. The MPC will have to remain vigilant about the pace of inflation generalisation to respond in a timely and effective way. For now, there is a case for incremental, mild repo rate hikes, not high-for-long rates.
39. I do not favour shifting the stance from neutral to tightening mode, as it may signal an extended cycle of rate hikes. This, in turn, can neutralise the benefits of growth-supportive monetary and fiscal policies in the recent past. Current inflation is primarily due to supply-side factors, rising fuel, food, and commodity prices, and their effects. The classic signs of economic overheating —such as a wage-price spiral or demand-driven capacity overstretch or abnormal growth in private consumption and capex —are largely absent. The Q1 growth rate (7.8%) is in line with the average growth rate in recent years (7.9% during FY 2021-22 to 2025-26). Growth is expected to moderate in the coming quarters, especially in sectors like real estate and automobiles, as the GST boost peters out. PMI manufacturing and services both show some signs of moderation.
40. Expectations of significant rate increases can undermine demand not only in interest rate-sensitive sectors such as vehicles, real estate, and discretionary spending, but also drag on recent momentum in private investment. Coming on the heels of stress on the farm sector due to below-normal rains and El Niño, rising input costs and global uncertainty, significant rate hikes would hurt profit margins and the sustainability of capex plans of large and small firms.
41. Therefore, I vote for a 25-bps increase in the repo rate to 5.50% without changing the stance.
Statement by Shri Indranil Bhattacharyya
42. Notwithstanding an adverse external backdrop and despite an erratic domestic monsoon, the Indian economy has fared much better than expectations with economic activity on a sound footing and poised to register more than 7 per cent growth in 2026-27.
43. On the inflation front, there are, however, reasons for concern. Inflation is clearly on the rise, averaging about 5.8 per cent in the immediate three quarters, driven by food and fuel prices. The weighted share of items in the CPI basket experiencing inflation above 6 per cent has increased noticeably in August, as suggested by the diffusion index. Core inflation (CPI excluding food and fuel) also indicates a similar shift in distribution, albeit of a lower magnitude. The momentum of underlying inflation is also high as evident from the weighted median and trimmed mean measures in recent months.2 These are corroborated by the latest round of survey findings which suggests that inflation expectations are significantly higher in both the urban and rural areas.3 Moreover, there is increasing evidence of pass-through of input cost pressures in certain segments such as restaurants and cooked meals. PMI surveys and producer price indices also suggest some pent-up pass-through. Greater pass-through is expected going ahead, especially when demand conditions are strong.
44. Therefore, the inflation outlook merits greater attention, given supply side pressures from crude and food prices are unlikely to relent quickly. With demand holding strong and in the wake of strong growth in monetary and credit aggregates, the interplay of both supply and demand factors could ratchet up inflation pressures significantly in the period ahead. Therefore, I feel it is better to set aside the “cautiousness bias”4 and act in a pre-emptive manner at this juncture rather than wait and watch. Accordingly, I vote for a 25-bps policy rate hike. Going ahead, the trajectory of the policy path would be calibrated based on the evolving macroeconomic developments and emerging inflation prints. Given the present global and domestic circumstances, rate cuts are not an option in the near term. Therefore, I feel it is also appropriate to change the stance from neutral to calibrated tightening. While the neutral stance is consistent with all three policy options (cut, hike and pause), calibrated tightening conveys an unequivocally clear message that rate hikes or pause are the only options in the near term, depending on the evolving outlook. Besides signalling, this would also reaffirm our commitment to price stability as the primary objective of monetary policy.
Statement by Dr. Poonam Gupta
45. The global backdrop has continued to evolve since the last policy meeting, feeding heightened uncertainty. Two developments in particular stand out: first, the flare-up in the West Asia conflict and persistently elevated oil prices; second, the implications of high demand for financial resources from sovereigns and the private sector in some advanced economies on global interest rates and cost of funding in other countries including emerging market economies.
46. Domestically, the economy has done exceptionally well, growing at 7.8 per cent in Q1:2026-27, well above the forecast in the August policy. A range of high-frequency indicators support the growth momentum in Q2 as well. Meanwhile, inflation, primarily driven by food, fuel and gold, with limited generalisation to core, has inched up to 4.5 per cent in July and further to 4.8 per cent in August. Consequently, the MPC has revised upward its inflation forecast to 5.2 per cent while increasing real GDP growth forecast for 2026-27 to 7.1 per cent. Inflation is projected to accelerate to 6.0 per cent in Q3 before moderating to 5.7 per cent in Q4 and 5.6 per cent in Q1 next year.
47. At this point in time, inflation is mostly driven by external supply-side shocks, with insignificant signs of it becoming entrenched or impacting inflation expectations. Yet, with projections indicating the likelihood of headline inflation hitting the upper tolerance limit of 6 per cent, one may not want to wait for more definitive evidence of generalisation, and instead be mindful of the fact that monetary policy works with a lag.
48. In fact, in the post pandemic inflation targeting period, whenever inflation has reached or breached the lower or upper tolerance limits, appropriate policy action has been taken. This has helped retain the credibility of the framework and has kept inflation expectations aligned to the target. Thus, rather than waiting any longer, in view of rising inflation and resilient growth, I favour raising the policy repo rate by 25 bps in this policy.
49. Meanwhile, inflationary pressures are mounting around the world, driven by high fuel and commodity prices. Domestically, weather-related adversities and global oil and commodity prices may continue to put upward pressure on headline inflation. At some point, a larger pass-through of input costs to output prices may materialise. Under these circumstances, it is conceivable that a further increase in the policy rate might be needed to keep inflation low and inflationary expectations anchored. The pace, extent, and duration of such actions would depend on the incoming data on inflation, its diffusion, and evidence of second-round effects.
50. Hence, I propose to change the stance to calibrated tightening, which would be consistent with any such warranted future course of action.
Statement by Shri Sanjay Malhotra
51. Amidst the turbulent global backdrop, the Indian economy has shown remarkable resilience. Growth for the full year 2026-27 is now projected at 7.1 per cent, 40 bps higher than the projection of 6.7 per cent in August.
52. Inflationary pressures are, however, building up. Headline CPI is projected to touch the upper tolerance band in Q3 and remain significantly above 5 per cent in the next two quarters.
53. In terms of the diffusion index, there are increasing signs of generalisation of inflation as 37 per cent of the commodities in the CPI basket had inflation above 4 per cent in August – it was merely 20 per cent in March. While core inflation increased from 3.9 per cent in July to 4.2 per cent in August, core inflation, excluding precious metals, increased to 2.9 per cent in August, driven by a strong momentum of 0.5 per cent. Underlying inflation, as measured by core ex precious metals is also anticipated to move above target in the coming months. This indicates a normalisation of inflation from the benign levels seen earlier.
54. As regards supply side inflation requiring a monetary policy response, it is pertinent to mention that monetary policy primarily acts by curtailing second round effects (wage expectations and firm level pricing behaviour) of a supply shock. It is difficult to distinguish between the second-round effects and the indirect impact of supply side pressures (in production cost through energy and other inputs) as both are present in core inflation.
55. Similarly, there are risks of demand side pressures in view of the growth in monetary and credit aggregates.
56. Considering the above growth-inflation dynamics, I consider it appropriate to recalibrate the policy rate. Accordingly, I vote for a 25-bps hike in the policy rate. The duration and extent of the rate hiking cycle would be contingent on the actual growth-inflation developments and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, the broadening of price pressures, second round effects of the supply shock, and the impact of demand impulses. Nevertheless, I feel it is appropriate to change the stance to calibrated tightening, essentially signalling that rate cuts are off the table in the near term and policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on the evolving circumstances and the outlook.
(Brij Raj)          
Chief General Manager
Press Release: 2026-2027/1361
1 BIS Quarterly Review Sep ’26, “Yields Climb, yet Risk Appetite stays firm”.
2 Various measures of trimmed mean (5%, 10% and 25%) suggest that it has increased from the range 2.2-2.7 per cent in March to 3.7-4.2 per cent in August 2026. Similarly, the weighted median has increased from 2 per cent to 3.5 per cent over the same period.
3 In the Reserve Bank’s September 2026 survey, urban households’ inflation expectations for the next three months as well as one year ahead rose by 70 bps and 60 bps, respectively. According to the bi-monthly Rural Consumer Confidence Survey (RCCS), the current perception of inflation in rural and semiurban households increased by 70 bps while it rose by 50 bps for expectations one-year ahead in September 2026.
4 From monetary policy perspective, concerns about uncertainty create a cautiousness bias: acting less is justified when the private sector’s expectations of inflation are assumed to remain unchanged, but acting less may lead to sharp spike in inflation and unhinge inflation expectations. In response to the de-anchoring of expectations, the central bank can easily end up tightening much more than it initially intended to do, hurting growth but without succeeding in aligning inflation back to its target quickly (see Stephane Dupraz, Sophie Guilloux-Nefussi and Adrian Penalver (2023), A Pitfall of Cautiousness in Monetary Policy, International Journal of Central Banking, Vol 19(3), August.

items.content:
… Say Nigeria’s Mental Health Act needs action, not just legislation
By Chioma Obinna
Nigeria and other African countries must invest in home-grown mental health research and translate policies into action to improve care for millions of people facing mental health challenges, psychiatrists have said.
The experts warned that Africa’s low contribution to global mental health research was limiting the continent’s capacity to develop evidence-based responses suited to its population, while weak implementation of policies threatened to widen the gap between legislation and access to care.
They spoke at the ninth International Research Conference of the Federal Neuro-Psychiatric Hospital, Yaba, Lagos, themed, “Mental Health Research at the Crossroads: Challenges, Policies and Reforms in Africa.”
Professor Taiwo Lateef Sheikh, a professor of psychiatry at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, said Africa accounted for less than two per cent of global mental health research output, a situation he said underscored the urgent need to strengthen local research capacity.
Sheikh called for increased investment in African-led studies, arguing that research priorities should reflect the realities of local communities and provide evidence for policies and interventions.
He also drew attention to the implementation gap surrounding Nigeria’s Mental Health Act, stressing that the existence of a law was not enough without concrete action, institutional commitment and adequate resources.
For Nigeria, the challenge is not only to develop mental health policies but also to ensure that research informs decisions, services reach people who need them and reforms translate into practical improvements in care.
The Medical Director of the Federal Neuro-Psychiatric Hospital, Yaba, Dr Olugbenga Owoeye, said research was essential to improving clinical practice and strengthening the delivery of mental health services.
He stressed the need to bridge the gap between research findings and their application, noting that studies should provide useful evidence for decision-making and improvements in patient care.
The conference chairperson, Professor Mashudat Bello-Mojeed, also emphasised the need to strengthen mental health research and ensure that evidence played a greater role in shaping policies and reforms across Africa.
She highlighted the importance of addressing the challenges confronting research development and building systems capable of supporting meaningful progress in mental healthcare.
Another speaker, Dr Tolu Ajomale highlighted the role of legal and policy frameworks in addressing mental health challenges, pointing to the need for stronger links between legislation, institutional action and access to care.
The discussions brought into focus the relationship between research, legislation and service delivery, with the experts calling for greater collaboration among governments, researchers and healthcare institutions.
They said locally generated evidence could help identify the needs of African populations, guide the design of appropriate interventions and strengthen the continent’s response to mental health challenges.
The conference called attention to the need for sustained investment in research and reforms that go beyond policy statements to deliver practical results.
The experts insisted that mental health research must become a stronger foundation for policymaking, while existing laws and commitments must be translated into action that improves access to care.
The post Psychiatrists seek home-grown research to tackle Africa’s mental health crisis appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja
The Federal Government has commissioned two solar mini-grids in Kano State, providing 2,214 electricity connections to homes and businesses in underserved communities.
The projects, delivered through the Rural Electrification Agency (REA) under the Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up (DARES) programme of the Nigeria Electrification Project (NEP), are funded by the World Bank.
Located in Ballagaza, Gabasawa Local Government Area, and Marayar Rogo, Warawa Local Government Area, the facilities have a combined installed capacity of 268.4 kilowatt-peak (kWp).
A statement by the REA on Thursday said the Ballagaza mini-grid has a capacity of 195.2kWp, while the Marayar Rogo facility has 73.2kWp.
The projects have provided 1,564 electricity connections in Ballagaza and 650 in Marayar Rogo.
Speaking at the commissioning, the Minister of Power, Chief Joseph Tegbe, said the projects demonstrated the importance of investment in renewable energy and collaboration with the private sector in expanding electricity access.
He said the Federal Government would continue to encourage partnerships that accelerate the delivery of reliable and sustainable electricity, particularly to rural communities.
According to him, the projects would bring electricity closer to underserved populations, support small businesses and create an enabling environment for economic growth.
The REA said the mini-grids were expected to support productive activities, including milling, welding, tailoring, cold storage and other commercial services, improving business operations, productivity and household incomes.
Representing Kano State Governor, the Managing Director of the Kano State Rural Electricity Board, Abba Kabir Yusuf, commended the Federal Government and the REA for extending electricity infrastructure to the benefiting communities.
He said improved electricity supply would support commercial activities, enhance productivity and contribute to the state’s socio-economic development.
The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of the REA, Abba Abubakar Aliyu, said the agency’s objective went beyond installing electricity infrastructure to ensuring that communities derived tangible economic benefits from the projects.
“With 2,214 connections across Ballagaza and Marayar Rogo, we are creating opportunities for households, supporting local businesses and providing a dependable foundation for productive work, stronger enterprises and improved incomes,” Aliyu said.
He added that the agency remained committed to ensuring that electricity access translated into better livelihoods and economic opportunities for rural communities.
The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Alfuttaim Nigeria Limited, Femi Kumuyi, whose company delivered the projects, said the facilities demonstrated the benefits of collaboration among the Federal Government, the REA, development partners and private-sector developers.
He said the company would continue to support the expansion of reliable renewable energy solutions in underserved communities.

items.content:
… As partnership connects nearly 2,000 schools, trains over 19,000 teachers
By Chioma Obinna
Nearly one million Nigerian students across the country are benefiting from free digital learning opportunities through a partnership between Airtel Africa, the United Nations Children’s Fund, UNICEF, and the Federal Government, as stakeholders move to bridge the digital divide and equip young people with skills for future employment.
The initiative, which has connected nearly 2,000 schools and reached more than 20,000 teachers, is removing data-cost barriers to digital education through free access to learning platforms, while equipping students with digital literacy, artificial intelligence, entrepreneurship, and employability skills.
The impact of the programme came into focus during a joint Airtel Africa-UNICEF delegation’s assessment tour of selected schools and youth programmes in Lagos, where students demonstrated how technology is changing their learning experience and opening new opportunities beyond the classroom.
The delegation, led by Garreth Spillane, Chief of Staff to the Chairman of Airtel Africa, visited Government Senior College, Agege; St George’s U.N.A. Primary School, Ipaja; and Yaba College of Technology, where students, teachers and young people showcased the practical benefits of digital learning and skills acquisition.
At Government Senior College, students demonstrated how digital learning tools, including artificial intelligence, are supporting classroom activities, while young people at Yaba College of Technology showed how digital platforms are helping them develop skills for employment, entrepreneurship and self-reliance.
Speaking during the tour, UNICEF Deputy Representative in Nigeria, Dr Rownak Khan, said free access to digital learning was helping young people acquire the knowledge and skills needed to prepare for their future.
“I’m very impressed to see how these girls are learning digital skills, and I really would like to thank the Ministry of Education at both the federal and state levels,” Khan said.
“But our biggest appreciation goes to Airtel Nigeria for this partnership. Airtel has supported us with zero-rating, providing free access so these girls can learn the skills they need to prepare for school and their future careers.”
She said the initiative was particularly important for girls, children with disabilities and learners in underserved communities, who must not be left behind as education increasingly embraces technology.
“Access to free digital learning not only bridges the digital divide but also brings children and young people closer to the knowledge, skills and opportunities they need to shape their and their country’s future,” Khan said.
“Our partnership with Airtel and the Government of Nigeria is supporting teachers and creating pathways from learning to earning. Girls, children with disabilities and those in underserved communities must be among the first to benefit.”
The Nigeria Learning Passport, one of the programme’s major platforms, provides online, mobile and offline access to curriculum-aligned educational resources for pre-primary, primary and secondary school pupils.
The platform hosts more than 15,000 educational resources, including lessons in English, Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba. It has recorded more than 2.5 million registered students and nearly 100,000 registered teachers.
The initiative, introduced in Nigeria during the COVID-19 pandemic when school closures disrupted learning nationwide, is now hosted by the Federal Ministry of Education as part of efforts to expand access to educational resources.
Through the partnership, Airtel provides zero-rated access to the Nigeria Learning Passport, the ministry’s Inspire and Ignite platforms, the Digital National Education Management Information System and the Youth Agency Marketplace, also known as YOMA.
The arrangement allows users to access the designated platforms without incurring mobile data charges, addressing one of the major obstacles to digital learning for families with limited resources.
Head of Programmes at the Airtel Africa Foundation, Esi Asare Prah, said digital inclusion in education was central to preparing young Africans for an increasingly technology-driven world.
“One of the biggest missions for the foundation is driving faster digital inclusion in education to improve learning outcomes,” Prah said.
“For Airtel as an organisation, digital inclusion is a major priority. We want to ensure that young people across Africa are equipped for the future.”
She said the visit demonstrated how access to digital resources could help young learners, particularly girls, gain confidence in technology and develop practical skills.
“It was wonderful to see young girls taking full advantage of the opportunity afforded by the zero-rated Learning Passport,” she said. “Because they can learn free of charge, they are able to absorb information and, within minutes, develop content from what they’ve learned.”
Prah said the Airtel Africa Foundation was committed to strengthening digital infrastructure, expanding access in underserved rural communities, empowering marginalised groups and promoting long-term educational equity.
She added that young people across Nigeria with an Airtel connection could access the Nigeria Learning Passport free of charge.
For students, the benefits extend beyond lessons delivered in school.
The Head Girl of Government Senior College, Tosin Adeola, said the platform had improved students’ academic performance and study habits by allowing them to revisit lessons and review difficult topics at home.
She thanked UNICEF and Airtel for providing the opportunity, saying students were determined to make effective use of the platform.
Airtel Africa Foundation committee member, Spillane, said connectivity could transform education when it enabled students to access quality learning materials and teachers to use digital tools effectively.
“Connectivity brings transformative opportunities when it helps students access quality digital learning and enables teachers to use digital tools effectively, as we’ve seen demonstrated so ably here in Nigeria,” he said.
“Working with UNICEF and governments, we will continue to connect schools, remove data-cost barriers through zero-rated learning platforms and support teachers across the continent.”
The Minister of State for Education, Prof. Suwaiba Sa’idu Ahmad, said collaboration among government, development partners and telecommunications providers was necessary to improve learning outcomes and ensure that digital education reached children regardless of their location.
“Transforming education in Nigeria requires strong partnerships aligned with government priorities and learners’ needs,” Ahmad said.
“We must strengthen teachers’ capacity, expand access to quality digital content, protect children online and ensure digital learning reaches every child, wherever they live.”
In Abuja, the delegation also met with the Office of the Vice President and the Federal Ministry of Education to discuss reliable connectivity, quality learning content, teacher training, inclusive digital design, stronger education data systems, child online safety and sustainable financing.
The partners reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening these areas to improve learning outcomes and expand access to digital education.
Across 13 African countries, the five-year Airtel Africa-UNICEF partnership has connected more than 3,000 schools, provided zero-rated access to more than 60 learning platforms and reached over 2.5 million children.
The partners said continued collaboration with governments would be critical to expanding the initiative and ensuring that more children and young people, particularly those in underserved communities, could benefit from digital learning and the opportunities it creates.
The post Free digital learning reaches 1m Nigerian students — UNICEF, Airtel appeared first on Vanguard News.

‎–Says friendship between two nations has begun to yield visible results
‎
‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru
‎
‎ABUJA — THE First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu on Thursday, received the Chinese Ambassador to Nigeria,
‎Yu Dunhai at the presidential villa, Abuja.
‎
‎At the visit, Ambassador Dunhai said the ongoing reforms in Nigeria, under President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda are yielding tangible and life-changing results that should be consolidated beyond 2027.
‎
‎The Ambassador said having seen the half year trade volume between the two countries grow to 18 billion dollars and having watched Nigeria in the last three years take a new shape, on strong macroeconomic footing, the country must continue the path by putting their faith in ongoing reforms.
‎
‎Yu Dunhai noted that the there is renewed and stronger confidence by foreign investors and his country will not shy away from the keying into this.
‎
‎The envoy pointed out that in the last three years, Nigeria’s export to China has increased tremendously.
‎
‎He said in deepening the bilateral relations between the two countries, China will ensure to work with the principle that Africa’s resources belong to Africa, stick to high quality investment, make use of domestic human capital among others.
‎
‎He explained that the visit, being his first since assuming office in Nigeria two years ago, is to convey his government’s admiration for the Renewed Hope Agenda, ably complemented by the First Lady’s Renewed Hope Initiative, and to explore further areas of support, particularly in health, education and promoting food security.
‎
‎Responding the First Lady of Nigeria Senator Tinubu noted that an endorsement for a second term in office for President Tinubu, from a strong ally such as China is cheering.
‎
‎She commended China’s interest in the agricultural sector, especially with a promise to collaborate on use of technology to enhance food security.
‎
‎The First Lady promised to encourage a collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security.
‎
‎“When friendship have transcended this long, it begins to yield results and we are beginning to see the results now”.
‎
‎“We are looking for how the vulnerable ones would be lifted, we know this will help us a lot. Nigeria is transforming. And we must embrace the new Nigeria”.
‎
‎Nigeria and China elevated their bilateral relations to a comprehensive strategic partnership, since year 2024 during President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s state visit to China.

items.content:
By Dapo Akinrefon
The Aare Ona Kakanfo of Yorubaland, Iba Gani Adams, has described the late leader of the pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere, Pa Reuben Fasoranti, as a symbol of integrity, discipline and selfless service to the Yoruba nation and Nigeria.
Adams, who expressed sorrow over Fasoranti’s death on Tuesday at the age of 100, said his passing marked the end of an era in Yoruba leadership and Nigeria’s socio-political history.
In a tribute, Adams said Nigeria had lost a leader whose wisdom and principled positions on justice, true federalism and good governance had guided generations.
“We have lost a leader whose wisdom and principled stance on issues of justice, true federalism, and good governance had been a guiding light for generations,” he said.
He described Fasoranti’s contributions to Yorubaland as immense and multifaceted, noting that, as Afenifere leader, he championed Yoruba unity and cultural pride while advocating the protection of Yoruba interests within the Nigerian federation.
According to Adams, Fasoranti’s commitment to democratic values and justice earned him respect beyond the Yoruba nation, across Nigeria’s diverse ethnic groups.
The Aare Ona Kakanfo said the late elder statesman played a pivotal role in shaping Nigeria’s socio-political discourse, particularly through his advocacy for true federalism.
He said Fasoranti believed that Nigeria’s unity could only be sustained through equitable power-sharing and respect for the autonomy of its constituent regions.
Adams also recalled that Fasoranti helped preserve the ideals of the late Chief Obafemi Awolowo’s progressive vision for Nigeria, which emphasised education, social justice and economic development.
He said the late Afenifere leader remained committed to national unity despite his strong advocacy for Yoruba rights.
Adams further described Fasoranti’s leadership style as inclusive and conciliatory, saying he consistently favoured dialogue and peaceful conflict resolution.
He noted that the approach contributed to peace and stability in Yorubaland and Nigeria during turbulent periods.
The post Fasoranti stood for integrity, selfless service — Adams appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Henry Oduah
items.content:
A US judge on Thursday issued President Donald Trump a December 11 deadline to testify under oath in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC.
Judge Enjolique Lett in Miami gave the order in response to complaints by the British broadcaster that Trump has refused to sit for a deposition, including canceling a previously agreed date of October 16.
If Trump fails to attend the deposition by then, he risks sanctions, including dismissal of his lawsuit, the court said.
Trump has accused the BBC of deceptively editing its documentary “Trump: A Second Chance” to make it seem as if he was inciting violence when he told supporters to march on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, after losing the presidential election.
The crowd proceeded to storm Congress in an attempt to stop the formal certification of Democrat Joe Biden’s victory.
While the BBC has apologized for the incident, which prompted the resignation of multiple senior executives, the broadcaster has denied it caused Trump any real injury and moved for the case to be dismissed.
Trump filed his suit against the BBC in December 2025 and is seeking at least $5 billion on each of two counts.
Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, said in court that Trump had no real excuse not to testify and that on October 16, he had only been campaigning, “participating in party politics.”
“No plaintiff is above the law,” Tobin said.
In a court filing Wednesday, Trump’s legal team argued that he was not seeking to avoid a deposition but had been constrained by “matters of national importance.”
The lawyers said Trump would be able to give a deposition between January 11 and 22.
Trump has made attacks on the media a signature of his two presidential terms, insulting reporters who ask questions he doesn’t like and seeking to ban outlets airing critical reports from the White House.
Most recently, the administration has plunged into a legal dispute with CNN, MSNOW and Politico over attempts to bar them from the White House.
With his approval ratings in the low 30 percent range and polls showing his Republican Party likely to lose control of the House of Representatives in the November 3 midterm elections, Trump faces increasing headwinds as he approaches his final years in power.
AFP

items.author: Henry Oduah
items.content:
The All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council has accused former Vice-President, Atiku Abubakar, of politicising Nigeria’s Ebola response, insisting that approved emergency funds remain untouched.
The council’s spokesperson, Mr Dele Alake, said this in a statement issued on Thursday in Abuja.
Alake said President Bola Tinubu approved N10 billion for the Ebola emergency in June, but relevant agencies deployed other available resources.
“On accountability, the Atiku camp should note that the N10 billion the President approved for the Ebola emergency in June remains untouched,” he said.
He said the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN) and other agencies strengthened surveillance at entry points.
According to him, the surveillance network alerted the government to the index case and facilitated contact tracing for 44 contacts.
The council commended the agencies for their contributions to monitoring the Ebola threat and supporting the public health response.
It also criticised Atiku’s reference linking President Tinubu’s name to Ebola, saying it risked turning a serious health concern into political ridicule.
“We believe linking and rhyming President Bola Tinubu’s name to Ebola only risks turning a serious health concern into a vehicle to ridicule the President,” Alake said.
The council also defended the handling of the infected Nigerian’s detection, citing the virus’s incubation period and the timing of symptoms.
“For anyone infected with the virus, the incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, with symptoms typically appearing eight to 10 days after exposure.
“An infected person cannot spread or transmit Ebola to others until they actively develop symptoms,” he said.
Alake urged opposition politicians to support health authorities rather than criticise the government’s response to the public health threat.
“A responsible opposition will applaud the Task Force for being responsive. But the Atiku camp always goes for cheap shots at the government,” he said.
The council also rejected Atiku’s allegation that a ministerial briefing was intended to discourage Nigerians from attending campaign rallies or voting.
Alake described the allegation as speculative, adding that the briefing instead urged Nigerians to comply with protocols announced by the task force.
He called on Atiku and his supporters to avoid politicising public health concerns, urging Nigerians to shun rumours and follow health authorities’ guidance.
“We advise Atiku Abubakar and his hirelings to avoid politicising public health issues,” he said.
The council said protecting Nigerians from the deadly disease should remain the priority. (NAN)

Presidential candidate of the African Action Congress, Omoyele Sowore, has defended his party’s request to hold the inauguration of its 2027 Presidential Campaign Council at the Presidential Villa in Abuja, arguing that opposition parties should enjoy the same access as the ruling All Progressives Congress.
Sowore made the remarks on Thursday at an event organised by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria, explaining that the request was prompted by the APC’s use of the facility for political activities.
The AAC had written to President Bola Tinubu seeking approval to inaugurate its Presidential Campaign Council at the Villa ahead of the 2027 general elections.
“We asked to use Aso Rock because the APC uses Aso Rock to do political party events. So we are saying, as a matter of right, since Aso Rock is our own, other political parties must be granted the opportunity to use Aso Rock the way APC uses Aso Rock,” Sowore said.
In addition to the venue, the party requested food, drinks and other logistical arrangements for attendees at the proposed inauguration scheduled for November 11, 2026.
A letter dated October 21 and signed by the AAC National Secretary, Oshiokhai Ikpeminioghena, stated that the request was anchored on multiparty democracy, political inclusiveness and equal treatment of political parties.
The party maintained that approving the request would affirm the Presidency’s commitment to fairness and demonstrate that public institutions were available to all Nigerians, irrespective of political affiliation.
The request triggered a disagreement between Sowore and the APC National Secretary, Ajibola Basiru, who criticised the AAC candidate and questioned the party’s electoral strength.
Sowore insisted that the move was aimed at securing equal access to the Presidential Villa. He also ruled out joining a proposed opposition coalition ahead of the 2027 elections.
“I don’t want to be part of your coalition because your rainbow coalition is going to die after 2027,” he said.
The AAC candidate also lamented the economic and social difficulties facing Nigerians, saying, “They have brought sorrow, and honestly, things are hard for the people of this country.”

US President Donald Trump lashed out at NBA superstar LeBron James on Thursday for what he called disrespectful behaviour during the playing of the national anthem.
Trump posted a video of the basketball legend doing apparent warm-up movements while lined up with his Philadelphia 76ers teammates.
“While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country! I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.
“LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!” he wrote.
The video used by Trump had an internal caption that read: “LeBron working on his golf swing pregame.” It showed him doing lateral swing motions and basketball shooting movements.
It was not immediately clear when the video was filmed.
There was no immediate reaction from James, 41, who is entering a record-extending 24th NBA season with his fourth team, the 76ers.
Trump has been critical of athletes before — particularly Black athletes — for their behaviour during the playing of the US national anthem before games.
During his first term, Trump singled out NFL star Colin Kaepernick for his decision to kneel during the “Star-Spangled Banner” to protest racial injustice and police brutality.

items.author: Henry Oduah
items.content:
The Federal Government has directed the strict implementation of the National Guideline on Debarment of Contractors, Consultants and Service Providers.
The directive is contained in a circular issued by the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), Sen. George Akume, with reference number 59780/S.2/B/585.
This is according to a statement by Ngozi Anyaelezu, Acting Head of Public Relations, Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP), in Abuja on Thursday.
Anyaelezu said that the guidelines provide for the exclusion of defaulting contractors from public procurement for up to five years.
She said the circular mandated all Accounting Officers in Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs) to ensure full compliance with the guidelines.
“It aims to prevent fraud and corruption in contract execution by ensuring that contractors who violate the provisions of the Public Procurement Act, 2007, are promptly reported and excluded from further participation in government procurement.”
The guidelines said that the BPP may initiate debarment proceedings following findings from its reviews, surveillance or audits, or based on a properly supported recommendation from a procuring entity approved by its Accounting Officer.
It provides that an affected contractor must be notified of the allegations and given 10 working days to respond, with provision for a limited extension in appropriate circumstances.
“Where the Debarment Committee establishes a case against a contractor, it may impose a debarment period of between three years and five years.
“A debarred contractor will be prohibited from being invited to bid for or awarded Federal Government contracts.
“The contractor will also be barred from conducting government business as an agent or representative of another contractor, consultant or service provider.”
The guideline further provides that the name of every debarred entity will be entered into the BPP database and published on the Bureau’s website, the Federal Tenders Journal and other relevant platforms.
It, however, allows for the reinstatement of debarred contractors after the expiration of the sanction, subject to an application supported by evidence of reform.
“The Federal Government reiterated its commitment to transparency, accountability and fiscal discipline in public expenditure.
“All Accounting Officers are to ensure that the guidelines are brought to the attention of Tenders Boards, Procurement Planning Committees, procurement departments and all officers involved in public procurement.”
Meanwhile, following the circular, Dr Adebowale Adedokun, Director-General of the BPP, said the guideline was designed to eliminate corrupt, fraudulent and non-performing contractors from the public procurement system.
Adedokun said the measure would safeguard public funds and promote value for money in government expenditure.
He said that the government would no longer tolerate compromises that undermined the integrity of public procurement processes.
The director-general said that any Accounting Officer or procuring entity that bypassed the debarment registry or violated the provisions of the Public Procurement Act would face administrative and legal sanctions.
“Moving forward, all procuring entities are mandated to verify compliance,” he said.
He said the guidelines identify several grounds for debarment, including offering money, gifts or other benefits to influence procurement decisions, and providing employment or financial benefits to procurement officials for improper purposes.
“Other grounds include conviction for fraud relating to public contracts, falsification of documents, and wilful or persistent failure to fulfil contractual obligations.
“It also allows the Federal Government to consider for debarment contractors already sanctioned by multilateral organisations,” he said.
(NAN)

items.author: Henry Oduah
items.content:
Olujonwo Obasanjo, son of former President Olusegun Obasanjo, has joined the Tinubu Must Stay Movement, pledging to promote policy continuity and explain President Bola Tinubu’s reforms.
He announced his decision at a news conference in Abuja on Thursday, where the leadership of the Tinubu Movement for Sustainable Governance Foundation (TMS) welcomed him.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that TMS is a political advocacy platform promoting policy continuity, sustainable governance and public understanding of Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda.
Olujonwo said his decision was shaped by his political experience, understanding of Nigeria’s reform history and belief in sustaining government policies across administrations.
“I’ve been in the APC since 2014. I was there when my father hosted late President Muhammadu Buhari and President Bola Tinubu to form the movement. I’m not new to the party,” he said.
He said inadequate communication about the Tinubu administration’s policies had created opportunities for misinformation and misinterpretation among Nigerians.
“There’s a lot of noise out there, and people are distorting what’s going on. ASUU has had no strikes. Students now have access to education loans.
“Nigeria has become a massive construction site and an investors’ haven again. These are things we need to promote,” he said.
Olujonwo said communicating government policies required explaining their objectives, implementation processes and implications for citizens rather than relying solely on political slogans.
The National Coordinator of TMS and Director-General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Kashifu Abdullahi, welcomed him into the movement.
Abdullahi said Olujonwo’s family background gave him an understanding of economic reforms and their implications for national development.
“You grew up in a family that led the second wave of reforms in Nigeria. Telecommunications liberalisation and banking reforms — these laid a solid foundation.
“Being raised in that family, you understand what reforms mean,” he added.
Abdullahi said policy consistency was essential for national development, warning that frequent reversals could undermine investor confidence and disrupt long-term planning.
“We are building investors’ confidence; the naira is becoming strong, our stock exchange is one of the fastest-growing.
“The Dangote Refinery is a game changer. If we start reversing these policies, we’ll go back to where we were,” Abdullahi said.
He said TMS would expand its nationwide structures and engage stakeholders across professional, political and social groups.
Abdullahi said the movement supported policy continuity beyond 2027, while seeking to strengthen institutional development and the sustainability of government programmes.
The Director-General of TMS, Marcel Ngogbehei, described Olujonwo’s entry as significant, citing his family’s association with economic reforms and democratic consolidation.
Ngogbehei, a former coordinator of the Obidient movement, recalled former President Obasanjo’s telecommunications liberalisation policies and Nigeria’s external debt relief.
He said those reforms helped lay the foundations for subsequent economic development.
“We are happy you have decided to take this step. Your father was one of those who revolutionised this country.
“The debt was paid off, and major innovations were introduced in liberalising the economy,” he said.
Ngogbehei said TMS was established to encourage informed public engagement on government policies, address misconceptions about ongoing reforms and promote assessments based on evidence and measurable outcomes. (NAN)

items.title: UEL: Juventus denied at the death, Sunderland make point in Poland
items.summary:
Bayer Leverkusen made it three straight wins in the Europa League with a Jonas Hofmann double earning a 2-0 away win at OFI Crete as both Juventus and Sunderland lost ground in Thursday’s third matchday.
The once mighty Hungarian side Ferencvaros kept pace with Leverkusen on nine points thumping Portuguese outfit Torreense 4-1, while Belgium’s Union Saint-Gilloise won 4-0 against Israeli outfit Hapoel Be’er Sheva.
Saint-Gilloise, Sunderland and Juve all have seven points from three games.

Bayer Leverkusen made it three straight wins in the Europa League with a Jonas Hofmann double earning a 2-0 away win at OFI Crete as both Juventus and Sunderland lost ground in Thursday’s third matchday.
The once mighty Hungarian side Ferencvaros kept pace with Leverkusen on nine points thumping Portuguese outfit Torreense 4-1, while Belgium’s Union Saint-Gilloise won 4-0 against Israeli outfit Hapoel Be’er Sheva.
Saint-Gilloise, Sunderland and Juve all have seven points from three games.

“The Federal Government is taking every necessary step to contain this case and protect Nigerians. Accurate and timely information is one of our strongest defences,” the minister said.

items.author: Henry Oduah
items.content:
By Henry Umoru
Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC ahead of the 2027 elections, Peter Obi has urged political opponents to keep the Pope, Pope Leo XIV and the Catholic Church out of partisan campaigns.
The former Anambra State governor condemned in very strong terms the circulation of an artificial intelligence-generated image allegedly showing him and an Enugu State governorship candidate seeking Pope Leo XIV’s blessing for electoral victory, describing the image as misleading and unwarranted.
In a statement signed on Thursday by the Spokesman of his Campaign Media Office, POMR, Idris Zekeri, Obi said the office had become aware of the image depicting Cardinal John Onaiyekan and described in the statement as the NDC presidential candidate, and Sir Chinyeaka Oha, the party’s Enugu State governorship candidate, standing before the Catholic Pontiff.
The statement condemned the alleged use of artificial intelligence to create the image and urged political actors to refrain from involving religious leaders and institutions in partisan disputes.
Obi maintained that his political campaign focused on addressing Nigeria’s pressing challenges, including poverty, insecurity, corruption and economic hardship. He also highlighted the need to expand opportunities for young people and build a country where citizens could live with dignity and hope.
He challenged political opponents to focus their campaigns on policy issues, records and leadership capacity rather than religious controversies.
He expressed disappointment over the incident, insisting that the 2027 general election should centre on Nigeria’s future and the issues affecting citizens, just as he also called for the Pope and the Catholic Church to be allowed to carry out their spiritual responsibilities without being drawn into partisan political disputes.
The statement read, “The Peter Obi Media Office has become aware of a deceptive AI-generated image depicting the NDC Presidential Candidate, revered Cardinal John Onaiyekan, and the Enugu State NDC gubernatorial candidate, Sir Chinyeaka Oha, standing before the Catholic Pontiff, Pope Leo XIV, and seeking his blessing for electoral victory.
“The Media Office strongly condemns this conduct and calls on political opponents to stop involving the Holy Father, the Pope, and the Catholic Church in partisan campaigns. Such an act is misleading and entirely unwarranted.
“The Church is a sacred institution that must be respected rather than exploited for political gain.
Peter Obi’s campaign is centred on issues. It seeks to rescue Nigeria from poverty, insecurity, corruption, and economic hardship; expand opportunities for our youths; and build a nation in which every Nigerian can live with dignity and hope.
“He also welcomes vigorous political debate and challenges his opponents to address Nigerians on these urgent matters. “Let us debate our records, policies, competence, character, and vision for the country.”
“The 2027 election must focus on Nigeria’s future, not fabricated religious controversies,” Obi said, expressing his disappointment over the incident.
“The Pope and the Catholic Church should be permitted to carry out their spiritual responsibilities without being drawn into partisan disputes.
“Let us keep the Church separate from politics and focus the campaign on the genuine issues facing Nigerians. A New Nigeria Is Possible.”

By Hadiza Yusuf
Kano State Governor Abba Yusuf has promised that the All Progressives Congress (APC) will focus on issues, achievements and plans rather than personal attacks in its campaign ahead of the 2027 general election.
Yusuf gave the assurance on Thursday during the inauguration of the APC 2027 presidential and gubernatorial campaign council management team in Kano.
He said the party would explain its achievements to voters, present its plans for the future and listen to the needs of the people.
“We are going to campaign based on what the APC leaders have done, not campaign full of insults,” the governor said.
Yusuf said members of the campaign council were selected based on their capacity to carry out the responsibilities assigned to them.
He urged them to work hard to ensure that the APC secured more votes in Kano than in any other state during the 2027 elections.
“Kano should garner a lot of votes for President Tinubu. The number of votes the APC gets in Kano should be the highest in the country. This is possible if you go out and campaign as required,” he said.
The governor described the council members as representatives of the party who must work towards securing victory for the APC and President Bola Tinubu.
“The members of this council are APC soldiers, and I urge you to carry out your responsibilities with commitment and work towards the party’s victory,” Yusuf said.
He also urged them not to be intimidated by opposition parties or allow fear to affect their campaign activities, insisting that the APC had established itself in the state.
Yusuf appealed to party members and supporters whose names were not included in the initial campaign council list not to feel disappointed, explaining that additional lists and subcommittees would be announced.
He called on party members to remain committed and work together to mobilise support for the APC ahead of the 2027 elections.
Among the key appointments, Abdullahi Tijjani Muhammad Gwarzo was named Director-General of the campaign council, while Hon. Bala Muhammad Gwagwarwa will serve as First Deputy Director-General.
Dr. Yunusa Adamu Dangwani was appointed Deputy Director-General for Kano South, while Dr. Ali Haruna Abubakar Makoda and Senator Abdussalam Abdulkarim Zaura will serve as Deputy Directors-General for Kano North and Kano Central, respectively.
Dr. Mariya Mahmoud Bunkure was also named Assistant Director-General for Women Affairs, while Hon. Garba Yusuf Abubakar will serve as Assistant Director-General for Operations, among other appointments.
Stakeholders present at the event included Senators Kawu Sumaila and Barau Jibrin, as well as Mariya Bunkure.

items.author: Akinbayo Wahab
items.content:
By Adegboyega Adeleye
The Deputy Director-General, Media and Communications of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential campaign, Dele Momodu, has accused the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) of using economic statistics to mislead Nigerians, alleging that President Bola Tinubu’s administration is fighting criticism from international institutions while struggling to win public confidence ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
Momodu, who is backing ADC presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar, made the remarks on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Thursday, while questioning the government’s presentation of economic figures and the credibility of the electoral process.
“I saw the speech of an Emir in the North, I wish we had a lot of time, I would have read it to you. They were told the brutal truth that you should never lie to the people. What the APC is doing today is to use those statistics to tell lies and to say The World Bank are for us, The IMF are for us,” he said.
He accused the government of attacking international institutions when their assessments raise concerns about Nigeria’s economic direction and borrowing.
“Whenever the World Bank says, oh, we are worried about the direction you are going, the loans you’re taking is becoming horrendous, then they fight the World Bank.
“If the Economist comes and writes and says, oh, the direction Nigeria is going, we know you are likely to force your way in to win the election, they will fight The Economist. So they are fighting on all fronts,” Momodu said.
Momodu questions INEC over voter register
The ADC chieftain also questioned the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), arguing that the commission should publish the voters’ register to enable Nigerians to scrutinise the electoral process.
He said the figures being cited for registered voters and party membership raised questions about the relationship between party strength and the wider electorate.
“For INEC just to do a simple job is obligatory. Publish the voters’ register. Now they say we have 103 million registered voters. Fantastic. Yesterday, I saw your guest, a senator of APC, boasting, we have 12 million registered members of our party. And the next party has maybe about 4 million registered voters.
“But INEC is telling us we have 103 million registered voters. So tell me, will 12 million people override the will and wishes of 103 million people?” he asked.
Momodu argued that Nigerians who were not firmly aligned with any political party could play a decisive role in the election, describing them as the “floaters party”.
“What that tells you immediately is that the largest political party in Nigeria, it’s not APC, it’s not ADC, it is the floaters party and the floaters are the ones crying today that their lives are in a big mess,” he said.
‘Hunger’ can defeat Tinubu
Momodu also blamed a lack of sincerity within the government for what he described as shortcomings in economic management, arguing that officials were not giving the president the full picture.
“What is lacking in this government is that sincerity. Everything is about one man. The people who are running our economy today have to tell Nigerians only what they think the president wants to hear. They are not telling him the truth, and when tomorrow comes, he will realise it, it’s just that it may be too late,” he said.
Asked how the opposition could defeat Tinubu in 2027, Momodu argued that economic hardship could prove decisive regardless of the ruling party’s political support.
“There is no permutation that will beat hunger. That is the truth. Bola Tinubu can bring all the governors in the world, and I just told you we saw it in Osun…” he said.
The post APC using statistics to tell lies, fighting on all fronts — Dele Momodu appeared first on Vanguard News.

Nollywood filmmaker Biodun Stephen has urged colleagues to stop announcing cinema earnings, warning that the practice puts unnecessary pressure on other filmmakers and creates a narrow definition of success in the industry.
Stephen made the remarks during Paul & Baaj: In Character podcast, where she argued that publicising box office figures could distract filmmakers from focusing on the quality and impact of their work.
“I think that we really should do away with the announcements,” she said.
“I feel like this is a distractions and it puts pressure on those other people who… feel as if that is the determine and that’s how you determine my success,” she added.
The filmmaker explained that frequent announcements of cinema earnings could make others feel unsuccessful if their projects failed to achieve similar figures.
Using a slippers business as an example, Stephen said people often rush to replicate successful ventures without understanding the effort and strategy behind them.
“Somebody starts selling slippers and people are rushing to buy slippers, the next one… is going to sell slippers… because they think that slippers sells, meanwhile they don’t understand what you have put in to ensure the slipper sells.”
Biodun Stephen also questioned the tendency among some filmmakers and actors to pursue international recognition before establishing a strong presence in Nigeria.
“It’s great to hunger for more, but I always say, have you even conquered Nigeria that can you stand and say that if I go to Kano they know me as an actor?”
She further argued that box office earnings alone were insufficient to determine a film’s quality, longevity or potential to reach international audiences.
According to her, a film could generate substantial cinema revenue without necessarily being outstanding, while a well-made production with export potential might earn less and receive little recognition.
“The film go tough but it can be a lot of crap and then the film that is really good that can travel, that has export value can do 40 million… the only yard stick for measuring success is this very shallow number.”
Explaining her approach to filmmaking, Stephen said her motivation was rooted in purpose rather than the pursuit of box office records or audience numbers.
“I’m doing it because I am living a life of purpose, I’m not chasing the numbers, I’m not chasing the audience.”
She added that the emotional impact of her stories and the difference they made in people’s lives were more meaningful to her than industry awards.
“When people call me to pray… and cry and say thank you so much, Jesus, my work is done, no award.”
